pages.title: How do ThreadLocals leak or cross- contaminate requests?
pages.fullText:
Q029 · References, cleanup and retention leaks INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q029. How do ThreadLocals leak or cross-
contaminate requests?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Pooled threads outlive requests, so an uncleared ThreadLocal may leak data
or expose it to the next request.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Values stored on long-lived threads can survive a request unless removed or replaced. ThreadLocal
maps have implementation lifecycle details that do not guarantee prompt value release. Use finally
to clean scoped state and avoid carrying one user's context into another task.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
try {
 context.set(requestContext);
 handleRequest();
} finally {
 context.remove();
}
Why it matters: Pool threads outlive the request that created the value.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would asynchronous work complicate context propagation?
Answer: Tasks can move between threads, so ThreadLocal context does not reliably follow
them. Pass context explicitly or use a deliberately scoped mechanism.
Interview trap: A weak reference to a ThreadLocal key does not guarantee its associated value
immediately disappears.
Source guide p. 23 · Technical references J17, J24-J27
Request context Async task boundary Explicit propagation
JVM / GC / PERFORMANCE

pages.title: How do you distinguish an intentional cache from a memory leak?
pages.fullText:
Q030 · References, cleanup and retention leaks INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q030. How do you distinguish an intentional cache
from a memory leak?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
A cache is intentional only when it has a useful size/TTL policy and a
measurable eviction plan.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Compare retention with the defined policy and workload. A cache that exceeds its intended size/TTL
or retains unnecessary object graphs is a correctness or design problem. Track post-reclamation
live-set trends and inspect retaining paths before labeling every rise a leak.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Cache policy: bounded entries and measured byte budget
Observe: retained graph after comparable workload phases
Investigate: owners, eviction and references
Why it matters: A flat object count can still hide larger values.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
Which cache metrics would you record alongside a heap comparison?
Answer: Track entries, estimated bytes, hit/miss rate, evictions, load failures, live-set size
and the cache's effect on backend calls.
Interview trap: A single heap snapshot cannot prove a growth trend.
Source guide p. 23 · Technical references J17, J24-J27

JVM / GC / PERFORMANCE

pages.title: How do you choose a collector?
pages.fullText:
Q031 · Choosing a garbage collector INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q031. How do you choose a collector?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Choose a collector by measuring user latency, throughput, CPU and memory
on the real workload.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Define acceptable tail latency, throughput, memory footprint and CPU budget, then test suitable
collectors on the same runtime and representative workload. Start with supported defaults. Verify
collector availability in the actual vendor build and platform.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Compare: same app, heap, load and resource limits
Measure: throughput, p99, GC pauses, CPU and RSS
Keep: correctness, error rate and startup observations
Why it matters: Collector selection is an experiment constrained by service objectives.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What evidence would justify changing from G1 to ZGC?
Answer: Move from G1 to ZGC only if a repeatable improvement in tail latency outweighs
CPU, heap/RSS and throughput costs under comparable load.
Interview trap: Smaller GC pauses alone do not establish a better application.
Source guide p. 24 · Technical references J08, J18, J20, J36, J37

pages.title: When is Serial GC useful?
pages.fullText:
Q032 · Choosing a garbage collector INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q032. When is Serial GC useful?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Serial GC uses one GC worker; it may suit tiny heaps or tightly limited CPUs
when pauses are acceptable.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Serial GC performs collection with a single GC worker and is suited to some small-footprint or
limited-resource workloads. Evaluate its simplicity and overhead against pause behavior for the
actual live set. It is not a generic choice for all latency-sensitive services.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
java -XX:+UseSerialGC -Xmx128m SmallApp
Why it matters: A small workload may not benefit from a large parallel collection workforce.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What would you measure before using Serial in a small container?
Answer: Measure p95/p99 pauses, throughput, peak RSS, warmup, CPU quota and total
job duration with realistic data.
Interview trap: A low thread count does not guarantee acceptable pauses as the live set
grows.

Small workload Serial trial Check pauses

pages.title: When is Parallel GC useful?
pages.fullText:
Q033 · Choosing a garbage collector INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q033. When is Parallel GC useful?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Parallel GC prioritizes useful throughput while allowing stop-the-world
collection work.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Parallel GC emphasizes throughput using multiple workers for stop-the-world collection. It can fit
batch workloads with acceptable pause tolerance. Compare total completion time and resource use
rather than assuming concurrent collection is always superior.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
java -XX:+UseParallelGC -Xmx2g BatchJob
Why it matters: More parallel collection work can reduce some collection durations when CPU
is available.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
Why might a batch job prefer Parallel over a lower-pause collector?
Answer: For a batch job with flexible pauses, faster completion and lower total CPU/
memory cost may matter more than p99 response latency.
Interview trap: Parallel workers compete within limited CPU quotas and can still cause
substantial application pauses.

pages.title: What is Epsilon GC and why is it unusual?
pages.fullText:
Q034 · Choosing a garbage collector INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q034. What is Epsilon GC and why is it unusual?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Epsilon allocates but never reclaims objects; it is useful only for bounded
experiments.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Epsilon manages allocation without reclaiming unused objects. It is useful for bounded experiments
and specialized workloads that complete within their memory budget. In HotSpot it requires
experimental-option unlocking and is not an ordinary long-running service collector.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
java -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions \
  -XX:+UseEpsilonGC -Xmx128m BoundedExperiment
Why it matters: Once available heap is exhausted, unreachable objects are not recovered for
reuse by Epsilon.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you bound a useful Epsilon experiment?
Answer: Choose a fixed operation count, -Xmx, input size and duration; run in an isolated
process and expect exhaustion once the budget is spent.
Interview trap: 'No GC pause' is not proof of a sustainable memory lifecycle.
Source guide p. 25 · Technical references J08, J18, J20, J36, J37
Fixed heap No reclamation Bounded exit
JVM / GC / PERFORMANCE

Q035. What happened to CMS and what is the
modern default?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
CMS was removed in JDK 14; G1 is a common server default, but always
inspect runtime flags.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →

CMS was removed in JDK 14. G1 became the default for common server configurations in JDK 9,
with ergonomic and build/platform qualifications. Inspect the effective collector instead of copying a
historical CMS flag set into a modern launch command.

# Confirm the collector selected by this runtime.

What is your migration process for old production JVM flags?
Answer: Inventory all launch flags, confirm target-JDK support, remove obsolete settings,
test performance and failure cases, then canary the rollout.

pages.title: How does G1 organize the heap?

Q036 · G1 architecture and phases INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q036. How does G1 organize the heap?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
G1 divides the heap into regions that can play Eden, survivor, old or
humongous roles.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
G1 divides its heap into equally sized regions used for young, old, free and humongous allocation
roles. The generational arrangement is logical rather than one permanently contiguous young
block. Region selection helps spread reclamation work across pauses.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Regions: Eden | Survivor | Old | Free | Humongous
Collection set: selected regions for this evacuation
Live objects: copied to suitable destination space
Why it matters: Region roles can change as storage is reused.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
Why does evacuation require destination capacity?
Answer: Live objects need free destination regions when copied; without enough suitable
space, evacuation can fail.
Interview trap: A region map is not a fixed Java object-addressing contract.
Source guide p. 27 · Technical references J09, J10

Q037. What is a G1 young collection?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
A G1 young GC copies reachable objects from selected young regions and
reclaims the rest.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
A young evacuation pause processes the young collection set, relocating live survivors and making
the collected regions reusable. Survival, root work and reference processing affect duration.
Frequent young pauses can be normal for an allocation-heavy service.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
New allocations -> Eden regions
Young pause -> survivors copied
Dead temporary objects -> storage reused
Why it matters: Allocation frequency and surviving volume are separate tuning inputs.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
Why might fewer allocations still produce a slower pause?
Answer: Pause time also depends on survivor bytes, references, remembered-set/root
work and CPU scheduling, not just allocation count.
Interview trap: Every young pause is not evidence of a leak.

Q038. What is a G1 mixed collection?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
A G1 mixed collection includes young regions plus selected older regions after
marking.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION

identified suitable candidates. It differs from collecting the whole heap. Observe which portions of
evacuation work contribute to the pause.

Answer: More smaller pauses may reduce individual duration but increase frequency and
overhead. Compare both tail latency and useful throughput.

Q039. What do remembered sets and barriers do in
G1?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
G1 remembered sets track relevant references across regions so a young
collection need not scan the entire heap.

→ →

They help track relevant cross-region references so selected regions can be collected without
blindly rescanning the entire heap every time. Barriers record information when references change;
maintaining and processing it costs CPU and memory.

Recorded cross-region information -> root discovery

work, which costs CPU and memory.

pages.title: What are humongous objects in G1?
pages.fullText:
Q040 · G1 architecture and phases INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q040. What are humongous objects in G1?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Very large G1 objects use special humongous regions, which can increase
space and fragmentation pressure.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Objects at or above roughly half a G1 region, including the threshold defined by the implementation,
receive special allocation treatment across contiguous regions. This can increase old-space
pressure and fragmentation. Inspect actual region size and humongous allocation evidence.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Example region: 1 MiB
Large byte array: inspect total aligned object size
Payload buffering -> possible humongous allocation
Why it matters: Large arrays used for request bodies can change the collector's allocation path.

How would streaming a payload alter this behavior?
Answer: Stream bounded chunks instead of building one giant byte array; then check
humongous allocation events, p99 and memory peaks.
Interview trap: The exact boundary is based on object size and the selected region size, not a
universal payload byte count.

Large full buffer Stream chunks Smaller allocations

pages.title: Does MaxGCPauseMillis guarantee a maximum pause?

Q041 · Evidence-driven G1 tuning INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q041. Does MaxGCPauseMillis guarantee a maximum
pause?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
MaxGCPauseMillis is a G1 planning target, not a maximum-pause promise.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
No. For G1 it is a soft target used in collection planning, not a hard real-time bound. A tighter target
can change collection frequency and overhead without guaranteeing application p99. Keep the
target tied to a measured service objective.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100
# Illustrative target; not a 100 ms guarantee.
Why it matters: Target planning operates within live-set, capacity and CPU constraints.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What should you measure after lowering the target?
Answer: Measure actual pause percentiles, frequency, GC CPU, throughput, allocation
stalls and the service's end-to-end p99.
Interview trap: A target lower than the available work budget cannot make necessary work
vanish.

pages.title: Why should you avoid fixing young-generation size blindly for G1?
pages.fullText:
Q042 · Evidence-driven G1 tuning INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q042. Why should you avoid fixing young-generation
size blindly for G1?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
G1 sizes young collections adaptively; forcing a fixed young size may prevent
useful adaptation.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
G1 adapts its young collection set to meet objectives. Options that constrain young sizing can
reduce this freedom and create unexpected behavior. First inspect allocation, survival and pause
phases; change constraints only for a specific measured hypothesis.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Baseline: selected G1 defaults and measured heap
Avoid inherited -Xmn without understanding its effect
Compare pause phases and useful throughput
Why it matters: A flag that helped another collector may interfere with G1's policy.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What evidence would justify constraining G1's young generation?
Answer: Only constrain it if logs show a repeatable phase-specific problem and
controlled A/B testing improves user latency without harming throughput.
Interview trap: There is no universal 'young must be 30% of heap' rule.

pages.title: What causes G1 evacuation failure or Full GC?
pages.fullText:
Q043 · Evidence-driven G1 tuning INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q043. What causes G1 evacuation failure or Full GC?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
G1 may fail evacuation when too much live data must move but too little
suitable free space remains.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Insufficient suitable destination space, high retained occupancy, late reclamation and allocation
patterns can prevent successful evacuation. Full collection can follow, but explicit requests or other
causes also exist. Read the stated cause and preceding events.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Inspect: evacuation-failure evidence
Compare: live set, free regions and allocation spikes
Correlate: marking progress and CPU availability
Why it matters: The first relevant warning often explains the later long pause.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you distinguish capacity pressure from a leaking cache?
Answer: Check whether post-GC live set keeps rising under equal workloads and inspect
cache ownership/eviction; a stable live set with sharp peaks suggests capacity pressure.
Interview trap: Raising heap without addressing unbounded retention may only postpone
recurrence.
Source guide p. 30 · Technical references J09, J10

pages.title: How does initiating heap occupancy affect G1?
pages.fullText:
Q044 · Evidence-driven G1 tuning INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q044. How does initiating heap occupancy affect G1?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
G1 starts concurrent marking based on occupancy and predictions; it needs
CPU time to finish.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
G1 uses occupancy and adaptive predictions to decide when to begin marking. Earlier marking can
create time to reclaim old regions, while CPU constraints can still prevent timely completion.
Inspect adaptive behavior before forcing a static threshold.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Observe marking start versus old occupancy
Check allocation during the marking cycle
Verify CPU headroom for concurrent work
Why it matters: The useful variable is time available before pressure, not one threshold in
isolation.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What would happen if a container's CPU limit is cut sharply?
Answer: Less CPU can delay concurrent marking, lengthen wall-clock work and increase
risk of old-space pressure or Full GC.
Interview trap: A copied IHOP value is not a guarantee that marking finishes before
exhaustion.
Source guide p. 31 · Technical references J09, J10
CPU quota cut Marking slows Less headroom

Q045. How should you respond to long mixed pauses
or humongous pressure?

Diagnose which G1 work is slow before tuning; large buffers or retention may
be better fixed in code.

alternative whose throughput and memory effects must be tested.

Change: stream bounded chunks

overhead.

size, repeat runs and compare large-object counts, pauses and throughput.

fragmentation cure.

Q046 · ZGC and Shenandoah INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q046. What makes ZGC different from G1?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
ZGC moves more GC work into concurrent phases to keep pauses low; G1
evacuates selected regions during pauses.

→ →

specific reference/barrier mechanisms. G1 evacuates selected regions during pauses and balances
throughput and latency. Compare full application results under the same resources.

ZGC: substantial concurrent marking and relocation

starvation can cause an allocation stall despite tiny STW pauses.

pages.title: How did ZGC change across Java 17, 21 and 25?
pages.fullText:
Q047 · ZGC and Shenandoah INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q047. How did ZGC change across Java 17, 21 and
25?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Java 17 ZGC is non-generational; Java 21 can opt into generational ZGC; Java
25 uses generational ZGC.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Java 17 ZGC is non-generational. Java 21 introduced an opt-in generational mode. Generational
mode became the default for ZGC in Java 23; Java 24 removed the non-generational mode. Java
25 uses generational ZGC without the old mode-selection option.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Java 17: -XX:+UseZGC
Java 21: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational
Java 25: -XX:+UseZGC
Why it matters: The mode is selected within ZGC; this does not make ZGC the general default
collector.

What must you compare when moving a Java 17 ZGC workload to Java 25?
Answer: Compare collector mode, effective flags, heap/RSS, CPU, allocation stalls, pause
distribution, throughput, startup and error rates on the real service.
Interview trap: Do not carry ZGenerational into a Java 25 launch recipe.

pages.title: How do Xms and Xmx differ?
pages.fullText:
Q051 · Heap sizing and OutOfMemoryError INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q051. How do Xms and Xmx differ?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Xms sets the starting/minimum heap and Xmx sets its maximum; neither
limits the whole process.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Xms controls the initial/minimum heap sizing contract in HotSpot and Xmx controls the maximum
heap. Neither caps total process memory. Equal values can reduce heap resizing, but increase
baseline commitment expectations and reduce footprint flexibility.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
java -Xms256m -Xmx1g Application
# Initial/minimum and maximum object-heap settings.
# Native allocations and thread stacks are additional.
Why it matters: Collector behavior and OS page residency still affect physical memory.

pages.title: Does increasing heap always improve performance?
pages.fullText:
Q053 · Heap sizing and OutOfMemoryError INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q053. Does increasing heap always improve
performance?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
More heap can postpone GC, but can increase memory use, pressure
elsewhere and some pause costs.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
No. More heap can reduce collection frequency and provide headroom, but can increase footprint,
affect layout or work per cycle, and violate process limits. Compare useful throughput and tail
latency within the same deployment budget.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Hypothesis: too little allocation headroom
Experiment: modest heap increase within process budget
Compare: GC work, p99, RSS and throttling
Why it matters: A larger heap is a capacity change that needs evidence.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What result would make you reject a heap increase?
Answer: Reject it if tail latency, total RSS, container OOM risk or throughput becomes
worse, even if GC events become less frequent.
Interview trap: An unbounded live set eventually consumes a larger heap too.

pages.title: What does GC overhead limit exceeded mean?
pages.fullText:
Q054 · Heap sizing and OutOfMemoryError INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q054. What does GC overhead limit exceeded mean?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
GC overhead limit exceeded means the VM spends excessive time collecting
but recovers little memory under its policy.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
On collectors and configurations that enforce it, the JVM detects excessive time spent collecting
with insufficient reclamation. It is a symptom of an unsustainable memory/workload situation.
Investigate retained data and capacity instead of merely disabling the check.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Repeated costly collections
Little useful reclamation
Application makes inadequate progress
Why it matters: The exception reports poor progress rather than naming the retaining owner.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you compare the live set with the allowed heap?
Answer: Compare post-full-collection occupancy with Xmx over repeated comparable
periods; near-capacity retained data suggests a live-set or leak issue.
Interview trap: Disabling the overhead limit does not create memory or repair retention.
Source guide p. 36 · Technical references J04, J06, J23, J24

pages.title: How do you capture evidence around heap exhaustion?
pages.fullText:
Q055 · Heap sizing and OutOfMemoryError INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q055. How do you capture evidence around heap
exhaustion?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Capture logs, heap evidence and process/container events before failures
when safe; guard sensitive dumps.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Use appropriate GC logs and a reviewed heap-dump policy, correlate process/container termination
and retain deployment identity. Heap dumps can be large, disruptive and sensitive. Store them
securely on a path with capacity rather than assuming every failure produces one.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/controlled/path
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:uptime,level,tags
Why it matters: A Java heap OOME and an OS/container kill have different evidence paths.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you manage dump storage for many replicas?
Answer: Use per-instance bounded dump paths, disk quotas/retention, centralized
restricted storage and a tested cleanup/collection plan.
Interview trap: A heap-dump-on-OOME flag does not guarantee a dump after an external kill.

pages.title: How do you enable modern GC and safepoint logging?
pages.fullText:
Q056 · GC logs and quantitative interpretation INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q056. How do you enable modern GC and safepoint
logging?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Use unified -Xlog settings for GC and safepoints in supported HotSpot
versions.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Use unified logging on modern HotSpot. Select tags, level, decorators and output rotation
appropriate to the investigation. Verify support on the actual JDK and ensure logs do not create
uncontrolled storage or I/O overhead.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
-Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:uptime,level,tags:
  filecount=5,filesize=10M
# Join as one option; shown across lines for reading.
Why it matters: Decorators and GC identifiers help connect phases belonging to one cycle.

Which extra phase detail would you enable for a long G1 evacuation pause?
Answer: Enable focused G1 phase tags such as gc+phases at debug level for a short
window; measure logging overhead and disk growth.
Interview trap: Old PrintGCDetails-style recipes do not map unchanged to every modern
release.

pages.title: How do you read heap before/after and pause duration?
pages.fullText:
Q057 · GC logs and quantitative interpretation INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q057. How do you read heap before/after and pause
duration?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
GC logs show heap occupied before/after events and how long the reported
phase took.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Identify the event, cause, heap values and unit, then compare across equivalent workload phases. A
before-to-after decrease describes reclamation during that event, not a standalone proof of leak
absence or an exact retained-live-set measurement.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Illustrative: GC(7) Pause Young ... 96M->24M(128M) 8.0ms
Before: 96M; after: 24M; shown heap capacity: 128M
Duration: 8.0ms for this reported event
Why it matters: A young event can leave garbage in uncollected old regions.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
Which trends would suggest increasing long-term retention?
Answer: Watch post-GC occupancy across similar traffic windows; an upward baseline
after major reclamation suggests retained growth.
Interview trap: Treating every after-young value as the complete live set is incorrect.

pages.title: How can GC duty fraction and allocation rate help?
pages.fullText:
Q058 · GC logs and quantitative interpretation INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q058. How can GC duty fraction and allocation rate
help?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
GC duty fraction estimates the share of an interval spent in pauses; allocation
rate estimates new object bytes per time.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Compute event time and allocation over a defined observation window with clear counting rules.
They expose memory-management demand but must be paired with collector CPU and application
metrics. Concurrent cycle wall time is not an STW pause.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Example: 0.5 s STW time / 10 s wall window = 5%
Allocation: 200 MiB over 2 s = 100 MiB/s
Separate: concurrent GC CPU and cycle duration
Why it matters: The arithmetic is useful only when the selected measurements match the
question.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you estimate bytes allocated per successful request?
Answer: Combine allocation bytes in JFR or profiler with successful request count over
the same window; exclude background work or report it separately.
Interview trap: Summing concurrent cycle duration as application stopped time inflates a
pause estimate.

pages.fullText:
Q059 · GC logs and quantitative interpretation INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q059. What do User, Sys and Real mean in GC
timing?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
User/Sys are CPU time consumed in different modes; Real is elapsed clock
time, including scheduling delays.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
They report CPU and elapsed-time perspectives for the event. Parallel worker CPU time can exceed
elapsed time. High wall time with limited CPU progress can suggest scheduling pressure; high
system time can motivate OS memory/I/O investigation.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Illustrative: User=0.08s Sys=0.01s Real=0.03s
CPU time can sum across workers
Wall time reflects elapsed duration
Why it matters: These values help form a hypothesis, not a complete diagnosis by themselves.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What other evidence would confirm CPU throttling?
Answer: Look at cgroup throttled time/periods, container CPU usage versus quota,
runnable queues and GC wall-clock-to-CPU gaps.
Interview trap: User plus Sys need not equal Real for parallel execution.

pages.fullText:
Q060 · GC logs and quantitative interpretation INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q060. What is a safepoint and is every safepoint a
GC pause?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
A safepoint is a JVM coordination state; many events besides GC can request
one.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
A safepoint is a VM coordination state used for operations requiring participating threads to reach
suitable execution states. GC is one use, but other operations can require safepoints. Time to reach
coordination can differ from time executing the operation.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Request coordination -> threads reach suitable state
VM operation executes -> application resumes
Log: inspect reaching and operation duration
Why it matters: A latency spike can involve coordination delay rather than a long collector
phase.

How would you investigate a long time-to-safepoint?
Answer: Enable safepoint logs and inspect time-to-safepoint, busy thread states, native
transitions and OS scheduling/CPU starvation.
Interview trap: Every application stall is not visible as a long GC pause.
Source guide p. 39 · Technical references J04, J06, J09, J10, J19

A thread dump shows what Java threads are doing, including stacks, waits and

JVM thread dump for the same process/time.

consumption.

pages.title: How do CPU and allocation profiles differ?

Q065 · JFR, dumps and native-memory tools INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q065. How do CPU and allocation profiles differ?

allocation sites and rates. A wall-clock or blocking view helps when threads wait. Choose the
evidence according to whether work, memory demand or waiting dominates.

pages.title: Why can p99 rise when average latency stays low?

Q066 · CPU, locks and tail latency INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q066. Why can p99 rise when average latency stays
low?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
p99 captures the slowest user requests; a small slow group can increase p99
while mean stays stable.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
A small subset of requests can encounter pauses, queueing, slow dependencies, contention or cold
execution. An average dilutes those outliers. Measure percentiles with enough observations and a
defined population, then correlate the slow path.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Most requests: 20 ms
Small tail: 1,000 ms
Average can look acceptable while p99 is poor
Why it matters: Endpoint and tenant segmentation can reveal a concentrated problem.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you separate one slow endpoint from a whole-service regression?
Answer: Break down histograms by endpoint, status and region; compare each route's
traffic share and dependency timing.
Interview trap: p99 estimates from a tiny sample are not stable evidence.

pages.title: What is the difference between service time and queueing time?
pages.fullText:
Q067 · CPU, locks and tail latency INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q067. What is the difference between service time
and queueing time?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Service time is active work; queueing time is waiting before work or a scarce
resource.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Service time is time spent executing the required work, while queueing time is time waiting for
admission or resources. As utilization approaches a bottleneck, waiting can grow sharply.
Instrument acquisition and execution separately.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Request total = admission + pool wait + work + I/O
JDBC acquisition: 400 ms
SQL execution: 10 ms
Why it matters: Optimizing the 10 ms SQL step alone may miss the dominant pool delay.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
Which pool and dependency metrics would you correlate?
Answer: Correlate executor queue age, Hikari pending/acquisition duration, HTTP client
pool waits, DB query time and arrival rate.
Interview trap: More threads can increase contention and waiting rather than throughput.

pages.title: How do you diagnose lock contention?
pages.fullText:
Q068 · CPU, locks and tail latency INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q068. How do you diagnose lock contention?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Lock contention makes threads wait for exclusive access even when
application code is otherwise fast.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Use repeated stacks and lock-related recording events to identify waiting threads, owners and
critical sections. Then reduce unnecessary lock scope or contention while preserving correctness.
Evaluate throughput and tail latency under the same concurrency.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Many requests -> one synchronized critical section
Owner -> slow I/O while holding lock
Candidate repair -> separate I/O from guarded state
Why it matters: The right change depends on the protected invariant.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you verify the correctness of a lock-scope reduction?
Answer: Add concurrency tests for invariants and race conditions, then measure
contention and p99 before and after the narrower lock.
Interview trap: Replacing a lock with a concurrent collection does not preserve every multi-
step atomic operation.
Source guide p. 44 · Technical references J21, J22, J28, J38
Wide lock Narrow lock Prove invariants
JVM / GC / PERFORMANCE

pages.title: Why is high CPU not always a GC problem?
pages.fullText:
Q069 · CPU, locks and tail latency INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q069. Why is high CPU not always a GC problem?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
High CPU can come from business loops, serialization, retries, spinning or GC;
profile before guessing.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
CPU can be consumed by application loops, serialization, cryptography, compilation or collector
work. Use CPU sampling, GC events and per-thread evidence to identify the owner. Diagnose the
hot path before changing collector settings.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
CPU: high
GC pause fraction: low
Profile: repeated JSON serialization dominates
Hypothesis: reduce redundant serialization work
Why it matters: A collector experiment is useful only if it addresses a measured contribution.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you quantify concurrent collector CPU versus application CPU?
Answer: Use JFR/CPU profiles and process CPU; compare GC worker activity in logs or
OS thread samples against application hot stacks.
Interview trap: The coexistence of GC activity and high CPU does not prove GC is the
dominant cost.

pages.title: How can retries create performance collapse?
pages.fullText:
Q070 · CPU, locks and tail latency INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q070. How can retries create performance collapse?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Retries multiply load when a dependency is slow, potentially creating a
positive feedback loop.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Retries multiply offered load when a dependency is already slow. Extra waiting requests retain state
and consume pools, threads and memory. Use deadlines, bounded attempts, backoff/jitter and
concurrency limits with idempotent or resolvable operations.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Client retries x service retries x SDK retries
Effective attempts can multiply
Budget: end-to-end deadline and bounded admission
Why it matters: The memory and latency symptom may originate from failure policy rather than
GC tuning.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What would you cap first during a dependency incident?
Answer: Cap in-flight dependency calls and retry attempts first, apply deadlines and
jittered backoff, and shed noncritical work.
Interview trap: An unlimited retry queue can become an unbounded retained object graph.
Source guide p. 45 · Technical references J21, J22, J28, J38
Slow dependency Retried load Overload spiral
JVM / GC / PERFORMANCE

Q071 · Allocation-aware Java coding INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q071. How do boxing and collections affect
allocation?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Boxed values and collection nodes allocate extra objects compared with many
primitive representations.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Boxing and reference-based data structures can add object and pointer overhead, though caching
and optimization change exact allocation. Primitive arrays or specialized approaches can help
measured hot paths. Compare semantics, workload and retained footprint.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
List<Integer> -> references and possible boxed values
int[] -> primitive payload in one array
IntStream -> primitive operations where appropriate
Why it matters: The data representation can matter more than a collector flag.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you measure the allocation cost of a real collection workload?
Answer: Profile allocation bytes and objects per operation on realistic inputs; validate with
JMH where helpful and end-to-end behavior.
Interview trap: Not every boxing expression necessarily creates a fresh object.

Q072 · Allocation-aware Java coding INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q072. How can string and logging work create
allocation pressure?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Formatting, concatenating and logging strings can allocate many short-lived
objects.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Repeated formatting, concatenation or payload construction can allocate substantial temporary
data. Parameterized logging can avoid some formatting when disabled, but argument expressions
still evaluate. Guard expensive computation where justified and keep sensitive payloads out of logs.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
log.debug("value={}", cheapValue);
if (log.isDebugEnabled()) {
 log.debug("summary={}", buildExpensiveSummary());
}
Why it matters: The logging API does not automatically defer every method argument.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
When would a logging supplier API be useful?
Answer: Supplier-style lazy messages help when disabled log levels would otherwise
construct expensive data; avoid capturing large objects unnecessarily.
Interview trap: Enabling verbose payload logs during load can change the performance being
diagnosed.

Q073 · Allocation-aware Java coding INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q073. Should every temporary object be pooled?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Pooling small objects can add state, contention and retention costs; measure
first.

→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
No. Ordinary allocation can be cheap and the collector may handle short-lived objects efficiently.
Pools introduce retained memory, ownership, concurrency and reset complexity. Pool only a
measured expensive resource or representation with a clear bounded lifecycle.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE

Connection/socket -> managed bounded lifecycle
Pooled buffer -> explicit ownership and size bound
Why it matters: A pool can convert short-lived data into a long-lived retained graph.

What would make a buffer pool worth its complexity?
Answer: A buffer pool helps if allocation/GC cost is material, reuse is frequent, and
bounded pool size improves actual throughput/latency.
Interview trap: Reusing an object without clearing request-specific state can leak data
between users.

Q074. How do you reduce large-payload memory
spikes?

Stream large data in bounded pieces rather than holding whole files or
payloads in heap.

→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Use bounded streaming, pagination, chunking and admission limits rather than buffering every
payload or result at once. Ensure downstream APIs and transaction behavior support the intended
stream. Measure peak concurrent memory, not just one request.

Answer: Throttle a test client/consumer, limit producer buffering and verify stable RSS,
bounded queue length and correct cancellation.

source was already fully materialized.

Q075. Are parallel streams always faster?

Parallel streams use shared parallel execution resources and can hurt small

→ →

Q076 · Benchmarking and experiment design INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q076. Why are naive nanoTime microbenchmarks
unreliable?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
A tiny loop using nanoTime is affected by JIT warmup, dead-code removal
and measurement noise.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Compilation, dead-code elimination, constant folding, timer cost and environmental noise can
dominate an ad hoc loop. JMH provides a structured harness, but its setup must still model the
question. A microbenchmark does not replace an end-to-end load test.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
long start = System.nanoTime();
// Tiny loop with unused result: misleading experiment.
long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - start;
Why it matters: The measured program might not execute the work you intended.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What would you change before claiming one collection implementation is faster?
Answer: Use JMH with controlled inputs, warmups, forks and allocation profiling;
compare confidence intervals and actual service performance.
Interview trap: A precise timer does not make a flawed experiment accurate.

pages.title: How does dead-code elimination affect a benchmark?
pages.fullText:
Q077 · Benchmarking and experiment design INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q077. How does dead-code elimination affect a
benchmark?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
The compiler may eliminate work if its result cannot be observed, making
timings unrealistically fast.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
If a result has no relevant observable use, optimized code may remove all or part of the
computation. Return benchmark results or use suitable JMH consumption mechanisms. Inspect
generated behavior or allocation evidence when the result seems implausible.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
@Benchmark
public int sum() {
 return values[0] + values[1];
}
// JMH consumes the benchmark result.
Why it matters: The measured operation needs a meaningful escape to the harness.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you keep an allocation benchmark representative without forcing
unrelated overhead?
Answer: Return or consume realistic results via JMH, keep data dependencies, and
compare allocation profiles without adding artificial heavy sinks.

pages.title: Why do JMH warmup and forks matter?
pages.fullText:
Q079 · Benchmarking and experiment design INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q079. Why do JMH warmup and forks matter?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
JMH warmup measures optimized hot paths; separate JVM forks reduce
contamination from prior measurements.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Warmup lets the runtime reach a defined execution condition. Forks isolate JVM execution histories
and reduce cross-test profile contamination. Choose iterations, forks and measurement modes from
the workload and variability; default values are not universal proof of rigor.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Record: JDK, JVM flags, forks, warmup and measurement
Observe: distribution and error, not one best number
Validate: representative inputs and consumed outputs
Why it matters: Different execution histories can produce different compiled code.

How would you compare startup-sensitive operations instead of warmed
throughput?

repeatable startup inputs, instead of relying on warmed JMH scores.

pages.title: How do you design a fair collector experiment?

Q080 · Benchmarking and experiment design INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q080. How do you design a fair collector
experiment?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
A collector comparison needs identical workload, JVM build, heap, CPU limits
and valid end-to-end metrics.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Hold application version, workload, resource limits and most settings constant; record unavoidable
collector-specific differences. Repeat runs, separate warmup from observation and measure the
service objective with error rates. Include memory and CPU cost alongside pauses.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
A: G1, same image and representative traffic
B: ZGC, same budget and deployment placement
Compare: p99, successful throughput, CPU, RSS, stalls
Why it matters: A fair comparison explains any changed variable, including JDK version.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you disentangle a JDK upgrade from a collector change?
Answer: Use a matrix: run old/new JDK each with its supported matching collector/mode,
then compare within-JDK and cross-JDK separately.
Interview trap: Comparing Java 17 G1 with Java 25 ZGC cannot isolate collector choice alone.

pages.title: How does HotSpot become container-aware?
pages.fullText:
Q081 · Containers and Kubernetes JVM budgets INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q081. How does HotSpot become container-aware?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Container-aware HotSpot reads applicable cgroup resource limits to choose
defaults and ergonomics.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Supported modern HotSpot builds on supported platforms can use container resource information
for ergonomics. Verify the detected memory and processors, effective flags and runtime build.
Detection and limits differ by OS, cgroup version and deployment configuration.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
java -XshowSettings:system -version
java -XX:+PrintCommandLineFlags -version
# Inspect what the actual deployment detects.
Why it matters: The same image can choose different ergonomics under different limits.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What would you inspect after moving from cgroup v1 to v2?
Answer: Inspect java -XshowSettings:system -version, cgroup files, actual Xmx,
availableProcessors and runtime logs after the migration.
Interview trap: Running on a host does not validate behavior in your Kubernetes pod.
Source guide p. 50 · Technical references J04-J06, J23

pages.title: How do MaxRAMPercentage and Xmx interact?
pages.fullText:
Q082 · Containers and Kubernetes JVM budgets INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q082. How do MaxRAMPercentage and Xmx
interact?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
MaxRAMPercentage helps choose heap ergonomically when Xmx is not
explicitly set; an explicit Xmx wins.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Heap-percentage flags affect ergonomic sizing when applicable; an explicit Xmx sets the heap
maximum rather than making the percentage a second independent cap. The denominator
depends on effective memory detection and configuration. Inspect the resulting heap.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Option A: -Xmx512m
Option B: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50
# Alternatives to evaluate, not equivalent everywhere.
Why it matters: Neither option bounds total native memory or guarantees container headroom.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you choose a budget for a 1 GiB Java container?
Answer: Reserve memory for metaspace, thread stacks, code, direct buffers, native
libraries and safety headroom; measure RSS before fixing Xmx.
Interview trap: A high percentage may leave too little memory for threads and buffers.
Source guide p. 51 · Technical references J04-J06, J23

pages.title: Why can a pod be OOMKilled while heap usage is below Xmx?
pages.fullText:
Q083 · Containers and Kubernetes JVM budgets INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q083. Why can a pod be OOMKilled while heap
usage is below Xmx?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
A container memory kill can happen when native and heap memory together
exceed the cgroup limit.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
The platform enforces its own charged-memory limit, which includes more than the Java heap.
Native allocations, stacks, direct buffers and other charged resources can exceed that limit. Inspect
termination and cgroup evidence alongside JVM metrics.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Heap used: below Xmx
Direct buffers and stacks: additional memory
Platform charged memory: exceeds container limit
Outcome: external kill may produce no heap dump
Why it matters: The failing boundary is the container, not necessarily Java heap allocation.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
Which deployment and process metrics would distinguish this from heap OOME?
Answer: Check termination reason, cgroup OOM events, RSS, heap-after-GC, NMT, direct
buffers and thread counts.
Interview trap: Raising Xmx can worsen the external kill risk.
Source guide p. 51 · Technical references J04-J06, J23
Heap below Xmx Native bytes OOMKilled
JVM / GC / PERFORMANCE

pages.title: How does CPU throttling affect GC and latency?
pages.fullText:
Q084 · Containers and Kubernetes JVM budgets INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q084. How does CPU throttling affect GC and
latency?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
CPU throttling delays application and GC workers, increasing real time even if
GC work itself is unchanged.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
A CPU quota can delay application and collector progress even when the host has spare
processors. Concurrent collectors need time to keep up, and parallel phases share the same
effective resource constraint. Inspect throttling and runnable demand together with GC timing.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
CPU demand > quota -> scheduling delay
Concurrent marking slower -> less reclamation headroom
Request queues -> longer end-to-end latency
Why it matters: A collector can appear slower because its environment changed.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you test whether a long pause is primarily scheduling delay?
Answer: Compare GC User+Sys with Real under throttling metrics; repeat at a higher
CPU quota and test whether wall-time gaps shrink.
Interview trap: Adding GC threads does not create more CPU quota.
Source guide p. 51 · Technical references J04-J06, J23
CPU quota GC waits for CPU Longer wall pause
JVM / GC / PERFORMANCE

Q085 · Containers and Kubernetes JVM budgets INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q085. How should you budget process memory?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Total Java process memory includes heap, metadata, code cache, native
buffers, stacks and overhead.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Start from measured peak charged memory and break down plausible contributors: heap, metadata,
code, thread stacks, direct/native buffers and other process/deployment charges. Leave justified
headroom and validate under peak and failure traffic. Estimates are not exact additive OS
accounting.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Example 1 GiB limit:
512 MiB heap + measured native budget + headroom
Check concurrent requests, thread count and buffers
Validate actual charged-memory peak
Why it matters: The budget must survive realistic concurrency, not only startup.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would the budget change for thousands of platform threads?
Answer: Many platform threads consume stacks and scheduling/native-thread resources;
multiply observed per-thread costs and include concurrency limits.
Interview trap: A universal 'set heap to 75%' recipe ignores workload-dependent native use.
Source guide p. 52 · Technical references J04-J06, J23
Heap + native areas Thread stacks Headroom

pages.title: How can connection-pool sizing affect JVM performance?
pages.fullText:
Q087 · Spring Boot production tuning INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q087. How can connection-pool sizing affect JVM
performance?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
More JDBC connections are not always better; too many can saturate the
database and amplify wait costs.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Blocked requests can retain object graphs and occupy platform threads while waiting for a
connection. A larger pool may overload the database rather than help. Budget connections across
all replicas and instrument waiting separately from SQL execution.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
20 replicas x pool maximum 15 = 300 connections
Database capacity and other clients constrain budget
Waiting requests -> retained context and response data
Why it matters: The bottleneck can be a database concurrency budget expressed as a JVM
memory symptom.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What should happen when the pool is full and the request deadline expires?
Answer: Return a controlled timeout/503 or suitable overload response; release caller
resources and do not let requests wait beyond their deadline.
Interview trap: Pool max is multiplied by replicas and can change during autoscaling.
Source guide p. 53 · Technical references J21-J24, J34, J35, J38, J39

Q088. How do WebFlux and virtual threads change
resource needs?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
WebFlux changes the I/O concurrency model; virtual threads allow blocking-
style code with many virtual tasks, but resources remain finite.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →

They change how waiting work occupies execution resources, but do not remove downstream limits
or per-request state. Avoid blocking event-loop code in reactive applications. With virtual threads,
bound resource access and admitted work rather than assuming cheap threads make unlimited
concurrency safe.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Reactive: event loop -> nonblocking composition
Virtual thread: simpler blocking style where suitable
Both: DB, remote API and memory budgets still apply
Why it matters: The concurrency model changes the cost profile, not the service's business
invariants.

Which limit would you enforce around a slow external API?
Answer: Use a bulkhead/semaphore on concurrent external calls plus connection limits
and timeouts; neither model grants infinite downstream capacity.

scheduling.

pages.fullText:
Q089 · Spring Boot production tuning INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q089. How do you tune startup for autoscaling?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Autoscaling succeeds only if new JVM instances warm up before traffic
overwhelms the existing fleet.

→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Measure time spent in loading, bean creation, database checks, initialization and compilation.
Remove unnecessary eager work while keeping readiness truthful. Use supported startup
instrumentation and evaluate startup features for your selected JDK and framework version.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Start process -> initialize -> readiness -> traffic
Measure each phase and first-request latency
Avoid moving failures invisibly into customer requests
Why it matters: Lazy initialization can shift work and failure from startup into request handling.

How would you verify that a newly scaled replica is truly useful?
Answer: Replay realistic traffic against newly Ready replicas; monitor startup time, first-
request p99, error rate, cache warmup and capacity.
Interview trap: A faster readiness signal that precedes required initialization can worsen
service reliability.

pages.title: How do you roll out a JVM tuning change safely?
pages.fullText:
Q090 · Spring Boot production tuning INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q090. How do you roll out a JVM tuning change
safely?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Tune JVM settings with a baseline, a small controlled change, canary
observation and a rollback plan.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Change a small reviewed set of variables, deploy to representative limited traffic and compare
customer, GC and resource metrics. Define abort criteria and keep a compatible rollback
configuration. Record exact JDK, flags, image and environment.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Hypothesis -> one controlled change -> canary
Observe -> p99, errors, useful rate, RSS, CPU
Decision -> expand or restore prior configuration
Why it matters: A flag-only release still changes runtime behavior and resource demand.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What would trigger immediate rollback of a heap-size experiment?
Answer: Rollback if user p99, errors, OOM kills, CPU throttling or RSS exceeds predefined
safe thresholds.
Interview trap: A canary with only idle traffic does not validate a peak-load memory change.

pages.title: Do virtual threads eliminate platform threads and memory costs?
pages.fullText:
Q092 · Modern Java version traps INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q092. Do virtual threads eliminate platform threads
and memory costs?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Virtual threads reduce per-request platform-thread costs but still consume
memory and downstream resources.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
No. Virtual threads run on carrier platform threads and retain their own execution state. They can
improve scalability for suitable waiting workloads, but cannot make CPU work infinitely parallel or
remove memory and dependency budgets. Available since Java 21 as a final feature.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Many waiting tasks -> virtual-thread candidates
CPU-heavy tasks -> limited by actual processors
In-flight state -> still consumes memory
Why it matters: Improved thread economics can expose a downstream bottleneck sooner.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you prevent unbounded virtual-thread work from exhausting memory?
Answer: Set admission/semaphore limits, timeouts and bounded request queues; monitor
heap, native usage and active external calls.
Interview trap: Virtual threads should not be described as a faster garbage collector.

Q093. How did virtual-thread monitor pinning
change?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Monitor pinning behavior changed across newer Java releases, so use the
specific JDK's rules and diagnostics.

→ →

monitor-related pinning limitation; other contexts such as relevant native execution can still matter.

identify monitor/native blocking call stacks.

and correctness needs.

Q094. What are compact object headers in Java 25?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Compact object headers in Java 25 can reduce header footprint under the
selected supported HotSpot mode.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →

JEP 519 made compact object headers a product feature after experimentation in Java 24. This is a
HotSpot layout feature, not a new Java object model. Verify support and enablement, then measure
footprint and performance; it is not an automatic reduction of every object to one fixed size.

Check: other selected VM options and platform support

may benefit, if CPU and compatibility measurements also improve.

Q095 · Modern Java version traps INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q095. How should you evaluate a JDK upgrade for
performance?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
A JDK upgrade can change GC, JIT and runtime defaults; test correctness
and performance together.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →

Test correctness and compatibility first, then compare startup, steady-state capacity, latency and
resources using the same workload. Separate runtime changes from collector/configuration
changes where possible. Review release notes and effective options rather than relying on expected
speedups.

Test B: new JDK, comparable supported config

What would block an upgrade despite better average throughput?
Answer: Block on incompatible libraries, crashes, data corruption, unacceptable tail
latency, higher OOM risk or failed rollback/recovery tests.
Interview trap: A single faster run after an upgrade is not a reliable attribution.

Q096. A service's heap keeps rising. How do you
investigate?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
When heap climbs, compare allocation and post-GC live memory, then identify
which owners retain growing object graphs.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Establish workload phases and compare retained/live-set behavior after relevant reclamation, not
just instantaneous used heap. Correlate cache, queue and session counts. Capture suitable
histograms or dumps, identify retaining roots and test the suspected owner's policy.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
Trend: baseline after comparable reclamation rises
Histogram: growing payload objects
Root path: retry queue retains failed requests
Repair: bounded queue, deadlines and safe discard
Why it matters: The retaining owner often explains why more heap only delayed failure.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
How would you validate that the repair stops growth under sustained failures?
Answer: Run sustained-load and failure-path tests, verify stable post-GC baselines,
bounded caches/queues and safe OOM headroom over time.
Interview trap: A sawtooth graph with temporary growth can be normal.

Q097. RSS rises while Java heap looks stable. What
next?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Stable heap with rising RSS suggests checking off-heap memory, threads,
metaspace and OS accounting.

→ →

Inspect direct buffers, threads, tracked native categories, libraries and OS mappings, along with
memory-accounting context. Use NMT diffs where enabled and OS evidence where it is not.
Compare workload and deployment changes before assigning the growth to a leak.

Inspect: stacks and thread ownership

allocations?

retained native allocations rise differently from reusable allocator arenas.

Q098 · Senior diagnosis and design scenarios INTERVIEW ANSWER CARD
Q098. p99 is poor but GC pauses are short. What do
you do?
SHORT ANSWER · SAY THIS FIRST
Short GC pauses do not rule out request queuing, DB waits, network stalls or
CPU contention.
VISUAL MEMORY SKETCH
→ →
PRECISE TECHNICAL EXPLANATION
Follow the request timeline through admission, locks, CPU scheduling and dependencies. Inspect
allocations and collector stalls only when evidence connects them. Compare endpoint-level traces
and saturation rather than assuming all tail latency comes from GC.
JAVA / COMMAND / SCENARIO EXAMPLE
GC pauses: short
Trace: 600 ms JDBC acquisition, 15 ms query
Bottleneck: connection availability/admission
Repair: workload and DB budget, not random GC flags
Why it matters: Low-pause GC removes one possible contributor rather than every source of
delay.
ANSWERED FOLLOW-UP · NO MEMORIZED FILLER
What evidence would change your diagnosis back toward memory management?
Answer: Change direction if allocation stalls, safepoint delays, native-memory pressure or
retained-heap trends line up in time with p99 spikes.
Interview trap: Changing to another low-pause collector can leave the dominant wait
untouched.

pages.title: VISUAL REFERENCE / 01
pages.fullText:
VISUAL REFERENCE / 01
JVM memory is more
than the heap
Think of the Java process as a shared memory budget, not a single heap graph.
→ →
Java heap: object allocation and garbage collection. Xmx is the Java object-heap
ceiling, not total resident memory.
Outside the heap: class metadata, compiled code, thread stacks, JIT/GC structures,
direct buffers and native libraries use additional memory.
Container: Linux cgroups account for process memory. An external OOM kill can
occur without a Java OutOfMemoryError or heap dump.
Heap objects + arrays Metaspace + JIT code Stacks + native buffers
Example estimate (not an exact RSS equation): 1,024 MiB budget − 512 MiB heap −
320 MiB other use = 192 MiB arithmetic headroom. Measure actual resident/
charged memory.
JVM / GC / PERFORMANCE
LEARN · DRAW · MEASURE · EXPLAIN 124

pages.title: VISUAL REFERENCE / 02
pages.fullText:
VISUAL REFERENCE / 02
How a young G1
collection works
G1 divides the heap into regions. It evacuates reachable survivors out of chosen regions.
→ →
Before: Some objects in young regions are dead; others can still be reached from
roots or references in older regions.
During: G1 pauses application threads, identifies live objects in its collection set and
copies them into destination regions.
After: Collected source regions become reusable. Copied bytes, roots and
remembered-set work all influence pause duration.
An evacuation failure means that suitable destination space could not be provided. Check live-
set pressure, free regions, large allocations and allocation rate.
New Eden objects STW evacuation Survivor / Old regions
JVM / GC / PERFORMANCE

pages.title: VISUAL REFERENCE / 03
pages.fullText:
VISUAL REFERENCE / 03
Collector phases
are not synonyms
→ →
Parallel: Several GC workers can run together. A parallel GC phase can still stop
application threads.
Concurrent: GC overlaps application work and competes for CPU, cache and
memory bandwidth.
Low-pause: ZGC and Shenandoah use substantial concurrent work, but can still
encounter pauses, stalls or throughput cost.
Stop-the-world pause Concurrent work + app Next collection phase
Version trap: Java 17 ZGC is non-generational; Java 21 added an opt-in
generational mode; Java 25 uses generational ZGC. Collector defaults and
availability are separate questions.

Three diagnoses,
three different fixes
Heap leak
Post-GC live occupancy rises under comparable load; retaining roots show
unbounded cache/queue.
Next: Cap ownership and fix retention, then soak-test.
High RSS, stable heap
Inspect direct memory, threads, metaspace, native memory and OS mappings.
Next: Fix the actual native owner; consider container budget.
p99 high, tiny GC pauses
Inspect queuing, DB acquisition, CPU throttling, locks and dependency latency.
Next: Tune the delayed layer rather than guessing new GC flags.
Always correlate a symptom with a timeline, not one screenshot of a heap meter.

pages.fullText:
SOURCE REFERENCE · ORIGINAL P. 62
A real G1 log entry
Understand the event, before/after heap and pause duration.
Walkthrough: a real G1 log entry
The following event came from L03 on this environment using G1 with Xms=Xmx=32 MiB. It is one
real local observation from a synthetic bounded workload, not a latency claim for Spring Boot.
[0.076s][info][gc          ] GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 14M->2M(32M) 10.862ms
FIELD
READING
Uptime
Time since this JVM began, not a wall-clock date.
GC(0)
Identifier connecting this collection with its associated phase lines.
Pause Young (Normal)
Young collection event and its stated classification.
G1 Evacuation Pause
The event includes relocating live objects in the selected collection set.
Heap values
14M before, 2M after, 32M shown heap capacity. They are log-reported
units.
Duration
10.862 ms reported for this event; subsequent runs can differ.
What this establishes: The workload ran with G1 and produced a young collection with a
before/after heap change. The selected log shows a real event that you can interpret.
What remains unknown: This one event does not establish p99, collector superiority, leak
absence, full live-set size or behavior under container CPU throttling.
Next evidence: Inspect repeated events, old-region trends, allocation/survival patterns and phase
times. Correlate with customer metrics only in a representative application workload.
References: J09, J10, J19

Use the least expensive tool that can answer your question.

every command is installed.

COMMAND / EVIDENCE
What launch
configuration?
jcmd PID VM.command_line jcmd PID VM.flags

waiting?

pages.fullText:
SOURCE REFERENCE · ORIGINAL P. 64
Worked diagnosis: rising retained data
Compare retained ownership under comparable workload.
Illustrative Spring API incident: memory usage rises during downstream failures. More heap delays
exhaustion, but the recovered baseline still rises across comparable workload windows.
OBSERVATION
HYPOTHESIS / NEXT CHECK
More failed outbound requests
Retry policy may retain requests longer than their useful
lifetime.
Increasing post-reclamation
occupancy
Investigate persistent owners, not only allocation rate.
Histogram shows many request
payloads
Inspect a graph and root path to find the owner.
Path leads to retry queue
Check queue bounds, expiry, cancellation and response
ownership.
Queue accepts unlimited failed
work
Bound admission and deadlines; preserve required durable
work elsewhere.
Repair: Use a bounded retry/admission policy consistent with business durability. Cancel expired
in-memory work, avoid retaining full payloads unnecessarily and define controlled failure or durable
queuing behavior.
Verification: Repeat representative traffic with a deliberately slow dependency. Check that retained
baseline stabilizes, useful successes recover, queue age stays bounded and rejected/expired
operations remain correct.
Interview answer: The collector could reclaim only unreachable objects. The retry owner kept
failed request graphs reachable; tuning GC could not correct that ownership policy.
No production incident or improvement measurement is claimed; this is a design and diagnosis 
exercise.

SOURCE REFERENCE · ORIGINAL P. 65
Worked diagnosis: latency without long GC
Look at blocked and queued work before changing GC.
Illustrative incident: p99 rises after more API replicas are added. GC pause evidence stays short, 
but
request traces show long JDBC acquisition waits.
CHECK
REASON
Total possible connections
Replica count multiplies per-process pool maxima.
Acquisition versus execution
Separate waiting for a connection from SQL time.
DB sessions and waits
Determine whether more connections increase useful work or
contention.
Request admission and deadline
Bound the number and lifetime of waiting request graphs.
Autoscaling signals
Scaling JVMs cannot guarantee more database capacity.
Repair candidate: Adjust service concurrency and pool budgets against measured database
capacity. Reduce query/transaction cost where evidence supports it; apply deadlines and explicit
overload behavior.
Verification: At equivalent offered load, compare successful throughput, p99, pool acquisition, DB
waits, allocation and charged memory. Test a database slowdown as well as normal load.
Interview answer: GC was investigated and was not the dominant observed delay. Pool waiting
explained the tail; a different collector would not create database execution capacity.

pages.fullText:
SOURCE REFERENCE · ORIGINAL P. 66
Worked diagnosis: external memory kill
Linux memory enforcement and JVM heap are not identical.
Illustrative Kubernetes case: a replica is OOMKilled while Java heap-used is below its configured
maximum. No heap dump appears.
EVIDENCE
QUESTION
Termination and cgroup events
Was the platform memory limit the failing boundary?
Memory graph under peak traffic
What charged-memory peak preceded termination?
Direct-buffer pools and request
sizes
Did concurrent payload buffers grow?
Thread and stack trends
Did platform-thread counts or stack demand increase?
NMT and OS mappings where
available
Which tracked or untracked native categories account for
growth?
Repair candidate: Rebudget heap and measured native contributors. Bound payload buffering,
thread creation and in-flight requests. Choose limit changes only when justified by capacity and 
cost.
Verification: Run the same image with the actual pod constraints and representative peak/failure
traffic. Observe charged memory, CPU throttling, GC, errors and useful throughput over a sufficient
window.
Interview answer: Xmx bounded the object heap, while the platform enforced a wider
charged-memory boundary. Heap-dump-on-OOME could not guarantee evidence for the external kill.

safe conclusions.

L10. Calculate pause fraction and a memory
estimate
Concurrent cycle durations must not be counted as stopped time. Estimated memory
categories are not a perfect additive RSS model.
TEST SCRIPT PRESERVED FROM SOURCE
set -euo pipefail
python3 - <<'PY'
pauses_ms = [8, 12, 10, 20]
window_ms = 10000
fraction = sum(pauses_ms) / window_ms
assert fraction == 0.005
limit_mib = 1024
heap_mib = 512
estimated_other_mib = 320
headroom_mib = limit_mib - heap_mib - estimated_other_mib
assert headroom_mib == 192
print("PASS: illustrative STW fraction =", fraction)
print("Illustrative remaining headroom MiB =", headroom_mib)
PY
Expected observation: The illustrative STW fraction is 0.005, or 0.5%, and arithmetic
headroom is 192 MiB. These are calculations on example inputs, not measurements.
Verification: Bash syntax and local execution passed using a Java 17 full JDK. Results illustrate the
test inputs; they do not prove performance rankings in deployed services.

QUICK REVISION
Collector decision sheet
Serial
Few GC worker threads; consider small heaps and tolerant pause goals.
Parallel
High-throughput batch work when pauses are acceptable.
G1
Region-based general-purpose collector balancing throughput and pause targets.
ZGC
Low-pause collector using concurrent work; needs CPU and allocation headroom.
Shenandoah
Low-pause collector with vendor/build/mode availability constraints.
Epsilon
Allocates without collection; use only bounded experiments.
CMS
Removed from JDK 14; not a modern production option.

pages.title: What is a design pattern?
pages.fullText:
JAVA DESIGN PATTERNS
PREMIUM STUDY NOTES
DESIGN-PATTERN FOUNDATIONS

Q001
FOUNDATION
What is a design pattern?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A design pattern describes a reusable collaboration of objects for a recurring
design problem in a context.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP
Real problem
Choose intent
Test tradeoff
SOURCE EXAMPLE / JAVA IDEA
Problem: several payment algorithms vary independently.
   Design: checkout delegates to a PaymentStrategy.
IN PLAIN ENGLISH
A pattern is not a library or a copy-paste class diagram. Adapt its roles to the actual requirements and
explain the change it makes easier. The implementation can be small, including a Java function.
INTERVIEW TRAP
More pattern classes do not automatically improve design.
FOLLOW-UP EXPLAINED
What requirement justifies the extra abstraction?
Answer: Add an abstraction when a second real behavior must be substituted, tested separately, or
changed independently. If no change axis exists, keep the simpler method.

pages.title: What are the three GoF pattern categories?
pages.fullText:
JAVA DESIGN PATTERNS
PREMIUM STUDY NOTES
DESIGN-PATTERN FOUNDATIONS
10
Q002
FOUNDATION
What are the three GoF pattern categories?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Creational patterns organize object creation; structural patterns organize
composition; behavioral patterns organize responsibilities and interactions.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP
Real problem
Choose intent
Test tradeoff
SOURCE EXAMPLE / JAVA IDEA
Creation: Builder
   Structure: Adapter
   Behavior: Strategy
IN PLAIN ENGLISH
The GoF catalog contains 23 patterns. Categories describe intent, not which Java keyword is used.
Factory Method uses inheritance, while Abstract Factory commonly uses composition to create a
family.
INTERVIEW TRAP
Similar class shapes can express different intents.
FOLLOW-UP EXPLAINED
Why can a wrapper be either Adapter or Decorator?
Answer: A wrapper is an Adapter when it converts one contract to another. It is a Decorator when
it preserves the contract but adds behavior such as tracing or compression.

Q003
FOUNDATION
How do design patterns differ from architectural
patterns?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Design patterns usually describe object-level collaboration; architectural
patterns describe broader system organization and constraints.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP
Real problem
Choose intent
Test tradeoff
SOURCE EXAMPLE / JAVA IDEA
Strategy: choose a discount algorithm
   Hexagonal architecture: isolate domain from delivery and persistence
IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Layered architecture, event-driven architecture and ports/adapters operate at different scales from
GoF patterns. A system may use several together. Explain their boundaries instead of calling every
useful arrangement a GoF pattern.
INTERVIEW TRAP
Repository and outbox are useful patterns but are not among the 23 GoF entries.
FOLLOW-UP EXPLAINED
Where would an Adapter sit in hexagonal architecture?
Answer: An Adapter sits on the infrastructure side of a port. Domain code calls the port; the
adapter translates that call into a database, HTTP, or vendor API.

pages.title: What does favor composition over inheritance mean?
pages.fullText:
JAVA DESIGN PATTERNS
PREMIUM STUDY NOTES
DESIGN-PATTERN FOUNDATIONS
12
Q004
FOUNDATION
What does favor composition over inheritance mean?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Prefer delegation when behavior should vary without coupling it to one fixed class
hierarchy.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP
Real problem
Choose intent
Test tradeoff
SOURCE EXAMPLE / JAVA IDEA
class Checkout {
     private final DiscountPolicy discount;
   }
IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Composition can swap independently varying behavior and reduce fragile superclass dependencies.
Inheritance remains useful for genuine substitutable abstractions and stable algorithm skeletons. Do
not turn the principle into an absolute ban.
INTERVIEW TRAP
Delegation still needs a coherent contract and lifecycle.
FOLLOW-UP EXPLAINED
When is Template Method a reasonable choice?
Answer: Template Method fits a stable sequence with limited, well-defined steps subclasses must
implement. Use composition when steps need independent runtime selection.

pages.title: What does program to an interface mean?
pages.fullText:
JAVA DESIGN PATTERNS
PREMIUM STUDY NOTES
DESIGN-PATTERN FOUNDATIONS
13
Q005
FOUNDATION
What does program to an interface mean?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Depend on the smallest useful abstraction or contract rather than unnecessary
implementation details.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP
Real problem
Choose intent
Test tradeoff
SOURCE EXAMPLE / JAVA IDEA
class OrderService {
     private final PaymentPort payments;
   }
IN PLAIN ENGLISH
An interface can be a Java interface or a stable abstraction. It should reflect the consumer's needs
and permit meaningful substitution. Creating an interface for every class without variation or
boundary value can add noise.
INTERVIEW TRAP
An interface does not automatically eliminate coupling to concrete semantics.
FOLLOW-UP EXPLAINED
What error/outcome contract should PaymentPort expose?
Answer: Return a documented success, rejection, or unknown outcome, with stable IDs and error
codes. A timeout must not automatically mean a payment definitely failed.

pages.title: When should you avoid introducing a pattern?
pages.fullText:
JAVA DESIGN PATTERNS
PREMIUM STUDY NOTES
DESIGN-PATTERN FOUNDATIONS
14
Q006
FOUNDATION
When should you avoid introducing a pattern?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Avoid it when it solves no current variation, makes the simple path harder, or
hides an important invariant.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP
Real problem
Choose intent
Test tradeoff
SOURCE EXAMPLE / JAVA IDEA
Two stable branches in one small method
   May be clearer than a registry + factories + reflection
IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Use the simplest structure that keeps the relevant change safe. Introduce a pattern when duplication,
variation or dependency boundaries provide evidence. Measure readability, testing and change impact
rather than pattern count.
INTERVIEW TRAP
Speculative extension points can become maintenance obligations.
FOLLOW-UP EXPLAINED
What concrete change would trigger refactoring?
Answer: Refactor when a third distinct algorithm arrives, branches have different owners, or a new
dependency needs its own test boundary. Show this with change history.
