pages.title: Find shortest unweighted distances with BFS.
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 · GRAPHS AND REACHABILITY QUESTION 081 / 120
Q081. Find shortest unweighted distances with BFS.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Start from the source, mark its distance zero and discover each neighbor once. Queue order
processes increasing edge distance.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
Find shortest unweighted
distances with BFS. ➜
KEY LOGIC
Start from the source, mark its
distance zero and discover each
neighbor once.
➜
RESULT
1 -> 2 and isolated 3; source 0 ->
[0,1,2,-1]
💡 The first discovery uses a shortest edge-count path.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
Time O(V+E) for adjacency lists; space O(V).
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
Neighbor indices must be valid; the graph may be
directed.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
Why is this insufficient for unequal weighted edges?
BFS minimizes the number of edges, not total weight. With different nonnegative edge costs, Dijkstra finds
minimum total weight; with negative edges use a suitable Bellman-Ford-style algorithm.
JAVA 17 · SOLUTION Source Q081 · 12 lines
static int[] bfsDistances(List<List<Integer>> graph,int source) {
  if(source<0 || source>=graph.size()) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
  int[] distance=new int[graph.size()]; Arrays.fill(distance,-1);
  Deque<Integer> queue=new ArrayDeque<>(); queue.add(source); distance[source]=0;
  while(!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int u=queue.remove();
    for(int v:graph.get(u)) if(distance[v]==-1) {
      distance[v]=distance[u]+1; queue.add(v);
    }
  }
  return distance;
}

pages.shortAnswer:
Use three DFS states: unseen, currently active, and finished. An edge to an active vertex is a back
edge and proves a directed cycle.

currently active, and finished.

Valid neighbor indices required; a deep graph can

pages.title: Produce a topological ordering or reject a cycle.
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 · GRAPHS AND REACHABILITY QUESTION 083 / 120
Q083. Produce a topological ordering or reject a
cycle.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Count incoming edges and repeatedly remove zero-indegree vertices, reducing their neighbors'
counts. If fewer than V vertices are emitted, a cycle prevents a complete order.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
Produce a topological ordering or
reject a cycle. ➜
KEY LOGIC
Count incoming edges and
repeatedly remove zero-indegree
vertices, reducing their neighbors'
counts.
➜
RESULT
1 -> 2 -> [0,1,2]
💡 A zero-indegree vertex has no unresolved predecessor.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
Time O(V+E); space O(V), excluding output.
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
A DAG can have several valid orders; tests should
normally verify edge ordering.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
How would a priority queue provide the lexicographically smallest order?
In Kahn's topological algorithm, put every zero-indegree node in a min-heap instead of a FIFO queue.
Repeatedly take the smallest available node and decrement neighbors; the result is the lexicographically
smallest valid order.
JAVA 17 · SOLUTION Source Q083 · 13 lines
static List<Integer> topological(List<List<Integer>> graph) {
  int[] degree=new int[graph.size()];
  for(List<Integer> edges:graph) for(int v:edges) degree[v]++;
  Deque<Integer> queue=new ArrayDeque<>();
  for(int u=0;u<degree.length;u++) if(degree[u]==0) queue.add(u);
  List<Integer> out=new ArrayList<>();
  while(!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int u=queue.remove(); out.add(u);
    for(int v:graph.get(u)) if(--degree[v]==0) queue.add(v);
  }
  if(out.size()!=graph.size()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cycle");
  return out;
}

pages.title: Generate distinct permutations, including duplicate input values.
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING QUESTION 086 / 120
Q086. Generate distinct permutations, including
duplicate input values.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Sort a copy and backtrack over unused positions. At each depth, skip an equal value when its
preceding equal position is still unused; that eliminates duplicate choice orders.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
[1,1,2] ➜
KEY LOGIC
Sort a copy and backtrack over
unused positions.
➜
RESULT
[1,1,2], [1,2,1], [2,1,1]
💡 Skip same-value alternatives at one decision depth, not every occurrence globally.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
Worst O(n*n!) time and output; auxiliary space O(n),
plus sorting copy.
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
Empty input has one permutation: the empty list.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
How would you generate permutations lazily rather than store all?
Implement an iterator-like depth-first generator with explicit state or yield one permutation to a callback as
soon as a complete assignment is found. Memory can be O(depth) instead of storing factorially many
results.
JAVA 17 · SOLUTION Source Q086 · 12 lines
static List<List<Integer>> permutations(int[] input) {
  int[] a=input.clone(); Arrays.sort(a); List<List<Integer>> out=new ArrayList<>();
  permutationDFS(a,new boolean[a.length],new ArrayList<>(),out); return out;
}
static void permutationDFS(int[] a,boolean[] used,List<Integer> path,List<List<Integer>> out) {
  if(path.size()==a.length) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); return; }
  for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++) {
    if(used[i] || (i>0 && a[i]==a[i-1] && !used[i-1])) continue;
    used[i]=true; path.add(a[i]); permutationDFS(a,used,path,out);
    path.remove(path.size()-1); used[i]=false;
  }
}

pages.title: Generate every subset of distinct values.
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 · RECURSION AND BACKTRACKING QUESTION 087 / 120
Q087. Generate every subset of distinct values.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Backtrack from a start index and record the current path at every call. Advancing the start
prevents choosing earlier positions again.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
[1,2] ➜
KEY LOGIC
Backtrack from a start index and
record the current path at every
call.
➜
RESULT
[], [1], [1,2], [2]
💡 The path corresponds to positions selected in increasing index order.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
Time/output O(n*2^n); auxiliary space O(n).
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
Large n creates exponential output even when
recursion is correct.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
How would duplicate values require a sorted skip rule?
Sort first. At each recursion depth, skip value a[i] when i>start and a[i]==a[i-1] so equivalent choices at the
same depth are not repeated. This preserves unique subsets without a global result set.
JAVA 17 · SOLUTION Source Q087 · 10 lines
static List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] a) {
  Set<Integer> unique=new HashSet<>(); for(int x:a) if(!unique.add(x)) throw new 
IllegalArgumentException();
  List<List<Integer>> out=new ArrayList<>(); subsetDFS(a,0,new ArrayList<>(),out); return out;
}
static void subsetDFS(int[] a,int start,List<Integer> path,List<List<Integer>> out) {
  out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));
  for(int i=start;i<a.length;i++) {
    path.add(a[i]); subsetDFS(a,i+1,path,out); path.remove(path.size()-1);
  }
}

than opens are used. These constraints ensure every prefix remains valid.

CHAPTER 19 · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING FOUNDATIONS QUESTION 091 / 120
Q091. Count stair-climbing ways with steps of one or
two.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
The last move comes from n-1 or n-2, so counts follow an adjacent-value recurrence. Use
BigInteger to avoid primitive overflow and define one empty way for zero stairs.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
n=4 ➜
KEY LOGIC
The last move comes from n-1 or
n-2, so counts follow an adjacent-
value recurrence.
➜
RESULT
ways(0)=ways(1)=1; ways(2)=2;
ways(3)=3; ways(4)=5.
💡 ways(0)=ways(1)=1; ways(2)=2; ways(3)=3; ways(4)=5.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
O(n) big-integer additions; storage and bit cost grow
with result size.
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
This convention counts the empty path at n=0.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
How would allowed step sizes change the state transition?
Let ways[i] = sum(ways[i-step]) for each allowed positive step with i-step >= 0. Set ways[0]=1 and fill upward.
Duplicated step sizes should not count as different moves unless specified.

static BigInteger stairs(int n) {
  if(n<0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
  BigInteger previous=BigInteger.ONE,current=BigInteger.ONE;
  for(int i=2;i<=n;i++) {
    BigInteger next=previous.add(current); previous=current; current=next;
  }
  return current;
}

pages.title: Find the minimum coins for an amount.
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING FOUNDATIONS QUESTION 092 / 120
Q092. Find the minimum coins for an amount.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
For each amount, consider taking one allowed coin after an already solved smaller amount. Use
an unreachable sentinel and return -1 when no combination forms the target.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
[1,2,5], amount=11 ➜
KEY LOGIC
For each amount, consider taking
one allowed coin after an already
solved smaller amount.
➜
RESULT
Optimal substructure follows by
removing the last selected coin.
💡 Optimal substructure follows by removing the last selected coin.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
Time O(amount*coinCount); space O(amount).
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
Pseudo-polynomial in numeric amount; huge amounts
can exhaust memory.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
Why does greedy selection fail for coins [1,3,4] and amount 6?
Greedy takes 4+1+1, using three coins, but the optimal answer is 3+3, using two. General coin systems need
DP or a proof of greedy optimality; always test coin-system assumptions.
JAVA 17 · SOLUTION Source Q092 · 8 lines
static int minCoins(int[] coins,int amount) {
  if(amount<0 || amount==Integer.MAX_VALUE) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
  for(int c:coins) if(c<=0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
  int[] dp=new int[amount+1]; Arrays.fill(dp,amount+1); dp[0]=0;
  for(int a=1;a<=amount;a++) for(int c:coins)
    if(c<=a && dp[a-c]<=amount) dp[a]=Math.min(dp[a],dp[a-c]+1);
  return dp[amount]>amount ? -1 : dp[amount];
}

  }

}

contiguous subarray.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Kadane's recurrence either extends the best subarray ending at the previous position or starts at
the current value. Track the global best separately and use long sums.

How would you return start and end indices?
Track a candidate start for the current Kadane sum. When starting at a[i] beats extending, reset the
candidate start to i; whenever a better maximum appears, store candidateStart and i as answer indices.

  long ending=a[0],best=a[0];
  for(int i=1;i<a.length;i++) {
    ending=Math.max((long)a[i],ending+a[i]); best=Math.max(best,ending);
  }
  return best;
}

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING FOUNDATIONS QUESTION 095 / 120
Q095. Find length of the longest strictly increasing
subsequence.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Maintain the smallest possible tail for every attained length. Replace the first tail at least as large
as the current value; append when all tails are smaller.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
[10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] ➜
KEY LOGIC
Maintain the smallest possible tail
for every attained length.
➜
RESULT
A smaller tail preserves more
opportunities for future extension.
💡 A smaller tail preserves more opportunities for future extension.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
Time O(n log(n+1)); space O(n).
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
Equal values replace rather than extend because
increasing is strict.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
What extra predecessor metadata reconstructs a subsequence?
For each input index, store the predecessor index of the best subsequence ending there, and remember the
tail index for each length. Backtrack from the longest tail, then reverse the collected indices/values.

CHAPTER 20 · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING ON SEQUENCES AND GRIDS QUESTION 097 / 120
Q097. Compute edit distance.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Solve all prefix pairs with insertion, deletion and replacement transitions. Equal final characters
add no cost; other choices cost one.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
"kitten", "sitting" ➜
KEY LOGIC

deletion and replacement
transitions.
➜

Base row/column represent
inserting/deleting an entire prefix.
💡 Base row/column represent inserting/deleting an entire prefix.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
Time O(n*m); space O((n+1)*(m+1)).
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
Transposition is not one operation under this contract.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
How would weighted operations or Damerau distance change the recurrence?
Replace the unit insertion/deletion/substitution costs with the selected weights in the recurrence. Damerau-
Levenshtein also allows transposition of adjacent characters, requiring additional neighboring states and a
precise variant definition.
JAVA 17 · SOLUTION Source Q097 · 10 lines
static int editDistance(String a,String b) {
  int[][] dp=new int[a.length()+1][b.length()+1];
  for(int i=0;i<=a.length();i++) dp[i][0]=i;
  for(int j=0;j<=b.length();j++) dp[0][j]=j;
  for(int i=1;i<=a.length();i++) for(int j=1;j<=b.length();j++) {
    if(a.charAt(i-1)==b.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1];
    else dp[i][j]=1+Math.min(dp[i-1][j-1],Math.min(dp[i-1][j],dp[i][j-1]));
  }
  return dp[a.length()][b.length()];
}

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 · DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING ON SEQUENCES AND GRIDS QUESTION 099 / 120
Q099. Solve 0/1 knapsack with a one-dimensional
table.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
For each item, update capacities backward so each item contributes at most once. If iterating
forward, this recurrence could reuse the same item.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
weights [2,3,4], values [4,5,7],
capacity 5 ➜
KEY LOGIC
For each item, update capacities
backward so each item
contributes at most once.
➜
RESULT
Descending capacity uses the
previous item set for the
referenced sm
💡 Descending capacity uses the previous item set for the referenced smaller capacity.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
Time O(itemCount*capacity); space O(capacity).
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
Pseudo-polynomial; zero-weight items are included at
most once; impractically large capacity is outside the
resource scope.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
How would unbounded knapsack change iteration order?
For unbounded knapsack, iterate capacity upward for each item so the current item's new result can be
reused in the same pass. In 0/1 knapsack, iterate downward to prevent selecting the same item twice.
JAVA 17 · SOLUTION Source Q099 · 10 lines
static long knapsack(int[] weights,int[] values,int capacity) {
  if(capacity<0 || weights.length!=values.length) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
  long[] dp=new long[capacity+1];
  for(int i=0;i<weights.length;i++) {
    if(weights[i]<0 || values[i]<0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
    for(int c=capacity;c>=weights[i];c--)
      dp[c]=Math.max(dp[c],dp[c-weights[i]]+values[i]);
  }
  return dp[capacity];
}

static BigInteger gridPaths(int rows,int cols) {

  for(int r=1;r<rows;r++) for(int c=1;c<cols;c++) dp[c]=dp[c].add(dp[c-1]);

}

Q110. Sum int values with a safe parallel reduction.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Map each value to long and use the built-in sum reduction. It avoids a shared mutable
accumulator and has an associative identity/combination for sums in the stated finite int-array

racing on

otherwise valid.

CHAPTER 23 · PRACTICAL JAVA CORRECTNESS QUESTION 112 / 120
Q112. Add decimal amounts and round once at the
result boundary.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Parse decimal strings into BigDecimal, sum exactly, then round the aggregate to two places using
a specified policy. This contract deliberately rounds the total rather than every input item.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
["0.10","0.20"]
➜
KEY LOGIC
Parse decimal strings into
BigDecimal, sum exactly, then
round the aggregate to two places
using a specified policy.
➜
RESULT

💡 Decimal text avoids introducing binary floating-point approximation before aggregation.

storage grows with numeric representation.
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
Rounding per item can produce a different total;
currency/scale policy must be specified separately.

Why do equals and compareTo treat scale differently?
BigDecimal.equals checks value and scale, so 2.0 != 2.00 by equals; compareTo compares numeric value
and returns zero for these. Use compareTo for amount ordering and deliberate scale policy for keys or
serialization.

  for(String amount:amounts) total=total.add(new BigDecimal(amount));
  return total.setScale(2,RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
}

Q114. Design a stable composite map key.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
An immutable record generates value-based equality and hash code from its components. Use

Q115. Sort integer extremes without comparator
overflow.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Use Integer.compare through comparingInt instead of subtraction. Subtracting keys can overflow

CHAPTER 24 · CONCURRENT PROGRAMMING TASKS QUESTION 118 / 120
Q118. Run independent calculations and combine
completion results.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Supply an explicitly owned executor and combine results through thenCombine. Avoid shared
mutable side channels.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
20 and 22 ➜
KEY LOGIC
Supply an explicitly owned
executor and combine results
through thenCombine.
➜
RESULT
Combination depends on both
normal completions and uses
their return
💡 Combination depends on both normal completions and uses their returned values.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
O(1) synthetic work; scheduling/executor overhead
dominates; bounded task resources.
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
Timed get is not a universal cancellation guarantee; the
tasks here do not block externally.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
How would you recover one failed dependency while preserving semantics?
Attach exception handling to the dependency stage that is optional, replacing its result with a documented
fallback. Use thenCombine for independent results, and never silently turn a required payment/authorization
failure into success.
JAVA 17 · SOLUTION Source Q118 · 8 lines
static long combineAsync(int a,int b) throws Exception {
  ExecutorService pool=Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
  try {
    CompletableFuture<Integer> left=CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(()->a,pool);
    CompletableFuture<Integer> right=CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(()->b,pool);
    return left.thenCombine(right,(x,y)->(long)x+y).get(5,TimeUnit.SECONDS);
  } finally { stopPool(pool); }
}

pages.title: Verify executor tasks run in FIFO order with one worker.
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 · CONCURRENT PROGRAMMING TASKS QUESTION 119 / 120
Q119. Verify executor tasks run in FIFO order with
one worker.
✎  SIMPLE ANSWER
Use a single-worker executor and submit tasks that append to an owned list. Retrieve every
completion before copying the output.
SKETCH THE PATTERN
EXAMPLE / INPUT
Submit 0,1,2 ➜
KEY LOGIC
Use a single-worker executor and
submit tasks that append to an
owned list.
➜
RESULT
output [0,1,2]
💡 One worker consumes the factory's FIFO work queue; completion handoff precedes observer copying.
⏱ TIME & SPACE
Work O(count); space O(count) for queued tasks,
handles and output.
⚠ INTERVIEW PITFALL
The factory queue is unbounded; this finite
demonstration is not a production admission design.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION · ANSWERED
Would a multiworker executor preserve completion order?
No. Multiple workers can start and complete tasks in a different order because task durations and
scheduling vary. A single-worker FIFO queue normally orders task start; use ordered result collection when
output order is required.
JAVA 17 · SOLUTION Source Q119 · 11 lines
static List<Integer> singleWorkerOrder(int count) throws Exception {
  if(count<0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
  ExecutorService pool=Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
  List<Integer> output=new ArrayList<>();
  try {
    List<Future<?>> futures=new ArrayList<>();
    for(int i=0;i<count;i++) { int value=i; futures.add(pool.submit(()->output.add(value))); }
    for(Future<?> future:futures) future.get(5,TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    return List.copyOf(output);
  } finally { stopPool(pool); }
}

pages.title: What is Spring Boot?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 • SPRING BOOT FOUNDATIONS
What is Spring Boot?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Spring Boot builds on Spring to provide opinionated dependency management, auto-
configuration, executable packaging, and operational features.
DRAW THE IDEA — Question focus
BEFORE
Java application ➜
FOCUS
Boot setup ➜
AFTER
Running context
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@SpringBootApplication
public class App {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    SpringApplication.run(App.class, args);
  }
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The launcher creates a Spring application context and, for a web application, starts its configured server. Boot
reduces setup; your business behavior still belongs in application code.
04 / WATCH OUT
Do not describe Boot as a replacement for Spring.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which decisions remain your responsibility?
Answer: You still design domain rules, API contracts, security, transactions, data ownership, limits, testing
and operations. Boot configures infrastructure; it does not decide the right business behavior.
Source guide p. 12 • Beginner • References: B01, B02, B03

pages.title: How are Spring, Spring MVC and Spring Boot different?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 • SPRING BOOT FOUNDATIONS
How are Spring, Spring MVC and Spring Boot different?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Spring supplies dependency injection and infrastructure; MVC handles servlet web
requests; Boot assembles and configures applications using them.
DRAW THE IDEA — MVC different
BEFORE
Java application ➜
FOCUS
Boot setup ➜
AFTER
Running context
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
spring-context -> bean container
spring-webmvc  -> DispatcherServlet and controllers
Spring Boot   -> application assembly and defaults
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A Boot MVC service uses all three roles. Boot can also run a command-line job with no MVC server. These names
identify different layers, not competing frameworks.
04 / WATCH OUT
Boot does not require REST or microservices.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can Boot run without an embedded web server?
Answer: Yes. Set spring.main.web-application-type=none or configure SpringApplication with
WebApplicationType.NONE. The context can run batch jobs or command-line tasks without starting a web
server.
Source guide p. 13 • Beginner • References: B01, B02, B03

pages.title: What does @SpringBootApplication combine?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 • SPRING BOOT FOUNDATIONS
What does @SpringBootApplication combine?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It combines @SpringBootConfiguration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and
@ComponentScan.
DRAW THE IDEA — @SpringBootApplication combine
BEFORE
Java application ➜
FOCUS
Boot setup ➜
AFTER
Running context
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@SpringBootApplication
class App { /* main method omitted */ }
// Configuration + auto-configuration + component scanning
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The application class can declare bean methods, Boot can contribute conditional infrastructure, and scanning
discovers components below the application package. These mechanisms can also be configured separately.
04 / WATCH OUT
Scanning does not search every package in every dependency.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why put the application class in a root package?
Answer: Component scanning normally starts at the application class package and its children. A root
package places controllers and services inside that default scan area.
Source guide p. 13 • Beginner • References: B01, B02, B03

pages.title: What is a starter?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 • SPRING BOOT FOUNDATIONS
What is a starter?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A starter is a convenient dependency descriptor for a capability; it is not itself the
entire runtime implementation.
DRAW THE IDEA — starter
BEFORE
Java application ➜
FOCUS
Boot setup ➜
AFTER
Running context
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
For the Boot 3.x baseline, the web starter brings MVC, an embedded servlet server and supporting libraries through
transitive dependencies. Boot's managed dependency versions keep the selected ecosystem aligned.
04 / WATCH OUT
A dependency starter and an auto-configuration module are distinct roles.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do you replace the default embedded server?
Answer: Exclude the default Tomcat starter and add the matching Jetty or Undertow starter for your
compatible Boot version. Check the dependency tree and run an HTTP smoke test.
Source guide p. 14 • Beginner • References: B01, B02, B03

pages.title: Why use Boot dependency management instead of assigning every version?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 • SPRING BOOT FOUNDATIONS
Why use Boot dependency management instead of
assigning every version?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Its tested version set reduces incompatible combinations; override a dependency only
with compatibility evidence.
DRAW THE IDEA — dependency management instead assigning
BEFORE
Java application ➜
FOCUS
Boot setup ➜
AFTER
Running context
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>${chosen-boot-3.5-patch}</version>
</parent>
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
This version is a selection placeholder, not a ready-to-run POM. The parent supplies dependency and plugin
conventions. A BOM import supplies dependency management when another parent must be retained.
04 / WATCH OUT
A BOM does not automatically apply every build-plugin convention.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you investigate a dependency conflict?
Answer: Inspect mvn dependency:tree or Gradle dependencyInsight, find the selected transitive version,
compare Boot BOM versions, then test a compatible exclusion or override.
Source guide p. 14 • Beginner • References: B01, B02, B03

pages.title: Does Boot generate application source code at runtime?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 • SPRING BOOT FOUNDATIONS
Does Boot generate application source code at runtime?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Boot configures objects through Spring infrastructure; ordinary auto-configuration does
not generate your business classes.
DRAW THE IDEA — generate source code runtime
BEFORE
Java application ➜
FOCUS
Boot setup ➜
AFTER
Running context
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Dependency present + condition matches
  -> configuration contributes bean definitions
Context refresh -> beans created and wired
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Adding a JDBC dependency can lead to a DataSource when the required configuration and conditions are satisfied.
It does not generate your repository's business logic.
04 / WATCH OUT
AOT build-time generation is a separate feature.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How can you see why an auto-configuration matched?
Answer: Start with --debug or inspect the Actuator conditions endpoint in a secured environment. The
condition evaluation report explains matched, unmatched and excluded configurations.

pages.title: What does SpringApplication.run do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 • APPLICATION STARTUP AND CONTEXT
What does SpringApplication.run do?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It prepares the environment, creates and refreshes an appropriate application context,
and completes startup callbacks.
DRAW THE IDEA — SpringApplication.run
BEFORE
Environment ➜
FOCUS
Context refresh ➜
AFTER
Ready service
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
ConfigurableApplicationContext context =
    SpringApplication.run(App.class, args);
OrderService service = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The returned context owns managed beans and their lifecycle. A web context also manages server integration. If a
required bean cannot be created, run fails instead of returning a healthy application.
04 / WATCH OUT
Startup involves more than invoking main.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Where would a missing required property fail?
Answer: Missing required configuration usually fails during property binding, validation or bean creation
as the context refreshes. The root cause tells which property was absent.
Source guide p. 16 • Beginner • References: B01, B03

pages.title: What is ApplicationContext?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 • APPLICATION STARTUP AND CONTEXT
What is ApplicationContext?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It is Spring's bean container with additional services such as events, resources,
messages, and environment access.
DRAW THE IDEA — ApplicationContext
BEFORE
Environment ➜
FOCUS
Context refresh ➜
AFTER
Ready service
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Service
class PricingService { BigDecimal price() { return BigDecimal.TEN; } }
// context.getBean(PricingService.class) returns the managed bean.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The container constructs and wires managed objects according to definitions. Calling new PricingService manually
creates an ordinary object outside those lifecycle and proxy rules.
04 / WATCH OUT
A Java object is not managed merely because its class has an annotation.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How can a library object become a bean?
Answer: Declare it with a @Bean factory method in a @Configuration class, or register a BeanDefinition.
Spring then owns its creation and lifecycle.
Source guide p. 17 • Beginner • References: B01, B03

pages.title: How does BeanFactory differ from ApplicationContext?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 • APPLICATION STARTUP AND CONTEXT
How does BeanFactory differ from ApplicationContext?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
BeanFactory supplies core bean creation and lookup; ApplicationContext adds
application-level facilities and commonly creates non-lazy singletons during refresh.
DRAW THE IDEA — BeanFactory ApplicationContext
BEFORE
Environment ➜
FOCUS
Context refresh ➜
AFTER
Ready service
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
BeanFactory -> create and resolve beans
ApplicationContext -> BeanFactory capabilities + events,
                      environment, resources, integration
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Boot normally works with an ApplicationContext. Lazy behavior depends on the actual context and bean definitions;
avoid treating every factory implementation as having one identical startup policy.
04 / WATCH OUT
The terms are related, not interchangeable in every API.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why do eager singletons help detect errors early?
Answer: Creating required non-lazy singletons at startup exposes missing dependencies and invalid
configuration before production requests arrive, rather than at the first use.

pages.title: CHAPTER 02 • APPLICATION STARTUP AND CONTEXT
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 • APPLICATION STARTUP AND CONTEXT
How do ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner
differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Both run after context refresh; ApplicationRunner exposes parsed ApplicationArguments,
while CommandLineRunner receives raw strings.
DRAW THE IDEA — ApplicationRunner CommandLineRunner
BEFORE
Environment ➜
FOCUS
Context refresh ➜
AFTER
Ready service
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Bean
ApplicationRunner warmup() {
  return args -> System.out.println(args.containsOption("warmup"));
}
// java -jar app.jar --warmup=true -> prints true
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Use runner callbacks for controlled startup work. An exception can fail startup, and slow work postpones completion.
@Order can order runners but does not create a general dependency graph.
04 / WATCH OUT
Do not hide endless background loops in a runner.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When should warmup finish before readiness?
Answer: If a warmup result is required before safe traffic, make it a bounded startup action and do not
report readiness until it completes. Optional warmup should not block indefinitely.
Source guide p. 18 • Beginner • References: B01, B03

pages.title: What is the difference between started and ready events?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 • APPLICATION STARTUP AND CONTEXT
What is the difference between started and ready events?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
ApplicationStartedEvent occurs after refresh before runners; ApplicationReadyEvent
follows successful runner completion.
DRAW THE IDEA — difference started ready events
BEFORE
Environment ➜
FOCUS
Context refresh ➜
AFTER
Ready service
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Refresh complete -> ApplicationStartedEvent
Run application and command-line runners
Successful completion -> ApplicationReadyEvent
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A server may already be bound before all warmup completes. Use readiness state to control traffic admission rather
than assuming a listening port means business readiness.
04 / WATCH OUT
An event callback is not a distributed deployment coordinator.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What if a runner throws?
Answer: The application startup fails and ApplicationReadyEvent is not published. Record the cause and
leave traffic readiness disabled instead of accepting requests with incomplete initialization.
Source guide p. 18 • Beginner • References: B01, B03

pages.title: How do you diagnose startup failure?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 • APPLICATION STARTUP AND CONTEXT
How do you diagnose startup failure?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Find the first meaningful cause, then check definitions, conditions, configuration,
versions, and external resource availability.
DRAW THE IDEA — diagnose startup failure
BEFORE
Environment ➜
FOCUS
Context refresh ➜
AFTER
Ready service
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
java -jar app.jar --debug
# Inspect the condition evaluation report and failure analysis.
# Check the deepest relevant cause rather than the final wrapper.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
An UnsatisfiedDependencyException can wrap a connection or binding failure. The outer exception describes where
construction failed; the cause explains why. Keep debug logs controlled because configuration diagnostics can
contain sensitive context.
04 / WATCH OUT
Repeatedly adding @ComponentScan can mask the real issue.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do you distinguish missing bean from failed bean creation?
Answer: A missing bean often causes NoSuchBeanDefinitionException; a found bean that fails initialization
yields BeanCreationException with a nested cause. Trace the first useful root cause.

pages.title: Why prefer constructor injection?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 • DEPENDENCY INJECTION AND BEAN SELECTION
Why prefer constructor injection?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It makes required dependencies explicit, supports final fields, and permits plain unit
testing without a Spring context.
DRAW THE IDEA — prefer constructor injection
BEFORE
Dependency ➜
FOCUS
Container selection ➜
AFTER
Injected bean
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Service
class Checkout {
  private final PaymentGateway gateway;
  Checkout(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; }
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Spring resolves the constructor dependency. A test can pass a fake gateway directly. With one constructor,
@Autowired is usually unnecessary. The object cannot be constructed successfully without its required collaborator.
04 / WATCH OUT
Constructor injection does not make dependency methods thread safe.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When is setter injection appropriate?
Answer: Setter injection fits genuinely optional or reconfigurable collaborators; document the absent-state
behavior. Use constructors for required dependencies.

pages.title: What is the difference between @Component, @Service and @Repository?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 • DEPENDENCY INJECTION AND BEAN SELECTION
What is the difference between @Component, @Service
and @Repository?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
All can register scanned components; @Service communicates business intent, while
@Repository also supports configured exception translation.
DRAW THE IDEA — difference @Component @Service @Reposit
BEFORE
Dependency ➜
FOCUS
Container selection ➜
AFTER
Injected bean
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Repository
class JdbcCustomerStore { /* data access */ }
@Service
class CustomerService { /* business policy */ }
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Stereotypes communicate architecture. Repository exception translation depends on the relevant post-processor and
persistence integration; it is not a blanket translation of every arbitrary exception.
04 / WATCH OUT
@Service does not automatically start a transaction.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What annotation defines a transaction boundary?
Answer: @Transactional marks the intended transaction boundary, subject to the configured transaction
manager and proxy/weaving invocation path. @Service by itself does not start one.

pages.title: How does @Bean differ from @Component?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 • DEPENDENCY INJECTION AND BEAN SELECTION
How does @Bean differ from @Component?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
@Component discovers a class through scanning; @Bean defines a managed object
through a configuration method.
DRAW THE IDEA — @Bean @Component
BEFORE
Dependency ➜
FOCUS
Container selection ➜
AFTER
Injected bean
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Configuration
class ClockConfig {
  @Bean Clock clock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); }
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Clock is a library type you need not annotate. Its factory result becomes a managed bean. @Bean is also useful
when construction needs arguments or policy that cannot be expressed by component scanning alone.
04 / WATCH OUT
Calling a factory outside Spring can create an unmanaged object.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do bean names get chosen?
Answer: Default scanned bean names usually derive from the class name; @Bean uses the method name.
You can assign explicit names and qualifiers to remove ambiguity.

pages.title: How do @Primary and @Qualifier resolve multiple beans?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 • DEPENDENCY INJECTION AND BEAN SELECTION
How do @Primary and @Qualifier resolve multiple beans?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
@Primary supplies a preferred candidate; @Qualifier narrows a dependency to matching
qualified candidates.
DRAW THE IDEA — @Primary @Qualifier resolve multiple
BEFORE
Dependency ➜
FOCUS
Container selection ➜
AFTER
Injected bean
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Checkout(@Qualifier("upiGateway") PaymentGateway gateway) {
  this.gateway = gateway;
}
// Both cardGateway and upiGateway may implement PaymentGateway.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The constructor chooses the UPI-qualified bean rather than guessing by implementation type. Primary is useful for
a default choice; qualifiers express dependency-specific selection.
04 / WATCH OUT
Qualifiers can be custom annotations, not only bean-name strings.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What if no candidate matches?
Answer: A required injection usually fails with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException, often wrapped by
UnsatisfiedDependencyException. Either register a matching bean or fix the qualifier.

pages.title: How should optional dependencies be represented?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 • DEPENDENCY INJECTION AND BEAN SELECTION
How should optional dependencies be represented?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use an explicit optional provider or Optional only when absence is a supported behavior.
DRAW THE IDEA — optional dependencies represented
BEFORE
Dependency ➜
FOCUS
Container selection ➜
AFTER
Injected bean
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
class Reporter {
  Reporter(ObjectProvider<AuditSink> sinks) {
    AuditSink sink = sinks.getIfAvailable();
    // Define a deliberate no-sink policy.
  }
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The provider defers lookup and can support optional or scoped access. Required security or payment collaborators
should generally fail startup when absent. Multiple candidates may still need resolution.
04 / WATCH OUT
Optional wiring must not silently weaken a required invariant.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When would getIfUnique be useful?
Answer: getIfUnique returns the only matching bean, if one exists; it is useful when a default is optional
and multiple candidates must not be chosen arbitrarily.

pages.title: How do you handle circular dependencies?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 • DEPENDENCY INJECTION AND BEAN SELECTION
How do you handle circular dependencies?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Treat a cycle as a design signal and separate responsibilities; do not assume every
circular graph can or should be auto-resolved.
DRAW THE IDEA — handle circular dependencies
BEFORE
Dependency ➜
FOCUS
Container selection ➜
AFTER
Injected bean
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Before: OrderService -> PaymentService -> OrderService
After:  CheckoutCoordinator -> OrderService
                           -> PaymentService
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Constructor cycles prevent constructing either dependency first. A coordinator or event boundary can remove the
cycle. Lazy wiring can postpone resolution but leaves the architectural dependency intact.
04 / WATCH OUT
Enabling circular references is not a universal repair.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can event callbacks introduce another cycle?
Answer: Yes. Event listeners that call back into the publishing service can make a logical cycle even if
constructor injection is acyclic. Map the full call and event path.

pages.title: What does singleton scope mean in Spring?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 • SCOPES, LIFECYCLE AND PROXIES
What does singleton scope mean in Spring?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A singleton is one bean instance per definition per container, not necessarily one object
per JVM.
DRAW THE IDEA — singleton scope mean
BEFORE
Bean definition ➜
FOCUS
Lifecycle / proxy ➜
AFTER
Managed object
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Service
class Counter {
  private int count;
  void increment() { count++; }
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Concurrent requests can reach this same Counter. Its scope supplies sharing, not atomicity. Use request-local
variables, immutable state, or suitable synchronization. Several application contexts can have separate singleton
instances.
04 / WATCH OUT
Singleton scope does not imply thread safety.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why is mutable request state unsafe in a singleton field?
Answer: Two requests may overwrite one another's user or order data because the same singleton
instance receives both calls. Keep request values local or properly request-scoped.

pages.title: When do prototype and request scopes help?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 • SCOPES, LIFECYCLE AND PROXIES
When do prototype and request scopes help?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Prototype creates a fresh instance per container lookup; request scope supplies state
associated with one web request.
DRAW THE IDEA — prototype request scopes help
BEFORE
Bean definition ➜
FOCUS
Lifecycle / proxy ➜
AFTER
Managed object
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Component
@RequestScope
class RequestData { String correlationId; }
// Injection into a singleton can use a scoped proxy.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A request-scoped proxy routes each request to its current target. Injecting a prototype once into a singleton instead
fixes that one prototype instance at injection time unless lookup is deferred.
04 / WATCH OUT
Spring does not manage complete destruction of ordinary prototypes.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would ObjectProvider supply a new prototype?
Answer: Inject ObjectProvider<MyPrototype>, then call getObject() each time a new instance is needed. A
one-time prototype constructor injection into a singleton does not create per-call instances.

pages.title: What do @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 • SCOPES, LIFECYCLE AND PROXIES
What do @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy do?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
They supply managed initialization and destruction callbacks; Boot 3 uses the
jakarta.annotation namespace.
DRAW THE IDEA — @PostConstruct @PreDestroy
BEFORE
Bean definition ➜
FOCUS
Lifecycle / proxy ➜
AFTER
Managed object
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@PostConstruct
void init() { validateConfiguration(); }
@PreDestroy
void close() { releaseOwnedResources(); }
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Initialization runs after dependency injection. Destruction runs when the context destroys a managed bean under
normal lifecycle handling. Abrupt process termination can prevent cleanup. Keep heavyweight remote startup work
deliberate.
04 / WATCH OUT
Prototype destruction and forced termination need separate handling.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why can transaction advice be unreliable in @PostConstruct?
Answer: Lifecycle callbacks may execute before the final externally used proxy is active. Move
transactional startup work to a separate proxied service invoked at a supported later lifecycle stage.

How does BeanPostProcessor differ from a factory post-
processor?

pages.title: What is the difference between full and lite @Bean configuration?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 • SCOPES, LIFECYCLE AND PROXIES
What is the difference between full and lite @Bean
configuration?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Full proxy-enabled configuration intercepts inter-bean calls; lite or
proxyBeanMethods=false calls use ordinary Java semantics.
DRAW THE IDEA — difference full lite @Bean
BEFORE
Bean definition ➜
FOCUS
Lifecycle / proxy ➜
AFTER
Managed object
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class Config {
  @Bean Clock clock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); }
  @Bean Report report(Clock clock) { return new Report(clock); }
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Method-parameter injection obtains the managed Clock without relying on intercepted calls. In this mode, directly
calling clock() is an ordinary factory invocation and can create another instance.
04 / WATCH OUT
Do not assume every @Bean method call is a container lookup.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When can disabling configuration proxies help?
Answer: Use proxyBeanMethods=false when @Bean methods do not call one another for managed
instances. It avoids unnecessary CGLIB interception; inject dependencies as method parameters instead.

pages.title: Why does self-invocation bypass common Spring advice?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 • SCOPES, LIFECYCLE AND PROXIES
Why does self-invocation bypass common Spring advice?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
In proxy-based AOP, a call through this does not pass through the proxy that applies
transaction, cache, or async advice.
DRAW THE IDEA — self-invocation bypass common advice
BEFORE
Bean definition ➜
FOCUS
Lifecycle / proxy ➜
AFTER
Managed object
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Service
class Importer {
  void run() { save(); } // Direct self-call
  @Transactional
  public void save() { /* write */ }
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Calling run through the proxy does not make its internal save call pass through that proxy again. Move the advised
boundary to a collaborator or redesign the entry point. AspectJ weaving is a different execution model.
04 / WATCH OUT
Adding another annotation does not change this call path.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which caller-to-proxy path would activate the transaction?
Answer: A caller must invoke the advised method on the Spring-managed proxy, for example another
service injected with the transactional bean. A this.save() self-call bypasses that proxy.

Adding another annotation does not change this call path.
05 / INTERVIEWER

service injected with the transactional bean. A this.save() self-call bypasses that proxy.

pages.title: Which property wins when the same setting appears in several sources?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 • EXTERNAL CONFIGURATION AND PROFILES
Which property wins when the same setting appears in
several sources?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Boot has a documented source order; for normal runs, command-line arguments
override environment variables and application files.
DRAW THE IDEA — property wins same setting
BEFORE
Config sources ➜
FOCUS
Binding + validation ➜
AFTER
Effective settings
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
# application.properties:
server.port=8080
# Environment: SERVER_PORT=8081
java -jar app.jar --server.port=8082
# Effective port: 8082 under ordinary command-line handling
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Later, higher-precedence sources replace earlier values. Tests and programmatic customization add more sources,
so do not memorize this simplified subset as the entire order. Diagnose the effective value and origin.
04 / WATCH OUT
Editing a file may have no effect when an environment override exists.

Does spring.config.location add to or replace default locations?
Answer: spring.config.location replaces the default search locations. spring.config.additional-location adds
new locations while retaining defaults. Confirm import/order rules for the selected Boot version.

pages.title: What are profiles and how are they activated?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 • EXTERNAL CONFIGURATION AND PROFILES
What are profiles and how are they activated?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Profiles select configuration or bean definitions for an environment or capability, using
an explicitly active profile set.
DRAW THE IDEA — profiles they activated
BEFORE
Config sources ➜
FOCUS
Binding + validation ➜
AFTER
Effective settings
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Profile("dev")
@Bean
MailSender fakeMail() { return new FakeMailSender(); }
# Launch: java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The dev bean participates only when its condition matches. Profiles should express controlled variants, not conceal
essential production dependencies. Profile-specific files can supply settings for the same codebase.

A profile name is not a security boundary.

Can several profiles be active together?

Conflicts still follow property-source precedence.

pages.title: How do you validate configuration at startup?

How do you validate configuration at startup?

Primitive default values can hide omitted settings without constraints.

pages.title: How should secrets be configured?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 • EXTERNAL CONFIGURATION AND PROFILES
How should secrets be configured?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Inject secrets from an appropriate secret store or protected runtime source and avoid
committing, logging, or exposing them.
DRAW THE IDEA — secrets configured
BEFORE
Config sources ➜
FOCUS
Binding + validation ➜
AFTER
Effective settings
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
# DB_PASSWORD is supplied at runtime.
# Restrict process, platform, and management access to this value.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A placeholder externalizes the secret; it does not encrypt the environment. Use a managed secret mechanism and
rotation policy appropriate to deployment. Sanitize diagnostic outputs and avoid including secrets in exception
messages.
04 / WATCH OUT
Environment variables alone are not an automatic secrecy guarantee.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will rotated credentials reach pooled connections?
Answer: Rotate secrets through the approved provider and explicitly refresh or recreate clients/
connections as needed. Existing pooled connections may keep the old credentials until closed.

pages.title: How do configuration imports and locations differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 • EXTERNAL CONFIGURATION AND PROFILES
How do configuration imports and locations differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Imports load additional config data; spring.config.location replaces default search
locations, while additional-location adds to them.
DRAW THE IDEA — configuration imports locations
BEFORE
Config sources ➜
FOCUS
Binding + validation ➜
AFTER
Effective settings
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
spring.config.import=optional:file:./local-overrides.properties
# optional tolerates this file being absent.
# For required production config, absence should usually fail.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The optional prefix deliberately changes missing-resource behavior. Configuration order and profile rules determine
the effective result. Use a clear required-versus-optional policy instead of silently accepting incomplete production
settings.
04 / WATCH OUT
A config import is not automatic live refresh.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would make a missing secret mount fatal?
Answer: Use an appropriate non-optional config import/location or validate the secret as required at
startup. Missing required configuration should fail fast and keep readiness false.

pages.title: How does auto-configuration choose beans?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 • AUTO-CONFIGURATION AND CUSTOM STARTERS
How does auto-configuration choose beans?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It evaluates conditions based on available classes, properties, existing bean definitions,
and application type.
DRAW THE IDEA — auto-configuration choose beans
BEFORE
Classpath + conditions ➜
FOCUS
Auto configuration ➜
AFTER
Default / override
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(PaymentClient.class)
class PaymentAutoConfiguration {
  @Bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean
  PaymentClient paymentClient() { return new PaymentClient(); }
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The library class must be present. If the user already supplies a matching PaymentClient bean, this default backs off.
This sketch assumes the client has an appropriate constructor.
04 / WATCH OUT
Conditions do not infer business intent beyond their tests.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why should an infrastructure default back off?
Answer: A starter default must back off under @ConditionalOnMissingBean so an application can supply
its own implementation without duplicate candidates or an accidental override.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 • AUTO-CONFIGURATION AND CUSTOM STARTERS
What does @ConditionalOnProperty actually check?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It tests selected property values using its prefix, name, havingValue, and matchIfMissing
policy.

BEFORE

FOCUS

@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix="audit", name="enabled", havingValue="true")
AuditSink auditSink() { return new AuditSink(); }
# audit.enabled=true -> candidate enabled; absent -> disabled

The explicit comparison and default make activation clear. Conditions choose definitions during startup; changing a
file later does not automatically create or remove a running bean.
04 / WATCH OUT
Collection-indexed properties need careful handling.

When would matchIfMissing=true be appropriate?
Answer: Use it only when absence should mean enabled by design; for sensitive or expensive features
prefer explicit opt-in instead of matchIfMissing=true.

CHAPTER 06 • AUTO-CONFIGURATION AND CUSTOM STARTERS
How can you exclude an unwanted auto-configuration?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use a targeted exclusion when the capability is intentionally absent, or provide a
supported custom bean when replacing a default.

BEFORE

FOCUS
Auto configuration ➜
AFTER
Default / override
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
class App { /* launch code omitted */ }

Exclusion can hide a broken requirement.

configuration exclusion mechanism accepting class names; avoid requiring an absent class literal.

pages.title: How should a company starter be designed?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 • AUTO-CONFIGURATION AND CUSTOM STARTERS
How should a company starter be designed?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Separate useful dependencies from conditional setup, expose typed properties, and
permit consumer overrides.

FOCUS

AFTER
Default / override

payment-spring-boot-autoconfigure -> conditional beans
payment-client -> core transport behavior

Keep business logic independent of Boot where useful. Test activation, absence, user overrides, and invalid settings.
Pick a company namespace rather than pretending to be an official Spring starter.

Broad component scanning can register unwanted consumer beans.

through properties or beans, while keeping secure defaults and validation.

pages.title: What does DispatcherServlet do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 • SPRING MVC REQUEST PROCESSING
What does DispatcherServlet do?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It coordinates MVC handler mapping, handler invocation, exception resolution, and
response rendering or conversion.
DRAW THE IDEA — DispatcherServlet
BEFORE
HTTP request ➜
FOCUS
DispatcherServlet ➜
AFTER
HTTP response
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
GET /orders/7
 -> servlet filters
 -> DispatcherServlet
 -> matching controller method

How do @Controller and @RestController differ?

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 • SPRING MVC REQUEST PROCESSING
How do filters, interceptors and AOP differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Filters wrap servlet traffic; MVC interceptors surround handler execution; AOP advises
eligible bean method calls.
DRAW THE IDEA — filters interceptors AOP
BEFORE
HTTP request ➜
FOCUS
DispatcherServlet ➜
AFTER
HTTP response
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Filter -> request/response and security boundary
Interceptor -> handler metadata and MVC lifecycle
AOP -> service method calls through an advice boundary
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Choose the level that owns the concern. A servlet filter can affect unmapped requests; a handler interceptor can
inspect a matched controller. Service authorization or transaction logic often belongs beyond HTTP routing.

MVC async dispatch changes callback behavior.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Where should a correlation id be created and cleaned up?

logging context and remove it in finally to avoid reuse leaks.

pages.title: How does content negotiation work?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 • SPRING MVC REQUEST PROCESSING
How does content negotiation work?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
MVC selects response representation using request preferences and supported
converters or declared media types.
DRAW THE IDEA — content negotiation work
BEFORE
HTTP request ➜
FOCUS
DispatcherServlet ➜
AFTER
HTTP response
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@GetMapping(value="/status", produces="application/json")
Map<String, String> status() { return Map.of("state", "ready"); }
# Accept: application/json -> JSON representation
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The produces condition constrains matching; message converters serialize the result. Unsupported media
preferences can produce 406, and an unsupported request body media type can produce 415.
04 / WATCH OUT
Accept and Content-Type have different meanings.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if no converter can write the returned type?
Answer: Spring may return an error such as 406 Not Acceptable when no supported representation
matches the client's Accept header; an unwritable declared return can yield converter-related failures.

CHAPTER 07 • SPRING MVC REQUEST PROCESSING
Should you add @EnableWebMvc in a Boot MVC
application?

control of MVC configuration and affects Boot defaults.

02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Configuration
class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
  @Override public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
    registry.addInterceptor(new TimingInterceptor());

}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
This extends MVC behavior without intentionally replacing its Boot configuration path. Use @EnableWebMvc only
when you want that level of ownership and have checked the resulting differences.

A common tutorial annotation can change important defaults.

defaults remain. @EnableWebMvc changes the auto-configuration baseline significantly.

pages.title: When should an API return 200, 201, or 204?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 • REST CONTRACTS AND API DESIGN
When should an API return 200, 201, or 204?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use 200 for a successful representation, 201 for newly created resources, and 204 for
success without a body.
DRAW THE IDEA — API return 200 201
BEFORE
API operation ➜
FOCUS
Contract + status ➜
AFTER
Client outcome
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@PostMapping("/orders")
ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(@RequestBody CreateOrder request) {
  OrderDto dto = service.create(request);
  return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/orders/" + dto.id())).body(dto);
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The response sends 201 plus Location and the created representation. A 204 response must not include a response
body. Choose codes from the operation's actual contract rather than returning 200 for every outcome.
04 / WATCH OUT
HTTP success does not explain every domain state.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What status represents an asynchronous accepted operation?
Answer: 202 Accepted means processing has started or been queued but is not finished. Supply an
operation ID or status URL; never imply downstream success.

pages.title: How do PUT and PATCH differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 • REST CONTRACTS AND API DESIGN
How do PUT and PATCH differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
PUT requests replacement semantics for the target representation; PATCH requests a
defined partial modification format.
DRAW THE IDEA — PUT PATCH
BEFORE
API operation ➜
FOCUS
Contract + status ➜
AFTER
Client outcome
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
PUT /customers/7  -> replacement representation
PATCH /customers/7 -> selected modifications
// Define omitted fields, explicit nulls, and version conflicts.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A partial DTO blindly copied over an entity can erase fields unintentionally. PATCH needs documented semantics,
such as merge-patch or a domain-specific operation. Neither verb alone implements concurrency control.
04 / WATCH OUT
PATCH is not automatically idempotent.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you prevent lost updates?
Answer: Use an ETag/If-Match condition or a version field checked atomically. A stale version should fail
clearly, typically with 412 or a documented conflict.

pages.title: What makes an HTTP operation idempotent?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 • REST CONTRACTS AND API DESIGN
What makes an HTTP operation idempotent?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Repeating the same intended operation has the same intended effect as one execution,
even if response details differ.
DRAW THE IDEA — makes HTTP operation idempotent
BEFORE
API operation ➜
FOCUS
Contract + status ➜
AFTER
Client outcome
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
DELETE /orders/7 -> first request removes it
DELETE /orders/7 -> later request does not remove another resource
// The second status may differ without changing idempotent intent.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Idempotence concerns the intended server effect, not identical responses or zero audit activity. For POST payments,
implement operation identity and deduplication when safe retries are required.
04 / WATCH OUT
Retrying a timed-out POST can duplicate business effects.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How should an idempotency-key record be persisted?
Answer: Persist a scoped unique key, request fingerprint, processing state and final result in a durable
transaction. Replay must return the same result or a clear in-progress state.

pages.title: Why return DTOs instead of exposing JPA entities?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 • REST CONTRACTS AND API DESIGN
Why return DTOs instead of exposing JPA entities?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
DTOs keep the API contract separate from persistence, control fields, and avoid
accidental lazy loading and internal data exposure.
DRAW THE IDEA — return DTOs instead exposing
BEFORE
API operation ➜
FOCUS
Contract + status ➜
AFTER
Client outcome
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
record CustomerDto(long id, String displayName) {}
CustomerDto toDto(Customer c) {
  return new CustomerDto(c.getId(), c.getDisplayName());
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Only approved fields are serialized. Persistence associations and passwords do not become API output merely
because they exist in an entity. Mapping work can also be performed through query projections.
04 / WATCH OUT
A DTO alone does not enforce row-level authorization.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When is a projection better than loading a full entity?
Answer: A projection reads only required columns and avoids loading the full entity graph. Use it for read-
only API views; use entities when domain changes need managed state.

pages.title: How should pagination and sorting be designed?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 • REST CONTRACTS AND API DESIGN
How should pagination and sorting be designed?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Bound page size, whitelist sort fields, and provide a deterministic order with a tie
breaker.
DRAW THE IDEA — pagination sorting designed
BEFORE
API operation ➜
FOCUS
Contract + status ➜
AFTER
Client outcome
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Pageable p = PageRequest.of(0, 20,
    Sort.by("createdAt").descending().and(Sort.by("id")));
Page<Order> result = repository.findAll(p);
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The id tie breaker stabilizes rows sharing a timestamp. Offset pagination can become expensive or shift under
concurrent writes; cursor-based designs may suit large changing datasets.
04 / WATCH OUT
Raw client sort expressions must not become arbitrary query text.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What are the tradeoffs of Page versus Slice?
Answer: Page usually executes/needs total-count information; Slice determines only whether another
segment exists, often avoiding an expensive count query. Define consistent ordering.

pages.title: How should API versioning be chosen?

CHAPTER 08 • REST CONTRACTS AND API DESIGN
How should API versioning be chosen?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Version when compatibility changes, choosing a consistent path, header, or media-type
policy backed by deprecation rules.
DRAW THE IDEA — API versioning chosen
BEFORE
API operation ➜
FOCUS
Contract + status ➜
AFTER
Client outcome
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
GET /api/v1/customers/7 -> legacy contract
GET /api/v2/customers/7 -> revised incompatible contract
// Keep both supported during a planned migration window.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A new optional field may not require a new version, but changed field meaning can. Document client compatibility,
sunset dates, and observable usage. Version numbers do not replace a migration strategy.
04 / WATCH OUT
Creating a new version for every code change creates needless complexity.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you know when v1 can be retired?
Answer: Use traffic telemetry, consumer inventory, contract tests and a communicated deprecation window
to verify no supported client needs v1. Do not retire it just because v2 exists.

pages.title: What is the purpose of @Valid on a request body?

CHAPTER 09 • VALIDATION AND EXCEPTION RESPONSES
What is the purpose of @Valid on a request body?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It asks the configured Bean Validation integration to validate the bound object before
ordinary controller execution.
DRAW THE IDEA — purpose @Valid request body
BEFORE
Incoming DTO ➜
FOCUS
Validate + handle ➜
AFTER
Safe error / result

@PostMapping("/users")

  return service.create(request);
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
With the validation starter, blank names fail before the method body runs. JSON syntax and type conversion failures
are separate from constraint failures. @Email does not establish mailbox ownership.
04 / WATCH OUT
@Valid is not a business uniqueness check.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do you validate nested DTOs?
Answer: Annotate the nested property with @Valid and give nested fields constraints. The outer DTO's
@Valid triggers traversal into nested validated objects.

pages.title: How does @RestControllerAdvice help?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 • VALIDATION AND EXCEPTION RESPONSES
How does @RestControllerAdvice help?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It centralizes REST exception handlers and shared controller concerns without
duplicating catch logic in every endpoint.
DRAW THE IDEA — @RestControllerAdvice help
BEFORE
Incoming DTO ➜
FOCUS
Validate + handle ➜
AFTER
Safe error / result
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@RestControllerAdvice
class Errors {
  @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFound.class)
  ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> missing(OrderNotFound ex) {
    return ResponseEntity.of(ProblemDetail.forStatus(404)).build();
  }
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
This maps a specific domain absence to 404. Add a stable error code and safe details appropriate to the API.
Infrastructure failures should follow a separate contract.
04 / WATCH OUT
Servlet-filter security failures are not automatically handled here.

Where should authentication failures be translated?
Answer: Authentication failures should usually be handled in Spring Security's AuthenticationEntryPoint/
filter-chain mechanisms, rather than relying only on @RestControllerAdvice.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 • VALIDATION AND EXCEPTION RESPONSES
Where should uniqueness and cross-resource rules be
enforced?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Enforce business rules in the service and authoritative data constraints in the database,
not only in request validation.
DRAW THE IDEA — uniqueness cross-resource rules enforce
BEFORE
Incoming DTO ➜
FOCUS
Validate + handle ➜
AFTER
Safe error / result
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Check email availability -> insert user
Two concurrent requests can both pass the check.
Unique database constraint -> final authority
Constraint conflict -> controlled application response
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
An early check improves usability but cannot eliminate the race. Handle the specific constraint failure and define
normalization before uniqueness. Domain conflicts need a clear status and safe error code.
04 / WATCH OUT
A pre-insert SELECT is not a concurrency guarantee.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you distinguish duplicate email from another constraint failure?
Answer: Inspect the violated constraint name or trusted SQL error classification, translate known
uniqueness failures into a domain-specific conflict, and leave unknown failures generic.

pages.title: How do JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 • SPRING DATA JPA AND ENTITY OWNERSHIP
How do JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
JPA defines persistence contracts, Hibernate is a provider, and Spring Data JPA supplies
repository abstractions on top.
DRAW THE IDEA — JPA Hibernate Data JPA
BEFORE
Entity state ➜
FOCUS
JPA context ➜
AFTER
Database change
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
interface CustomerRepository extends JpaRepository<Customer, Long> {
  Optional<Customer> findByEmail(String email);
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Spring Data builds the repository implementation, which uses JPA infrastructure backed by the chosen provider.
Hibernate is common but not the specification itself. A derived query still runs a database query.
04 / WATCH OUT
Repository abstractions do not remove the need to understand SQL.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When would a custom repository implementation help?
Answer: Use a custom repository when an operation needs complex query construction, batch updates,
vendor features or persistence behavior not expressible cleanly by derived methods.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 • SPRING DATA JPA AND ENTITY OWNERSHIP
What are transient, managed, detached and removed
entities?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
They describe whether an entity is new, tracked by a persistence context, no longer
tracked, or scheduled for deletion.
DRAW THE IDEA — transient managed detached removed
BEFORE
Entity state ➜
FOCUS
JPA context ➜
AFTER
Database change
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Customer c = new Customer(); // Transient
entityManager.persist(c);     // Managed in this context
entityManager.detach(c);      // Detached
// remove requires an appropriately managed entity.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Managed changes can be detected and written at flush. Editing a detached object does not automatically update the
database. State and transaction boundaries determine which operations are valid.
04 / WATCH OUT
A non-null id does not always prove an object is managed.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would contains(entity) help diagnosis?
Answer: EntityManager.contains(entity) tells whether that exact instance is currently managed in the
persistence context; it does not establish that the database row still exists.

pages.title: How do persist, merge and repository save differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 • SPRING DATA JPA AND ENTITY OWNERSHIP
How do persist, merge and repository save differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
persist makes a new entity managed; merge copies state into a managed instance;
Spring Data save chooses persistence behavior from newness detection.
DRAW THE IDEA — persist merge repository save
BEFORE
Entity state ➜
FOCUS
JPA context ➜
AFTER
Database change
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Customer detached = loadDetached();
Customer managed = entityManager.merge(detached);
// Continue with managed, not an assumption that detached changed state.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
merge returns the managed object used by the persistence context. The supplied object need not become
managed. Spring Data newness can depend on version, identifier, or Persistable configuration.
04 / WATCH OUT
save is not an unconditional SQL INSERT.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would an assigned id affect newness detection?
Answer: With an assigned non-null ID and no version/newness policy, Spring Data may treat the entity as
existing and call merge. Implement Persistable or appropriate new-state detection when needed.

pages.title: What is dirty checking?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 • SPRING DATA JPA AND ENTITY OWNERSHIP
What is dirty checking?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The persistence provider detects relevant changes to managed entities and synchronizes
them at flush within the transaction.
DRAW THE IDEA — dirty checking
BEFORE
Entity state ➜
FOCUS
JPA context ➜
AFTER
Database change
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Transactional
public void rename(long id, String name) {
  Customer c = repository.findById(id).orElseThrow();
  c.setName(name);
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The entity is managed in the active transaction, so changes can be flushed without another save call. Flush timing
and SQL depend on provider behavior. The update still commits only if the transaction succeeds.
04 / WATCH OUT
Detached changes do not participate in dirty checking.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if the transaction rolls back after flush?
Answer: Flushing sends SQL but does not commit it. If the enclosing transaction rolls back successfully, its
database changes are undone despite the earlier flush.
Source guide p. 45 • Intermediate • References: D01, D02

pages.title: Who owns a bidirectional JPA relationship?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 • SPRING DATA JPA AND ENTITY OWNERSHIP
Who owns a bidirectional JPA relationship?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The owning side controls the relationship mapping update; maintain both Java sides for
consistent in-memory behavior.
DRAW THE IDEA — Who owns bidirectional JPA
BEFORE
Entity state ➜
FOCUS
JPA context ➜
AFTER
Database change
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@OneToMany(mappedBy="order") List<Line> lines;
// In Line:
@ManyToOne Order order;
// Add helper: order.lines.add(line); line.order = order;
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Here Line.order owns the relationship. Updating only the inverse collection can leave database linkage unchanged.
Cascade and orphanRemoval govern lifecycle behavior separately from ownership.
04 / WATCH OUT
Cascade is not a fetch policy.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When should orphanRemoval delete a child?
Answer: Use orphanRemoval when removing a child from its owning parent collection truly means
deleting it. Do not use it for children shared or transferred to another aggregate.

CHAPTER 10 • SPRING DATA JPA AND ENTITY OWNERSHIP
Why should schema migrations replace ddl-auto=update in
production?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Versioned migrations make changes reviewable and repeatable; automatic update is not
a controlled compatibility and rollback plan.
DRAW THE IDEA — schema migrations replace ddl-auto
BEFORE
Entity state ➜
FOCUS
JPA context ➜
AFTER
Database change
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
# Apply approved Flyway or Liquibase migrations separately.
# Expand schema, migrate consumers, then contract later.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Validation checks mapping compatibility; it does not perform a migration. A versioned change can be reviewed for
locks, data backfill, compatibility, and recovery. Use one clear owner for schema initialization.
04 / WATCH OUT
Rolling application code back may not roll schema back safely.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you add a required column without downtime?
Answer: Add the nullable column, deploy compatible readers/writers, backfill existing rows, then enforce
NOT NULL only after every writer supplies the value and old versions are gone.

pages.title: Where should @Transactional usually be placed?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 • TRANSACTIONS AND CONSISTENCY
Where should @Transactional usually be placed?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Place it on a service boundary that owns one database unit of work, rather than
scattering unrelated transactions across controller steps.
DRAW THE IDEA — @Transactional usually placed
BEFORE
Service invocation ➜
FOCUS
Transaction boundary ➜
AFTER
Commit / rollback
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Transactional
public void transfer(long from, long to, BigDecimal amount) {
  debit(from, amount);
  credit(to, amount);
  recordTransfer(from, to, amount);
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The database operations participate in one local transaction when the method is invoked through its configured
transaction boundary and uses the right manager. Internal helpers can share it.
04 / WATCH OUT
This does not automatically make a remote HTTP call atomic with the database.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you publish a durable transfer event?
Answer: Write the business change and an outbox event record in the same local transaction. A separate
relay publishes the event with retry and deduplication.

pages.title: Which failures trigger default rollback?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 • TRANSACTIONS AND CONSISTENCY
Which failures trigger default rollback?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
By default, runtime exceptions and Errors trigger rollback; checked exceptions require
an explicit rule when rollback is intended.
DRAW THE IDEA — failures trigger default rollback
BEFORE
Service invocation ➜
FOCUS
Transaction boundary ➜
AFTER
Commit / rollback
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
@Transactional(rollbackFor = IOException.class)
public void importOrders() throws IOException {
  repository.save(order);
  throw new IOException("Invalid source");
}
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
The explicit rule makes this checked failure roll back the participating transaction. If the exception is caught and
suppressed inside the boundary, the interceptor may not see it. Global rules can also be configured, so state your
assumptions.
04 / WATCH OUT
catch-and-return can accidentally commit partial work.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would a rollback-only marker affect the outer caller?
Answer: When a participating inner transaction marks rollback-only, the outer call may complete its logic
but fail on commit with UnexpectedRollbackException. Do not claim it committed.

pages.title: How do REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 • TRANSACTIONS AND CONSISTENCY
How do REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
REQUIRED joins an existing transaction or starts one; REQUIRES_NEW uses an
independent transaction while suspending an existing one.
DRAW THE IDEA — REQUIRED REQUIRES_NEW
BEFORE
Service invocation ➜
FOCUS
Transaction boundary ➜
AFTER
Commit / rollback
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Outer REQUIRED -> connection/transaction A
  Inner REQUIRES_NEW -> independent transaction B
  B can commit even if A later rolls back
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
This requires crossing an advised boundary. Independent propagation can need another database connection while
the outer one is held. Use it for a deliberate consistency contract, not as a generic exception workaround.
04 / WATCH OUT
Pool exhaustion can arise under nested independent transactions.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When is NESTED behavior different?
Answer: NESTED uses savepoints within one physical transaction when supported; REQUIRES_NEW uses
an independent transaction and often another connection. Support varies by manager.
