pages.title: Does changing a configuration file refresh running beans automatically?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
Does changing a configuration file refresh running beans
automatically?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Ordinary Boot startup binding is not a general live-refresh mechanism; dynamic
changes need an explicit supported design.
DRAW THE IDEA — changing configuration file refresh
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Startup -> bind timeout=2s into bean
Edit file -> existing bean normally remains unchanged
Refresh policy -> supported rebinding or new immutable snapshot
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Choose which settings may change, validate replacement atomically, and define resource reconfiguration. A new
password value does not automatically replace every connection in an existing pool.
04 / WATCH OUT
Restart-required and live settings should not be mixed implicitly.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would readers observe a complete new policy snapshot?
Answer: Publish one validated immutable configuration object through a volatile/atomic reference. Each
request reads the reference once so fields come from one version.

pages.title: How do local and distributed caches differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
How do local and distributed caches differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Local caches offer per-instance low-latency storage; distributed caches share data
across instances with network and consistency costs.
DRAW THE IDEA — local distributed caches
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Caffeine -> one process owns local entries
Redis -> service instances share remote cache state
Two-level cache -> additional invalidation and freshness policy
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A local cache hit can diverge from another pod's result. A shared store still needs serialization, TTL, key versioning,
availability, and invalidation semantics. Choose from workload and correctness requirements.
04 / WATCH OUT
Redis being shared does not guarantee immediately coherent local near-caches.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What is the stale-data tolerance?
Answer: Document maximum acceptable staleness by use case. Prices, authorization and stock may need
stronger reads than marketing descriptions or optional recommendations.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
Why is a Redis lock not automatically safe for irreversible
work?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Lease expiry, pauses and ownership transfer can let an old holder continue after a new
holder acquires the lock.
DRAW THE IDEA — Redis lock not automatically
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Owner A lease expires during a long pause
Owner B obtains new lease and proceeds
A resumes -> two actors may perform the protected effect
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Use appropriate fencing or an authoritative idempotent/transactional protocol when the effect requires it. Unlock
only the token you own and define renewal failure. The design must match the datastore and failure model.
04 / WATCH OUT
A lease is not proof that the old process stopped.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can the downstream service reject stale fencing tokens?
Answer: Only if the downstream storage/API checks monotonically advancing tokens and rejects obsolete
ones. A lease alone cannot prevent a paused owner from resuming a harmful write.

CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
How should multipart upload limits and file ownership be
designed?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Bound file and request size, validate accepted types, constrain storage paths, and clean
up temporary resources under failure.

FOCUS

spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size=12MB

The values are illustrative. Content-Type and extension are untrusted hints; inspect required content and avoid
loading huge files into memory. Virus scanning or quarantine depends on the product's needs.
04 / WATCH OUT
Multipart limits do not replace path traversal protection.

What happens if processing fails after a temporary file is created?

scheduled orphan cleanup. Make processing retryable by upload identity.

CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
What is the distinction between synchronous MVC and
MVC async timeout?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
MVC async request timeout governs supported asynchronous request processing; it is
not a universal timeout for ordinary blocking controllers.
DRAW THE IDEA — distinction synchronous MVC MVC
BEFORE

FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER

// Downstream clients and synchronous work need their own limits.

Map the specific servlet/async lifecycle before assuming cancellation. Expiring an HTTP response does not
guarantee a background task stopped. Propagate deadlines and handle unknown business outcomes.
04 / WATCH OUT
A proxy timeout may close the client while server work continues.

Which layer owns stopping an expensive export?
Answer: The job or request coordinator must own cancellation and limits; an MVC async timeout does not
guarantee expensive work or an external call stopped.

pages.title: How do client-side load balancing and discovery differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
How do client-side load balancing and discovery differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Discovery identifies service instances; load balancing chooses where a call should go,
with health and connection behavior part of the contract.
DRAW THE IDEA — client-side load balancing discovery
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Logical service name -> discover candidates
Load-balancer policy -> choose an instance
Client call -> deadline, retry, pool, outcome
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A Kubernetes Service may already provide routing, while another stack may use client-side selection. Avoid
duplicating mechanisms without evidence. Use compatible Spring Cloud release alignment where that ecosystem is
selected.

CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
What should you know when using OpenFeign with Boot?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Feign supplies declarative client interfaces; timeouts, encoding, errors, authentication,
pools and version alignment remain configuration responsibilities.

Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant

not treat it as a reactive client. Verify retry defaults for the integration rather than assuming raw Feign defaults.

pages.title: How do rate limiting and business quotas differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
How do rate limiting and business quotas differ?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Rate limiting controls request admission over time; a business quota tracks a durable
domain entitlement or consumption rule.
DRAW THE IDEA — rate limiting business quotas
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Rate: up to N calls per time window
Quota: purchased allowance remaining for this account
// Choose authoritative identity, storage, and concurrency policy.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A process-local limiter may multiply capacity across replicas. A durable quota needs consistent accounting,
idempotency and failure handling. Return a meaningful throttle contract with retry information where appropriate.
04 / WATCH OUT
IP address alone may be a poor account identity.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What must happen atomically when a paid quota is consumed?
Answer: Consume a paid quota with an atomic authoritative reservation and durable usage record. A read-
then-increment across replicas can overspend the quota.

pages.title: How should Spring Batch be distinguished from a scheduled method?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
How should Spring Batch be distinguished from a
scheduled method?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Spring Batch supplies job/step metadata, chunk processing and restart semantics;
scheduling only determines when work is triggered.
DRAW THE IDEA — Batch distinguished scheduled method
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Schedule -> launch Job
Job -> Step -> read/process/write chunks
Repository -> execution and restart metadata
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Choose a job identity and parameters carefully, then test restart after a failed chunk. The batch version and
transaction boundaries matter. A for-loop inside @Scheduled does not acquire durable recovery semantics
automatically.
04 / WATCH OUT
Re-running a job needs duplicate-effect policy.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What state should a restart skip versus repeat?
Answer: On restart, skip committed/recorded work and repeat only idempotent uncommitted items based
on durable job/step state and checkpoint semantics.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
How should a saga differ from a local @Transactional
method?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A saga coordinates multiple independently committed steps and compensations; a local
transaction rolls back participating resources atomically.
DRAW THE IDEA — saga local @Transactional method
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Reserve stock -> authorize payment -> create shipment
Failure later -> release stock or void authorization as defined
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Compensation is another business action, not time travel. It can fail or require manual resolution. Persist workflow
state, deadlines and operation ids, and make both forward and compensating actions idempotent.
04 / WATCH OUT
@Transactional does not turn remote services into one database.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which step is irreversible and needs special handling?
Answer: Mark irreversible steps such as external settlement or shipped goods explicitly; handle them with
manual/reconciliation paths rather than pretending compensation is a database rollback.

pages.title: What is the difference between business audit and application logging?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
What is the difference between business audit and
application logging?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Audit records prove defined business events and often require durability and controlled
access; diagnostic logs help operate and debug the service.
DRAW THE IDEA — difference business audit logging
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Audit: who approved order, when, under which operation identity
Log: dependency timed out, trace id, safe error context
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Do not assume sampled, rotating debug logs satisfy an audit requirement. Define retention, tamper resistance,
consistency, and sensitive-field policy. Conversely, avoid storing every diagnostic stack trace as a business audit
event.
04 / WATCH OUT
Both channels can expose confidential information.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Must an approval fail if its audit cannot be recorded?
Answer: If a required audit record is part of the business/legal invariant, approval must not commit
without durable audit intent. Put both in one local transaction if possible.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
How should an idempotency-key store handle concurrent
requests?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Atomically claim the key, bind it to the intended request, track completion, and return or
reconcile the same operation outcome.
DRAW THE IDEA — idempotency-key store handle concurrent
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Unique key -> claimed operation and payload fingerprint
Same key + same payload -> existing pending/completed outcome
Same key + different payload -> explicit conflict
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A cache-only check followed by work races across requests. Store enough state to recover after a crash between
external success and local completion. Define retention and pending-operation timeouts.
04 / WATCH OUT
Deleting a pending key can enable a duplicate effect.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Who reconciles an unknown provider outcome?
Answer: The payment owner and business workflow must reconcile by the stable operation ID, using status
lookup/callbacks and recorded uncertainty; a timeout alone is not a failure result.
Source guide p. 101 • Senior • References: F03, D03, M03, M04, I03

pages.title: Why can optimistic retries still violate a business rule?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
Why can optimistic retries still violate a business rule?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A retry must re-read and revalidate the full invariant, not blindly repeat arithmetic from
stale state.
DRAW THE IDEA — optimistic retries still violate
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Read stock=1 -> conflict -> re-read stock=0
Business rule: reserve requires available >= 1
Retry -> reject now rather than force another decrement
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A successful later write is not proof the original operation remained valid. Include other relevant rows and unique
constraints in the invariant. Bound retry attempts and return a clear conflict or insufficient-capacity outcome.
04 / WATCH OUT
Retrying every optimistic failure can amplify contention.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When would atomic conditional SQL be a better fit?
Answer: A conditional UPDATE ... WHERE available>=? enforces a simple stock invariant atomically at the
database, avoiding a stale read and repeat-update loop.
Source guide p. 102 • Senior • References: F03, D03, M03, M04, I03

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
How should sensitive fields be protected during JSON
serialization?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use explicit DTOs and field policies, and verify every output and error path rather than
relying only on one annotation.
DRAW THE IDEA — sensitive fields protected during
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
record PublicUser(long id, String name) {}
// passwordHash, token and internal flags are absent by design.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Serialization annotations can help but do not protect logs, exceptions, projections, alternate mappers, or toString.
Test response fields and review caching/tracing representations.
04 / WATCH OUT
Ignoring a password field in JSON does not make an entity safe for all uses.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you avoid accidentally echoing a rejected credential?
Answer: Use dedicated safe error DTOs and central exception handling. Never serialize the request object
or rejected credential into logs or response ProblemDetail properties.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 • ADVANCED DESIGN AND INTERVIEW DISTINCTIONS
What should change when a service is deployed across
regions?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Define data ownership, replication consistency, conflict handling, latency, and failover/
recovery semantics explicitly.
DRAW THE IDEA — change deployed across regions
BEFORE
Business rule ➜
FOCUS
Mechanism + proof ➜
AFTER
Safe invariant
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Local region routing -> lower request latency
Shared authoritative write region -> cross-region dependency
Multi-writer -> conflict and invariant policy required
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Boot packaging is not the limiting design issue. Operation identity, clocks, timeouts, caches, and database
consistency can behave differently across regions. Test partial partition and recovery using the chosen datastore's
guarantees.
04 / WATCH OUT
Two healthy deployments do not prove one consistent business state.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which operations can safely remain region-local?
Answer: Read-only caches, telemetry and optional personalization may stay region-local; monetary
balance, stock and other global invariants need an authority/replication protocol.

A bean exists in code but injection fails. What do you

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
Latency rises while CPU stays low. What is your first
hypothesis?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Investigate waits on pools, external I/O, locks, and queues using correlated thread and
latency evidence.
DRAW THE IDEA — Latency rises while CPU
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
CPU low + Hikari pending high -> pool ownership/query wait
CPU low + executor queue high -> blocked workers or admission excess
CPU low + outbound spans long -> dependency slowdown
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
These are hypotheses, not conclusions. Time-aligned metrics and stacks determine the bottleneck. Bound waiting
and repair the constrained dependency before blindly increasing threads.
04 / WATCH OUT
Adding replicas can multiply pressure on the same database.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would prove that connections are leaking?
Answer: Hikari active connections remain near max, pending requests grow, and connection-acquisition
timeouts appear while completed request load falls. Inspect leaked-resource stack traces and slow
transactions.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
A cache serves another tenant's data. What failed?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The key or cached representation omitted a result-affecting tenant or authorization
dimension, or access was not enforced at the boundary.
DRAW THE IDEA — cache serves another tenant
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Before: cache[productId]
After:  cache[(tenantId, productId)] for tenant-specific results
Permission check -> remains mandatory on each protected operation
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Stop the leakage, assess affected entries, and invalidate or rebuild the cache. A corrected key does not retroactively
remove old entries. Test cross-tenant requests and role changes.
04 / WATCH OUT
Valid authentication does not repair a wrong cache key.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would a tenant id be trusted rather than taken blindly from a request?
Answer: Derive tenant scope from verified authentication, not a user-editable header alone. Compare
resource ownership in the data query and test cross-tenant IDs explicitly.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
JWT requests work in Postman but fail in the browser.
Why?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Separate CORS/preflight behavior from token validation, cookie/CSRF rules, and the
browser's actual sent headers.
DRAW THE IDEA — JWT requests work Postman
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Inspect OPTIONS status and access-control headers.
Inspect actual Authorization header on the following request.
Check Origin allowlist and credential mode.
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Postman does not enforce browser CORS. A preflight may be rejected before the actual bearer request occurs. Use
server and browser evidence to locate the failure instead of disabling all security.
04 / WATCH OUT
CORS errors can mask an underlying 401/403 response.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you test the preflight in MockMvc?
Answer: Use MockMvc OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method headers; assert allowed
origins, methods, headers and no unintended 401.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
An API returns 403 after login. What should you check?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Check the required authority, role-prefix mapping, matched security chain, method
checks, CSRF, and object ownership.
DRAW THE IDEA — API returns 403 after
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Token scope: orders.read -> typical authority SCOPE_orders.read
Rule expects ROLE_ADMIN -> different authority
POST with cookie authentication -> may also require CSRF token
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A valid identity can fail authorization, and 403 can have multiple causes. Examine which component denied access.
Configure claim conversion deliberately rather than granting broad privileges.
04 / WATCH OUT
hasRole and hasAuthority are not identical string checks.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you verify scope conversion?
Answer: Load a token with the expected scope, inspect JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter mapping, and
assert the resulting SCOPE_ authority and effective SecurityFilterChain selection.

pages.title: CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
An endpoint charges twice after a retry. How should it be
repaired?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Persist one business operation identity and coordinate deduplication with the provider
or recover through reconciliation.
DRAW THE IDEA — endpoint charges twice after
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
First request: key=payment-42, result unknown after timeout
Retry: same key=payment-42
Server/provider: return existing outcome or continue same operation
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A timeout cannot prove the first attempt failed. Store request identity, state, and result under a concurrency-safe
protocol. Define key reuse, payload mismatch, expiry, and recovery.
04 / WATCH OUT
A local synchronized block does not deduplicate across replicas.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What if the provider succeeded before the application stored the result?
Answer: Use provider reconciliation by the original operation ID: recover the charge result and store it
once. A new idempotency key risks a second charge.
Source guide p. 108 • Senior • References: D03, S04, I04, O01, O02

CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
A Kafka consumer applies the same event twice. What is
required?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Make the business effect idempotent and inspect the commit, redelivery, retry, and
rebalance windows.
DRAW THE IDEA — Kafka consumer applies same
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Effect committed -> process stops before offset committed
Restart -> record delivered again
Dedup marker + effect -> authoritative atomic policy
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
This is expected under at-least-once delivery. A durable unique operation/event marker helps when it shares the
correct boundary with the effect. For remote effects, reuse provider idempotency identity.

effect and correct offset/retry behavior in an integrated broker/DB test.

pages.title: Async notifications run before an order commits. Why?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
Async notifications run before an order commits. Why?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A separate worker does not inherit the caller's thread-bound transaction and can
execute immediately after submission.
DRAW THE IDEA — Async notifications run before
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Transaction A writes order -> submits async task
Task B reads order before A commits -> absent or stale view
Repair -> after-commit handoff or durable outbox
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
After-commit callbacks fit some best-effort cases but can still lose work if the process stops. An outbox records the
intent with the business transaction and supports recovery.
04 / WATCH OUT
A delay or sleep is not a commit-order guarantee.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you prove task loss is recovered after restart?
Answer: Persist order and outbox intent atomically, crash after commit and before send, restart the relay,
and prove delivery/retry from the pending row.
Source guide p. 109 • Senior • References: D03, S04, I04, O01, O02

pages.title: Scheduled jobs run once per pod instead of once per cluster. How do you fix it?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
Scheduled jobs run once per pod instead of once per
cluster. How do you fix it?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use a deliberate distributed coordination or durable scheduling design when cluster-
wide singleton execution is required.
DRAW THE IDEA — Scheduled jobs run once
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
5 replicas x local @Scheduled -> 5 trigger sources
Cluster-wide requirement -> lease/lock or external scheduler
Business effect -> still idempotent under takeover and retry
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A lock can expire while an old owner continues, so consider fencing and ownership semantics. Durable scheduling
and progress recording can simplify recovery. Choose based on delivery requirements rather than suppressing logs.
04 / WATCH OUT
A single initial replica is not a future coordination policy.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would clock skew or a network partition affect the lease?
Answer: Clock skew and partitions can permit competing lease assumptions. Use database/cluster
coordination and fencing/ownership checks at the effect boundary; prefer idempotent job steps.
Source guide p. 109 • Senior • References: D03, S04, I04, O01, O02

pages.title: A startup runner waits forever for a remote service. What should change?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
A startup runner waits forever for a remote service. What
should change?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Bound startup waiting, define required versus optional readiness, and separate endless
background work from startup completion.
DRAW THE IDEA — startup runner waits forever
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Required dependency -> bounded verification, fail or stay unready
Optional warmup -> controlled degraded state and retry later
Infinite polling loop -> managed background lifecycle
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A never-ending runner prevents successful startup completion. The policy should match whether useful requests can
be served. Use backoff and limits rather than spinning or overwhelming the dependency.
04 / WATCH OUT
A listening port does not prove runners have completed.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would readiness report during fallback operation?
Answer: Readiness should report usable-with-documented-degradation only when the application can
safely serve its essential contract; otherwise remain unready while bounded startup retry continues.

CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
A database pool exhausts after traffic drops. What do you
inspect?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Inspect leaked or long-held connections, transaction duration, blocked queries, and pool
acquisition/ownership evidence.
DRAW THE IDEA — database pool exhausts after
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Active connections stay high + requests low

Thread stacks + database sessions -> correlate holders
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Enable appropriate temporary leak diagnostics carefully, then find the ownership defect. Leak warnings can also
identify a legitimately long transaction. Ensure every manual resource closes and avoid holding database
transactions over remote calls.
04 / WATCH OUT
Raising the pool size can delay the next outage.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which code path fails to release resources on an exception?
Answer: Inspect every response/error/timeout cancellation path, especially streams and HTTP client
bodies; track outstanding leases and stack traces showing acquisition without close.

pages.title: A REQUIRES_NEW audit call stalls under load. Why?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
A REQUIRES_NEW audit call stalls under load. Why?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The outer transaction may hold a connection while the independent inner transaction
waits for another, exhausting the pool.
DRAW THE IDEA — REQUIRES_NEW audit call stalls
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
20 outer transactions hold 20 pool connections
Each enters inner REQUIRES_NEW and requests another
No spare connection -> blocked acquisition
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Verify actual connection and propagation behavior. Redesign the audit durability boundary or budget concurrency
and connections deliberately. Crossing a proper proxy is also needed for this propagation to occur.
04 / WATCH OUT
Independent transactions are not free concurrency.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Would an outbox satisfy the audit requirement differently?
Answer: REQUIRES_NEW may need a second pool connection while an outer transaction holds one. An
outbox can persist audit intent in the outer transaction without the nested extra connection.

pages.title: Why is it risky?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
An API returns 200 with an empty list during an outage.
Why is it risky?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It disguises retrieval failure as valid absence, potentially driving incorrect downstream
decisions.
DRAW THE IDEA — API returns 200 empty
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
No customers -> successful empty result
Database unavailable -> separate failure contract
Cached fallback -> explicit degraded semantics if permitted
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A client may assume there is no data and delete or create resources. Preserve the failure cause and return the
defined error response. A fallback needs freshness and business approval, not just convenient typing.
04 / WATCH OUT
catch(Exception) returning empty is not universal robustness.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would a batch retain successes while reporting failed items?
Answer: Return per-item success/error records or a documented partial-success response, preserving
stable item IDs and retryability. Empty success must not camouflage dependency failure.

CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
A memory leak appears after enabling metrics. What do
you inspect?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Check high-cardinality meter tags and retained registries or listener state before
attributing the issue to all observability.
DRAW THE IDEA — memory leak appears after
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Timer tag customerId -> one series per unique customer
Meter count keeps increasing -> registry retains combinations
Fix -> normalized routes and bounded business categories
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Confirm the retention path and compare series count after the change. Do not disable all telemetry without an
alternative diagnostic plan. Sampling and label design solve different issues.
04 / WATCH OUT
A bounded request queue does not bound meter cardinality.

What memory evidence would distinguish it from a cache leak?
Answer: Inspect meter count, unique tag combinations, registry allocations and heap dominators. A
metrics leak retains meter/tag objects; a cache leak retains cached keys/values.

pages.title: CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
WebFlux requests stop progressing while one JDBC call
runs. Why?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Blocking work occupies a shared event-loop thread; isolate it or choose a stack aligned
with the blocking dependencies.
DRAW THE IDEA — WebFlux requests stop progressing
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Bad: Mono.just(jdbc.load()) -> call runs before publisher assembly
Better shape: Mono.fromCallable(() -> jdbc.load())
                  .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
fromCallable defers execution. The scheduler isolates the blocking operation, but downstream and in-flight
concurrency still need bounds. R2DBC is a different persistence model, not a drop-in Hibernate switch.
04 / WATCH OUT
Wrapping an already-computed result in Mono is not offloading.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Would MVC with virtual threads fit better?
Answer: MVC plus virtual threads may suit predominantly blocking JDBC workloads if the stack is
compatible, but DB connections still constrain concurrency. Compare performance under bounded load.
Source guide p. 113 • Senior • References: D03, S04, I04, O01, O02

pages.title: An integration test passes but production violates a constraint. Why?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
An integration test passes but production violates a
constraint. Why?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The test may use a different engine, skip commit/flush, mock the repository, or omit
real migrations and concurrency.
DRAW THE IDEA — integration test passes but
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Mock repository -> no database constraint exercised
H2 substitute -> dialect or locking differs
Rollback-only test -> commit-sensitive failure can be missed
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Test the required invariant against the deployment engine, with explicit flush or completion when appropriate. Add
concurrency tests when the defect depends on simultaneous requests.
04 / WATCH OUT
More assertions on mocks do not validate SQL behavior.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would two concurrent inserts test a uniqueness race?
Answer: Use two independent concurrent transactions starting together, attempt the same unique key and
assert one commits and the other receives the expected constraint failure.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
A rollout breaks old pods after a schema change. What
failed?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The schema transition was not backward compatible with versions running during
rollout or rollback.
DRAW THE IDEA — rollout breaks old pods
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Drop old column -> old pod query fails
Safer: add new shape -> dual-compatible code -> migrate -> retire old shape
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Inventory consumers, migration locks, data backfill, and mixed-version behavior. Verify both the new and previous
application versions against the transitional schema.
04 / WATCH OUT
Application rollback does not restore dropped data.

Which migration should be delayed until all old consumers are gone?
Answer: Delay dropping/renaming old columns or making formerly optional fields mandatory until all old
applications, jobs and consumers have migrated and rollback no longer needs the old schema.

pages.title: How do you repair it?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
Logging context disappears in async or reactive work.
How do you repair it?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use supported context propagation with clear lifecycle ownership rather than assuming
ordinary ThreadLocal state follows execution.
DRAW THE IDEA — Logging context disappears async
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Caller thread MDC -> executor task may use another thread
Reactor sequence -> context belongs to the reactive chain
Cleanup -> restore or remove owned context at the boundary
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Select propagation support for the actual framework and executor. Test both correct correlation and absence of
cross-request leakage. Do not copy authentication blindly into work with a different trust boundary.
04 / WATCH OUT
InheritableThreadLocal is not a general pooled-task solution.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would task reuse expose stale context?
Answer: Reused pool threads may retain ThreadLocal/MDC data from an earlier request. Capture/restore
explicitly and remove in finally; Reactor needs its supported context propagation approach.

pages.title: What should change?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
A tenant filter exists but direct repository calls bypass it.
What should change?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Enforce the invariant at an authoritative service or data-access boundary reachable
from every entry point.
DRAW THE IDEA — tenant filter exists but
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
HTTP interceptor only -> messaging path can bypass
Service authorization + tenant-scoped query -> common boundary
Test HTTP, batch, and message entry points
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A cross-cutting mechanism must actually cover the calls it claims to protect. Trust tenant identity from authenticated
context and ensure query predicates and key selection align. Consider database-enforced isolation where required.
04 / WATCH OUT
A client-supplied tenant header alone is insufficient authority.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would a cache interact with the same invariant?
Answer: Use tenant-qualified keys and recheck authorization on every sensitive hit path. A cache is part of
the security boundary, not an exemption from ownership checks.

pages.title: CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
Graceful shutdown still loses queued tasks. What contract
is missing?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Executor draining is bounded process behavior, not durable acceptance or recovery of
important queued work.
DRAW THE IDEA — Graceful shutdown still loses
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
HTTP accepts job -> in-memory queue -> process terminated
Durable job record -> accepted work can be recovered
Shutdown -> stop admission, bounded drain, record unfinished state
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
Return acceptance only after the durability requirement is met. Pending tasks and in-flight effects need replay/
idempotency rules. Tune platform grace and executor shutdown, but do not rely on an unlimited wait.
04 / WATCH OUT
shutdownNow does not atomically finish all accepted jobs.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would the client query after a restart?
Answer: Expose a durable job/order status endpoint keyed by the operation ID, so a client can discover
whether a previously accepted task completed or needs recovery after restart.

pages.title: CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 • SENIOR PRODUCTION DIAGNOSIS
How would you review a Spring Boot service before
production?
01 / THE SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
State its key invariants, failure boundaries, resource budgets, security rules,
observability, deployment compatibility, and recovery evidence.
DRAW THE IDEA — would review before production
BEFORE
Production symptom ➜
FOCUS
Evidence + diagnosis ➜
AFTER
Safe recovery
02 / THE ORIGINAL EXAMPLE
Review -> contract, authorization, transaction, idempotency
Limits -> DB, outbound pool, executor, cache, retries
Release -> readiness, probes, migrations, rollback
Evidence -> focused tests, load profile, operational signals
03 / WHY THIS WORKS
A successful startup proves wiring, not business correctness or capacity. Choose checks according to the actual
service rather than counting annotations. Resolve risks with an owner and a verifiable decision before release.
04 / WATCH OUT
A generic checklist is not evidence that a critical payment path is safe.
05 / INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which unresolved risk would block your release?
Answer: A critical unresolved risk such as cross-tenant access, duplicate charges, unsafe schema rollout or
missing recovery of committed orders should block release regardless of passing unit tests.

pages.fullText:
Defer and isolate a blocking client call
Original source page 128 • Add a compatible Boot project and dependencies
Source exercise: implement the method or project recipe, then verify its actual success and failure behavior.
C11 Defer and isolate a blocking client call
Create a reactive wrapper that defers blocking execution, isolates it, and exposes a result 
deadline.
Setup: webflux
Worked solution
Mono<Result> call() {
  return Mono.fromCallable(() -> blockingClient.call())
      .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())
      .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));
}
Verification and boundary policy
Check no client call occurs before subscription, execution does not occupy the event loop, and a 
slow
call produces timeout behavior. The operator does not guarantee transport cancellation; configure
the client's deadlines too. Bound in-flight work and verify actual cleanup.
After implementing, test the expected result and its failure path. Snippets may be partial project recipes.

pages.title: VISUAL CHEATSHEET Trust flow
pages.fullText:
VISUAL CHEATSHEET Trust flow
How Spring Security protects a
request
SERVLET SECURITY
HTTP request Selected chain Business handler
1. Choose the chain. Spring Security selects the first matching
SecurityFilterChain. A missing catch-all can expose unexpected routes.
2. Authenticate. Check the configured credential type: password, session,
bearer JWT, or opaque token. A valid signature alone is not an authorization
decision.
3. Authorize. Check method/endpoint permission and real object ownership.
Tenant safety must also hold on cache hits and asynchronous paths.
4. Verify denial. Wrong issuer, audience, key, owner, role, and missing CSRF
tokens must produce the intended response without a business side effect.
Default to secure, explicit rules Architecture reference

pages.title: PROVE TRUST BEFORE ACCESS Who issued it? Who is it for? What rights?
pages.fullText:
VISUAL CHEATSHEET JWT + OAuth
Three questions about every token
PROVE TRUST BEFORE ACCESS
Who issued it? Who is it for? What rights?
Issuer + signature + algorithm: Trust only configured issuers and known
verification keys. The kid header is a key selection hint, not an arbitrary fetch
URL.
Audience + time: A correctly signed token can still be for the wrong service,
expired, or not yet valid.
Permissions + ownership: Scopes and roles authorize selected operations.
They do not automatically authorize access to every customer's data.
JWT is not OAuth: JWT is a token representation. OAuth defines delegated
access. OIDC adds a client identity layer. A signed JWT is usually readable, not
encrypted.
Access tokens belong to resource APIs Protocol reference

pages.title: What problem does Spring Security solve?
pages.fullText:
SECURITY FOUNDATIONS Q001 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 001
What problem does Spring Security solve?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It supplies authentication, authorization, and common security protections
integrated with Spring applications.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Credential evidence ➜ Trusted identity ➜ Right to access?
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Request -> security processing -> permitted handler
Denied request -> defined authentication or access response
Why it works: The framework supplies mechanisms, but the application must define trusted
identities, permissions, credential handling and data ownership. A dependency alone cannot decide
who owns an order.
⚠ Interview trap: Security configuration is not a complete threat model.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
Which business rule cannot be inferred from a valid login?
A successful login does not prove that the user owns a particular order, invoice, or tenant
record. Check ownership for each requested object.

pages.title: How do authentication and authorization differ?
pages.fullText:
SECURITY FOUNDATIONS Q002 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 002
How do authentication and authorization differ?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides whether that
identity may perform a particular action.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Actor + resource ➜ Permission + owner rule ➜ Allowed / denied
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
User Sai signs in successfully.
Sai requests another tenant's invoice.
Identity valid -> ownership check can still deny access.
Why it works: A successful login is not universal permission. Protect both operation-level capability
and the target object's ownership. Keep denied outcomes distinct from malformed input or
unavailable data.
⚠ Interview trap: A valid token does not authorize every object id.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would you test cross-tenant denial?
Create tenants A and B, sign in as A, request B's record, expect denial and confirm the
database record was not read or changed.

pages.title: How do principal, credentials and authorities differ?
pages.fullText:
SECURITY FOUNDATIONS Q003 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 003
How do principal, credentials and authorities differ?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Principal identifies the caller, credentials are evidence used to authenticate,
and authorities describe granted capabilities.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Credential evidence ➜ Trusted identity ➜ Right to access?
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
Object principal = auth.getPrincipal();
Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> rights = auth.getAuthorities();
Why it works: The principal can be UserDetails, Jwt, or another supported identity object. Credentials
should be handled minimally and may be erased after authentication. Never assume a password
remains available in an authenticated token.
⚠ Interview trap: Casting every principal to your entity is unsafe.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
What principal type does JWT authentication normally expose?
With Spring's usual JWT resource-server setup, the principal is a Jwt, wrapped by
JwtAuthenticationToken. Custom converters may change that shape.

pages.title: How do roles and authorities differ?
pages.fullText:
SECURITY FOUNDATIONS Q004 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 004
How do roles and authorities differ?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Authorities are permission strings; role helpers conventionally add a ROLE_
prefix when checking a role.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Credential evidence ➜ Trusted identity ➜ Right to access?
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
hasAuthority("orders:approve") -> exact authority
hasRole("ADMIN") -> normally checks ROLE_ADMIN
// Role prefix can be configured in supported integrations.
Why it works: Use a consistent mapping policy. A token claim named roles is not automatically
mapped into Spring's expected strings. Grouping fine-grained permissions into roles is an
application decision.
⚠ Interview trap: hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN") commonly applies the wrong expectation.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would you map identity-provider groups?
Map only trusted, allowlisted provider groups into approved GrantedAuthority values; do not
accept an arbitrary roles claim from an untrusted issuer.

pages.title: What do 401, 403 and login redirects mean?
pages.fullText:
SECURITY FOUNDATIONS Q005 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 005
What do 401, 403 and login redirects mean?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
401 requests or reports authentication failure in an API contract; 403
denotes refused access; browser login entry points can redirect instead.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Credential evidence ➜ Trusted identity ➜ Right to access?
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Bearer API without valid credentials -> commonly 401
Authenticated caller lacking permission -> commonly 403
Form-login browser request -> commonly redirect to login
Why it works: The selected entry point, access-denied handler, and failure source determine the
actual response. A CSRF failure can also produce 403. Do not diagnose solely from status without
finding the denying component.
⚠ Interview trap: Anonymous access denial does not always produce the same response as an
authenticated denial.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
Which handler controls API unauthenticated responses?
AuthenticationEntryPoint controls unauthenticated API responses, normally 401 with an
appropriate WWW-Authenticate challenge.

SECURITY FOUNDATIONS Q006 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 006
Why does adding the security starter change a Boot
app?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Boot activates supported security defaults when its conditions match;
explicit beans let the application own configuration.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Credential evidence ➜ Trusted identity ➜ Right to access?
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
spring-boot-starter-security -> relevant security classes
No custom chain -> default Boot security behavior
Custom SecurityFilterChain -> application controls its rules
Why it works: For the baseline, default web authentication and generated credentials are
development starting points. Separate user-details defaults can have different back-off conditions
from the web chain.
⚠ Interview trap: A custom chain alone does not configure a production identity store.

Define your own UserDetailsService (or other authentication setup) to replace Boot's
generated in-memory user defaults.

pages.fullText:
SERVLET FILTER ARCHITECTURE Q007 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 007
How do DelegatingFilterProxy and FilterChainProxy
differ?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
DelegatingFilterProxy bridges the servlet container to a Spring bean;
FilterChainProxy selects and executes a Spring Security filter chain.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Incoming request ➜ Ordered chain + filter ➜ Handler or 401/403
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Servlet container
-> DelegatingFilterProxy
-> FilterChainProxy
-> selected SecurityFilterChain -> DispatcherServlet
Why it works: The bridge allows Spring-managed security infrastructure to participate in container
requests. FilterChainProxy owns chain selection and other security integration. These names refer to
different responsibilities, not alternative configurations.
⚠ Interview trap: A controller may never run when a security filter rejects the request.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
Where would you debug which chain matches?
Enable narrow Spring Security debug/TRACE diagnostics and inspect FilterChainProxy's
selected SecurityFilterChain; test route matching.

pages.title: What is a SecurityFilterChain bean?
pages.fullText:
SERVLET FILTER ARCHITECTURE Q008 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 008
What is a SecurityFilterChain bean?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It pairs request-matching behavior with an ordered set of security filters for
matching traffic.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Incoming request ➜ Ordered chain + filter ➜ Handler or 401/403
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain web(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults());
return http.build();
}
Why it works: This browser-oriented sketch retains default CSRF behavior and assumes a configured
user source. The DSL assembles filters; it is not a list of controller interceptors. Define the credential
mechanism and authorization together.
⚠ Interview trap: Configuration snippets from different app types cannot be merged blindly.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
What changes for a bearer-only API?
Use a dedicated matching API chain with oauth2ResourceServer JWT support, stateless
context policy, narrow permissions, and reviewed CSRF/credential transport.

pages.title: How are multiple security chains selected?
pages.fullText:
SERVLET FILTER ARCHITECTURE Q009 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 009
How are multiple security chains selected?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Only the first matching chain is selected, using chain order and its
securityMatcher; a fallback prevents uncovered requests.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Servlet request ➜ Select security chain ➜ Authenticate / deny
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
@Order(1) API chain: securityMatcher("/api/**")
@Order(2) Web chain: any remaining request
// Request /api/orders -> API chain only, not both chains.
Why it works: Rules in a later chain do not repair a permissive earlier match. Keep narrow chains
first and a deliberate catch-all last. Test endpoints outside the expected prefixes.
⚠ Interview trap: A request matching no chain can bypass security-chain protections.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would you detect a missing fallback?
Send a request outside every named chain and assert it is denied by a final catch-all
chain; include unknown paths and verbs.

pages.title: How do securityMatcher and requestMatchers differ?
pages.fullText:
SERVLET FILTER ARCHITECTURE Q010 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 010
How do securityMatcher and requestMatchers differ?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
securityMatcher chooses whether a chain applies; authorization
requestMatchers choose rules inside the selected chain.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Servlet request ➜ Select security chain ➜ Authenticate / deny
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
.requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()
.anyRequest().authenticated());
Why it works: /api/public belongs to this chain but receives a public authorization rule. /web/home
does not belong to this chain at all and needs another matching chain. The two matcher levels have
different scope.
⚠ Interview trap: anyRequest inside one chain does not protect unmatched chains globally.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
Where should a catch-all deny rule live?
Put a last, lowest-priority catch-all chain with anyRequest().denyAll() so unmatched routes
are not exposed.

Why does security filter order matter?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
A filter can act only on state prepared upstream; credential validation
normally precedes authorization using that identity.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Incoming request ➜ Ordered chain + filter ➜ Handler or 401/403

-> exception translation around downstream authorization

context before deciding permission.

INTERVIEW QUESTION 012
What does Exception TranslationFilter do?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH

pages.fullText:
AUTHENTICATION MODEL AND CONTEXT Q013 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 013
What does Authentication represent?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It can represent an authentication request or an authenticated result,
carrying principal, credentials, authorities and status.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Login token ➜ Provider decision ➜ Context lifecycle
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Authentication request = UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken
.unauthenticated("sai", "secret");
Authentication result = authenticationManager.authenticate(request);
Why it works: The manager delegates validation and returns the approved identity if successful.
User-controlled data must not be marked trusted simply to bypass validation. A result's
isAuthenticated state alone is not an object-level permission policy.
⚠ Interview trap: Application code should not fabricate trusted authorities from input.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
What happens on an unsupported token type?
If no provider supports the token, ProviderManager cannot authenticate it and throws an
appropriate authentication failure.

pages.fullText:

INTERVIEW QUESTION 014
How do AuthenticationManager, ProviderManager
and AuthenticationProvider differ?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
AuthenticationManager is the entry contract; ProviderManager delegates to
suitable providers; each provider validates supported authentication types.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Login token ➜ Provider decision ➜ Context lifecycle
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Authentication request -> ProviderManager
-> provider.supports(request class)
-> provider.authenticate(request)
-> authenticated result or failure
Why it works: A provider can return null when it does not handle that request. Several providers can
coexist. A custom provider should validate its mechanism and return authorities from a trusted
source.
⚠ Interview trap: supports is not the same as successful credential verification.

Register supported providers for each mechanism; each authenticates only tokens it
understands and returns a trusted result.

INTERVIEW QUESTION 015
What is SecurityContextHolder?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It exposes the current SecurityContext using a configured strategy; the
servlet default associates it with the executing thread.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Login token ➜ Provider decision ➜ Context lifecycle
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Authentication current = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
// Framework processing owns loading and clearing during requests.
Why it works: The context contains the current authentication. Manually setting it changes the
current execution's identity but does not automatically persist a login for later requests. Keep
lifecycle and trusted construction explicit.
⚠ Interview trap: ThreadLocal context does not automatically follow executor tasks.

A session-oriented implementation may use HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository; choose
the repository deliberately.

pages.title: What does SecurityContextRepository do?
pages.fullText:
AUTHENTICATION MODEL AND CONTEXT Q016 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 016
What does SecurityContextRepository do?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It loads and saves security context according to the application's
persistence policy, such as session or request-only storage.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Login token ➜ Provider decision ➜ Context lifecycle
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Context repository -> load existing context
Authentication succeeds -> save if persistent login is intended
Request completes -> thread-associated state cleared
Why it works: In modern explicit-save configurations, custom login code must save the context
deliberately. Built-in mechanisms coordinate their supported persistence behavior. Do not rely on an
old automatic-save assumption across versions.
⚠ Interview trap: Setting the holder is not sufficient proof that session login survives.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How does a stateless repository choice change the design?
A request-only or null repository does not preserve a login between requests; authenticate
every request or supply a different persistence policy.

pages.title: What is UserDetailsService responsible for?
pages.fullText:
PASSWORD AUTHENTICATION AND USER STORAGE Q019 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 019
What is UserDetailsService responsible for?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It loads user identity data, password representation, authorities and account
flags; it does not itself implement the entire password-authentication flow.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Entered password ➜ Verify stored hash ➜ Allow / reject
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) {
Account a = store.findNormalizedUsername(username).orElseThrow();
return User.withUsername(a.username()).password(a.passwordHash())
.authorities(a.authorities()).build();
}
Why it works: The sketch must translate absence into the supported UsernameNotFoundException
and preserve account-status rules. A password provider uses the loaded data with its encoder. Do not
expose the stored hash in an API response.
⚠ Interview trap: A database entity is not automatically the correct public principal.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would disabled accounts be represented?
Expose enabled=false in UserDetails or equivalent account policy; authentication must
reject disabled accounts.

pages.fullText:
PASSWORD AUTHENTICATION AND USER STORAGE Q020 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 020
How does DaoAuthenticationProvider use
PasswordEncoder?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It obtains user details and verifies supplied credentials against the stored
adaptive-hash representation through the configured encoder.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Entered password ➜ Verify stored hash ➜ Allow / reject
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
PasswordEncoder encoder = PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
String stored = encoder.encode("example");
System.out.println(encoder.matches("example", stored)); // true
Why it works: Salts mean two encode calls can produce different stored strings for the same
password. Verify with matches, not string equality after re-encoding. Use the supported provider
configuration for the exact baseline.
⚠ Interview trap: Do not log the supplied password during authentication.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
Why should cost be measured on production-class hardware?
A hashing cost that is safe on a laptop may overload production CPU; benchmark login
latency and throughput on representative hardware.

INTERVIEW QUESTION 021
What does DelegatingPasswordEncoder add?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It selects a password-hash implementation from an identifier prefix,
supporting verification and algorithm evolution.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Entered password ➜ Verify stored hash ➜ Allow / reject
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
{bcrypt}$2a$... -> bcrypt verification
{argon2}...     -> configured Argon2 verification
// Exact encoder ids and implementation availability depend on setup.
Why it works: The prefix describes the stored format rather than encrypting the password.

details password update service.
⚠ Interview trap: Missing or unknown ids need a deliberate migration policy.

On successful login, verify the old hash, check upgradeEncoding, and atomically store a
new adaptive hash without ever storing plaintext.

INTERVIEW QUESTION 022
Why is plain hashing with SHA-256 insufficient for
passwords?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Fast general-purpose hashes are cheap to guess at scale; use salted
adaptive password hashing with an appropriate cost and policy.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Entered password ➜ Verify stored hash ➜ Allow / reject
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Bad: SHA256(password) as a login database scheme
Better: supported adaptive PasswordEncoder + measured cost
Store hash, never reversible raw-password recovery data.
Why it works: Salt prevents identical-password equality from being visible through identical unsalted
hashes. Cost slows offline guessing. Pick a reviewed algorithm and implementation; do not invent a
custom cryptographic scheme.
⚠ Interview trap: Encoding, hashing and encryption solve different problems.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
What additional control slows online guessing?
Apply per-account/IP/device rate limits, progressive delays, abuse detection and MFA as
appropriate.

pages.title: How does session fixation protection help?
pages.fullText:
SESSIONS, LOGIN, LOGOUT AND REMEMBER-ME Q027 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 027
How does session fixation protection help?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It changes or replaces the session identifier/state at authentication
according to supported policy, preventing reuse of a pre-login identifier.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Browser identity ➜ Session + cookie policy ➜ Next-request proof
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Attacker knows pre-login session id
Victim authenticates -> session id changes
Attacker's old identifier should not grant the authenticated session.
Why it works: Modern servlet integration can use changeSessionId. Exact strategy and session-
attribute behavior depend on configuration. Validate the actual login flow when implementing custom
authentication.
⚠ Interview trap: Rotating the id does not prevent every stolen-session attack.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
What happens to concurrent tabs with the same browser session?
Tabs sharing the browser's session cookie generally follow the rotated session identifier;
verify custom clients and in-flight requests.

pages.title: How should logout behave for a session application?
pages.fullText:
SESSIONS, LOGIN, LOGOUT AND REMEMBER-ME Q028 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 028
How should logout behave for a session application?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Use the framework logout flow to clear security state and invalidate the
relevant session, with CSRF protection for state-changing browser behavior.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Browser identity ➜ Session + cookie policy ➜ Next-request proof
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
<form method="post" action="/logout">
<!-- Include framework CSRF token field. -->
<button>Log out</button>
</form>
Why it works: The exact endpoint and success response can be configured. Cookie cleanup and
remember-me cleanup should match your setup. A GET route that merely displays confirmation
differs from the actual state-changing logout.
⚠ Interview trap: Local logout does not automatically log out an identity provider.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How does logout differ for self-contained bearer tokens?
Session logout invalidates the server session and clears authentication; JWT logout needs
short lifetimes or a separate revocation mechanism.

SESSIONS, LOGIN, LOGOUT AND REMEMBER-ME Q029 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 029
What is remember-me authentication and what is its
limitation?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It provides longer-lived browser reauthentication through a cookie-based
policy; it is weaker than fresh full authentication for sensitive actions.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Browser credentials ➜ Persistent session ➜ Logout / expiry
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Remember-me cookie -> restored identity
Sensitive password change -> require fresh authentication/MFA
// fullyAuthenticated can distinguish supported remember-me state.
Why it works: Token storage, expiry, theft detection and revocation differ by implementation. Do not
confuse remember-me with an OAuth refresh token. Keep sensitive-operation assurance explicit.
⚠ Interview trap: A remembered identity is not proof the password was just supplied.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would password changes affect remember-me tokens?
Invalidate or rotate persistent remember-me tokens when passwords change; server-side
token records are easier to revoke.

pages.title: How are authorization request rules selected?
pages.fullText:
HTTP AUTHORIZATION AND CHAIN BOUNDARIES Q031 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 031
How are authorization request rules selected?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
The first matching authorization rule in the selected chain is applied; order
specific rules before broad ones.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Actor + resource ➜ Permission + owner rule ➜ Allowed / denied
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
.requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
.requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
.anyRequest().authenticated());
Why it works: A broad permitAll placed first can make narrower restrictions unreachable. This rule
ordering is separate from security-chain ordering. Inspect both levels when a protected route
unexpectedly succeeds.
⚠ Interview trap: anyRequest is normally the terminal fallback rule.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would you test an unexpected route?
Test a new unmatched URL and an unexpected HTTP method; require a specific allow rule
or a deny-all fallback.

pages.fullText:
HTTP AUTHORIZATION AND CHAIN BOUNDARIES Q032 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 032
How does permitAll differ from ignoring security
processing?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
permitAll allows authorization within the chain; ignoring bypasses the
selected security protections for that request.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Request + method ➜ Matcher + authority ➜ Allow / deny
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
/public/** -> permitAll, security headers can still apply
Ignored path -> security chain bypassed for that path
Why it works: Prefer permitAll when public routes should retain exploit protection and headers. An
ignored route cannot rely on that chain to populate or protect its context. Review static-resource
policy deliberately.
⚠ Interview trap: 'Public' need not mean 'outside all security filters'.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
Why can a permitted POST still fail CSRF?
permitAll skips authorization denial, not CSRF validation for unsafe browser requests; a
POST can still be rejected.

pages.title: QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
pages.fullText:
HTTP AUTHORIZATION AND CHAIN BOUNDARIES Q033 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 033
Why should authorization consider the HTTP
method?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Read and write operations on the same path can require different
permissions.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Actor + resource ➜ Permission + owner rule ➜ Allowed / denied
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/orders/**").hasAuthority("orders:read")
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/orders/**").hasAuthority("orders:create")
.anyRequest().denyAll()
Why it works: Route shape alone does not distinguish a safe read from a modifying operation.
Handle preflight and other dispatches in their correct mechanism. Backend ownership checks still
apply.
⚠ Interview trap: Method-specific rules do not prevent unsafe business semantics inside GET.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
What permission should a bulk export require?
Bulk export should require a dedicated, least-privilege permission plus row/tenant filtering
and audit logging.

pages.title: What is deny-by-default and why use it?
pages.fullText:
HTTP AUTHORIZATION AND CHAIN BOUNDARIES Q034 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 034
What is deny-by-default and why use it?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Unspecified operations are refused rather than accidentally opened as the
application grows.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Request + method ➜ Matcher + authority ➜ Allow / deny
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
.requestMatchers("/health/public").permitAll()
.requestMatchers("/api/orders/**").hasAuthority("orders:read")
.anyRequest().denyAll());
Why it works: New endpoints need an explicit policy instead of inheriting unrestricted access. Test
framework endpoints, error dispatches and static paths that should work intentionally. Deny-by-
default is useful only if rules express the real operation semantics.
⚠ Interview trap: An overly broad allowed prefix can still expose new sensitive routes.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would a new endpoint fail a security regression test?
A new endpoint should fail closed under anyRequest().denyAll(), and a regression test
should assert anonymous and underprivileged denial.

pages.title: How do authenticated and fullyAuthenticated differ?
pages.fullText:
HTTP AUTHORIZATION AND CHAIN BOUNDARIES Q035 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 035
How do authenticated and fullyAuthenticated differ?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
authenticated can include supported remembered authentication;
fullyAuthenticated excludes anonymous and remember-me authentication
states.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Request + method ➜ Matcher + authority ➜ Allow / deny
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Public page -> permitAll
Account overview -> authenticated
Sensitive credential change -> fresh assurance policy
Why it works: A helper expresses one trust distinction, not a complete MFA or recent-login policy. If
recent authentication is required, check the actual assurance and time evidence from a trusted
mechanism.
⚠ Interview trap: fullyAuthenticated is not universally equivalent to MFA.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
Where would step-up authentication be recorded?
Record assurance level and authentication time in trusted session/token context, then
enforce step-up on sensitive actions.

INTERVIEW QUESTION 036
How should ERROR and ASYNC dispatches be
considered?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Security matching can include dispatcher types, so test secondary
dispatches and intentionally choose their access policy.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Observe symptom ➜ Locate trust boundary ➜ Repair and retest
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
.requestMatchers(DispatcherType.ERROR, DispatcherType.FORWARD).permitAll()
// Illustrative choice: review error/forward behavior before adopting.
Why it works: An original authorized request can encounter another check during rendering or
error handling. Avoid masking the original error with an unexpected denial, while ensuring forwards
cannot reach sensitive operations unchecked.
⚠ Interview trap: Blanket dispatch exemptions require an actual boundary analysis.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would a protected forwarded handler be tested?
Test FORWARD/ERROR/ASYNC dispatches to protected handlers, checking that
authorization still prevents forbidden effects.

pages.title: How is method security enabled?
pages.fullText:
METHOD AND OBJECT-LEVEL SECURITY Q037 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 037
How is method security enabled?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Use @EnableMethodSecurity and supported annotations on eligible Spring-
managed method boundaries.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Actor + object ➜ Ownership check ➜ Guard business effect
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
class MethodSecurityConfig {}
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('orders:approve')")
public void approve(long id) { /* domain work */ }
Why it works: The call must cross the advice boundary. Enabling servlet request security does not
automatically enable every method-security annotation. Check proxy eligibility and invocation paths.
⚠ Interview trap: Self-invocation can bypass ordinary proxy advice.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
Which callers might bypass a controller's URL rule?
Service methods invoked by jobs, messages, or other controllers can bypass a particular
controller URL rule; enforce reusable business authorization.

pages.title: How do @PreAuthorize and @PostAuthorize differ?
pages.fullText:
METHOD AND OBJECT-LEVEL SECURITY Q038 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 038
How do @PreAuthorize and @PostAuthorize differ?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
PreAuthorize checks before invocation; PostAuthorize checks afterward and
can inspect the returned object.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Actor + object ➜ Ownership check ➜ Guard business effect
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
@PostAuthorize("returnObject.owner == authentication.name")
public OrderView load(long id) { return store.loadView(id); }
Why it works: Post-authorization can prevent returning a result but cannot undo arbitrary side
effects already performed. Use prechecks or authoritative tenant-scoped operations for modifying
methods. Query-level ownership can also avoid loading unrelated data.
⚠ Interview trap: PostAuthorize is unsuitable as the only guard on an irreversible write.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
What happens to a null or Optional return shape?
A null/empty Optional result may affect the expression; define and test the actual return
shape, especially for @PostAuthorize.

METHOD AND OBJECT-LEVEL SECURITY Q039 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 039
What do @PreFilter and @PostFilter do?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
They filter supported input or output collections according to per-element
expressions, rather than making every element safe automatically.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Incoming request ➜ Ordered chain + filter ➜ Handler or 401/403
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
@PostFilter("filterObject.owner == authentication.name")
public List<OrderView> list() { return store.findCandidateViews(); }
Why it works: Filtering can remove unauthorized results, but loading all candidates may be
expensive and counts/pagination can leak or mislead. Prefer appropriately scoped queries when
possible. The returned type must be supported for the selected annotation.
⚠ Interview trap: Filtering an in-memory page can produce inconsistent totals.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would row ownership be enforced in the query?
Apply tenant and ownership constraints in the database query itself, not only by filtering a
large returned collection.

INTERVIEW QUESTION 040
How can custom permission logic be used in
expressions?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
Delegate complex decisions to a trusted policy bean or supported
permission evaluator rather than packing them into fragile strings.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Actor + object ➜ Ownership check ➜ Guard business effect
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
@PreAuthorize("@orderPolicy.canRead(authentication, #id)")
public OrderView read(long id) { return store.read(id); }
Why it works: The policy checks the trusted identity and authoritative ownership. Preserve method
parameter names or use a supported explicit naming approach. Keep policy decisions testable
without granting privileges from request input.
⚠ Interview trap: Repeating a remote permission lookup can create latency and availability
coupling.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
What data should a policy cache include?
Include principal, tenant, effective permissions, resource/version, and policy-version/expiry
in the cache key or invalidate on change.

pages.title: What is IDOR or broken object-level authorization?
pages.fullText:
METHOD AND OBJECT-LEVEL SECURITY Q042 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 042
What is IDOR or broken object-level authorization?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It occurs when changing an object identifier lets a caller access another
user's or tenant's resource without the required permission check.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Actor + resource ➜ Permission + owner rule ➜ Allowed / denied
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
GET /invoices/7 -> caller-owned invoice
GET /invoices/8 -> another tenant's invoice
Query: WHERE id=:id AND tenant_id=:trustedTenant
Why it works: A valid role is not sufficient if ownership is part of the contract. Derive tenant identity
from trusted authentication, then enforce it in lookup and modification. Avoid distinguishing
forbidden existence where policy forbids disclosure.
⚠ Interview trap: Random UUIDs are not an authorization policy.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How would a message consumer enforce the same rule?
A consumer must validate the trusted initiator/tenant and resource ownership before
executing a message's business effect.

pages.title: What is CSRF?
pages.fullText:
CSRF AND BROWSER CREDENTIAL BEHAVIOR Q043 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 043
What is CSRF?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
It is unwanted state-changing action induced through a victim's browser
using credentials the browser supplies automatically.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Browser request ➜ CSRF / origin policy ➜ No forbidden write
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
Victim logged in with session cookie
Malicious site triggers a modifying request
Browser may attach victim's credential -> server needs CSRF defense
Why it works: The attacker need not read the response to cause the action. CSRF tokens establish a
request-bound proof unavailable to an unrelated origin under the expected browser model. XSS can
undermine that model.
⚠ Interview trap: CORS restrictions alone do not prevent every cross-site submission.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
Why must GET avoid state-changing semantics?
GET must remain safe: browsers and intermediaries can prefetch or repeat it, so do not
charge, delete or modify on GET.

pages.title: How does a synchronizer CSRF token help?
pages.fullText:
CSRF AND BROWSER CREDENTIAL BEHAVIOR Q044 / 144
INTERVIEW QUESTION 044
How does a synchronizer CSRF token help?
EXPLAIN IN ONE BREATH
The server checks a token associated with the legitimate session/request
flow for unsafe methods, in addition to the automatically sent credential.
QUICK VISUAL — WHAT HAPPENS?
Browser request ➜ CSRF / origin policy ➜ No forbidden write
ORIGINAL EXAMPLE / CODE
<form method="post" action="/orders">
<input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="SERVER_TOKEN">
</form>
Why it works: Use the actual framework-provided parameter/header name and token, not the literal
placeholder. Keep tokens out of logs and URLs. Missing or invalid tokens follow the CSRF failure
path.
⚠ Interview trap: A static shared token provides no meaningful per-client binding.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION — ANSWERED
How does a JavaScript client obtain the token safely?
Expose a token safely via approved token endpoint or cookie/header mechanism, then
send it in a request header; guard against XSS.
