An order page composes one order with payment status. A monthly revenue report uses a governed 
reporting store instead of issuing a remote join for every customer across live services.

Answer → Include source watermark/version, lag/last updated timestamps, reconciliation counts

pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 15 · Q074/120
CQRS, projections and caching
Q074. How does cache-aside work, and where
do races appear?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Cache-aside loads from the owner on a miss and caches the result. Concurrent updates
may race with an old load that writes stale data back.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Read the cache, load from the
authoritative store on a miss
and populate it...
➜
Tenant A's product price is
cached under tenant A and
product ID
➜ A TTL limits exposure duration;it is not strong consistency
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Tenant A's product price is cached under tenant A and product ID. After a price update, invalidation may 
race with an earlier read; a version check prevents an older value from replacing a newer entry.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
// Always scope cache keys to the verified tenant.
String key = tenantId + ":" + productId;
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
How would you test the stale-repopulation race?
Answer → Pause a cache miss after its DB read, update DB and invalidate, then allow stale load to
populate. Assert version checks or invalidation prevent stale replacement.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A TTL limits exposure duration; it is not strong consistency.

pages.title: CQRS, projections and caching Q075. How do you prevent a cache stampede?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 15 · Q075/120
CQRS, projections and caching
Q075. How do you prevent a cache stampede?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
A cache stampede is many identical misses rebuilding one expensive value. Coalesce
loads, bound concurrency and spread expiration times.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Reduce simultaneous misses
with per-key single-flight
loading, controlled...
➜ Ten replicas see a popularentry expire ➜ A lock with a long wait canturn a stampede into aqueueing outage
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Ten replicas see a popular entry expire. Jitter spreads expiries, while a bounded loader protects the 
database. Optional catalog data can serve a marked stale entry during refresh; authorization cannot use 
the same policy casually.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
// Only one refresh per key; bounded stale fallback.
computeIfAbsent(key, ignored -> loadFromOwner());
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
What happens when refresh fails repeatedly?
Answer → After repeated refresh failure, use a bounded stale-serve policy where safe, exponential
retry, breaker and per-key admission; never overload the origin.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A lock with a long wait can turn a stampede into a queueing outage.
MY ONE-LINE RECAP ______________________________________________________

microservices?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
OAuth is an authorization framework; OIDC adds login identity; JWT is one token format.
A valid signature alone does not authorize a business action.

access token

pages.title: Why must services enforce authorization even behind a gateway?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 16 · Q077/120
Security across service boundaries
Q077. Why must services enforce authorization
even behind a gateway?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
A gateway may authenticate a caller, but only the domain service knows whether that
caller owns a particular order or tenant resource.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
The gateway's policy may
authenticate requests or
protect routes, but...
➜
An authenticated user can
reach GET /orders/id, but the
order owner must verify...
➜
A user-controlled tenant
header must not override
verified tenant authority
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
An authenticated user can reach GET /orders/id, but the order owner must verify that this user or 
service may read that tenant's particular order. Route-level login is insufficient.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
if (!resource.tenantId().equals(currentTenant))
    throw new AccessDeniedException("tenant");
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
How would you test cross-tenant resource access?
Answer → Call with tenant A's token against tenant B's ID and assert denial across get/update/
export endpoints, including cached and batch paths.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A user-controlled tenant header must not override verified tenant authority.

pages.title: What do mTLS and workload identity provide?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 16 · Q078/120
Security across service boundaries
Q078. What do mTLS and workload identity
provide?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
mTLS authenticates connected workloads and encrypts transport. It does not prove the
end user's permission to read a specific invoice.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
mTLS authenticates peers at
the transport boundary and
encrypts traffic;...
➜
Only an approved order
workload can establish the
allowed payment connection
➜
Encryption does not prove that
the requested business action
is authorized
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Only an approved order workload can establish the allowed payment connection. The payment service 
still checks whether the request is permitted for the tenant and operation being charged.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
How do you rotate credentials without interrupting all traffic?
Answer → Overlap old and new certificates/credentials, rotate connections gradually, verify new
handshakes, then retire old trust material without restarting everything at once.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  Encryption does not prove that the requested business action is authorized.

pages.title: When should client credentials or user- token propagation be used?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 16 · Q079/120
Security across service boundaries
Q079. When should client credentials or user-
token propagation be used?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Client credentials identify service-to-service work; delegated user context is used only
when user identity truly matters. Never blindly forward every token.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Client credentials represent an
application's own authority ➜ A nightly settlement job usesservice authority ➜ Do not invent trusted claims inheaders unless the receivingboundary...
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
A nightly settlement job uses service authority. A user cancelling an order carries user context under a 
supported delegation contract, while the downstream service independently verifies its permission.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
// Audit both identities:
log(workloadId, userSubject, tenantId, operationId);
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
How do you audit both the calling workload and the end user?
Answer → Record workload identity and authorized end-user subject separately with trace ID,
tenant, action, decision and outcome; minimize sensitive token logging.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  Do not invent trusted claims in headers unless the receiving boundary verifies them.

pages.title: How do you reduce secret leakage and server-side request forgery?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 16 · Q080/120
Security across service boundaries
Q080. How do you reduce secret leakage and
server-side request forgery?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Keep secrets out of code/logs and stop services from fetching arbitrary URLs on behalf
of clients. Validate destinations and network egress.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Use approved secret storage,
restrict diagnostic exposure
and redact...
➜
A document service accepts
object IDs mapped to
approved storage, not
arbitrary...
➜
String-prefix URL checks can
be bypassed by parsing or
redirect behavior
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
A document service accepts object IDs mapped to approved storage, not arbitrary URLs that can target 
internal admin services. Access tokens and signed URLs are excluded from ordinary request logs.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Which egress controls would support the application checks?
Answer → Use egress allowlists, private DNS/VPC rules, proxy filtering, metadata endpoint
protection and restrictive workload network policies alongside URL validation.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  String-prefix URL checks can be bypassed by parsing or redirect behavior.

tell you?

Logs explain events, metrics show trends and alerts, and traces join the path of one

metrics aggregate
measurements over...

// Add traces + age-of-pending-order metrics.

Q082. How is trace context propagated across
services?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Trace context follows requests through services and messages so spans can be
correlated. A business operation ID must outlive trace retention.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Instrumentation injects and
extracts a supported context,
commonly W3C...

Order calls inventory with
trace context and publishes an
event with causation...
➜
A user-controlled baggage
field is not trusted
authorization or unlimited...

Order calls inventory with trace context and publishes an event with causation metadata. A later worker 
starts a causally linked processing span while retaining order ID for business recovery.

When is a span link more appropriate than a single parent?
Answer → Use a span link when batch or asynchronous work has multiple triggering contexts, or
when the processing relationship is not a simple single-parent child.

metadata.

● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 17 · Q083/120
Observability and reliability objectives
Q083. What are SLI, SLO, SLA and an error
budget?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
An SLI is what you measure, an SLO is your target, an SLA is a customer agreement, and
an error budget permits limited misses.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
An SLI measures a chosen
service outcome; an SLO sets
its target over a...
➜ For eligible checkout attempts,99 ➜ A process uptime metric is notnecessarily a checkout-successSLI
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
For eligible checkout attempts, 99.9% must complete successfully under one second over a rolling 30-
day window. Invalid customer input may be excluded by a documented policy, not hidden after an 
incident.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
SLI = goodBusinessOperations / eligibleOperations
errorBudget = (1 - SLO) * eligibleOperations
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
What should count as good when work completes asynchronously?
Answer → Count durable acceptance plus completion within the published window as good when
the product promises final completion; report pending/out-of-window separately.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A process uptime metric is not necessarily a checkout-success SLI.

Q084. How does error-budget burn-rate
alerting work?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Burn-rate compares how fast current bad events use up the allowed error budget. Fast
burn needs quick action; slower burn needs investigation.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Burn rate compares the
observed bad-event fraction
with the fraction...
➜ With a 99 ➜ Percentile latency and requestsuccess can require separate
SLIs
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
With a 99.9% objective, the allowed bad fraction is 0.1%. A sustained 1% bad fraction has a burn rate of 
10, consuming budget ten times faster than the target rate.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
What action should an alert trigger, and who owns it?
Answer → Page the on-call owner for rapid user-impacting burn with a runbook; slow burn can
create an actionable ticket and pause risky releases.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  Percentile latency and request success can require separate SLIs.

pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 18 · Q089/120
Testing distributed contracts and failures
Q089. Which failure tests are essential for
event processing?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Crash testing exposes lost updates, duplicate effects and offset races that normal
integration tests miss.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Test duplicate deliveries,
crashes before and after
business commit,...
➜ A payment double records acharge but drops its response ➜ Happy-path exactly-onceassertions do not coverambiguous outcomes
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
A payment double records a charge but drops its response. A repeated request with the same key 
returns that recorded charge; a test fails if the order creates a second charge identity.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
// Crash after DB commit, before message/offset ACK.
// Replay should create one ledger effect.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Where would you inject a crash to expose early offset commits?
Answer → Commit the Kafka offset before writing the business database result, kill the consumer
and restart. The test should show why that order can lose an effect.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  Happy-path exactly-once assertions do not cover ambiguous outcomes.

● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 18 · Q090/120

Q090. How should chaos and load tests be
designed?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Chaos tests test named failure hypotheses; load tests measure capacity under known
conditions. Keep abort criteria and measurable customer impact.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Choose a bounded experiment,
a hypothesis and a
measurable steady-state...
➜
Delay the recommendation
dependency while checking
that purchase success
remains...
➜
A random outage without a
hypothesis often produces little
learning
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Delay the recommendation dependency while checking that purchase success remains within its 
objective and recommendation concurrency stays bounded. Restore it and verify queue and circuit 
recovery.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
What would falsify your claimed isolation between workloads?
Answer → Show recommendations saturating checkout connections or raising checkout error rate
despite the claimed bulkhead; that falsifies the isolation claim.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A random outage without a hypothesis often produces little learning.

pages.title: How do startup, readiness and liveness probes differ in Kubernetes?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 19 · Q092/120
Deployment, Kubernetes and schema changes
Q092. How do startup, readiness and liveness
probes differ in Kubernetes?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Startup gates initial initialization; readiness controls traffic; liveness requests restart when
local process recovery is likely to help.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Startup probes allow
initialization before other
configured probes take over
➜ A slow schema warm-up needsstartup handling ➜ Use the selected Kubernetesversion and inspect actualprobe and routing...
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
A slow schema warm-up needs startup handling. A wedged process may fail liveness. A local inability to 
serve the API may fail readiness while the team repairs it without unnecessary restart churn.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
startupProbe -> initialization complete
readinessProbe -> admit traffic
livenessProbe -> local restart is helpful
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Why is an external payment outage usually a poor liveness check?
Answer → A remote payment outage is outside the pod's repair control. Restarting every pod
increases load and hides an otherwise recoverable dependency incident.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  Use the selected Kubernetes version and inspect actual probe and routing behavior.

pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 19 · Q094/120
Deployment, Kubernetes and schema changes
Q094. What is an expand-contract database
migration?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Expand-contract adds compatible schema first, runs old and new code together, backfills,
then removes obsolete fields after verification.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
First add compatible structure,
then deploy code that can
coexist with old...
➜
Add delivery_region beside
region, backfill safely, update
readers and writers in...
➜
A destructive migration can
make an otherwise healthy old
image unusable
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Add delivery_region beside region, backfill safely, update readers and writers in stages, verify 
completeness, then remove region in a later release after compatibility checks.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
ADD COLUMN new_status TEXT NULL;
-- Backfill in batches, switch readers, contract later.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
How do you prevent a backfill from overwriting a newer live update?
Answer → Read the current row version during backfill and update conditionally; never let an old
snapshot overwrite a newer application write.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A destructive migration can make an otherwise healthy old image unusable.

Q095. What does graceful shutdown require for
a service?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Graceful shutdown stops admitting new work, drains or transfers accepted work and
releases resources under a deadline.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Stop or reduce new work, allow
permitted in-flight work to
complete within...
➜
An instance becomes unready,
drains HTTP requests, finishes
or safely abandons a...
➜
A shutdown hook alone does
not make accepted in-memory
jobs durable
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
An instance becomes unready, drains HTTP requests, finishes or safely abandons a claimed batch, and 
releases resources. Unfinished durable jobs can resume elsewhere after their claim expires.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e

spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Which work must be recoverable if the process dies immediately?
Answer → Every uncommitted operation, accepted durable job, outbox intent and unacknowledged
message must be retryable or reconciled after an immediate crash.

● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 20 · Q096/120

Q096. How do you estimate concurrency and
capacity?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Concurrency is approximately arrival rate times time in system for stable averages.
Capacity depends on shared databases, thread pools, network and queues.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
For a stable system, Little's
Law relates average work in
the system to...
➜ At 500 requests per secondand 0 ➜ This average is not a sufficientcapacity limit or a p99 latencyguarantee
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
At 500 requests per second and 0.2 seconds average residence, average in-flight work is about 100. If 
residence rises to one second, the same stable rate implies about 500 in flight.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
// Stable-load approximation (not a capacity guarantee):
inFlight = arrivalRatePerSec * avgLatencySeconds;
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
What happens if arrival rate exceeds sustainable service rate?
Answer → If incoming work exceeds sustainable completion rate, queued requests and latency
grow until throttling, scaling, rejection or resource failure occurs.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  This average is not a sufficient capacity limit or a p99 latency guarantee.

Q101. What is the strangler-fig migration
pattern?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
The strangler pattern routes selected capabilities away from a legacy system to new
implementations over time. It needs careful ownership cutover.

capabilities gradually through
a controlled routing...

requests go to an extracted

A supposedly temporary

permanent coupling

path.

pages.title: How would you design checkout and order acceptance?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 22 · Q106/120
Business architecture case studies
Q106. How would you design checkout and
order acceptance?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Checkout coordinates Orders, Inventory and Payment through durable state transitions,
stable operation IDs and recoverable commands.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Separate order identity,
inventory reservation and
payment authority
➜
Order o-71 moves from
ACCEPTED to RESERVED to
PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED to
CONFIRMED
➜
Success is a business state, not
simply an HTTP 200 from the
orchestrator
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Order o-71 moves from ACCEPTED to RESERVED to PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED to CONFIRMED. A 
definitive payment rejection releases reservation r-8 and ends in REJECTED; an unknown payment 
outcome follows reconciliation instead.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
ACCEPTED -> RESERVE -> PAYMENT_PENDING -> CONFIRMED
// Every state transition is durably recorded.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Where does the workflow store each transition and pending command?
Answer → Store each workflow state and pending outbox command in one local transaction; a
relay publishes the command and a worker advances state conditionally.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  Success is a business state, not simply an HTTP 200 from the orchestrator.

Notifications should be accepted as durable jobs, processed asynchronously and retried

THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Loan origination can separate application intake, offers, underwriting and partner

pages.title: How would you prevent double booking in a reservation system?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 22 · Q110/120
Business architecture case studies
Q110. How would you prevent double booking in
a reservation system?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Prevent double booking using one authoritative conditional reservation/write for a slot,
with unique identity and lifecycle transitions.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Enforce the seat, room or slot
invariant at the authoritative
store through...
➜ Seat s-9 is held underreservation r-2 until its expiry ➜ A distributed cache lock alonemay not protect theauthoritative booking...
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Seat s-9 is held under reservation r-2 until its expiry. A confirmation succeeds only while r-2 is still the 
valid hold. If payment arrives late, reconcile payment and availability instead of silently granting the seat 
twice.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
UPDATE seats SET state='CONFIRMED'
 WHERE id=:id AND state='HELD' AND version=:v;
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
How do expiry and confirmation avoid racing into two final states?
Answer → Use conditional version/state updates so only ACTIVE may become CONFIRMED or
EXPIRED. The winning transaction defines the final state; retries return it.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A distributed cache lock alone may not protect the authoritative booking write.

pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 23 · Q111/120
Production diagnosis and recovery
Q111. How would you diagnose rising 504
responses?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
504s can come from queue waits, pool exhaustion, slow dependencies or improper
deadlines. Trace before changing timeouts or adding retries.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Find where the deadline
expires, then separate
upstream queueing,...
➜
Traces show 700 ms waiting
for payment connections
before a 300 ms remote call
➜ The layer returning 504 maynot be the layer causing delay
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Traces show 700 ms waiting for payment connections before a 300 ms remote call. Pool utilization and 
queue growth support a saturation diagnosis; a provider latency chart alone would miss it.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
504 -> trace -> pool wait -> downstream latency
// Never create a fresh payment ID during repair.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
What repair reduces waiting without increasing double-charge risk?
Answer → Reduce queues with bounded admission, isolate slow dependencies and recover
unknown charges by stable operation ID. Never blindly retry using a new payment identity.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  The layer returning 504 may not be the layer causing delay.

pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 23 · Q112/120
Production diagnosis and recovery
Q112. How would you investigate duplicate
business effects?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Duplicate effects often come from retries, broker redelivery or crashes between commit
and acknowledgement. Trace the operation identity end-to-end.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Trace the stable operation or
event identity across producer,
relay,...
➜
Two charges share one
checkout ID but different
payment operation IDs
➜
Exactly-once broker
processing does not cover new
logical identities
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Two charges share one checkout ID but different payment operation IDs. The caller generated a new 
key after each timeout, so consumer deduplication alone cannot repair the cause.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
// Regression: kill after ledger COMMIT, before ACK.
// Replay should not credit twice.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Which test should permanently reproduce the incident's crash window?
Answer → Keep a regression test that forces the exact crash after the business commit but before
the acknowledgement, then replays and asserts one durable effect.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  Exactly-once broker processing does not cover new logical identities.

pages.title: How would you diagnose a growing Kafka backlog?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 23 · Q113/120
Production diagnosis and recovery
Q113. How would you diagnose a growing Kafka
backlog?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Kafka lag rises when arrival exceeds throughput or one partition/message stalls. Check
per-partition progress and downstream delays.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Compare production rate,
processing rate, record age
and per-partition lag
➜
One partition contains a hot
tenant and lags while five
partitions are idle
➜
Low committed-offset lag can
hide an unbounded in-process
task backlog
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
One partition contains a hot tenant and lags while five partitions are idle. Additional group members 
cannot split that traditional partition assignment; key design or workload isolation needs review.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
// Keep aggregate events on a stable partition key.
producer.send(topic, aggregateId, event);
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
How would you rebalance the workload without breaking order guarantees?
Answer → Use stable aggregate keys, partition-aware scaling and controlled handover or
sequence gates; do not randomly redistribute events that require order.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  Low committed-offset lag can hide an unbounded in-process task backlog.

pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 23 · Q114/120
Production diagnosis and recovery
Q114. Why might every replica restart during a
dependency outage?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
A dependency outage can make readiness/liveness fail on all pods, triggering traffic
withdrawal or restart storms.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
A liveness policy may treat a
shared downstream outage as
a restart-worthy...
➜
All catalog Pods fail liveness
when recommendation is
down, even though catalog...
➜ Do not disable probes blindly;repair their failure model
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
All catalog Pods fail liveness when recommendation is down, even though catalog can serve product data. 
Restarting catalog cannot fix recommendation and interrupts otherwise usable traffic.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
// Do NOT make all downstream failures restart-worthy.
// Readiness and liveness answer different questions.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Which signal actually indicates that restarting this process may help?
Answer → Liveness should fail for a process-local condition a restart can repair, such as a
permanently wedged server thread loop, not just remote service unavailability.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  Do not disable probes blindly; repair their failure model.

pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 23 · Q115/120
Production diagnosis and recovery
Q115. How would you investigate stale or cross-
tenant cache results?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Stale or cross-tenant cache content can come from bad keys, unsafe invalidation or
missing authorization. Treat a data leak as security-critical.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Check the exact cache key,
trusted tenant context,
permissions, value...
➜
A product key omits tenant ID,
allowing tenant B to read A's
negotiated price
➜
A global cache can magnify a
local identity mistake across all
replicas
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
A product key omits tenant ID, allowing tenant B to read A's negotiated price. Adding a shorter TTL only 
shortens the leak; a scoped key and verified caller context fix the identity boundary.
IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH i l l u s t r a t i v e
cacheKey = verifiedTenantId + ":" + resourceId;
// Owner still checks permission on a miss.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Which test rejects the same resource ID under a different tenant?
Answer → Request the same order ID under a different authenticated tenant and assert a denial
even if the first tenant populated the cache.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A global cache can magnify a local identity mistake across all replicas.

Start by clarifying users, traffic, invariants, consistency and failure objectives. Then design

pages.title: What should an architecture decision record contain?
pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 24 · Q117/120

Q117. What should an architecture decision
record contain?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
An ADR records context, decision, alternatives, tradeoffs, risks, evidence and when to
revisit it—not just the chosen tool name.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Record the decision's context,
constraints, considered
options, chosen...
➜
An ADR chooses orchestration
for a five-step loan workflow
because audit and...
➜
A decision without a
measurable consequence is
difficult to evaluate later
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
An ADR chooses orchestration for a five-step loan workflow because audit and recovery need one visible 
progress record. It also documents coordinator durability, team ownership and a review point if workflow 
volume changes.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
What observation would make you reverse the decision?
Answer → Reverse it if measured lead time, latency, risk or operating cost violates the decision
criteria, or the expected ownership benefit fails to appear.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A decision without a measurable consequence is difficult to evaluate later.

pages.fullText:
● MICROSERVICES / HANDWRITTEN INTERVIEW NOTES CH 24 · Q118/120

Q118. How do you prove independent
deployability?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Independent deployment means one service can release a compatible change without
coordinated changes to others or shared data migrations.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Verify that compatible versions
coexist across APIs, events
and schemas,...
➜
Deploy a new inventory version
while old and new order
instances remain active
➜
A separate Git repository is
not evidence of runtime or
data compatibility
EXAMPLE FROM THE ORIGINAL GUIDE
Deploy a new inventory version while old and new order instances remain active. All supported 
reservation contracts pass; schema changes still allow rollback to the approved old inventory image.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Which release dependency would show that independence is still incomplete?
Answer → A release that requires consumers to deploy first, or requires a shared schema write
used by another service, shows the dependency is not yet independent.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  A separate Git repository is not evidence of runtime or data compatibility.

Q120. How do you balance architectural quality,
cost and team capability?
THE 30-SECOND ANSWER
Choose architecture that meets business guarantees with skills and budget available.
Smaller, cohesive services often beat fashionable complexity.
CONCEPT ➜ REAL EXAMPLE ➜ RISK
Optimize for the product's
goals under real staffing,
operational and cost...
➜
A team keeps three cohesive
services instead of twenty tiny
ones, invests in...
➜
More services can increase
coordination and on-call load
faster than...

A team keeps three cohesive services instead of twenty tiny ones, invests in contract tests and outbox 
recovery, and measures release lead time, incident rate and useful throughput per cost.
INTERVIEWER'S FOLLOW-UP
Which simplification would preserve the business guarantees at lower cost?
Answer → Keep cohesive modules together, replace unnecessary synchronous hops with a local
module call, or use a managed capability while preserving owned data contracts and recovery.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP:  More services can increase coordination and on-call load faster than capability.

pages.title: Define the invariant Who owns data? What must never be duplicated or lost? What state can a user see
pages.fullText:
BEFORE AN INTERVIEW
Final 60-second checklist
Define the invariant
Who owns data? What must never be duplicated or lost? What state can a user see
while work is pending?
Walk through one failure
What if the request times out after the remote effect succeeded? What if an outbox
relay crashes after send? Can a consumer replay safely?
Prove the recovery
Which database constraint, durable event, stable identity or reconciliation process
makes it correct? Which real integration test shows this?
Include the budget
What happens when requests, tasks or messages arrive faster than they finish? How
are retries, deadlines, memory and connections bounded?
Tell the truth about verification
Passing local models proves local behavior. PostgreSQL, Kafka, Kubernetes, Spring
Security and cloud recovery each require their own evidence.
MICROSERVICES / 120 INTERVIEW QUESTIONS 177

pages.title: What is system design, and how is it different from coding?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 / How to approach a system design interview QUESTION 001 / 120
What is system design, and how is it different from
coding?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
System design decides how components, data and operations work together to meet
functional and quality requirements. Coding implements behavior inside those
boundaries.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Java method: reserve(productId, quantity)
System question: who owns stock, what happens on retry,
and how do we prevent two orders selling the last unit?
WHY THIS WORKS
A correct method can still belong to an unreliable system. The design must explain storage, concurrent
requests, timeouts, recovery and ownership. A diagram is useful only when you can explain a request and
a failure through it.
COMMON PITFALL  Starting with Kafka or Kubernetes before describing the requirement usually hides the
main problem.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which invariant must survive a service crash?
Answer: Stock cannot go below zero and one seat cannot belong to two buyers. Enforce these rules
in durable database transactions.
Requirement
Service boundary
Correct behavior

CHAPTER 01 / How to approach a system design interview QUESTION 002 / 120
What should you clarify before drawing the
architecture?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Clarify the main operations, scale, latency, durability, consistency, security and scope.
Separate requirements from assumptions and confirm which user journey matters
most.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Ticket booking assumptions:
Search may be slightly stale.
A confirmed seat must have one owner.
Payment timeout must remain recoverable.
WHY THIS WORKS
These requirements allow a cached search path but require an authoritative booking transaction. Ask
about peak traffic, geographic scope and retention. When the interviewer does not provide numbers, use
explicit hypothetical values and revise the design if those values change.
COMMON PITFALL  Do not treat every endpoint as needing identical consistency or availability.

Is an unavailable checkout preferable to duplicate sales?
Answer: Usually yes: reject or delay checkout instead of making duplicate sales. Show the user a
clear retry message.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 / How to approach a system design interview QUESTION 003 / 120
How should you use a 45-minute design interview?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Spend a few minutes defining the problem, estimate the critical scale, draw a minimal
complete design, then deepen the highest-risk decisions and explain failures.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
0-5 min: scope and invariants
5-10: workload, APIs and data model
10-20: request path and architecture
20-38: concurrency, scaling and failure deep dive
38-45: tradeoffs, monitoring and evolution
WHY THIS WORKS
Treat this schedule as a practice aid. If the interviewer asks about partitioning early, adapt. A strong
answer connects decisions: the workload motivates a partition key, that key creates a hot-key risk, and
the mitigation changes cost or ordering.
COMMON PITFALL  Listing components without walking through a request does not demonstrate
correctness.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Where is the first bottleneck at ten times the traffic?
Answer: Measure database queries, hot keys, external calls and pool usage under a 10x load test;
optimize the first saturated part.

pages.title: What is the difference between high-level and low- level design?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 / How to approach a system design interview QUESTION 004 / 120
What is the difference between high-level and low-
level design?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
High-level design describes service boundaries, storage, communication and
deployment. Low-level design describes classes, interfaces, algorithms and state
transitions within a component.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
HLD: Booking service owns holds in a relational database.
LLD: enum HoldState { ACTIVE, CONFIRMED, EXPIRED }
Java command: confirm(holdId, paymentReference)
WHY THIS WORKS
The levels should agree. If the HLD promises idempotent confirmation, the LLD needs a stable command
key and duplicate handling. Avoid spending the whole interview on class diagrams when the central
challenge is distributed recovery.
COMMON PITFALL  A Java interface does not define a network reliability contract by itself.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if confirm arrives twice?
Answer: Use the same request ID. Read the stored confirmation result; never charge or reserve the
same seat again.
HLD: services
LLD: methods
Same guarantee

pages.title: What makes an architecture answer convincing?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 / How to approach a system design interview QUESTION 005 / 120
What makes an architecture answer convincing?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
State the invariant, explain the normal path, expose the failure path, quantify
assumptions and justify the tradeoff. Show how you will observe and evolve the design.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Claim: no overselling.
Mechanism: conditional stock update in one DB transaction.
Evidence: concurrent test and affected-row count.
Boundary: external payment is a separate workflow.
WHY THIS WORKS
This answer is stronger than saying that a database is ACID. It identifies the operation that enforces the
guarantee and the point at which that guarantee stops. Include one rejected alternative and why it
conflicts with the workload.
COMMON PITFALL  Avoid promising absolute availability, zero latency or universal exactly-once
processing.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you prove the invariant under concurrent requests?
Answer: Run many simultaneous purchase requests with one unit in stock; assert exactly one
reservation and stock never falls below zero.

pages.title: How do you convert daily requests into peak requests per second?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 / Requirements, estimates and capacity QUESTION 006 / 120
How do you convert daily requests into peak
requests per second?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Divide daily requests by 86,400 to get the average, then apply an explicit peak factor.
Estimate reads and writes separately because they stress different resources.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Assume 20,000,000 reads/day and 2,000,000 writes/day.
Average reads = 231.5/s; writes = 23.1/s.
At 8x peak: reads = 1,852/s; writes = 185/s.
WHY THIS WORKS
These numbers suggest a moderate write load and a read-heavy workload, but they do not determine
machine count. Benchmark the actual request path, payload, query and failure behavior. Include bursts
such as a sale opening rather than assuming a smooth average.
COMMON PITFALL  A peak multiplier is a stated assumption, not a universal industry constant.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What if a single key receives half the reads?
Answer: Cache or copy hot read-only data and use request coalescing. Do not split authoritative
stock without coordination.
Daily volume
/ 86400

pages.title: How do you estimate storage and bandwidth?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 / Requirements, estimates and capacity QUESTION 007 / 120
How do you estimate storage and bandwidth?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Multiply retained record count by average encoded size, then add indexes, replicas and
operational overhead. For bandwidth, multiply requests per second by transferred bytes.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
1,000,000 events/day x 500 bytes x 30 days = 15 GB.
Three copies: approximately 45 GB of raw event data.
2,000 responses/s x 10 KB = approximately 20 MB/s.
WHY THIS WORKS
This uses decimal units and excludes indexes, protocol overhead, compression and backups. Java heap
object size can be much larger than serialized size. A design should distinguish working-set memory,
authoritative storage, log retention and backup capacity.
COMMON PITFALL  Do not equate three replicas with three independent backups.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How much extra space is needed during rebalancing?
Answer: Allow spare capacity for temporary duplicate copies plus indexes, compaction and safety
margin. Estimate from the rebalancing plan.
Records x size
replicas
overhead

pages.title: What does Little's Law tell you about concurrency?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 / Requirements, estimates and capacity QUESTION 008 / 120
What does Little's Law tell you about concurrency?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
For a stable system, average in-flight work equals arrival rate multiplied by average
time in the system. It helps estimate concurrency and recognize queue growth.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Arrival rate = 1,000 requests/s.
Mean response time = 0.2 seconds.
Average in-flight requests = 200.
WHY THIS WORKS
The time includes waiting when your boundary includes the queue. This relationship does not directly
size a thread pool: requests may wait asynchronously or use several downstream resources. When
arrivals exceed completion capacity for a sustained period, the stable-system assumption fails and
queues grow.
COMMON PITFALL  Using p99 latency in place of the mean does not produce average concurrency.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How does a slower database change in-flight work?
Answer: For equal arrival rate, a slower database raises average in-flight work (L = arrival rate x
response time) and may grow queues.
Arrival rate
x mean latency

pages.title: Why do p95 and p99 matter more than average latency alone?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 / Requirements, estimates and capacity QUESTION 009 / 120
Why do p95 and p99 matter more than average
latency alone?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Percentiles describe how slow requests affect a portion of users. An acceptable mean
can hide a long tail caused by pauses, queueing, lock contention or slow dependencies.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
For 10,000 sorted request durations:
p99 is near the 9,900th duration.
Mean 40 ms with p99 2,000 ms can still hurt checkout.
WHY THIS WORKS
Measure the complete user operation and important internal stages. Fan-out often increases the chance
that at least one dependency is slow. Keep histogram boundaries suitable for the SLO, and aggregate
distributions rather than averaging percentile values across servers.
COMMON PITFALL  An average of instance p99 values is not the fleet p99.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Does the latency include queue and connection acquisition time?
Answer: Yes. Measure from arrival to final response, including waiting for queues, a connection and
downstream services.

pages.title: How do SLI, SLO and SLA differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 / Requirements, estimates and capacity QUESTION 010 / 120
How do SLI, SLO and SLA differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
An SLI is a measured service behavior, an SLO is its target, and an SLA is an
agreement with consequences. Define success from the user's perspective.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
SLI: successful valid checkout requests / valid requests.
SLO example: 99.9% over a rolling 30-day window.
At 1,000,000 eligible requests: budget = 1,000 failures.
WHY THIS WORKS
Document which errors count and how the denominator is measured. A request-based budget is
different from a time-based downtime allowance. A fast response containing an unusable result may still
be a failure. Use burn rate to detect rapid budget consumption.
COMMON PITFALL  Do not exclude overload failures simply to improve the reported success rate.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What signal detects a bad deploy before the monthly SLO fails?
Answer: Watch short-window error rate, p99 latency and error-budget burn during a canary; roll
back early if they spike.
Measure SLI
set SLO
alert burn

pages.title: What happens between entering a URL and reaching a Java service?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 / Networking and API contracts QUESTION 011 / 120
What happens between entering a URL and
reaching a Java service?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The client resolves a name, establishes or reuses a connection, negotiates transport
security when needed, and sends an HTTP request through routing layers to the
application.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Browser -> DNS -> edge/CDN -> load balancer
-> Spring controller -> service -> repository
WHY THIS WORKS
Connection reuse, DNS caching and HTTP version change the exact sequence. TLS protects transport
but does not replace authorization. Trace the time spent before the controller as well as inside it; a
controller log alone cannot reveal a DNS or handshake failure.
COMMON PITFALL  Assuming every request creates a fresh TCP connection gives misleading latency
estimates.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Where can a timeout occur before Java receives the request?
Answer: DNS lookup, connection setup, TLS handshake, proxy routing and the load balancer can all
time out before the controller.

DNS / TLS

pages.title: When should you choose REST, RPC or asynchronous messaging?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 / Networking and API contracts QUESTION 012 / 120
When should you choose REST, RPC or
asynchronous messaging?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Choose according to interaction semantics. Resource-oriented HTTP works well for
public APIs; typed RPC helps internal request-response calls; messages decouple
completion when the caller can accept a delayed outcome.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
POST /orders -> 202 + operation URL for long work.
GET /operations/op-42 -> PENDING or COMPLETED.
OrderCreated event -> independent notification consumer.
WHY THIS WORKS
The operation record must be durable before acknowledging accepted work. RPC still needs timeouts,
compatibility and authorization. Messaging shifts complexity to delivery, ordering, retention and status
tracking; it does not remove it.
COMMON PITFALL  Returning 202 before work is durably accepted can lose an acknowledged operation.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How can the client discover the final outcome?
Answer: Return an operation ID; support GET /operations/{id}. Optionally send a webhook or event
when finished.

durable operation
worker
status

pages.title: What does HTTP idempotency mean?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 / Networking and API contracts QUESTION 013 / 120
What does HTTP idempotency mean?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Repeating an idempotent operation has the same intended effect as performing it
once. Response codes or audit entries may differ. POST can gain application-level
idempotency through an explicit contract.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
PUT /profiles/42 with the same representation:
intended stored representation stays the same.
POST /payments with Idempotency-Key: pay-7:
the service must define duplicate handling.
WHY THIS WORKS
HTTP method semantics describe intent, not proof of an implementation. For a payment API, bind a key
to the caller and a validated request fingerprint, retain the result, and reject key reuse with different
intent. Scope and retention are part of the contract.
COMMON PITFALL  Generating a new idempotency key for every retry defeats deduplication.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What if the original payment committed but the response was lost?
Answer: A retry with the same idempotency key must return the saved outcome or current state,
not create another payment.
Same request key
one effect
saved result

pages.title: Why is cursor pagination often better than large offsets?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 / Networking and API contracts QUESTION 014 / 120
Why is cursor pagination often better than large
offsets?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A cursor seeks from a stable ordering key instead of scanning and discarding an ever-
growing prefix. A deterministic tie-breaker prevents ambiguity when timestamps are
equal.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
SELECT id, created_at FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = :customer
AND (created_at, id) < (:lastTime, :lastId)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50;
WHY THIS WORKS
An index starting with customer_id and continuing with the ordering columns supports this access
pattern. Sign or validate the cursor and bind it to the query scope. Concurrent edits can still change later
pages unless the API promises a snapshot.
COMMON PITFALL  A cursor is not an authorization credential; check ownership on every request.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What should happen when the sort key changes after page one?
Answer: Define whether pages are a snapshot. If the ordering key can change, accept documented
movement or use a stable snapshot cursor.
(lastTime,lastId)
index seek

pages.title: How do you evolve an API without breaking clients?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 / Networking and API contracts QUESTION 015 / 120
How do you evolve an API without breaking clients?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Prefer additive compatible changes, explicit semantics and a transition period. Validate
compatibility for serialized data and behavior, not just Java method signatures.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
record OrderView(String id, String status) {}
Later JSON may add estimatedDelivery.
Clients must tolerate unknown optional fields.
WHY THIS WORKS
Changing units, making a nullable value mandatory or reinterpreting a status can break clients even if
JSON still parses. Define unknown enum behavior, deprecation telemetry and rollout order. For events,
test old consumers against new producers and the reverse where required.
COMMON PITFALL  Renaming a field without a compatibility strategy can break independently deployed
services.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will you know the last old client has migrated?
Answer: Measure old-client traffic through version headers, API telemetry and compatibility
dashboards; retire only after an agreed cutoff.
Old clients
additive schema
gradual retirement

pages.title: How do vertical and horizontal scaling differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 / Scaling and load distribution QUESTION 016 / 120
How do vertical and horizontal scaling differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Vertical scaling increases resources in one machine. Horizontal scaling adds machines
and requires work and state to be distributed across them.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Vertical: a larger DB host reduces current CPU pressure.
Horizontal: four stateless Java API instances share load.
Shared bottleneck: one write-primary database.
WHY THIS WORKS
Vertical scaling can be a sensible first step with simpler operations. Horizontal scaling improves
aggregate capacity only when shared resources and partitioning permit it. Plan what happens when one
node fails and remaining nodes absorb its traffic.
COMMON PITFALL  Doubling Java instances while keeping a saturated database unchanged can increase
queueing.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can the service meet its SLO after losing one instance?
Answer: Test remaining-instance capacity using N-1 load testing. Keep SLO headroom, queues and
downstream limits in the model.
Bigger node
vertical scale
shared limit

pages.title: What makes a service stateless?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 / Scaling and load distribution QUESTION 017 / 120
What makes a service stateless?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A stateless request handler does not require a particular instance's memory to process
the next request. Durable business state and shared coordination live in appropriate
external systems.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Bad scaling assumption:
Map<String, Cart> carts = new HashMap<>();
One instance's map is invisible to another instance.
WHY THIS WORKS
Local caches and temporary request data are compatible with a stateless architecture if correctness does
not depend on them surviving or being shared. Store carts durably when the product promises recovery;
avoid making sticky sessions the only recovery mechanism.
COMMON PITFALL  Stateless does not mean that the business system has no state.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens to a cart when its instance restarts?
Answer: The cart survives only if stored in shared durable storage. An in-memory cart on one
instance disappears on restart.
Any instance
shared storage
recoverable cart

pages.title: How do load-balancing algorithms affect a design?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 / Scaling and load distribution QUESTION 018 / 120
How do load-balancing algorithms affect a design?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Round robin spreads requests by turn; least-connections considers current connection
counts; hashing provides affinity. Pick a method that matches request duration,
connection behavior and state needs.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Short HTTP calls: round robin can be adequate.
Long-lived sockets: connection-aware balancing helps.
Tenant affinity: hash routing may create hot tenants.
WHY THIS WORKS
A connection count is only a proxy for load: multiplexed connections or uneven request cost can make it
misleading. Health checks and draining are as important as the selection algorithm. Weighted routing can
support canaries or unequal capacity.
COMMON PITFALL  A healthy process can still be unable to serve a critical dependency.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will existing WebSocket connections move during deployment?
Answer: Open sockets usually remain on the old node until disconnected. Drain the node; clients
reconnect using a last-seen event cursor.

pages.title: What is the difference between a reverse proxy, gateway and service discovery?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 / Scaling and load distribution QUESTION 019 / 120
What is the difference between a reverse proxy,
gateway and service discovery?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A reverse proxy routes requests to backends; a gateway often adds API policy such as
authentication or quotas; service discovery finds the current addresses of service
instances.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Gateway: validate token and route /orders.
Discovery: locate healthy order-service endpoints.
Java service: enforce order ownership and business rules.
WHY THIS WORKS
These responsibilities may overlap in products, but explaining them separately avoids misplaced
guarantees. Discovery information can be stale, so callers still need bounded failures and endpoint
refresh. Keep critical object authorization in the owning service even if the edge authenticates users.
COMMON PITFALL  Putting every business rule in a gateway creates coupling and bypass risks.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens when discovery returns an instance that just terminated?
Answer: The call may fail or time out. Refresh discovery, retry safely within the deadline, and avoid
sending to draining nodes.

pages.title: How should autoscaling work under a traffic spike?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 / Scaling and load distribution QUESTION 020 / 120
How should autoscaling work under a traffic spike?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Scale using a signal related to the bottleneck, keep warm capacity for rapid bursts, and
bound queues while additional instances start. Scaling is part of admission control, not
a substitute for it.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Queue wait rises before CPU saturates for blocking I/O.
Scale on suitable request/queue signals.
Reject excess work when safe capacity is exhausted.
WHY THIS WORKS
Startup time, cold caches and database connection limits can make aggressive scaling harmful. Add
hysteresis and consider per-tenant fairness. For consumers, backlog age and sustainable processing rate
can matter more than CPU.
COMMON PITFALL  Creating many instances can create a simultaneous connection storm.

pages.title: When should you use a relational database?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 / Choosing storage and data models QUESTION 021 / 120
When should you use a relational database?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use it when relationships, constraints, transactions and flexible queries are central.
Start with the required queries and invariants, then assess whether one database can
support the workload.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
orders(id, customer_id, status, amount_minor)
order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity)
UNIQUE(customer_id, idempotency_key)
WHY THIS WORKS
A constraint protects the invariant across all application instances and scripts using that database.
Relational systems can scale through indexing, replicas, partitioning and workload separation, with
tradeoffs. A small service with relational data does not need a distributed database by default.
COMMON PITFALL  Enforcing uniqueness with a Java read-then-insert check is vulnerable to races.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which constraint prevents two retries creating different orders?
Answer: A unique index on (customer_id, idempotency_key), or the correct equivalent scope, rejects
duplicate order creation.

pages.title: When does a document or key-value store fit better?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 / Choosing storage and data models QUESTION 022 / 120
When does a document or key-value store fit
better?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A document store can fit aggregate-oriented reads and changing nested structures; a
key-value store fits direct lookup by key. Evaluate each product's actual consistency
and transaction capabilities.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Document: product catalog with category-specific attributes.
Key-value: sessionId -> session metadata.
Query requirement: list products by price and brand.
WHY THIS WORKS
The third requirement still needs suitable indexing or a separate query model. Embedding data can
improve reads while increasing update size and duplication. Avoid selecting a database solely because
the schema changes; a relational system can also store structured JSON where appropriate.
COMMON PITFALL  NoSQL does not mean no schema; the application still depends on data shape.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will an update to embedded shared data propagate?
Answer: Update the shared source record and rebuild or notify affected documents; version copied
fields to catch stale updates.
Key lookup

tailored index

pages.title: How do normalization and denormalization trade off?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 / Choosing storage and data models QUESTION 023 / 120
How do normalization and denormalization trade
off?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Normalization reduces duplication and update anomalies. Denormalization copies or
precomputes data to serve a known read path faster, at the cost of keeping copies
consistent.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Normalized: order references customer_id.
Historical snapshot: order stores shipping address at purchase.
Read projection: customer_order_summary stores counts.
WHY THIS WORKS
The address snapshot is part of historical business truth, not merely an optimization. A summary
projection needs an update or rebuild strategy. Name which copy is authoritative and whether the user
can tolerate projection lag.
COMMON PITFALL  Denormalized fields without ownership and repair rules become inconsistent silently.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can the summary be rebuilt from authoritative records?
Answer: Yes, if its source records and rules are retained. Replay or recompute it, then compare
totals before switching reads.
Source records

rebuild route

pages.title: How should indexes be designed for an API query?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 / Choosing storage and data models QUESTION 024 / 120
How should indexes be designed for an API query?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Design indexes around filters, ordering and selectivity, then verify with the database
query plan and representative data. Indexes trade faster reads for storage and write
maintenance.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Query: orders for one customer, newest first.
CREATE INDEX ix_order_customer_time
ON orders(customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);
WHY THIS WORKS
This index aligns with the cursor example. Whether it is used depends on data distribution, statistics and
the full query. Explain covering/index-only possibilities separately from the basic lookup; do not assume
every selected column should be indexed.
COMMON PITFALL  An index on each column separately is not equivalent to a useful composite index.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How does this index affect a high-volume insert workload?
Answer: Every insert must also maintain this index, adding write I/O and storage. Measure before
adding more indexes.
Query shape

pages.title: Why separate object storage from metadata storage?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 / Choosing storage and data models QUESTION 025 / 120
Why separate object storage from metadata
storage?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Large immutable files fit object storage, while ownership, status and queryable
metadata fit a database. This avoids routing all file bytes through the relational
database or application heap.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
DB: asset(id, owner_id, object_key, state, size_bytes)
Object store: binary bytes under a generated key.
State: UPLOADING -> SCANNING -> AVAILABLE.
WHY THIS WORKS
Access should depend on the metadata state and authorization. Because object storage and the
database are different systems, handle orphaned objects, missing objects and interrupted uploads with
cleanup and reconciliation.
COMMON PITFALL  A successful byte upload does not automatically mean the asset is safe to publish.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which job detects uploaded files whose finalization never completed?
Answer: A scheduled reconciler searches uploads stuck in UPLOADING/SCANNING, verifies object
state and completes or cleans them.
Direct upload
object store
scan
AVAILABLE

pages.title: What do ACID properties guarantee?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 / Transactions and concurrency control QUESTION 026 / 120
What do ACID properties guarantee?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Atomicity groups operations, consistency means declared invariants remain valid
through correct transactions, isolation controls concurrent interaction, and durability
concerns persistence of committed results under the system's failure model.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Transfer within one database:
BEGIN; debit account A; credit account B; COMMIT;
Both balance changes commit together or neither does.
WHY THIS WORKS
Application logic and constraints are still responsible for business correctness. Durability depends on the
database and storage configuration. A local database transaction does not automatically make an
external payment provider part of the same commit.
COMMON PITFALL  ACID consistency is different from distributed read consistency such as linearizability.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if an HTTP call succeeds before the DB transaction rolls back?
Answer: The outside call is not rolled back with the database. Record uncertainty and compensate
or reconcile safely.
DB transaction
atomic local change
commit

pages.title: How can two requests safely compete for the last stock unit?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 / Transactions and concurrency control QUESTION 027 / 120
How can two requests safely compete for the last
stock unit?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use an atomic conditional update and check the affected-row count, or use an
appropriate locking transaction. Enforce the stock change and related reservation in
one database transaction.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
UPDATE inventory
SET available = available - :qty
WHERE product_id = :id AND available >= :qty;
// require qty > 0; success means exactly one row changed
WHY THIS WORKS
A positive quantity check is essential. The database arbitrates concurrent updates; zero rows means
missing product or insufficient stock and may require a defined response. Record a stable reservation key
in the same transaction to handle duplicate commands.
COMMON PITFALL  A Java synchronized block protects only cooperating threads in one JVM.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Where will the reservation record be committed relative to the decrement?
Answer: Insert the reservation in the same transaction as the conditional decrement; commit both
or neither.
Competing requests
conditional UPDATE
one winner

pages.title: How do optimistic and pessimistic locking differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 / Transactions and concurrency control QUESTION 028 / 120
How do optimistic and pessimistic locking differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Optimistic locking detects conflicting versions at update time. Pessimistic locking
reserves access using database locks before making a decision. Choose based on
contention and transaction length.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
UPDATE orders SET status = :next, version = version + 1
WHERE id = :id AND version = :expected;
// zero rows: stale version or missing record
WHY THIS WORKS
Optimistic conflicts need a business-aware response; do not blindly retry decisions computed from stale
data. Pessimistic locks can serialize contention but increase waiting and deadlock risk. Keep locked
transactions short and acquire multiple locks in a consistent order.
COMMON PITFALL  Version checks protect only writes that participate in the protocol.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Should a stale address edit be retried or shown as a conflict?
Answer: Show a 409/conflict and ask the user to review changes; automatic retry could overwrite
another user's edit.
Read version
compare and swap
conflict

pages.title: Why can isolation level change the result of a business operation?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 / Transactions and concurrency control QUESTION 029 / 120
Why can isolation level change the result of a
business operation?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Isolation levels allow different concurrent histories. A read followed by a decision can
become invalid before commit unless the operation uses sufficient isolation, locks or
constraints.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Two doctors both read: another doctor is on call.
Each turns their own on_call flag off.
Row-version checks alone can still leave no doctor on call.
WHY THIS WORKS
This write-skew example touches different rows, so locking only the modified row is insufficient. Define
the cross-row invariant and protect it with a suitable serializable transaction or an explicit coordination
row. Database isolation names and guarantees vary by product.
COMMON PITFALL  PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED gives a new snapshot per statement, not one
immutable transaction snapshot.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What must be retried after a serialization failure?
Answer: Retry the entire transaction from a fresh read, with a bounded retry budget, not just its last
SQL statement.
Concurrent reads
cross-row invariant
serializable

pages.title: How should Java services handle transaction boundaries?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 / Transactions and concurrency control QUESTION 030 / 120
How should Java services handle transaction
boundaries?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Place the boundary around a complete local business operation, keep it short, and
understand the framework's interception rules. Avoid holding locks while waiting for
slow remote work.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
@Transactional
public void reserve(Command c) {
    inventory.decrementIfAvailable(c);
    reservations.insert(c.requestId());
}
WHY THIS WORKS
This Spring fragment assumes a transactional repository and an intercepted call. In default proxy mode,
self-invocation does not trigger transaction advice. Verify rollback rules for the exception types you use.
External calls belong in an explicit workflow with compensation or reconciliation.
COMMON PITFALL  Returning successfully after catching a business failure may accidentally commit
partial intended work.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you verify both rows roll back after an insert failure?
Answer: Force the reservation insert to fail in an integration test, then assert stock and reservation
rows are unchanged.
Local transaction
commit intent
async call

pages.title: What is the difference between replication and sharding?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 / Replication, partitioning and hot keys QUESTION 031 / 120
What is the difference between replication and
sharding?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Replication stores copies of the same data on multiple nodes. Sharding distributes
different subsets across nodes. Each shard may have its own replicas.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Shard A: customers 1-999, replicated three times.
Shard B: customers 1000-1999, replicated three times.
Replication changes copies; sharding changes placement.
WHY THIS WORKS
Replication can improve read capacity and fault recovery but does not remove the primary's write
workload in a single-leader design. Sharding spreads writes but complicates cross-shard queries,
rebalancing and transactions. Begin with partitioning only when workload or ownership requires it.
COMMON PITFALL  A replica and a shard are not interchangeable terms.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will a customer query route to the correct shard?
Answer: Hash or look up customer_id in the shard map; version routing so moves do not send
writes to two owners.
Key
shard owner
replicated copies

pages.title: Why can reading from a replica return stale data?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 / Replication, partitioning and hot keys QUESTION 032 / 120
Why can reading from a replica return stale data?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Asynchronous replication may not have applied the primary's latest commit. A
successful write on the primary does not mean every replica can immediately return it.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
User changes profile name and receives success.
Next GET is routed to a lagging replica.
Response briefly contains the old name.
WHY THIS WORKS
Possible policies include reading the primary for a session after a write, waiting for a relevant replication
position, or explicitly accepting stale data. Define read-your-writes expectations for each operation. A
routing timeout or failover can complicate a simple stickiness policy.
COMMON PITFALL  A healthy replica is not necessarily a sufficiently fresh replica.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which metric prevents reads from replicas with unacceptable lag?
Answer: Monitor replication lag in time or log position, and route consistency-sensitive reads to
primary when lag exceeds policy.
Primary commit
replica lag
stale read

pages.title: How do you choose a partition key?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 / Replication, partitioning and hot keys QUESTION 033 / 120
How do you choose a partition key?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Choose a key that distributes load while keeping common operations within one
partition. Consider traffic distribution, data size, ordering and future tenant growth.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Orders partitioned by customer_id:
customer history is local; global sales reports are not.
Events partitioned by order_id:
per-order event order is easier to preserve.
WHY THIS WORKS
The right key differs for storage and an event log. A tenant key simplifies isolation but a large tenant may
dominate one partition. Hashing improves distribution but range scans may need fan-out or a separate
index.
COMMON PITFALL  Even distribution of record counts does not guarantee even distribution of traffic.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens when one tenant grows one hundred times larger?
Answer: Split the tenant by a secondary key if feasible, dedicate it to a shard, or isolate its
workload; preserve required ordering.
Tenant key
partition
hot-tenant check

pages.title: What does consistent hashing solve?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 / Replication, partitioning and hot keys QUESTION 034 / 120
What does consistent hashing solve?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It maps keys to nodes so membership changes move a limited subset of keys instead
of remapping most keys as simple modulo hashing can. It does not solve storage
migration by itself.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Modulo routing: hash(key) % nodeCount.
Changing 4 nodes to 5 changes many destinations.
Hash ring: keys move mainly near the changed ownership range.
WHY THIS WORKS
Virtual nodes can smooth uneven placement. Rendezvous hashing is another approach: choose the node
with the highest key-node score, as demonstrated in the Java lab. Real changes require data movement,
versioned routing and handling old owners during transition.
COMMON PITFALL  Calling the algorithm consistent does not imply strong read consistency.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will reads work while a range is being copied?
Answer: Use a migration-aware router: check old and new owners during transition with versioned
ownership and cutover rules.
Hash ring
membership change
limited moves

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 / Replication, partitioning and hot keys QUESTION 035 / 120
How do you handle a hot key or a hot partition?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Measure whether the heat is reads, writes or fan-out, then use a mitigation that
preserves the required semantics. Options include replication, caching, batching or
partitioning the work differently.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Popular product reads: CDN/cache and local read copies.
Popular product stock: one authoritative reservation policy.
Analytics counter: split increments and later aggregate.

uncontrolled independent counters can oversell. Hot-key mitigation often sacrifices immediacy,
simplicity or exactness; state that cost explicitly.

stock and seat ownership may not.

pages.title: What does the CAP theorem actually say?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 / Consistency, CAP and consensus QUESTION 036 / 120
What does the CAP theorem actually say?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
During a network partition, a distributed read/write system cannot guarantee both
linearizable consistency and a successful response to every request reaching a non-
failing node under the theorem's model.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Two isolated replicas receive conflicting stock updates.
Option: reject some writes to protect one ordering.
Option: accept writes and later resolve divergence.
WHY THIS WORKS
Partition tolerance is not a feature you can disable while networks still fail. Outside a partition, systems
still make latency and coordination tradeoffs. Discuss the operation and its failure behavior rather than
branding a whole application as CP or AP.
COMMON PITFALL  CAP availability is not the same as a 99.9% business success SLO.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can stale catalog reads continue while stock writes are rejected?
Answer: Yes. Catalog viewing can tolerate staleness, but stock writes may be denied until one
authority is available.
Network split

unavailable writes

pages.title: How do strong, eventual and read-your-writes consistency differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 / Consistency, CAP and consensus QUESTION 037 / 120
How do strong, eventual and read-your-writes
consistency differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Linearizable operations behave as if they occur in one real-time order. Eventual
consistency promises convergence under its stated assumptions. Read-your-writes
ensures a session sees its own acknowledged updates.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Stock confirmation: require an authoritative decision.
Search index: accept documented update lag.
Profile edit: preserve the editor's read-your-writes experience.
WHY THIS WORKS
These guarantees are not synonyms for isolation levels. Specify convergence conditions, allowed
staleness and what happens during failover. Session guarantees may require tokens or routing; they
should not depend on accidental connection affinity.
COMMON PITFALL  Eventual consistency alone does not specify how many seconds stale data may
remain.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if updates stop but a replica cannot reconnect?
Answer: It will remain behind until it reconnects or is rebuilt. Eventual consistency does not
promise progress during permanent isolation.
Strong write
stale projection
session read

pages.title: Why is a majority quorum useful, and what are its limits?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 / Consistency, CAP and consensus QUESTION 038 / 120
Why is a majority quorum useful, and what are its
limits?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Overlapping majorities can support coordinated decisions when used by a correct
protocol. A simple read/write quorum arithmetic rule alone does not establish
linearizability.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
N = 3; majority = 2.
Any two majorities intersect.
R + W > N is an overlap condition, not a full protocol.
WHY THIS WORKS
Version handling, concurrent writes, membership changes, failures and read paths matter. Sloppy
quorums and asynchronous application can alter guarantees. When a design requires consensus, use a
proven implementation and explain what losing quorum means for operations.
COMMON PITFALL  Reading two arbitrary replicas is not automatically a linearizable read.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can a minority serve safe writes while disconnected from the majority?
Answer: Not as quorum-committed writes. It can reject or queue requests; accepting them as final
risks divergence.
Three nodes
two voters
overlapping majority
