pages.title: What problem does Raft solve?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 / Consistency, CAP and consensus QUESTION 039 / 120
What problem does Raft solve?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Raft coordinates a replicated log through leader election, log replication and safety
rules. It lets a replicated state machine agree on committed operations under its fault
assumptions.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Three voting nodes tolerate one unavailable node.
Five voting nodes can tolerate two unavailable nodes.
No majority: progress may stop, while safety is preserved.
WHY THIS WORKS
Raft is not a replacement for business validation, partitioning or disaster recovery. Followers may be
behind; safe reads require the implementation's read protocol. Leadership alone does not authorize
arbitrary local writes without commitment rules.
COMMON PITFALL  Do not claim that electing a leader makes every follower read current.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why does a three-node cluster need two votes to make progress?
Answer: A majority of 3 is 2; any two sets of 2 nodes overlap, helping preserve one committed log
history.
Leader election
replicated log
committed entry

pages.title: Why do distributed locks need ownership checks and sometimes fencing?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 / Consistency, CAP and consensus QUESTION 040 / 120
Why do distributed locks need ownership checks
and sometimes fencing?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A lease can expire while an old holder is paused. Ownership-safe release prevents
deleting another holder's lease, while fencing lets the protected resource reject stale
owners' writes.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Holder A gets fence 7, then pauses.
Holder B gets fence 8 and writes.
Resource rejects A's later write carrying fence 7.
WHY THIS WORKS
The resource must durably enforce monotonic fencing; adding a token without checking it does nothing.
A lock service and the database can fail independently. Prefer a local database constraint or conditional
transaction when it directly enforces the invariant.
COMMON PITFALL  A TTL does not guarantee the old holder stops executing when its lease expires.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Where is the last accepted fencing token stored?
Answer: The resource (often a database row) stores the highest accepted token and rejects writes
with smaller tokens.
Lease owner A7
new owner B8
reject stale A7

pages.title: How do cache-aside, write-through and write- behind differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Caching and content delivery QUESTION 041 / 120
How do cache-aside, write-through and write-
behind differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Cache-aside loads on a miss and writes authoritative storage separately. Write-through
includes cache updates in the write path. Write-behind defers persistence and therefore
changes the durability contract.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Cache-aside Java sketch:
var cached = cache.get(key);
if (cached != null) return cached;
var value = repository.find(key);
cache.put(key, value); return value;
WHY THIS WORKS
This fragment omits TTL, concurrent misses and invalidation intentionally. Write-through across two
independent systems still needs failure handling; it is not automatically atomic. Write-behind is suitable
only when acknowledged data-loss and recovery risks are acceptable or durably queued.
COMMON PITFALL  A successful cache write is not proof that a durable database write succeeded.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which store remains authoritative after a cache outage?
Answer: The durable database stays authoritative in cache-aside. A cache outage must not silently
become lost data.
Cache miss
database
populate cache

pages.title: Why is cache invalidation hard?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Caching and content delivery QUESTION 042 / 120
Why is cache invalidation hard?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A read can race with a write and refill old data after invalidation. Correctness depends
on update ordering, versions, retention and the consistency the API promises.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Reader loads version 4 from DB.
Writer commits version 5 and deletes cache entry.
Reader then places version 4 back into the cache.
WHY THIS WORKS
A TTL limits how long such data may remain only if the refill and expiry semantics are controlled; it does
not prevent the race. Version-aware writes, change events and bounded stale policies can help. For
correctness-critical decisions, consult authoritative state rather than trusting a cache.
COMMON PITFALL  Deleting after a database write alone does not eliminate all stale refill races.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can the cache reject a lower-version replacement?
Answer: Yes: attach a version and update only if the incoming version is not older than the cached
version.
Reader v4
writer v5
stale refill risk

pages.title: What causes a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Caching and content delivery QUESTION 043 / 120
What causes a cache stampede and how do you
prevent it?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A popular key expires or disappears and many callers reload it simultaneously.
Coalesce misses, spread expiry times, warm critical data or serve permitted stale values
while one refresh runs.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
100 callers miss product:42.
Single-flight: one loader; 99 wait for its result.
TTL jitter: avoid thousands of unrelated keys expiring together.
WHY THIS WORKS
Single-flight in one JVM still allows one load per application instance. A distributed refresh policy adds
lease and failure complexity. Bound waiting and loading time; a stuck loader should not block the key
indefinitely. Keep stale serving separate from availability of authoritative decisions.
COMMON PITFALL  Jitter alone does not prevent a stampede on one extremely hot key.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens to waiters if the loader throws an exception?
Answer: Fail or time out the shared load, release waiting callers with an error/fallback and permit a
later bounded retry.
100 concurrent misses
single loader
one DB call

pages.title: How do TTL and eviction differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Caching and content delivery QUESTION 044 / 120
How do TTL and eviction differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
TTL makes an entry logically expire after a time policy. Eviction removes entries to
manage capacity. A cache hit policy must account for both and tolerate entries
disappearing early.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
TTL: product data is fresh for 60 seconds.
Eviction: memory pressure removes it after 5 seconds.
Next request reloads even though TTL was not reached.
WHY THIS WORKS
Choose an eviction strategy based on access patterns and budget memory for implementation overhead.
A Redis cache can use approximate LRU or LFU policies; an authoritative Redis workload requires a
different persistence and eviction discussion. Cache size should cover the useful working set, not
necessarily the whole database.
COMMON PITFALL  TTL is not a guarantee that a key will remain resident for that duration.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will you detect cache churn that overloads the database?
Answer: Track miss ratio, eviction rate, hot-key reloads and database queries. A sharp miss/load
rise signals churn.
TTL expiry
cache miss; eviction
cache miss

pages.title: When should you use a CDN and HTTP caching?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Caching and content delivery QUESTION 045 / 120
When should you use a CDN and HTTP caching?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use edge caching for cacheable content that many users request, with explicit
freshness, validators and privacy rules. It reduces origin traffic and often improves
geographic latency.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Public asset: Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400.
Versioned path: /assets/app.a83f.js.
Private account response: use an appropriate private/no-store policy.
WHY THIS WORKS
An ETag can support conditional validation. Shared-cache keys must include every relevant response
variant; authenticated or personalized content needs careful policy. Purges and versioned URLs have
different costs. Cache directives do not replace access control at the origin.
COMMON PITFALL  A cache key missing tenant or language context can return the wrong user's variant.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens when a deleted public file is still cached at an edge?
Answer: The edge may keep serving it until expiry or purge. Use purge/versioning and choose
cache TTL to match revocation needs.
Browser
CDN
origin; purge on revoke

pages.title: What is the difference between a work queue and an event log?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 / Queues, logs and streaming QUESTION 046 / 120
What is the difference between a work queue and
an event log?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A work queue commonly distributes tasks among workers. A retained event log
supports replay and independent consumer positions. Product capabilities overlap, so
describe the required behavior.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Queue use: send one email task to a worker.
Log use: OrderCreated consumed by billing and analytics.
Each log consumer group tracks its own progress.
WHY THIS WORKS
A log can also distribute work within a group, while some queues retain history. Replay changes the
operational contract: old events must remain interpretable and side effects must not be repeated
accidentally. Decide retention, acknowledgement and poison-message handling.
COMMON PITFALL  A message broker is not automatically a permanent source of business truth.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can a new analytics consumer rebuild six months of history?
Answer: Only if the log still retains that data, or a snapshot/archive is available. Six months is not
guaranteed by default.
Queue: one worker
Task; Log: many groups

pages.title: How do at-most-once and at-least-once delivery differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 / Queues, logs and streaming QUESTION 047 / 120
How do at-most-once and at-least-once delivery
differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
At-most-once can lose work but avoids repeat delivery under its contract. At-least-once
can redeliver work, so effects need deduplication or natural idempotency.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Consumer updates DB, then crashes before acknowledging.
Broker redelivers the event after recovery.
Consumer must avoid applying the business effect twice.
WHY THIS WORKS
Acknowledging before an effect risks loss; acknowledging afterward risks duplication. A unique event
key stored in the same database transaction as the effect can close the local duplication window. It does
not make a remote side effect atomic with that transaction.
COMMON PITFALL  Duplicate transport delivery and duplicate business effect are different
measurements.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Where is the dedup marker committed relative to the effect?
Answer: Commit the dedup marker and local business update in the SAME database transaction so
neither can happen alone.
Apply effect + dedup ID
commit
ack

CHAPTER 10 / Queues, logs and streaming QUESTION 048 / 120
What ordering can a partitioned log provide?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A partition can maintain a sequence of records. Ordering across partitions or across
independently produced operations requires additional coordination or explicit business
versioning.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Kafka key = orderId.
Events for one key normally route to one partition.
Different orders may be processed concurrently.
WHY THIS WORKS
Producer configuration and concurrent producers also affect the business order represented by the log.
Consumers that dispatch to parallel workers can complete effects out of order even when delivery order
is stable. Sequence numbers can detect gaps and obsolete updates.
COMMON PITFALL  Partition delivery order does not guarantee ordered completion in a multithreaded
consumer.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How should a consumer handle version 8 arriving after version 9?
Answer: Ignore older version 8 after 9, or repair a detected gap; do not apply state transitions
backward.

ordered events

pages.title: How should retries and dead-letter handling work for consumers?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 / Queues, logs and streaming QUESTION 049 / 120
How should retries and dead-letter handling work
for consumers?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Retry transient failures within a bounded policy, preserve the needed order, and isolate
permanently failing records with enough context for investigation and safe replay.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Event e-17 fails validation permanently.
Record event ID, schema version and reason.
Move to a controlled failure workflow; do not retry forever.
WHY THIS WORKS
A retry topic can let later events overtake earlier ones. If an aggregate requires strict order, pause or
quarantine that aggregate rather than silently skipping its state transition. A dead-letter store needs
owners, alerts, retention and a replay procedure.
COMMON PITFALL  A dead-letter queue without monitoring turns visible failures into hidden backlog.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can replay repeat a notification or payment already completed?

pages.title: What does backpressure mean in a streaming system?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 / Queues, logs and streaming QUESTION 050 / 120
What does backpressure mean in a streaming
system?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Downstream limits should influence upstream admission or production so slow
processing does not create unbounded memory and latency. When slowing producers is
impossible, define shedding or durable buffering.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Consumer capacity: 500 events/s.
Producer rate: 700 events/s.
Backlog grows by 200 events/s while this imbalance continues.
WHY THIS WORKS
Measure oldest-message age as well as count. A durable log buys time, but finite retention and storage
still impose limits. Parallelism helps only if partitioning, downstream capacity and ordering allow it. Treat
replay throughput as a separate workload competing with live processing.
COMMON PITFALL  A larger queue postpones overload; it does not increase processing rate.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How long until retention is exceeded at the current growth rate?
Answer: Backlog growth is 200 events/s in the example. Time to exceed capacity = free retained
slots / 200 seconds.
700/s input
500/s output
+200/s backlog

pages.title: What problem does the transactional outbox solve?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Outbox, idempotency and distributed workflows QUESTION 051 / 120
What problem does the transactional outbox solve?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It records the business change and an event to publish in one local database
transaction, avoiding the gap between committing data and separately publishing an
event.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders(...);
INSERT INTO outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, payload) VALUES(...);
COMMIT;
WHY THIS WORKS
A relay or change-data-capture process publishes committed outbox rows. If publication succeeds but
marking completion fails, it may publish again. Consumers therefore still need duplicate handling. Track
oldest unpublished age and clean up only according to recovery and retention policy.
COMMON PITFALL  Outbox provides durable publish intent, not automatically exactly-once delivery.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if the relay crashes immediately after publishing?
Answer: It publishes again after restart because the relay did not mark success. Consumers must
ignore duplicate event IDs.
Order + outbox
one DB commit
relay

pages.title: How should an idempotency key be implemented?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Outbox, idempotency and distributed workflows QUESTION 052 / 120
How should an idempotency key be implemented?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Scope the key to a caller and operation, bind it to a canonical validated request,
atomically coordinate ownership and store a durable result or status. Define expiry and
duplicate-in-progress behavior.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
UNIQUE(caller_id, operation, request_key)
Fields: request_hash, state, result_reference.
Same key + different request hash -> conflict.
WHY THIS WORKS
Canonicalization must handle semantically equivalent input consistently. A local database operation can
commit the key and effect together. For an external effect, persist workflow state and use the provider's
stable key plus reconciliation. Never claim an in-memory map is a durable multi-instance idempotency
store.
COMMON PITFALL  Expiring keys too early can turn a delayed retry into a second operation.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What response should a concurrent duplicate receive while the first request is running?
Answer: Return the existing result if finished; otherwise respond with an in-progress status or wait
briefly and safely.
Request key + hash
local effect
cached outcome

pages.title: What is a saga, and when is it useful?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Outbox, idempotency and distributed workflows QUESTION 053 / 120
What is a saga, and when is it useful?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A saga coordinates local transactions across services using explicit steps and
compensating actions. It supports recoverable workflows when one global atomic
transaction is unavailable or undesirable.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Reserve inventory -> authorize payment -> confirm order.
If authorization fails: release reservation.
If later work fails: retry, reconcile or compensate by policy.
WHY THIS WORKS
Compensation is a business operation, not a database rollback of the past. It can fail and needs
idempotency, retry and audit. Orchestration centralizes workflow state; choreography reacts to events
but can make the overall process harder to inspect.
COMMON PITFALL  A payment refund may have different timing and rules from undoing an uncommitted
payment.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Who owns a workflow stuck between authorization and confirmation?
Answer: A durable workflow owner (saga coordinator/order service) stores state and runs recovery/
reconciliation jobs.
Order
Reserve
Charge
Confirm / Compensate

pages.title: Why is exactly-once processing a bounded claim?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Outbox, idempotency and distributed workflows QUESTION 054 / 120
Why is exactly-once processing a bounded claim?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It describes a guarantee within a specified system and protocol. It does not
automatically cover arbitrary external effects, replay, client retries and all failure
modes.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Kafka transaction: atomically write Kafka output and offsets.
HTTP email provider: outside that transaction.
DB unique event key: can protect one local DB effect.
WHY THIS WORKS
Name the boundary, isolation, producer/consumer configuration and effect. Producer idempotence
handles certain duplicate writes to Kafka; it is different from an end-to-end payment guarantee. A design
can often achieve effectively-once business behavior with stable identities and reconciliation.
COMMON PITFALL  Do not label the entire workflow exactly-once because one broker supports
transactions.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which side effect remains outside the coordinated commit?
Answer: Any provider call outside the coordinated database/log transaction, such as an email or
payment API, can repeat.

coordinated DB?
external gap

pages.title: How do reconciliation and audit improve reliability?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Outbox, idempotency and distributed workflows QUESTION 055 / 120
How do reconciliation and audit improve reliability?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Reconciliation compares durable records across boundaries and repairs or escalates
mismatches. Audit explains what commands and transitions occurred without relying on
temporary process memory.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Local payment state = PENDING, provider state = SUCCEEDED.
Reconciler queries using the original provider reference.
It advances the workflow without charging again.
WHY THIS WORKS
Run reconciliation on a schedule and after incident recovery. Use bounded scans or cursors, idempotent
repairs and an escalation state for ambiguous cases. An audit log should capture stable IDs and decisions
while avoiding secrets and unnecessary personal data.
COMMON PITFALL  Treating every unknown external outcome as failure can create duplicate effects on
retry.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What evidence distinguishes a failed charge from a lost success response?
Answer: Check the provider using its stable payment reference and webhook/status API; a timeout
alone proves neither success nor failure.
Unknown payment
provider query
reconcile

pages.title: How should you set timeouts and end-to-end deadlines?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Timeouts, retries and resilience QUESTION 056 / 120
How should you set timeouts and end-to-end
deadlines?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Bound each stage and carry a remaining deadline through the request path. Include
connection acquisition and queue waiting rather than budgeting only the remote
response time.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Client deadline: 800 ms.
Reserve 100 ms for local processing and response.
Calls, pool wait and permitted retries share the remainder.
WHY THIS WORKS
Choose budgets from observed latency, the user objective and acceptable false timeouts, then load-test
them. A timeout means the caller stopped waiting; it does not establish that the callee stopped work or
rolled back. Cancellation must be cooperative and propagated where supported.
COMMON PITFALL  Giving every nested call the full original deadline can exceed the user's budget.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How much time remains before starting the second attempt?
Answer: Subtract elapsed time and reserved safety budget from the overall deadline; skip retries
with too little time left.
Deadline
per-call timeout
response / stop

pages.title: When should you retry, and why add jitter?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Timeouts, retries and resilience QUESTION 057 / 120
When should you retry, and why add jitter?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Retry operations whose failures may be transient and whose effects are safe to repeat,
within a bounded attempt and time budget. Randomized delay reduces synchronized
retry waves.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Delay cap = min(maxDelay, base * 2^attempt).
Full jitter example: random delay from 0 to that cap.
Do not retry invalid input or an exhausted total deadline.
WHY THIS WORKS
Classify errors using the API contract. Retry at one deliberate layer to avoid multiplicative attempts. A
payment timeout requires an idempotency or status lookup contract, not an optimistic assumption of
failure. Respect relevant rate-limit signals and avoid retrying into a saturated dependency.
COMMON PITFALL  Three attempts at each of three nested layers can create 27 downstream attempts.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which layer owns retry policy for this business operation?
Answer: Choose one responsible layer for retries; prevent multiplied attempts across client, gateway
and each service.
Transient error
jitter retry
success / fail

pages.title: How does a circuit breaker work?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Timeouts, retries and resilience QUESTION 058 / 120
How does a circuit breaker work?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It stops most calls after a failure policy is triggered, then allows controlled probes to
see whether the dependency recovered. It limits repeated failures rather than fixing the
dependency.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Closed: normal calls, collect outcomes.
Open: fail fast or use a defined fallback.
Half-open: limited probes before normal traffic returns.
WHY THIS WORKS
Choose whether timeouts, selected errors and slow calls count as failures. Keep breaker scope aligned
with the dependency or operation; one broken tenant should not necessarily trip every tenant. Fallback
data must still satisfy the user contract.
COMMON PITFALL  Circuit breakers do not bound the number of successful but slow concurrent calls;
bulkheads can.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if all instances enter half-open together?
Answer: Use jitter, per-instance probe caps and half-open trial limits so all nodes do not hit
recovery at once.
Closed
Open
Half-open probe

pages.title: What is a bulkhead, and how is it different from rate limiting?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Timeouts, retries and resilience QUESTION 059 / 120
What is a bulkhead, and how is it different from rate
limiting?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A bulkhead limits concurrent work or isolates resources so one dependency cannot
consume the whole service. Rate limiting controls admission over time; the two address
different overload shapes.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Payment calls: semaphore permits = 20.
Reports: separate bounded executor and DB budget.
Request quota: 100 calls per user per minute.
WHY THIS WORKS
A low request rate can still exhaust concurrency if each call hangs. Acquire with a bounded wait or fail
fast; release permits in finally blocks. Separate resource pools only where the isolation benefit justifies
the extra overhead.
COMMON PITFALL  A semaphore does not enforce a fixed requests-per-second quota.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens when a report request blocks for several minutes?
Answer: Put reports in a separate bounded executor. When full, reject the new report rather than
block checkout threads.
Report bulkhead
queued cap
reject surplus

pages.title: What is graceful degradation?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Timeouts, retries and resilience QUESTION 060 / 120
What is graceful degradation?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It deliberately reduces optional behavior while preserving essential correctness and a
clear user experience. The fallback must be explicitly allowed by the product's
requirements.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Catalog page: omit recommendations during an outage.
Stock purchase: reject or remain pending if authority is unavailable.
Search: serve a documented stale index when acceptable.
WHY THIS WORKS
Define which dependencies are optional, which failure modes trigger fallback and how recovery happens.
Monitor degraded responses separately from fully successful ones. Avoid returning fabricated
confirmation for a write whose outcome is unknown.
COMMON PITFALL  A stale price or authorization decision may violate the contract even when it improves
uptime.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which user journey can continue safely without this dependency?
Answer: Keep login, read-only catalog or previously confirmed order lookup if safe; block uncertain
payment or inventory writes.

safe reduced feature

pages.title: How should you size a Java thread pool?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 / Java concurrency and resource budgets QUESTION 061 / 120
How should you size a Java thread pool?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Start with workload type and resource limits, then measure throughput and latency.
CPU-bound work is constrained by effective CPU capacity; blocking I/O also depends
on downstream capacity and wait time.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<Runnable>(200),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());
WHY THIS WORKS
This bounded example caps execution and queued tasks; it is not a universal recommendation of eight
threads. Rejection must become a controlled API outcome. Common fixed-thread-pool factory methods
can use unbounded queues, so inspect the actual executor. Count queued work in the deadline.
COMMON PITFALL  A huge queue can preserve acceptance while making every result too late to be
useful.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens when the 201st waiting task arrives?
Answer: If all workers and queue slots are occupied, reject or apply a documented backpressure
policy; never grow without bound.

reject overload

pages.title: Do virtual threads remove the need for concurrency limits?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 / Java concurrency and resource budgets QUESTION 062 / 120
Do virtual threads remove the need for concurrency
limits?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
No. Java 21+ virtual threads make many blocking tasks cheaper in thread resources,
but database connections, remote quotas, CPU and memory still need explicit limits.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Java 21+ concept:
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()
Still bound payment calls and database access separately.
WHY THIS WORKS
Use virtual threads for suitable blocking workloads, then observe actual behavior on the target JDK and
libraries. They do not make CPU-heavy work faster merely by adding concurrency. The runnable
exercises in this guide use Java 17 so they require no preview flags or newer runtime.
COMMON PITFALL  Unlimited cheap threads can still create unlimited expensive downstream work.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Where will you enforce the database concurrency budget?
Answer: Use a semaphore or pool limit before DB calls. Virtual threads do not create extra DB
connections.

pages.title: Why must database connection pools be budgeted across instances?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 / Java concurrency and resource budgets QUESTION 063 / 120
Why must database connection pools be budgeted
across instances?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Each application instance adds potential database sessions. The total must fit the
database's sustainable concurrency and leave room for administration, background jobs
and other applications.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
12 instances x 30 connections = 360 potential connections.
Autoscale to 24 instances -> 720.
The database does not automatically gain capacity.
WHY THIS WORKS
Pool size is not the same as useful database parallelism. Measure acquisition wait, active usage,
transaction duration and DB saturation. Use short transactions, bounded acquisition and backpressure.
Different workloads may require separate budgets even when they share one physical database.
COMMON PITFALL  Raising pool size to fix waiting can worsen a CPU- or lock-bound database.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which limit stops autoscaling from overwhelming the database?
Answer: Cap total connections across replicas: instances x maxPoolSize <= DB budget, with
headroom for failover and admin work.

Different workloads may require separate budgets even when they share one physical database.
pages.pitfall: Raising pool size to fix waiting can worsen a CPU- or lock-bound database.
pages.followup:
Which limit stops autoscaling from overwhelming the database?
Answer: Cap total connections across replicas: instances x maxPoolSize <= DB budget, with
headroom for failover and admin work.

pages.title: Why is ConcurrentHashMap not a distributed transaction?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 / Java concurrency and resource budgets QUESTION 064 / 120
Why is ConcurrentHashMap not a distributed
transaction?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It provides thread-safe map operations within one JVM. It neither shares memory
across instances nor atomically commits independent business resources with crash
durability.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
map.putIfAbsent(requestKey, result); // one JVM
check balance; debit account; add audit record;
// these three operations need a business transaction
WHY THIS WORKS
Per-key compute operations can coordinate a narrow local update, but a sequence across keys is not
automatically atomic. Process restart loses ordinary in-memory state. Use the map for caches or local
coordination only when the design tolerates these boundaries.
COMMON PITFALL  Thread-safe containers do not make a multi-step business operation thread-safe by
themselves.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What changes when a second application instance handles the retry?
Answer: Another JVM has a different map and lock. Use durable shared state and database
uniqueness for global correctness.
Map in JVM A
JVM B?
durable DB constraint

pages.title: How do JVM memory and GC affect system design?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 / Java concurrency and resource budgets QUESTION 065 / 120
How do JVM memory and GC affect system design?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Allocation rate, live data and pauses influence tail latency and capacity. Budget heap
plus native memory, thread stacks and buffers, and use evidence before tuning
collector settings.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Large request body -> allocation spike.
Unbounded queue -> retained tasks and payloads.
Container memory = heap + non-heap + native overhead.
WHY THIS WORKS
Use GC logs, allocation profiling, heap analysis and request traces to distinguish causes. Streaming
payloads and bounding queues can solve a design problem that a larger heap only delays. Cache entries
often contain object overhead beyond their serialized byte size.
COMMON PITFALL  Setting maximum heap equal to the container memory limit leaves no room for other
memory.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which retained objects grow with backlog rather than useful working data?
Answer: Queued events, retained payloads and unbounded collections may grow with backlog.
Measure heap, allocation and GC pauses.
Backlog
live heap
GC pauses

pages.title: When should you choose a modular monolith over microservices?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Service boundaries and architecture patterns QUESTION 066 / 120
When should you choose a modular monolith over
microservices?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A modular monolith fits when one deployment and local transactions meet current
needs. Microservices can help independent ownership or scaling but introduce network
and operational costs.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Modules: catalog, orders, payment workflow.
Enforce interfaces and data ownership inside one application.
Extract notifications when independent scale justifies it.
WHY THIS WORKS
A monolith can be well structured; microservices can still be tightly coupled. Judge team boundaries,
release needs, workloads and reliability. Avoid splitting every entity into a service, which can make one
business operation require many coordinated calls.
COMMON PITFALL  More network boundaries create more partial-failure states.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which measurable problem will this service extraction solve?
Answer: Name a measured need such as independent deployment, scaling or team ownership;
extraction has operational cost.
Modular monolith
proven boundary
extract later

pages.title: How should a service own its data?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Service boundaries and architecture patterns QUESTION 067 / 120
How should a service own its data?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
One service should control the writes and invariant for its business domain. Other
services use contracts or replicated projections rather than bypassing ownership with
shared-table writes.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Inventory owns stock and reservations.
Order service calls reserve or consumes reservation outcomes.
Analytics reads a projection, not live ownership tables.
WHY THIS WORKS
Physical databases may initially be shared for operational reasons, but access boundaries should remain
explicit. Cross-service foreign keys and direct updates make independent evolution harder. Define how
data is copied and how deletion or correction reaches projections.
COMMON PITFALL  Sharing a database does not justify every service modifying every table.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Who approves a schema change that affects another service's projection?
Answer: The owning service approves its schema. Consumers coordinate event/API contracts and
rebuild their own projections.
Service owner
publishes API / events
consumers

pages.title: What is CQRS, and when is it useful?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Service boundaries and architecture patterns QUESTION 068 / 120
What is CQRS, and when is it useful?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
CQRS separates command behavior from query behavior. It can use one database or
separate projections; it is useful when read and write models have meaningfully
different needs.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Command: reserve inventory with strict validation.
Query: product search with precomputed availability text.
Projection lag is shown or accepted by product policy.
WHY THIS WORKS
CQRS does not require event sourcing, Kafka or separate microservices. Separate read storage adds
update propagation, rebuild and lag management. Start with simple command/query separation and add
projections for a demonstrated read problem.
COMMON PITFALL  A read projection should not silently become the authority for stock confirmation.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will a newly deployed projection catch up?
Answer: Replay a retained event log or backfill from a snapshot, then apply live changes until a
measured lag threshold is met.
Write model
event
read projection

pages.title: What is event sourcing, and how does it differ from an event log?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Service boundaries and architecture patterns QUESTION 069 / 120
What is event sourcing, and how does it differ from
an event log?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Event sourcing stores domain events as the authoritative history from which current
state is derived. A transport event log may carry copies of changes while another store
remains authoritative.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Account events: Opened, Credited, Debited.
Current balance = replay of valid ordered account events.
Snapshot: acceleration, not replacement of authoritative history.
WHY THIS WORKS
The approach requires versioned events, aggregate concurrency, replay rules and handling of corrections.
External effects must not automatically repeat during replay. Historical data deletion and sensitive fields
need deliberate design. Event sourcing is useful for some domains but adds complexity.
COMMON PITFALL  Publishing OrderCreated after a normal database insert is not automatically event
sourcing.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you evolve an old event whose schema no longer matches current code?
Answer: Use versioned event upcasters or adapters, preserve old event meaning and test replay
against historical samples.
Events as truth
replay
current state

pages.title: How can a large system migrate safely to a new design?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Service boundaries and architecture patterns QUESTION 070 / 120
How can a large system migrate safely to a new
design?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Move one bounded capability at a time, define a single authority during transition, and
verify equivalence before switching traffic. Use reversible routing and a repair path.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Step 1: new read model receives change events.
Step 2: shadow compare selected responses.
Step 3: canary traffic, observe, then expand.
WHY THIS WORKS
Dual writes across independent stores are fragile without a durable coordination mechanism. Migration
checkpoints, validation counts and reconciliation reveal missed changes. After cutover, plan how rollback
interacts with writes that occurred only in the new authority.
COMMON PITFALL  Rolling back application code does not necessarily roll back changed data semantics.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What prevents both old and new services from owning the same write?
Answer: Use one write owner at a time; route commands through it and compare dual-read results
before a staged cutover.
Old owner
migrate
fence
new owner

pages.title: Why use a search index instead of the transactional database for text search?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Search, analytics and derived data QUESTION 071 / 120
Why use a search index instead of the transactional
database for text search?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A search engine offers specialized text indexing, relevance and query features. Keep
authoritative data ownership separate and define how updates reach the searchable
projection.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Product DB commit -> durable change event -> index update.
Search returns product IDs and display fields.
Checkout revalidates price and stock from authoritative services.
WHY THIS WORKS
The index may lag or contain a product that was just deleted. Handle tombstones, versions and
authorization filters. For simpler workloads, the database's built-in text features may be sufficient; a
separate search cluster creates operational overhead.
COMMON PITFALL  A relevant search hit is not proof that the user may access or purchase the item.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will you rebuild the index without blocking live search?
Answer: Build a new index from a snapshot while streaming live updates, compare it, then
atomically switch the search alias.
DB change
CDC stream
text index

pages.title: How do batch and stream processing differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Search, analytics and derived data QUESTION 072 / 120
How do batch and stream processing differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Batch processes bounded datasets at intervals. Stream processing handles ongoing
events with incremental state. Choose based on freshness requirements, cost and
correctness under late data.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Daily revenue report: batch may be enough.
Fraud signal during checkout: timely stream may be needed.
Both need rules for corrections and duplicated events.
WHY THIS WORKS
A hybrid design can use streaming for rapid visibility and batch reconciliation for authoritative correction.
Streaming does not inherently mean real-time completion; backlog and downstream delays still matter.
Track data freshness independently of request latency.
COMMON PITFALL  Fast ingestion does not establish accurate or timely final aggregates.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How late can an event arrive and still revise the result?
Answer: Choose a lateness watermark and correction policy. Very late events may update historical
results or go to adjustments.
Batch window
stream increments
merged result

pages.title: What is the difference between event time and processing time?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Search, analytics and derived data QUESTION 073 / 120
What is the difference between event time and
processing time?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Event time describes when the business event occurred. Processing time describes
when a processor observed it. Delays and clock issues can make those times differ
substantially.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Purchase happened at 23:59 yesterday.
Mobile device reconnects at 08:00 today.
A daily sales metric must choose the intended time basis.
WHY THIS WORKS
Define timezone, trustworthy timestamp source and late-event handling. Watermarks or lateness
policies guide when a computation treats a window as sufficiently complete; they cannot make all late
events impossible. Reprocessing may update earlier totals.
COMMON PITFALL  Device clocks are not necessarily accurate enough to enforce business ordering.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Should a late refund alter yesterday's report or today's adjustment ledger?
Answer: For finance, keep an immutable original period and post a dated correction if accounting
rules require that approach.
Event timestamp
watermark
late correction

pages.title: How can you maintain a materialized aggregate safely?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Search, analytics and derived data QUESTION 074 / 120
How can you maintain a materialized aggregate
safely?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Define the source of truth, stable event identities, update ordering and recovery
strategy. Apply each local increment with deduplication or rebuild from authoritative
records.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Event e-5: order total + 1,250 minor units.
Atomic transaction: insert processed event ID, update total.
Duplicate e-5: no additional increment.
WHY THIS WORKS
This is a local database pattern, not universal exactly-once streaming. Corrections need explicit negative
or replacement operations. High-volume counters may be partitioned and merged when delayed totals
are acceptable. Decide what the dashboard should display during lag or rebuild.
COMMON PITFALL  Summing repeated delivery records without deduplication overstates revenue.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will you reconcile the aggregate against the ledger?
Answer: Replay ordered IDs from the ledger into a versioned aggregate and compare sums/record
counts to authoritative rows.
Ledger entries
projection
reconcile

pages.title: How should you rebuild a projection while writes continue?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Search, analytics and derived data QUESTION 075 / 120
How should you rebuild a projection while writes
continue?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Take a consistent baseline or a defined source position, replay changes from the
matching position, and switch only after checking catch-up and correctness. Track
versions to avoid older replay overwriting newer data.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Build index-v2 from a baseline at source position P.
Replay changes after P while live writes continue.
Validate and switch a read alias when caught up.
WHY THIS WORKS
Snapshot and change positions must align; otherwise the gap can lose or duplicate changes.
Deduplication handles duplicates, while version checks preserve latest state. T ombstones matter as much
as inserts. Use resource budgets so rebuilding does not starve production traffic.
COMMON PITFALL  Copying rows and then listening for events without a gap strategy can miss writes.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What evidence shows the new projection is complete enough for cutover?
Answer: Verify source coverage, event catch-up position, counts and sampled results; then switch
reads and monitor mismatches.
Snapshot
replay delta
alias switch

pages.title: When should you use polling, server-sent events or WebSockets?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 / Realtime connections and fan-out QUESTION 076 / 120
When should you use polling, server-sent events or
WebSockets?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Polling is simple for infrequent updates; server-sent events provide server-to-client
streaming; WebSockets support bidirectional communication. Choose according to
interaction, infrastructure and recovery needs.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Status every minute: polling.
Live job progress: SSE may fit.
Interactive chat: WebSocket plus durable history API.
WHY THIS WORKS
Persistent connections require authentication renewal, heartbeat policy, load balancing and draining.
Reconnect should resume from a stable position rather than assume nothing happened while
disconnected. The transport does not store messages or prove delivery to a person.
COMMON PITFALL  A successful socket write does not prove that a user read a message.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How does the client recover messages missed during reconnect?
Answer: Keep a last-seen event ID/sequence. On reconnect, fetch the missing interval and
deduplicate delivered events.
Poll / SSE / WebSocket
replay cursor

pages.title: How should a chat system define message ordering?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 / Realtime connections and fan-out QUESTION 077 / 120
How should a chat system define message ordering?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use an explicit conversation sequence or another deterministic contract. Distinguish
server acceptance order, delivery order and display order, and do not rely solely on
client clocks.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Client sends clientMessageId = m-7.
Server commits conversation sequence = 104.
Retry m-7 returns the same accepted message.
WHY THIS WORKS
Serializing sequence assignment per conversation can become a hot partition for a huge room. If strict
global ordering is unnecessary, relax the requirement explicitly. Delivery through multiple gateways may
differ, so clients can sort or detect gaps using the server sequence.
COMMON PITFALL  Two timestamps can be equal or inaccurate and still need a tie-breaker.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens when sequence 106 arrives before 105?
Answer: Buffer version 106 briefly until 105 arrives, then replay missing history; do not assume
network arrival order is truth.
Client ID
durable seq no
dedup on reconnect

pages.title: How do you route messages to connected users?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 / Realtime connections and fan-out QUESTION 078 / 120
How do you route messages to connected users?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Track which connection gateway currently hosts a user's sessions, route live delivery
there, and keep durable message history independent of the connection directory.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Directory: user-42 -> gateway-A + gateway-C.
Message committed -> delivery event -> active gateways.
Offline or missed delivery -> recover from history cursor.
WHY THIS WORKS
Directory entries expire and can become stale during disconnection or deployment. Multi-device users
may need delivery to several sessions. A failed live route should not delete the durable message.
Presence is often approximate and should have a TTL-based contract.

Answer: The first push may fail, but durable messages remain in storage. Reconnect and replay
must not rely on that directory.

pages.title: How do fan-out on write and fan-out on read compare?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 / Realtime connections and fan-out QUESTION 079 / 120
How do fan-out on write and fan-out on read
compare?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Fan-out on write precomputes recipient feeds, making reads cheaper. Fan-out on read
combines sources at read time, making writes cheaper but reads more expensive. A
hybrid handles uneven audience sizes.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Normal author: add post ID to follower feed projections.
Celebrity author: merge recent posts during feed read.
Rank and paginate using a stable feed contract.
WHY THIS WORKS
Audience size and read frequency decide the tradeoff. Precomputed fan-out needs retry, duplicate
handling and deletion propagation. Read-time merging needs bounded source queries and caching.
Ranking changes can complicate cursor semantics.
COMMON PITFALL  A post with millions of followers can overwhelm naive synchronous fan-out.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How long may a follower wait before a new post appears?
Answer: State an explicit freshness SLO, e.g., a few seconds for normal feed updates, and test it
under fan-out load.
New post

pages.title: How do you control slow realtime clients?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 / Realtime connections and fan-out QUESTION 080 / 120
How do you control slow realtime clients?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Bound per-connection buffers and define disconnect, resume or coalescing behavior
when a client cannot keep up. Preserve durable events separately from ephemeral
updates.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Chat messages: durable history with resume cursor.
Typing indicators: coalesce or drop if the buffer is full.
Slow client: disconnect with a recoverable session policy.
WHY THIS WORKS
Do not let one connection retain unlimited heap or block a shared event loop. Backpressure policies vary
by message type; a missed typing indicator is less serious than a missing committed message. Monitor
queue bytes and age, not just message count.
COMMON PITFALL  An unbounded per-socket queue can exhaust a server before CPU is busy.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which events are safe to drop and which require replay?
Answer: Drop typing indicators or presence updates if allowed; retain chat messages and replay by
durable ID.
Slow socket
bounded buffer
replay later

pages.title: How do authentication and authorization differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Security and tenant isolation QUESTION 081 / 120
How do authentication and authorization differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides whether that identity may
perform this action on this resource. Validate both for synchronous and asynchronous
work.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
GET /orders/42
Authenticated user: customer-7.
Service checks that order 42 belongs to customer-7 or an allowed role.
WHY THIS WORKS
A gateway can validate a token, but the owning service still knows the object-level business rule. Scope
background jobs to the original authority or an explicit service identity. Permission changes may require
fresh checks rather than trusting old cached decisions.
COMMON PITFALL  Knowing an unguessable resource ID does not grant permission to access it.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if a queued command runs after permission is revoked?
Answer: Recheck permission at execution, or cancel the command if authorization was revoked;
queue-time checks may become stale.

pages.title: How should a multitenant system isolate data?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Security and tenant isolation QUESTION 082 / 120
How should a multitenant system isolate data?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Bind every operation to a validated tenant context and enforce isolation in queries,
keys, caches, events and operational tooling. Larger or sensitive tenants may need
stronger physical separation.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE tenant_id = :authorizedTenant AND id = :orderId;
Cache key: tenantId + ':' + orderId.
WHY THIS WORKS
Do not trust a tenant ID from the request without connecting it to the caller's authority. T enant quotas
and workload budgets protect performance isolation as well as privacy. Consider row-level controls,
separate schemas or dedicated databases according to requirements and operating cost.
COMMON PITFALL  A correctly scoped SQL query can still leak data through an incorrectly scoped cache.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How are support tools prevented from bypassing tenant boundaries?
Answer: Use tenant-aware repository policies, row-level security where suitable, scoped support
roles and audited access.
Tenant ID
scoped query
audited access

pages.title: Why are encryption, secrets and key rotation separate design concerns?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Security and tenant isolation QUESTION 083 / 120
Why are encryption, secrets and key rotation
separate design concerns?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Transport and storage encryption protect different paths. Secret management controls
credentials, and key rotation limits long-lived exposure. Each requires an ownership
and rollout plan.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
TLS: protects request bytes in transit.
DB/object encryption: protects stored bytes under its threat model.
Service credential: delivered securely and rotated without downtime.
WHY THIS WORKS
Encryption does not prevent an authorized application from returning the wrong user's data. Avoid
placing secrets in source code, logs or ordinary config artifacts. Design overlapping credential validity
and revocation so services can transition safely.
COMMON PITFALL  A token in a trace or error log can bypass otherwise strong transport protection.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will old and new keys coexist during rotation?
Answer: Publish a new key ID, accept old and new during migration, re-encrypt/expire old data,
then revoke the old key.
Ciphertext + key ID
rotate
retire old key

pages.title: How should signed upload or download URLs be secured?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Security and tenant isolation QUESTION 084 / 120
How should signed upload or download URLs be
secured?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Authorize the request before issuing a narrowly scoped, short-lived capability. Bind the
operation to a generated object key and validate content and ownership again during
finalization.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
User requests upload for an owned draft asset.
Server issues URL for that specific object and operation.
Finalization checks object metadata and approved workflow state.
WHY THIS WORKS
Treat the URL as a bearer capability and avoid logging it. Depending on the storage API, restrictions and
reuse behavior differ; expiry is not always a one-use guarantee. Size, type, checksum and scanning
requirements should be enforced by supported policy or validation.
COMMON PITFALL  A client-provided object key can overwrite another user's content if accepted blindly.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can an issued URL be reused before it expires?
Answer: Often yes until expiry, depending on the signing policy. Use short TTLs, narrow scope and
storage-level controls.
Signed limited URL
direct object access
expiry

pages.title: How should deletion work when data has replicas and projections?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Security and tenant isolation QUESTION 085 / 120
How should deletion work when data has replicas
and projections?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Define a deletion lifecycle covering authoritative rows, search indexes, caches, objects,
events, exports and backups. Track completion and prevent deleted data from
reappearing during replay.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Mark account deletion request durably.
Propagate tombstones to projections and storage owners.
Rebuild logic respects tombstones and retention policy.
WHY THIS WORKS
Some audit or financial records may follow separate documented retention requirements; this guide does
not prescribe legal policy. Minimize sensitive fields in immutable events before creating them. Backup
expiry and restore procedures must respect the intended deletion lifecycle.
COMMON PITFALL  Removing one database row does not delete copies in a search cluster or cache.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What prevents a replay from recreating a deleted user profile?
Answer: Record tombstones/deletion versions and prevent event replay from recreating them;
purge dependent projections.
Deletion tombstone
replicas
replay suppression

pages.title: How do metrics, logs and traces complement each other?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Observability and performance diagnosis QUESTION 086 / 120
How do metrics, logs and traces complement each
other?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Metrics summarize behavior over time; logs record detailed events; traces connect
stages of a distributed operation. Use stable correlation IDs and consistent semantic
fields.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Metric: checkout latency histogram.
Log: order=o-7, state=PAYMENT_PENDING, reason=timeout.
Trace: gateway -> order -> inventory -> provider.
WHY THIS WORKS
Not every request needs a verbose log or stored trace. Sampling, cardinality and retention affect cost and
diagnostic coverage. Carry trace context across messages and record the relationship between
acceptance and later processing. Avoid logging payloads with secrets.
COMMON PITFALL  A trace that starts after a long queue wait can understate the user latency.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which signal links an HTTP request to its asynchronous workflow?
Answer: Use one correlation/trace ID plus the durable operation/event ID across HTTP, outbox and
consumer logs.
Trace ID
logs + spans
async event ID

pages.title: Which golden signals should you monitor?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Observability and performance diagnosis QUESTION 087 / 120
Which golden signals should you monitor?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Track latency, traffic, errors and saturation, plus domain-specific correctness and
freshness. Pair user symptoms with resource causes so alerts support diagnosis.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
User signals: successful bookings and confirmation latency.
Resource signals: DB lock wait, pool wait and queue age.
Correctness: oversell count and unresolved payment outcomes.
WHY THIS WORKS
CPU alone can look healthy while requests wait on a database or remote service. A business invariant
alert may matter more than a small latency increase. Define ownership and runbooks for actionable
alerts and suppress noisy non-actionable events.
COMMON PITFALL  A broker being reachable does not mean consumers are keeping up.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which alert fires when accepted work stops progressing?
Answer: Alert on oldest pending age, processing success rate and stuck-state counts, not only API
success at acceptance.
Latency / traffic
errors / saturation

pages.title: Why can metric cardinality become a production problem?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Observability and performance diagnosis QUESTION 088 / 120
Why can metric cardinality become a production
problem?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Every unique label combination can create another time series. Unbounded labels such
as user ID or request ID increase memory, storage and query costs.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Good bounded label: operation='checkout', result='timeout'.
Risky label: request_id='unique-for-every-request'.
Put detailed identifiers in controlled logs or traces instead.
WHY THIS WORKS
Even several individually bounded labels can multiply into a large set. Establish budgets for tenant, route
and exception labels. Normalize dynamic URL paths into route templates. Use exemplars or trace links
when supported to connect a metric spike to diagnostic detail.
COMMON PITFALL  Labeling by raw URL can create one series for every object ID.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How many combinations can this label schema produce?
Answer: Multiply the number of unique values for all label dimensions; avoid unbounded user_id/
request_id metric labels.
Many labels
time series explosion
aggregation

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Observability and performance diagnosis QUESTION 089 / 120
How do you find the bottleneck in a slow Java API?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Break down queue, executor, connection acquisition, database, remote call and
serialization time. Correlate traces with resource metrics and profiles before changing
pool or heap settings.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Observed p99 = 1.8 s.
Trace: pool acquisition = 1.5 s; SQL = 20 ms.
Investigate long transactions and connection budget first.
WHY THIS WORKS
If SQL itself is slow, inspect plans, row counts and lock waits. If CPU is busy, profile allocation and
compute paths. T est a candidate change under representative load and compare the user SLO, not only
one local metric.
COMMON PITFALL  Increasing threads without locating the wait can increase downstream contention.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Is the connection pool empty because of slow queries, leaks or long transactions?
Answer: Check active/idle/awaiting connections, slow-query times, blocked transactions and leaks
with trace evidence.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Observability and performance diagnosis QUESTION 090 / 120
How should you validate capacity and failure
behavior?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use representative data and workload distributions, measure sustainable throughput
and tails, then inject specific failures. Verify invariants and recovery, not just happy-
path request counts.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Load: normal + burst + hot tenant + large payload.
Fault: kill consumer after DB commit before acknowledgement.
Expected: duplicate delivery but one local business effect.
WHY THIS WORKS
Include cold cache, dependency slowness and recovery backlog. A small deterministic lab proves an
algorithmic behavior, not production capacity or distributed correctness. Document environment and
assumptions so measurements are reproducible.
COMMON PITFALL  A benchmark with only cache hits cannot size the database fallback path.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can recovery traffic coexist with live traffic without missing the SLO?
Answer: Run load plus failover/replay together, measuring user SLOs and recovery times, not only
steady-state throughput.
Load test
fail a dependency

CHAPTER 19 / Deployment, shutdown and disaster recovery QUESTION 091 / 120
How do liveness, readiness and startup probes
differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Liveness guides restart of a stuck process; readiness guides traffic admission; startup
protects slow initialization before other probes begin. Use each for its intended lifecycle
question.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Startup: initialization completed.
Readiness: able to handle this service's traffic.
Liveness: process is irrecoverably unhealthy without restart.
WHY THIS WORKS
Probe semantics and orchestration actions must match the platform. Making liveness depend on every
remote service can cause cascading restarts during a shared outage. Readiness can reflect critical
dependencies while optional features degrade. Avoid expensive probes that worsen overload.
COMMON PITFALL  A temporarily unavailable database is not always a reason to restart every API process.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How should readiness behave during connection-pool exhaustion?
Answer: Mark unready when the node cannot serve essential requests; prevent tight readiness
flapping with sane thresholds.

pages.title: What does graceful shutdown require?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 / Deployment, shutdown and disaster recovery QUESTION 092 / 120
What does graceful shutdown require?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Stop taking new work, remove the instance from traffic, drain or checkpoint existing
work within a budget, and release resources. Durable uncompleted work should be
safely redeliverable.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Mark unready -> propagate routing change -> stop admission.
Finish short requests; checkpoint/ack completed consumer work.
Close pools before the termination deadline.
WHY THIS WORKS
Load balancer propagation and existing connections introduce races. For long-lived sockets,
communicate reconnect and provide resume positions. Never acknowledge unfinished message effects
just to make shutdown faster. A forced kill remains possible, so correctness must survive it.
COMMON PITFALL  Graceful shutdown is an optimization for clean exits, not a replacement for crash
recovery.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens when termination arrives before a payment workflow finishes?
Answer: Persist workflow state first. On termination, stop admitting work, drain briefly, then resume
from durable state later.

finish in-flight
resume durable work

Load balancer propagation and existing connections introduce races. For long-lived sockets,
communicate reconnect and provide resume positions. Never acknowledge unfinished message effects
just to make shutdown faster. A forced kill remains possible, so correctness must survive it.

Graceful shutdown is an optimization for clean exits, not a replacement for crash
recovery.
pages.followup:
What happens when termination arrives before a payment workflow finishes?
Answer: Persist workflow state first. On termination, stop admitting work, drain briefly, then resume
from durable state later.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 / Deployment, shutdown and disaster recovery QUESTION 093 / 120
How do rolling, canary and blue-green deployment
differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Rolling replaces instances gradually; canary exposes a small portion of traffic first;
blue-green keeps two deployment environments and switches routing. All need
compatible data and contracts.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Canary: send 1% of checkout traffic to version B.
Compare error rate, latency and business invariants.
Increase traffic only after the defined observation gate.
WHY THIS WORKS
Percentages are illustrative, not a fixed safe policy. Mixed versions can share queues and schemas, so
validate compatibility in both directions where required. Rollback must consider new data states and side
effects, not only code images.
COMMON PITFALL  A healthy process startup is not proof that a deployment is safe for users.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What signal detects a canary creating duplicate reservations?
Answer: Compare canary duplicate-key conflicts, duplicate reservations per request ID and
invariant alerts; abort if they rise.

pages.title: What is an expand-and-contract database migration?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 / Deployment, shutdown and disaster recovery QUESTION 094 / 120
What is an expand-and-contract database
migration?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Add compatible structures first, migrate readers and writers through a transition,
validate backfill, then remove old structures only after old consumers are gone.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
1. Add nullable delivery_window_v2.
2. Deploy compatible writers; backfill with checkpoints.
3. Switch reads after validation.
4. Later enforce constraints and remove old field.
WHY THIS WORKS
DDL locking and online behavior differ by database and operation. Avoid a single unbounded backfill
transaction. A dual-write phase within one local transaction can be manageable; across independent
databases it needs additional coordination. T est old application code against the expanded schema.
COMMON PITFALL  Dropping the old column before the last old instance stops can break a rolling deploy.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will you resume a backfill after interruption?
Answer: Backfill in small, idempotent batches with a checkpoint/cursor and verification so restart
resumes safely.

pages.title: How do RPO and RTO differ, and why are replicas not enough?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 / Deployment, shutdown and disaster recovery QUESTION 095 / 120
How do RPO and RTO differ, and why are replicas
not enough?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
RPO is the acceptable data-loss window; RTO is the acceptable recovery time. Replicas
can copy corruption or accidental deletion, so recovery also needs protected backups
and tested restoration.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Hypothetical target: RPO 5 minutes; RTO 30 minutes.
Need compatible backup/log retention and restore process.
Test actual restore time and recovered data integrity.
WHY THIS WORKS
Targets are requirements, not guarantees produced by naming a replication mode. Include credentials,
configuration, object data and dependencies in the recovery plan. A failover drill and a backup restore
drill verify different failure scenarios.
COMMON PITFALL  Three live copies can all reproduce the same erroneous delete.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do you restore a correct point in time without losing later valid work unnecessarily?
Answer: Restore from backup and WAL to a verified point; reconcile later valid operations from
independent logs/ providers where possible.
Backup + WAL
restore drill

pages.title: How do active-passive and active-active regions differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Multi-region and global systems QUESTION 096 / 120
How do active-passive and active-active regions
differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Active-passive routes normal writes to one active region and keeps another for
recovery. Active-active serves work in multiple regions and needs explicit data
ownership or conflict resolution.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Active-passive: simpler write authority, slower failover path.
Active-active: local service paths, harder concurrent-write rules.
Home-region model: each account has one write owner.
WHY THIS WORKS
The right design depends on recovery targets, latency and the business invariant. Active-active
application traffic does not necessarily imply multi-primary writes to every record. Cross-region
synchronous coordination can increase write latency and reduce progress during partition.
COMMON PITFALL  Two regions accepting the same account debit independently can violate balance
rules.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Where is the write authority for a user traveling abroad?
Answer: Route to an explicit home/write authority. Traveling users may read locally but send strict
writes to their owner.
One writer region
standby / active reads

pages.title: Why is failover more than changing DNS?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Multi-region and global systems QUESTION 097 / 120
Why is failover more than changing DNS?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Failover must ensure the new authority is ready, old writers cannot continue conflicting
writes, data loss is understood, and clients and dependent systems reconnect safely.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Detect failure -> confirm authority decision.
Fence old writer -> promote suitable replica.
Update routing -> reconcile pending external operations.
WHY THIS WORKS
DNS caching and existing connections make traffic changes gradual. Promotion after asynchronous
replication may lose acknowledged writes under some configurations. T est role changes, retries and
idempotency during failover. A control-plane error can be more dangerous than a short outage.
COMMON PITFALL  Promoting a replica without preventing old-primary writes can create split brain.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How are requests to the old region rejected after promotion?
Answer: Use leader epochs, fencing tokens or storage leases so a demoted region cannot accept
writes after promotion.
Old leader fenced
new leader promoted
route update

pages.title: What does data locality change in a design?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Multi-region and global systems QUESTION 098 / 120
What does data locality change in a design?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Placing data near its main access path can reduce latency, transfer cost and
coordination. It also affects partition routing, recovery and requirements for where
particular data may reside.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Tenant home region stores authoritative records.
Global directory maps tenant -> home region.
Public static assets can be replicated near readers.
WHY THIS WORKS
Directory updates become part of tenant migration. Region requirements may arise from contracts or
policy; verify the applicable requirement rather than assuming all data must be globally copied. Model
cross-region access explicitly for users and background workers.
COMMON PITFALL  A global cache can undermine an otherwise carefully scoped locality policy.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do you move a tenant without two simultaneous write owners?
Answer: Pause its writes, copy/verify state, flip versioned routing, then enable one new owner; reject
stale route versions.
Tenant home region
data move
new home

pages.title: How can conflict resolution change business meaning?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Multi-region and global systems QUESTION 099 / 120
How can conflict resolution change business
meaning?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Last-write-wins, merging and conflict-preserving strategies each encode a policy.
Choose a strategy that matches the data, rather than using timestamps as a universal
correctness solution.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Profile nickname: last-write-wins may be acceptable.
Set of likes: merge identities under a defined model.
Account balance: arbitrary last-write-wins loses valid money movements.
WHY THIS WORKS
Wall-clock skew and ties can distort timestamp ordering. Some data types support useful convergent
merge semantics, but reversals and business constraints still require care. For critical operations, avoid
conflicting independent writers or use an appropriate coordinated protocol.
COMMON PITFALL  Eventual convergence does not establish that the converged value is correct for the
business.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can two concurrent valid operations both be preserved?
Answer: Some operations are commutative (two increments); two purchases for one remaining item
are not. Merge only with business rules.
Concurrent update
business merge / reject

pages.title: What should a region-outage runbook include?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Multi-region and global systems QUESTION 100 / 120
What should a region-outage runbook include?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Describe detection, authority and fencing, promotion, traffic admission, dependency
readiness, recovery validation and eventual return. Assign owners and define a stopping
condition for unsafe ambiguity.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Check replication position and expected loss window.
Verify identity, secrets, DB, broker and object access.
Track pending workflows through stable request IDs.
WHY THIS WORKS
Practice with partial outages, not just complete region disappearance. Returning to the old topology
needs synchronization and ownership transfer just like initial failover. Communication and status
systems should not rely only on the failing region.
COMMON PITFALL  A second region without tested credentials and dependencies is not a complete
recovery capability.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will you prove the system is safe before restoring normal write traffic?
Answer: Identify owners, promotion steps, write fencing, data checks, DNS/client routing, rollback,
contacts and drills.
Detect outage
fence writes
restore + verify

pages.title: How do fixed-window and sliding-window rate limits compare?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 21 / Rate limiting, fairness and admission QUESTION 101 / 120
How do fixed-window and sliding-window rate
limits compare?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Fixed windows count requests in discrete periods and are simple, but allow boundary
bursts. Sliding-window approaches smooth the boundary with more state or an
approximation.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Fixed limit: 100/minute.
100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:00:
200 requests can arrive within two seconds.
WHY THIS WORKS
A sliding log stores request times for exact rolling counts but uses memory proportional to traffic.
Bucketed or weighted counters reduce cost with approximate behavior. Choose precision according to
abuse risk and budget. The rejection response should explain retry behavior when useful.
COMMON PITFALL  A per-minute quota does not necessarily protect short-term concurrency.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What burst can a caller create near a window boundary?
Answer: A caller can send nearly a full limit just before reset and another full limit just after it:
almost 2x briefly.
Fixed boundary
burst spike; sliding
smoother
