pages.title: How does a token bucket work?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 21 / Rate limiting, fairness and admission QUESTION 102 / 120
How does a token bucket work?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Tokens accumulate up to a capacity; each admitted request consumes tokens. The refill
rate controls long-term throughput and capacity controls the permitted burst.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Capacity = 10 tokens; refill = 2 tokens/s.
Initially allow a burst of 10.
After exhaustion, roughly 2 new unit requests/s can proceed.
WHY THIS WORKS
Use an appropriate monotonic time source for elapsed time in a local limiter. Concurrent checks and
consumption must be atomic. Weighted operations can consume different token amounts. A distributed
implementation needs a shared atomic state transition or an explicitly approximate policy.
COMMON PITFALL  Running this bucket independently in five instances multiplies the aggregate
permitted rate.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What should happen when the request costs more than bucket capacity?
Answer: Reject an oversized request rather than wait forever; validate cost > 0 and document
whether partial tokens are allowed.
Capacity tokens
refill rate
accept / reject

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 21 / Rate limiting, fairness and admission QUESTION 103 / 120
How do you enforce a distributed quota?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Choose a single authoritative state transition per quota key, or explicitly allocate
approximate budgets to nodes. Define accuracy, latency and behavior when the
coordinator is unavailable.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Key: tenant + operation + policyVersion.
Atomic check/refill/decrement in shared storage.
Local emergency concurrency caps protect each process.
WHY THIS WORKS
An atomic Redis script or dedicated quota service can coordinate a key, but storage failover and partition
behavior still matter. For some APIs, temporary approximate quotas are acceptable; for financial limits,
they may not be. Global coordination can become a latency or hot-key bottleneck.
COMMON PITFALL  An eventually consistent read-then-write counter does not provide an exact global
quota.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which policy is used during a quota-store outage?
Answer: Use a central atomic counter/script or partitioned quota allocation; define consistency and
fallback when unavailable.

pages.title: How do quotas and fairness differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 21 / Rate limiting, fairness and admission QUESTION 104 / 120
How do quotas and fairness differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A quota caps usage; fairness prevents one workload from starving others within shared
capacity. Use per-tenant budgets, bounded queues or scheduling policies according to
the product contract.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Tenant A: 10,000 queued reports.
Tenant B: 1 interactive request.
A single FIFO can make B wait behind all of A's work.
WHY THIS WORKS
Separate interactive and batch traffic or use weighted scheduling. Reserve capacity for control and
recovery work when necessary. T enant-specific limits should avoid high-cardinality metric explosions and
have a manageable configuration lifecycle.
COMMON PITFALL  Global rate limiting can protect the system while still allowing one tenant to dominate
it.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What maximum wait can a small tenant experience during a large import?
Answer: Use per-tenant queues/weights and maximum waits; a big import must not monopolize
shared capacity.

fair queues
small tenant progress

CHAPTER 21 / Rate limiting, fairness and admission QUESTION 105 / 120
Should a limiter fail open or fail closed?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Choose per operation based on the consequence of excess work versus denied work.
Document the fallback, apply local protection, and expose degraded enforcement to
monitoring.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Public product reads: may use a cautious local fallback.
Paid external SMS: tighter admission may be required.
Critical money limit: do not invent availability guarantees.
WHY THIS WORKS
There is no universal safe setting. A fail-open policy can overload an already damaged dependency; a fail-
closed policy can create an outage from the limiter itself. Use cached policy and bounded local budgets
when appropriate, with clear accuracy limits.
COMMON PITFALL  Treating every quota as a security invariant can unnecessarily reject harmless reads.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How long may degraded quota enforcement continue?
Answer: Only a short, documented period with extra alarms and reduced access, based on risk and
capacity.

pages.title: How do database sequences, random IDs and time- based IDs compare?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Identifiers and useful algorithms QUESTION 106 / 120
How do database sequences, random IDs and time-
based IDs compare?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Sequences simplify compact uniqueness in one authority; random IDs enable
decentralized generation; time-based layouts can improve ordering but need clock and
node-identity handling.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Sequence -> compact, may reveal volume.
Random UUID -> decentralized, larger keys.
Time-based ID -> timestamp + node + local sequence.
WHY THIS WORKS
Uniqueness and unpredictability are separate requirements. A unique ID is not an access-control
mechanism. Distributed time-based generators need defined behavior on clock rollback, sequence
exhaustion and duplicated node identifiers. Index locality and storage overhead should influence the
choice.
COMMON PITFALL  Encoding a sequential number does not make it secret.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if two nodes accidentally use the same generator identity?
Answer: Detect duplicate generator IDs, fence the node, and use collision-resistant IDs or a durable
unique constraint.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Identifiers and useful algorithms QUESTION 107 / 120
Why use Base62 for short codes, and what does it
not solve?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Base62 represents numbers with letters and digits to make a compact URL-friendly
code. Encoding alone neither creates unique IDs nor protects against guessing.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Alphabet size = 62.
Six characters offer 62^6 = 56,800,235,584 combinations.
Random selection still needs collision detection and retry.
WHY THIS WORKS
Use a unique database constraint on the code and an appropriate allocation strategy. Sequential IDs
encoded in Base62 avoid random collisions but can reveal patterns. Add moderation and redirect safety
rules independently. Confirm allowed characters and case sensitivity across clients and storage.
COMMON PITFALL  A huge namespace does not make random collision probability zero.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you allocate a user-selected custom alias safely?
Answer: Enforce a unique alias index/conditional insert and return conflict when someone else
owns it.
Base62 bytes
short code
unique mapping

pages.title: What is a Bloom filter useful for?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Identifiers and useful algorithms QUESTION 108 / 120
What is a Bloom filter useful for?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It is a compact probabilistic membership structure that can say definitely absent or
possibly present, under its normal no-deletion and consistent-population assumptions.
Verify positive results in authoritative storage.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Request for code XYZ.
Filter says absent -> skip lookup only if filter coverage is valid.
Filter says present -> check the database.
WHY THIS WORKS
False positives create extra lookups. Stale population, unsafe deletion or incomplete rebuilds can create
application-level false negatives even when the core algorithm does not. Estimate capacity and false-
positive rate before choosing bit and hash counts.
COMMON PITFALL  Never use a possibly-present answer as proof that a record exists.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens to newly created records before the filter update arrives?
Answer: A stale filter can say 'not found' for a new record. Read source-of-truth during refresh or
choose a freshness protocol.
Bloom positive
verify DB; negative
freshness

pages.title: When is rendezvous hashing useful?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Identifiers and useful algorithms QUESTION 109 / 120
When is rendezvous hashing useful?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It assigns a key to the node with the highest deterministic key-node score. Adding a
node moves only keys won by the new node, which makes membership changes easier
to reason about.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
score = hash(key + delimiter + stableNodeId).
owner = node with the maximum unsigned score.
Use identical encoding and tie-breaking on every client.
WHY THIS WORKS
The simple method checks each node, so cost grows with membership size. Weighted versions can
account for unequal capacity. The Java lab verifies the limited-remapping property when adding one
node, but it does not implement distributed migration or failure detection.
COMMON PITFALL  Java hashCode is not a complete stable cross-language routing specification.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How will routing configurations be versioned during membership changes?
Answer: Distribute a routing epoch; old clients must refresh or be rejected/redirected during
rebalance.
Key + candidates
max hash score
owner

pages.title: How can probabilistic structures and approximate counters be used responsibly?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Identifiers and useful algorithms QUESTION 110 / 120
How can probabilistic structures and approximate
counters be used responsibly?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use approximation where the product can tolerate bounded error, document the error
model, and keep correctness-critical decisions on an authoritative path.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Approximate distinct visitors: useful analytics.
Approximate item popularity: useful ranking signal.
Available money or remaining tickets: enforce exact policy.
WHY THIS WORKS
Error bounds, merge behavior and reset semantics differ by algorithm. A metric approximation can be
useful without being valid for billing. Include estimation error and pipeline lag in the dashboard meaning.
Avoid claiming exact totals because repeated runs happen to match small test data.
COMMON PITFALL  An approximate traffic estimate should not silently determine an exact financial
settlement.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which decisions remain correct when the estimate is wrong?
Answer: Use estimates for caching, analytics or hints; never authorize charges, ownership or hard
quotas from a guessed count.
Requirement
Critical decision
Verified result

pages.title: How should money be represented in Java and storage?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 / Business invariants: money, stock and reservations QUESTION 111 / 120
How should money be represented in Java and
storage?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use a defined currency and exact representation, such as integer minor units or
BigDecimal with explicit scale and rounding policy. Do not use binary floating point for
authoritative monetary calculations.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
record Money(String currency, long minorUnits) {}
USD 12.34 -> minorUnits 1234 under a two-decimal policy.
Use checked arithmetic and validate matching currencies.
WHY THIS WORKS
Currencies and business instruments can have different scales, so do not assume two decimals
universally. Overflow, rounding and exchange rates need explicit rules. A ledger records movements and
supports reconciliation more reliably than overwriting a balance without history.
COMMON PITFALL  BigDecimal constructed from a double can preserve an unintended binary
approximation.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
At which boundary is tax or exchange rounding applied?
Answer: Round at the defined business stage and currency scale; persist the rounding rule and
exact resulting minor units.
Price + currency
exact minor units
ledger

pages.title: Why use reservation states instead of immediately reducing final availability?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 / Business invariants: money, stock and reservations QUESTION 112 / 120
Why use reservation states instead of immediately
reducing final availability?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A reservation models temporary ownership while a workflow completes. Expiry,
confirmation and release are explicit transitions with one authoritative decision per
resource.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
AVAILABLE -> HELD -> CONFIRMED
HELD -> EXPIRED or RELEASED
Confirm only if hold is active and belongs to the caller.
WHY THIS WORKS
An expiry worker and confirmation can race, so the database must arbitrate using conditional updates or
locks. The timeout shown to a client should reflect server policy, not only a local countdown. Decide the
outcome of payment success after the hold expired.
COMMON PITFALL  A scheduled Java timer in one instance is not a durable global expiry mechanism.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which transition wins if confirmation and expiry execute simultaneously?
Answer: One atomic state transition wins. The losing worker rereads the final status and must not
reverse confirmation.
ACTIVE hold
CONFIRMED or EXPIRED
no double sale

pages.title: How should payment states handle an unknown outcome?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 / Business invariants: money, stock and reservations QUESTION 113 / 120
How should payment states handle an unknown
outcome?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Persist an explicit pending or unknown state, reuse a stable provider key, and query or
reconcile before issuing a new effect. A timeout is not evidence that the provider failed.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
CREATED -> SUBMITTED -> SUCCEEDED or DECLINED
SUBMITTED -> UNKNOWN after a lost response
UNKNOWN -> reconciled final state using the same provider reference
WHY THIS WORKS
Callbacks can arrive before or after polling results; duplicate and out-of-order updates need a valid
transition policy. Keep order state separate from payment state when they have different ownership.
Manual review is a valid terminal escalation for unresolved ambiguity.
COMMON PITFALL  Automatically charging again after every timeout can create duplicate payments.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do you handle a success callback after the UI has shown pending?
Answer: Keep the order PENDING/RECONCILING, accept a verified late callback idempotently and
update the UI safely.
Payment initiated
UNKNOWN
confirmed / reversed

pages.title: How can a local ledger transfer remain correct under retries?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 / Business invariants: money, stock and reservations QUESTION 114 / 120
How can a local ledger transfer remain correct under
retries?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use a stable command identity, balanced ledger entries and a transaction enforcing
account and currency rules. Commit deduplication and the local transfer together.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Command transfer-9:
Debit A by 500; credit B by 500 in the same currency.
UNIQUE(command_id) prevents repeated local application.
WHY THIS WORKS
Lock ordering, insufficient funds and serialization conflicts require explicit handling. A transfer to another
independent institution is a distributed workflow with settlement and reconciliation, not merely a two-
row update. Define whether account balances are derived or materialized and how they are checked.
COMMON PITFALL  A globally unique ID alone does not stop duplicate execution unless it is enforced.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do concurrent debits avoid taking an account below its permitted balance?
Answer: Lock/conditionally update the balance in one transaction, enforce minimum balance and
deduplicate transfer IDs.
Transfer key
debit + credit
one DB commit

pages.title: What does a notification delivery guarantee actually mean?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 23 / Business invariants: money, stock and reservations QUESTION 115 / 120
What does a notification delivery guarantee actually
mean?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Accepted, sent to provider, delivered to a device and read by a person are different
states. Promise only the state you can observe and control, and retain stable identities
across retries.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Notification n-42:
QUEUED -> PROVIDER_ACCEPTED -> DELIVERED when reported.
Read receipts are a separate product behavior.
WHY THIS WORKS
Provider callbacks can be duplicated or delayed. Email and SMS may not support perfect deduplication
or delivery evidence. Opt-out and preference changes should be checked at the appropriate sending
boundary. Define expiration so stale messages do not arrive long after they are useful.
COMMON PITFALL  A successful provider HTTP response does not necessarily prove device delivery.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which state should the dashboard display during provider ambiguity?
Answer: Show 'delivery unknown / checking' rather than 'failed' or 'delivered' until provider
evidence arrives.
Send intent
provider ambiguity
reconcile

pages.title: The cache disappears and the database collapses: what would you change?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 / Senior deep dives and production scenarios QUESTION 116 / 120
The cache disappears and the database collapses:
what would you change?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Treat cache loss as a planned workload, bound fallback concurrency, coalesce reloads
and prioritize essential requests. Rebuild gradually instead of flooding the database.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Before: every miss immediately queries DB.
After: bounded loaders + short waits + permitted stale serving.
Cold-cache load test verifies recovery budget.
WHY THIS WORKS
Separate cache misses, cache timeouts and total cache outage in metrics. A circuit breaker on the cache
can reduce repeated delays, but the database still needs admission control. Warm-up should avoid all
instances loading the same keys simultaneously.
COMMON PITFALL  Increasing database connections without checking DB capacity can accelerate
collapse.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which requests will be rejected while the cache warms?
Answer: Reject low-value/nonessential fallback queries first, protect critical checkout and cap DB
reload concurrency.
Cache outage
limit misses
protect DB

pages.title: Consumer lag rises while CPU is low: how do you investigate?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 / Senior deep dives and production scenarios QUESTION 117 / 120
Consumer lag rises while CPU is low: how do you
investigate?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Measure queue age, partition skew, database or provider waits, retry volume and
processing concurrency. Low CPU suggests waiting or uneven work, not necessarily
spare usable capacity.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
One partition contains a huge tenant.
Other consumers idle while that partition waits on DB locks.
Adding consumers does not divide this partition automatically.
WHY THIS WORKS
Inspect per-partition lag and duration, not only total backlog. Check ordering constraints before
parallelizing effects. A poison event can block progress, while repeated transient failures can consume
the entire retry budget. Fix the bottleneck and test backlog recovery alongside live traffic.
COMMON PITFALL  Scaling consumers beyond partition or downstream limits may create no throughput
gain.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can the hot tenant be repartitioned without breaking ordering?
Answer: Only with a new partition key/mapping and replay plan. Per-entity order must still be
defined and preserved.
Lag per partition
hot lock / retry
fix limit

pages.title: A deployment produces duplicate orders: where do you look first?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 / Senior deep dives and production scenarios QUESTION 118 / 120
A deployment produces duplicate orders: where do
you look first?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Verify stable request identities, durable uniqueness, transaction boundaries and
compatibility between versions. Trace one duplicate from client retries through
gateways, services and event consumers.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Version A scopes key by customer + request ID.
Version B accidentally scopes by instance + request ID.
Mixed deployment can admit the same command twice.
WHY THIS WORKS
Compare the actual persisted records and constraint definitions, not just code annotations. Check
whether keys expired, payload fingerprints changed or a proxy interception was bypassed. Stop
expansion of the bad version and reconcile effects according to business policy.
COMMON PITFALL  Deleting duplicates without understanding payment and inventory effects can corrupt
state.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which database constraint would have prevented the regression?
Answer: A unique constraint on the real caller scope and stable request key would reject the
duplicate even across versions.
Stable request key
unique DB row
one order

pages.title: What should a strong design tradeoff explanation sound like?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 / Senior deep dives and production scenarios QUESTION 119 / 120
What should a strong design tradeoff explanation
sound like?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Name the chosen guarantee and its cost, describe the alternative, and connect the
choice to a requirement. Avoid presenting technologies as universally better.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
WORKED EXAMPLE
Choice: route stock confirmation to one write authority.
Benefit: one correct reservation ordering.
Cost: higher remote latency and unavailable writes on lost authority.
Alternative: regional stock allocation with explicit budgets.
WHY THIS WORKS
The alternative can improve local availability but adds allocation and rebalancing complexity. Quantify
the assumptions that make the decision reasonable. Describe the trigger for revisiting it, such as regional
demand or a tighter latency target.
COMMON PITFALL  Saying 'it scales better' without naming the bottleneck and cost is incomplete.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What changed requirement would make you choose the alternative?
Answer: Choose regional allocation when low local write latency or regional independence becomes
a hard requirement and quotas can be split.
Requirement change
cost comparison
choice

pages.title: How should you finish an interview design answer?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 24 / Senior deep dives and production scenarios QUESTION 120 / 120
How should you finish an interview design answer?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Summarize the user journey, guarantees, bottleneck, failure behavior and next
evolution. Check that every important requirement maps to an explicit mechanism and
observable signal.
DRAW THE IDEA trace the decision, not just the technology
CODE / QUERY EXAMPLE
Booking guarantee -> conditional DB transition.
Retry guarantee -> durable request key and stored result.
Recovery -> outbox, reconciliation and tested restoration.
Scale -> indexed reads, cache, partitioning when justified.
WHY THIS WORKS
Invite a deep dive into the highest-risk boundary if time remains. Explain one limitation honestly and
how you would validate it before production. The goal is a defensible system with clear assumptions, not
an elaborate diagram filled with tools.
COMMON PITFALL  Do not finish with an unsupported claim that the design has no single point of failure.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What experiment would you run first before implementing this system?
Answer: Run a concurrent invariant test or failure-injection prototype around the riskiest
component, such as last- seat booking.
Guarantee
failure test
measured next step

pages.title: URL shortener
pages.fullText:
WORKED ARCHITECTURE A01 DESIGN + NORMAL PATH
URL shortener
Design creation and redirect for short URLs, with expiry and click analytics.
REQUIREMENTS AND GUARANTEE
Create a short code, resolve it, support optional expiry and a custom alias. Redirect should be fast; click
analytics can be delayed. The code must identify one mapping, and moderation or revocation must have
a defined propagation delay.
CAPACITY ASSUMPTIONS (HYPOTHETICAL)
Assume 2 million new links/day and 20 million redirects/day, with an 8x peak. This is approximately 185
peak writes/s and 1,852 peak reads/s. At 500 bytes/mapping, a year of new mappings is approximately
365 GB before indexes, replicas and backups. These are planning assumptions.
FOLLOW THE NORMAL REQUEST
Creation validates the destination and allocates a code, inserts the mapping under a unique constraint,
and returns it after commit. Redirect checks permitted edge/cache entries and falls back to the indexed

pages.title: Distributed rate limiter
pages.fullText:
WORKED ARCHITECTURE A02 DESIGN + NORMAL PATH
Distributed rate limiter
Protect a multitenant API with burst allowance and per-tenant quotas.
REQUIREMENTS AND GUARANTEE
Apply tenant and operation policy, allow a controlled burst, return a useful rejection, and prevent one
tenant from exhausting shared work. Decide acceptable quota error and outage behavior per endpoint
before choosing coordination.
CAPACITY ASSUMPTIONS (HYPOTHETICAL)
Assume 20,000 requests/s across 10,000 active quota keys. If each request performs one remote atomic
quota operation, the store must sustain at least that operation rate plus headroom. At an assumed 200
bytes/key, raw state is 2 MB, excluding substantial store overhead. Measure the hot-key distribution and
network latency.
FOLLOW THE NORMAL REQUEST
Resolve the validated tenant and policy version. Atomically refill and consume tokens for the key. Allow
only if all mandatory policies pass, using a clearly defined multi-policy accounting rule. Reject excess work
with 429 where appropriate. Enforce local concurrency separately. If quota storage fails, apply the
endpoint-specific degraded policy and monitor it.
Interview technique: point to the one owner that can make the authoritative decision.

pages.title: E-commerce checkout
pages.fullText:
WORKED ARCHITECTURE A03 DESIGN + NORMAL PATH
E-commerce checkout
Create an order without overselling or charging twice when clients retry.
REQUIREMENTS AND GUARANTEE
Accept an idempotent checkout command, reserve stock, coordinate payment, expose pending/final
status and reconcile unknown outcomes. A cart or search result can be stale; final price and inventory
decisions must use authoritative policy.
CAPACITY ASSUMPTIONS (HYPOTHETICAL)
Assume 2,000 checkout commands/s at peak, average four items/order and 5 KB of order-plus-items
payload. Raw new order data is approximately 10 MB/s before indexes and copies. At an assumed 200
ms mean request duration, about 400 requests are in flight. Payment latency and per-product contention
need separate measurements.
FOLLOW THE NORMAL REQUEST
Validate customer and cart, calculate the authoritative quote and store a command-scoped order in
PENDING. Commit its outbox record locally. A workflow reserves each inventory item through
idempotent commands and authorizes payment with a stable provider key. It confirms the order only
after required outcomes are known. On failure it releases reservations or follows the documented
compensation policy; on timeout it remains pending and reconciles.
Interview technique: point to the one owner that can make the authoritative decision.

pages.title: Ticket booking and expiring holds
pages.fullText:
WORKED ARCHITECTURE A04 DESIGN + NORMAL PATH
Ticket booking and expiring holds
Sell assigned seats fairly under a burst while preventing duplicate ownership.
REQUIREMENTS AND GUARANTEE
Browse availability, hold selected seats for a limited time, confirm on a known payment outcome, and
expire unused holds. One confirmed seat has one owner. Define fairness, bot controls and behavior when
payment finishes near hold expiry.
CAPACITY ASSUMPTIONS (HYPOTHETICAL)
Assume 50,000 people arrive in one minute: about 833 arrivals/s on average, with a larger stated burst to
test. If 5% attempt a hold, that is roughly 42 hold commands/s on average, but a popular section may
concentrate most writes. Capacity depends on contention, not merely total QPS. Buyers Admission /
queue Search projection Java booking API Seat / hold DB Payment workflow Expiry worker Search may
be stale; the seat database decides ownership. Admission protects burst capacity. Expiry and
confirmation compete through one authoritative transaction policy.
FOLLOW THE NORMAL REQUEST
Admit a bounded number of buyers and authorize the request. Lock requested seats in a consistent order
or use an equivalent atomic protocol. Verify availability and create one hold with an authoritative expiry
in the same transaction. Confirm only an active owned hold. An expiry worker releases eligible holds
through conditional transitions. Display countdowns as estimates of server expiry and return the
authoritative result of confirmation.
Interview technique: point to the one owner that can make the authoritative decision.

pages.title: Durable chat
pages.fullText:
WORKED ARCHITECTURE A05 DESIGN + NORMAL PATH
Durable chat
Support multi-device chat, offline history and reconnect without duplicate messages.
REQUIREMENTS AND GUARANTEE
Accept a message once under a stable client key, assign conversation order, persist history, deliver live
when possible and resume missed messages. Separate accepted, delivered and read states. Huge public
rooms need a different fan-out budget from small conversations.
CAPACITY ASSUMPTIONS (HYPOTHETICAL)
Assume 1 million daily active users sending 20 messages/day: 20 million/day, or about 231/s average and
2,315/s at a stated 10x peak. At 1 KB/message, raw message bytes are about 20 GB/day before replicas
and indexes. Separately assume 200,000 concurrent sockets to size gateways. Client devices Socket
gateways Connection directory Message owner Message DB / outbox Delivery log Delivery worker The
DB is the history authority. The delivery-log arrow includes an outbox relay. The connection directory is
ephemeral; failed live routing is repaired by history resume.
FOLLOW THE NORMAL REQUEST
Authenticate the connection and authorize conversation membership. Accept clientMessageId under
sender scope, assign a server sequence and commit message plus outbox. Deliver the resulting event to
current gateways and devices. Each client deduplicates by server message ID and detects sequence gaps.
On reconnect, request history after the last acknowledged sequence. Read receipts follow a separate
idempotent state policy.
Interview technique: point to the one owner that can make the authoritative decision.

Chat gateway
Message DB
Delivery fan-out

pages.fullText:
WORKED ARCHITECTURE A06 DESIGN + NORMAL PATH
Social feed
Build a personalized feed with popular authors and stable pagination.
REQUIREMENTS AND GUARANTEE
Create posts, follow authors, retrieve a useful feed, propagate deletion and enforce privacy. New posts
may appear after a defined lag. Ranking, chronological order and pagination behavior must be clarified.
CAPACITY ASSUMPTIONS (HYPOTHETICAL)
Assume 10 million users, 10% daily active and 20 feed reads each: 20 million reads/day. If an ordinary
post has 500 followers but a celebrity has 10 million, average fan-out hides the dominant worst case.
Model the audience distribution, read frequency and allowable freshness. Reader / author Java feed API
Post owner DB Feed cache Fan-out log Projection worker Feed store Follow graph Post-to-log
publication uses durable change capture or an outbox. Ordinary author posts populate feed projections;
high-audience posts can be merged at read time.
FOLLOW THE NORMAL REQUEST
Commit the authoritative post and change intent. Fan-out workers obtain an appropriate follower view
and add stable post IDs to recipient feed projections with duplicate-safe writes. Feed reads fetch the
projection, merge designated high-audience sources and apply ranking and authorization. Use a cursor
tied to the chosen ranking/snapshot policy. Deletion and privacy changes must hide content even if
projection cleanup is delayed.

pages.title: Large file upload and media processing
pages.fullText:
WORKED ARCHITECTURE A07 DESIGN + NORMAL PATH
Large file upload and media processing
Accept large user files without filling Java heap, and publish only validated assets.
REQUIREMENTS AND GUARANTEE
Authorize upload, support retry/resume, validate expected content, process safely and serve authorized
downloads. An asset is available only after the declared checks complete. Clean up abandoned uploads
and orphaned objects.
CAPACITY ASSUMPTIONS (HYPOTHETICAL)
Assume 100,000 uploads/day at 50 MB average: 5 TB/day of raw ingress. Routing every byte through
Java APIs adds application bandwidth and memory pressure. Direct object upload separates the control
plane from the data plane; transformations, replicas, egress and retention need additional budgets.
Uploader Java control API Metadata DB Object storage Finalize event Scan / transform Download / CDN
The API issues a scoped upload capability after authorization. Object bytes bypass application heap.
Finalization records durable processing intent; publication depends on metadata state and validation.
FOLLOW THE NORMAL REQUEST
Create a draft asset and generate a unique object key. Issue a short-lived upload capability with
supported restrictions. The client uploads directly and retries or resumes according to the storage
contract. Finalization verifies object ownership, size and checksum and records processing intent.
Workers scan and transform into versioned objects, then atomically publish metadata. Downloads check
authorization before issuing a capability or serving allowed public content.
Interview technique: point to the one owner that can make the authoritative decision.

Resource IDs and cursors always require

state: UPLOADING, SCANNING, AVAILABLE, 
REJECTED, DELETED

FAILURE PLAYBOOK
DESIGNED RESPONSE Client abandons upload Expire draft and clean incomplete/orphaned objects.
Upload succeeds, finalize lost Retry stable finalization or reconcile draft object state. Duplicate transform
job Use versioned deterministic outputs and an atomic publish decision. Malicious/invalid file Quarantine
or reject; never publish before validation policy.
TRADEOFF
Direct upload saves API bandwidth but exposes a capability and introduces two-system reconciliation.
Proxying small files can be simpler. Prefer streaming and bounded buffers when proxying is required.
Multiple versions make processing and rollback safer but increase storage and cleanup costs.
OBSERVE
Upload/finalize success; draft age; processing
lag; rejected scans; checksum failures; orphan
bytes; object-store and CDN egress.
NEXT EVOLUTION
Add multipart/resumable upload, processing
pools by workload and lifecycle retention. Keep
public CDN content separate from private
delivery policy. T est interrupted upload and
metadata/object mismatch recovery.

1. What if a client finalizes a different file than the one authorized?
Answer: Bind the upload grant to object key, owner, size/checksum and validate these again during finalization.
2. How do you prevent a signed URL from overwriting another asset?
Answer: Issue unique, short-lived, scoped object keys; reject overwrites and validate at finalize.

pages.title: Notification platform
pages.fullText:
WORKED ARCHITECTURE A08 DESIGN + NORMAL PATH
Notification platform
Deliver email, push and SMS under preferences, provider limits and recoverable
failures.
REQUIREMENTS AND GUARANTEE
Accept durable intent, choose allowed channels, respect current preferences, rate-limit expensive
providers and expose meaningful status. Notifications can expire; provider acceptance is different from
device delivery or human reading.
CAPACITY ASSUMPTIONS (HYPOTHETICAL)
Assume 10 million notifications/day: approximately 116/s average and 1,160/s at a stated 10x peak. A
provider limited to 500/s will accumulate backlog at 660/s during that peak unless traffic is delayed,
rerouted or dropped by policy. Compute backlog duration against notification expiry. Business services
Notification API Intent DB / outbox Channel workers Preferences Providers Callbacks / reconcile A local
commit accepts notification intent. Channel workers enforce policy and budgets. Callback/reconciliation
paths update durable states without assuming every provider response is final delivery.
FOLLOW THE NORMAL REQUEST
Validate and deduplicate a caller-scoped notification intent, then commit it with publish intent. Resolve
channel preferences according to the sending policy, render a versioned template and enqueue a channel
attempt. Enforce provider rate and concurrency limits, use stable provider keys where supported, and
retain ambiguous attempts for reconciliation. Apply duplicate-safe callbacks, expire obsolete work and
expose accepted/provider/delivery states separately.
Interview technique: point to the one owner that can make the authoritative decision.
Clients
Notify API
Outbox / queue
Provider send

Notification platform: make it reliable
API CONTRACT
Resource IDs and cursors always require

key

These are logical schema sketches;

FAILURE PLAYBOOK
DESIGNED RESPONSE Provider timeout Retain ambiguity; reconcile or retry by provider contract.
Preference changed Recheck at sending boundary according to policy. Callback duplicated Persist
provider event identity with state transition. Backlog exceeds expiry Expire obsolete intents and prioritize
essential classes.
TRADEOFF
Provider failover improves resilience but can create duplicates when the first outcome is unknown. If a
provider lacks idempotency or status lookup, document the residual duplicate/loss risk. Keep urgent
transactional messages separate from bulk campaigns and ensure quotas preserve fairness.
OBSERVE
Intent acceptance; queue age by bounded
channel/class; provider errors; ambiguous
attempts; suppression and expiry; reported
delivery lag; paid usage.
NEXT EVOLUTION
Partition work by channel and tenant budget,
introduce provider-specific adapters and isolate
campaigns. Add replay tooling with a dry-run
view and explicit duplicate-risk policy.
TWO SENIOR FOLLOW-UPS WITH ANSWERS
1. Can an SMS be sent twice when switching providers after a timeout?
Answer: Yes: a timeout leaves delivery uncertain, so use provider idempotency where supported and reconcile before
fallback.
2. What should happen to a password-reset message that waited past its useful lifetime?
Answer: Enforce an expiry or deadline and discard the stale message rather than delivering an unusable reset link.

pages.title: System guarantees checklist
pages.fullText:
ARCHITECT INTERVIEW CHEAT SHEET REVISE FAST
System guarantees checklist
No overselling Atomic check-and-reserve in the authoritative store, plus duplicate command handling.
Idempotency Scoped stable key, validated request intent, durable outcome and in-progress behavior.
Event publication Business update and outbox intent committed together; relay can redeliver.
Cache
consistency
State the stale-data policy; never make stock or money decisions from an untrusted
cache.
Fault tolerance Specify how retries, timeouts, admission and recovery behave during failure.
Regional failure Name the data owner, failover consistency, RPO and RTO.
Queue processing Budget backlog age, partitions, redelivery, poison records and consumer effects.
Security Authorize the resource and operation at its owner, with tenant-scoped queries/cachekeys.
Performance Quantify workload and measure p95/p99, queue wait, pool pressure and bottlenecks.
Strong interview pattern: Requirement → Invariant → Normal request → Failure path →
Tradeoff → Validation signal.
Keep guarantees specific Revision sheet

CHAPTER 01 · EVENT-DRIVEN FOUNDATIONSQUESTION 001 / 100 
What is Kafka and why use it with Spring Boot?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Kafka is a distributed event log; Spring Boot supplies the
application wiring for publishing and consuming records.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Order service ➔ orders topic ➔ billing and shipping groups
WORKED EXAMPLE
Order service -> orders topic -> billing and shipping groups
WHY IT WORKS
One published order event can feed
independent services. Consumers keep their
own progress and can replay retained records.
Kafka adds asynchronous delivery, but the
application still owns business correctness.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Kafka is not a substitute for a database
transaction.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
When would a direct REST call be simpler?
Choose REST when the caller must receive a small, immediate answer, and the target
service is available within the request deadline. Example: checking an address before
submitting a form.

pages.title: How does an event differ from a command?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 · EVENT-DRIVEN FOUNDATIONSQUESTION 002 / 100 
How does an event differ from a command?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
An event states something that happened; a command asks a
specific capability to do something.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Service owns fact ➔ Kafka keeps record ➔ Independent consumers
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
Event: OrderPlaced(orderId=42)
   Command: ReserveInventory(orderId=42)
WHY IT WORKS
An order event should describe a committed
fact. A reservation command can be rejected
and needs an outcome. Naming and

pages.title: When should Kafka replace synchronous REST?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 · EVENT-DRIVEN FOUNDATIONSQUESTION 003 / 100 
When should Kafka replace synchronous REST?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Use Kafka when independent processing, buffering or replay
matters more than an immediate response from the downstream
service.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
POST /orders ➔ Kafka keeps record ➔ 202 + orderId
WORKED EXAMPLE
POST /orders -> 202 + orderId
   GET /orders/42 -> PENDING, CONFIRMED or REJECTED
WHY IT WORKS
The HTTP response confirms the documented
acceptance boundary, not completion of every
consumer. Expose an explicit status model and
failure path. Use synchronous calls where the
caller genuinely needs the downstream result
now.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A fast HTTP response does not prove the
event was durably accepted.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What does 202 mean in your API?
HTTP 202 means the request was accepted for later handling, not that all business steps
finished. Return an operation ID and offer a status endpoint showing PENDING,
COMPLETED or FAILED.

pages.title: CHAPTER 01 · EVENT-DRIVEN FOUNDATIONSQUESTION 004 / 100
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 · EVENT-DRIVEN FOUNDATIONSQUESTION 004 / 100 
How is Kafka different from a traditional work
queue?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Kafka retains a partitioned log and tracks progress per consumer
group instead of deleting each record after one consumer receives
it.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Service owns fact ➔ Kafka keeps record ➔ Independent consumers
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
orders: offsets 0,1,2,3 remain within retention
   billing group next=4; analytics group next=2
WHY IT WORKS
Within a group, partition ownership distributes
work. Across groups, each application can
read the same records independently.
Retention is a storage policy, so a slow
consumer can fall behind the available history.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Consumption does not reset the retention
clock.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you detect data lost to retention?
Track each group's oldest available offset against its next committed offset. Alert when
retention advances past unprocessed data; compare processing history and recover
missing data from a trusted source.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 8

pages.title: CHAPTER 01 · EVENT-DRIVEN FOUNDATIONSQUESTION 005 / 100
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 01 · EVENT-DRIVEN FOUNDATIONSQUESTION 005 / 100 
What is eventual consistency in an event-driven
system?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Related services can temporarily show different states while events
travel and are processed.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Service owns fact ➔ Kafka keeps record ➔ Independent consumers
WORKED EXAMPLE
Order: CONFIRMED at 10:00:00
   Search projection: PENDING until 10:00:02
WHY IT WORKS
Define an acceptable lag, user-visible pending
state and reconciliation process. A broken
consumer is not automatically eventual
consistency: without recovery the projection
may never converge.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Do not promise immediate reads from an
asynchronous projection.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What convergence metric would you monitor?
Measure time from authoritative event commit to successful projection update, especially
the oldest pending event age. Alert on exceeded freshness SLOs and on projections that
stop advancing.

pages.title: What are a topic, partition and offset?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 · TOPICS, PARTITIONS AND RECORD IDENTITYQUESTION 006 / 100 
What are a topic, partition and offset?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
A topic groups records; partitions are ordered logs; offsets identify
positions within one partition.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Business key ➔ Partition log ➔ Offset and consumer
WORKED EXAMPLE
orders-0 offset 19 != orders-1 offset 19
   Record identity: topic + partition + offset
WHY IT WORKS
Offsets are assigned by the broker and are
not global sequence numbers. Compaction
and transactions can leave gaps in visible
records. Use a separate eventId for business
deduplication across republishing.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
An offset alone is not globally unique.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Why can a consumer see offset gaps?
Offsets can be absent from what a consumer sees because of compaction, aborted
transactions under read_committed, retention, or filtering. Do not assume every numeric
offset has a visible record.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 11

pages.title: Where does Kafka guarantee ordering?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 · TOPICS, PARTITIONS AND RECORD IDENTITYQUESTION 007 / 100 
Where does Kafka guarantee ordering?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Kafka preserves log order within a partition, not a global order
across partitions.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
customer A ➔ Partition log ➔ partition 0: Created, Updated
WORKED EXAMPLE
customer A -> partition 0: Created, Updated
   customer B -> partition 1: Created, Updated
WHY IT WORKS
Choose a stable aggregate key when updates
for that aggregate must share a partition.
Consumer worker pools, retry topics and
application logic can still reorder side effects
after records are read.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Partition order does not guarantee ordered
asynchronous completion.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you preserve account-level processing order?
Send all events for an account with the same stable account ID as key, process each
partition in sequence, and avoid asynchronous handlers that finish out of order.
Repartitioning requires a migration plan.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 12

pages.title: How does a record key affect partition selection?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 · TOPICS, PARTITIONS AND RECORD IDENTITYQUESTION 008 / 100 
How does a record key affect partition selection?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
The producer partitioner uses the key and partition metadata
unless an explicit partition or custom partitioner changes that
choice.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Business key ➔ Partition log ➔ Offset and consumer
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
template.send("orders", order.customerId(), json);
WHY IT WORKS
A stable key normally routes related events to
the same partition for a fixed topic layout. Null
keys follow the configured partitioner behavior.
Do not rely on an undocumented hand-written
modulo formula to match every client version.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A business key can create a hot partition.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which key would you choose for a payment ledger?
Use the payment or account identity whose operations must stay ordered (for example
accountId), not a random eventId. Consider hot accounts and make the partitioning
policy explicit.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 13

pages.title: What happens when a topic gains partitions?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 02 · TOPICS, PARTITIONS AND RECORD IDENTITYQUESTION 009 / 100 
What happens when a topic gains partitions?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It increases possible parallelism, but key-to-partition mapping can
change for future records.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Before: account-7 ➔ Partition log ➔ partition 1
WORKED EXAMPLE
Before: account-7 -> partition 1
   After expansion: account-7 may -> partition 4
WHY IT WORKS
Older records remain in their original
partitions. If a key moves, strict ordering
across old and new history needs an explicit
migration strategy, drain or versioned topic.
Partition reduction is not a normal in-place
operation.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Adding partitions is not a harmless ordering
change.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you migrate an ordered topic?
Create a versioned topic with the desired partition count, establish a controlled cutover
point, drain old work, and route new writes to the new topic. Reconcile versions and
consumer progress before retirement.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 14

CHAPTER 02 · TOPICS, PARTITIONS AND RECORD IDENTITYQUESTION 010 / 100 
Are timestamp and offset the same?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
A timestamp describes record time semantics; an offset describes
position in a partition log.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Business key ➔ Partition log ➔ Offset and consumer
WORKED EXAMPLE
partition 0: offset 20 timestamp 10:05
   partition 0: offset 21 timestamp 10:03

because clocks and sources differ. Broker
append-time policy is a different choice. Event

explicit in the event contract.

Sorting across topics by timestamp does not
establish causality.

How would you handle late events?

results until a grace limit; after that use a correction event, reconciliation or a
documented late-data policy.

pages.title: What are leader, follower and ISR?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 · REPLICATION AND BROKER GUARANTEESQUESTION 011 / 100 
What are leader, follower and ISR?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
The leader handles partition writes; followers replicate; ISR is the
set of replicas currently sufficiently caught up.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Producer policy ➔ Leader and ISR ➔ Ack or uncertainty
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
Replication factor=3; ISR={broker1, broker2}
   Leader=broker1; broker3 is lagging
WHY IT WORKS
ISR membership changes as replicas fail or
catch up. Replication factor is the desired
replica count, while ISR describes current
replication health. Observe under-replicated
partitions and shrinking ISR during incidents.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Replication factor three does not mean three
healthy copies right now.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What metric would trigger your durability alert?
Alert on under-replicated partitions, offline replicas, ISR shrinkage and partitions below
min.insync.replicas. Include broker and availability-zone health so an alert signals actual
durability risk.

pages.title: What do acks=0, acks=1 and acks=all mean?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 · REPLICATION AND BROKER GUARANTEESQUESTION 012 / 100 
What do acks=0, acks=1 and acks=all mean?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
They choose no broker acknowledgment, leader acknowledgment,
or acknowledgment from the current in-sync replica set.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Producer policy ➔ Leader and ISR ➔ Ack or uncertainty
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
acks=0: no response confirmation
   acks=1: leader confirms
   acks=all: ISR acknowledgment requirement
WHY IT WORKS
acks=all is not acknowledgment from every
configured replica, including lagging ones. It
works with min.insync.replicas to enforce a
minimum healthy replica count for accepted
writes.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Acknowledgment does not mean a consumer
processed the record.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What can still fail after acks=1 succeeds?
The leader can acknowledge before followers copy the record. If the leader then fails
and a different replica wins, the acknowledged record can be lost under relevant
recovery settings.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 18

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 · REPLICATION AND BROKER GUARANTEESQUESTION 013 / 100 
How do min.insync.replicas and acks=all work
together?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
The broker rejects all-ack writes when the ISR falls below the
configured minimum.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Producer policy ➔ Leader and ISR ➔ Ack or uncertainty
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
replication.factor=3
   min.insync.replicas=2
   acks=all
WHY IT WORKS
With one in-sync replica remaining, this policy
sacrifices write availability rather than
accepting under-replicated writes. The exact
failure can appear during or after append, so
the producer must handle uncertain outcomes
and retries.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
min.insync.replicas alone does not enforce this
producer policy for acks=1.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Why might a timeout still mean the record was appended?
The broker might append the record, but its acknowledgment may be delayed or lost.
Treat the response as unknown and retry using a compatible idempotent producer plus
stable business identity.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 · REPLICATION AND BROKER GUARANTEESQUESTION 014 / 100 
Why can a successful send still have durability
limits?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
A send confirms the configured broker acknowledgment boundary,
not protection against every correlated failure.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
RF=3 on one physical host ➔ Leader and ISR ➔ one host failure losesavailability
WORKED EXAMPLE
RF=3 on one physical host -> one host failure loses availability
WHY IT WORKS
Replica placement, fault domains, recovery
policy and storage health matter. Kafka
replication does not make application retries
or external side effects automatically safe.
Design for realistic rack or zone failures.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Three replicas in the same failure domain are
weak protection.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What failure would your deployment survive?
With three replicas across independent zones and suitable ISR/minimum settings, one
broker or zone failure may be tolerated. Correlated failure, quorum loss or misplacement
remain outside that guarantee.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 03 · REPLICATION AND BROKER GUARANTEESQUESTION 015 / 100 
What is KRaft and how does it relate to
ZooKeeper?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
KRaft manages Kafka cluster metadata through a controller
quorum; older Kafka deployments used ZooKeeper.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Controller quorum ➔ Leader and ISR ➔ metadata decisions
WORKED EXAMPLE
Controller quorum -> metadata decisions
   Partition replicas -> record storage
WHY IT WORKS
Kafka 4.x is KRaft-only. Controllers and
partition leaders have different responsibilities.
For an interview, separate the broker/client
version from the Spring Boot library version
and ask which deployment generation is in
scope.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Do not prescribe ZooKeeper for a new Kafka
4.x cluster.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How does controller loss differ from a partition leader failure?
Controller loss affects metadata leadership and cluster coordination until controller
quorum recovers. Partition-leader loss affects writes/reads for that partition until an
eligible replica takes leadership.

pages.title: CHAPTER 04 · SPRING BOOT INTEGRATIONQUESTION 016 / 100
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 · SPRING BOOT INTEGRATIONQUESTION 016 / 100 
Which dependency enables Spring Kafka
integration?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Add spring-kafka and let the Spring Boot dependency
management select compatible library versions.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Boot configuration ➔ Spring Kafka client ➔ Listener / template
WORKED EXAMPLE
<dependency>
     <groupId>org.springframework.kafka</groupId>
     <artifactId>spring-kafka</artifactId>
   </dependency>
WHY IT WORKS
The Boot parent or BOM manages versions.
Broker binaries are a separate deployment
concern. This guide targets Boot 3.5 and
Spring Kafka 3.3 style APIs; check your
resolved dependency tree before copying a
version-specific configuration.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Mixing arbitrary client and framework
versions can break compatibility.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you inspect the effective dependency versions?
Run `mvn dependency:tree` (or Gradle dependencyInsight) and inspect the resolved
`spring-kafka`, `kafka-clients` and Boot versions. Use the chosen Boot BOM as the
compatibility baseline.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 23

pages.title: What does Boot auto-configure for Kafka?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 · SPRING BOOT INTEGRATIONQUESTION 017 / 100 
What does Boot auto-configure for Kafka?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It can configure producer and consumer factories, KafkaTemplate,
administration and a default listener container factory from
properties and available beans.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Boot configuration ➔ Spring Kafka client ➔ Listener / template
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers=localhost:9092
   spring.kafka.consumer.group-id=orders-worker
WHY IT WORKS
Properties supply client settings; listener
annotations supply application behavior.
Custom beans can cause parts of auto-
configuration to back off. Inspect conditions
when a template or factory is unexpectedly
absent.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Boot does not provision a production broker
cluster.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What would a custom ConsumerFactory override?
A custom ConsumerFactory replaces or customizes consumer construction, including
deserializers, authentication, bootstrap addresses and group settings. Confirm the listener
factory uses that bean.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 24

pages.title: What is Kafka T emplate?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 · SPRING BOOT INTEGRATIONQUESTION 018 / 100 
What is Kafka T emplate?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
KafkaTemplate is Spring's publishing abstraction over the Kafka
producer.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Boot configuration ➔ Spring Kafka client ➔ Listener / template
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
CompletableFuture<SendResult<String,String>> future =
       template.send("orders", "42", "placed");
WHY IT WORKS
In modern Spring Kafka, send returns a
CompletableFuture. Completion carries broker
metadata or an error. A send can also fail
synchronously before a future is returned,
such as during serialization or unavailable
metadata.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Starting a send is not the same as confirming
its success.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which two failure paths must publishing code handle?
Handle a synchronous exception from `send(...)` and asynchronous exceptional
completion of its `CompletableFuture`. Neither successful invocation nor a pending future
is proof of broker acceptance.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 25

pages.title: What does @KafkaListener do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 · SPRING BOOT INTEGRATIONQUESTION 019 / 100 
What does @KafkaListener do?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It declares a listener endpoint that a Spring-managed container
invokes for consumed records.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Boot configuration ➔ Spring Kafka client ➔ Listener / template
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
@KafkaListener(topics="orders", groupId="billing-v1")
   public void receive(String value) { service.apply(value); }
WHY IT WORKS
The container owns polling, dispatch and
configured offset/error behavior. A bean
method is needed for endpoint registration.
The listener should finish the required durable
work before the container treats the record as
successfully handled.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A swallowed exception can make failed work
appear successful.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
When should the listener throw?
Throw when the required durable business effect failed and the configured error handler
should retry or quarantine the record. Do not swallow a database exception and permit
offset progress.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 26

pages.title: How do you create a topic from an application?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 · SPRING BOOT INTEGRATIONQUESTION 020 / 100 
How do you create a topic from an application?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Declare a NewTopic bean for KafkaAdmin when application-
managed topic creation is appropriate.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Boot configuration ➔ Spring Kafka client ➔ Listener / template
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
@Bean NewTopic orders() {
     return TopicBuilder.name("orders")
         .partitions(6).replicas(3).build();
   }
WHY IT WORKS
The cluster must support the replica count
and the principal must have administration
permission. Production teams often provision
topics separately through reviewed
infrastructure configuration. Existing topics
and changes need deliberate operational
control.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A one-broker local cluster cannot satisfy
replication factor three.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Who should own topic configuration in production?
The platform or streaming team usually owns approved topic declarations, ACLs,
retention and replication through infrastructure-as-code; application teams define the
contract and request reviewed changes.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 27

05. Producer reliability and tuning
Handle both synchronous send errors and asynchronous future completion.
Record and key → Batch and broker → Future result
Five original interview questions follow, each with its own answer, visual model, worked
example, pitfall, and solved follow-up.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 28

pages.title: What does producer idempotence prevent?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 · PRODUCER RELIABILITY AND TUNINGQUESTION 021 / 100 
What does producer idempotence prevent?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It prevents duplicate log appends from eligible retries within the
producer's protocol session.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Record and key ➔ Batch and broker ➔ Future result
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
spring.kafka.producer.acks=all
   spring.kafka.producer.properties[enable.idempotence]=true
WHY IT WORKS
Idempotence uses producer identity and
sequence numbers. It does not deduplicate
two business sends with the same eventId, or
prevent a consumer from charging twice.
Compatible retry and max-in-flight settings
are required.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Idempotent producer does not mean
idempotent business workflow.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you deduplicate application resends?
Give the event a stable business ID, and deduplicate it at the consumer's durable write
boundary (such as a unique inbox key in the same DB transaction). Producer
idempotence alone cannot do this.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 29

pages.title: What is max.in.flight.requests.per.connection?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 · PRODUCER RELIABILITY AND TUNINGQUESTION 022 / 100 
What is max.in.flight.requests.per.connection?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It limits producer requests awaiting responses on a broker
connection.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Record and key ➔ Batch and broker ➔ Future result
WORKED EXAMPLE
Idempotent producer: supported max-in-flight <= 5
WHY IT WORKS
Without idempotence, multiple outstanding
requests and retries can reorder batches. With
compatible idempotence settings, ordering is
preserved for supported values. Do not tune
this value in isolation from latency, throughput
and retry behavior.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Setting it arbitrarily high conflicts with
idempotence requirements.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Why might setting it to one reduce throughput?
Only one batch can be in flight, which prevents pipeline overlap. On high-latency broker
links it can substantially reduce throughput; benchmark compatible idempotent settings
instead.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 30

It limits producer requests awaiting responses on a broker
connection.

pages.title: How do linger.ms and batch.size affect publishing?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 · PRODUCER RELIABILITY AND TUNINGQUESTION 023 / 100 
How do linger.ms and batch.size affect publishing?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
They influence waiting and batching of records, trading latency for
throughput and compression efficiency.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Record and key ➔ Batch and broker ➔ Future result
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
linger.ms=10
   batch.size=32768
WHY IT WORKS
The producer batches per partition. A full
batch can send before the linger interval
expires. Defaults vary by Kafka client version,
so measure the resolved client's behavior
rather than memorizing one default forever.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
batch.size is not the maximum event size.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you benchmark latency at low traffic?
Publish small messages at controlled low rates, measure p50/p95/p99 end-to-end
latency with linger set to multiple values, and record producer batch size, network use
and CPU.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 31

pages.title: How do delivery.timeout.ms and request.timeout.ms differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 · PRODUCER RELIABILITY AND TUNINGQUESTION 024 / 100 
How do delivery.timeout.ms and
request.timeout.ms differ?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Request timeout bounds an individual response wait; delivery
timeout bounds the overall delivery lifecycle including retry-related
time.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Record and key ➔ Batch and broker ➔ Future result
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
delivery.timeout.ms=120000
   request.timeout.ms=30000
WHY IT WORKS
The delivery budget includes batching delay
and retries under the producer's rules.
max.block.ms separately bounds selected waits
during send, such as metadata or buffer
availability. Use budgets aligned with API
expectations.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
An HTTP timeout does not cancel a Kafka
record already sent.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What response should an API return for an unknown send outcome?
Return an explicit PENDING/UNKNOWN state with a stable operation ID if the business
contract allows it. Reconcile the send result from durable intent; do not claim failure or
success from timeout alone.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 32

pages.title: CHAPTER 05 · PRODUCER RELIABILITY AND TUNINGQUESTION 025 / 100
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 · PRODUCER RELIABILITY AND TUNINGQUESTION 025 / 100 
Why use compression and bounded producer
buffers?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Compression can reduce network/storage work, while bounded
buffers expose overload instead of hiding it indefinitely.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Record and key ➔ Batch and broker ➔ Future result
WORKED EXAMPLE
compression.type=zstd
   buffer.memory=33554432
WHY IT WORKS
Compression effectiveness depends on
batches and payloads. Buffer exhaustion can
block publishing up to the configured limit and
then fail. Track enqueue rate, request latency
and buffer wait metrics before changing
memory.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Increasing buffers does not fix a permanently
slow broker.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you shed load safely?
Reject or defer excess requests with a documented 429/503 or a durable queue if the
contract supports it. Bound memory and requests, protect critical workloads and expose
retry-after guidance.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 33

06. Consumer groups and scaling
Consumers in one group divide partitions; separate groups progress
independently.
Subscribed group → Partition assignment → Progress checkpoint
Five original interview questions follow, each with its own answer, visual model, worked
example, pitfall, and solved follow-up.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 34

pages.title: What is a consumer group?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · CONSUMER GROUPS AND SCALINGQUESTION 026 / 100 
What is a consumer group?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
A group coordinates consumers that share progress and divide
partition ownership for subscribed topics.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Subscribed group ➔ Partition assignment ➔ Progress checkpoint
WORKED EXAMPLE
orders has 6 partitions
   billing group: 3 consumers -> roughly 2 partitions each
   shipping group: independent progress
WHY IT WORKS
A partition is normally assigned to one
consumer at a time within the group. Different
groups receive independent copies of the
logical stream. Assignment details depend on
topics, strategy and protocol.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Consumers in different groups do not share
the workload.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you add an audit subscriber?
Create a new consumer group ID for audit, subscribe it to the same topic, grant
minimum ACLs and define its offset starting policy. Billing's group progress remains
independent.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 35

pages.title: How many consumers can usefully process one topic in a group?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · CONSUMER GROUPS AND SCALINGQUESTION 027 / 100 
How many consumers can usefully process one
topic in a group?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Parallel partition ownership is bounded by the topic's partition
count.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Subscribed group ➔ Partition assignment ➔ Progress checkpoint
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
6 partitions; 10 consumers in one group
   At most 6 own partitions for this topic
WHY IT WORKS
Extra consumers can be idle. A consumer can
own several partitions, and a group can
subscribe to multiple topics. Scale using
measured partition load and downstream
capacity, not only replica count.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
More pods cannot split one hot partition
between group members.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you fix a single hot key?
First measure why the key is hot. If operations need one total order, increase per-
partition processing capacity or redesign the aggregate; splitting the key sacrifices its
single-partition order.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 36

pages.title: CHAPTER 06 · CONSUMER GROUPS AND SCALINGQUESTION 028 / 100
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · CONSUMER GROUPS AND SCALINGQUESTION 028 / 100 
What does listener concurrency mean in Spring
Kafka?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It configures multiple child listener containers, each with its own
consumer.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Subscribed group ➔ Partition assignment ➔ Progress checkpoint
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
@KafkaListener(topics="orders", concurrency="3")
   public void receive(String value) { ... }
WHY IT WORKS
Two application instances with concurrency
three create up to six consumers. Their useful
assignments still depend on partitions and
group strategy. Shared listener state and
injected collaborators must be safe for
concurrent invocation.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Concurrency is not a worker pool for one
consumer instance.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What state should not be stored on the listener bean?
Do not keep mutable currentOrder, currentRecord, tenantId, counters or unsynchronized
maps as listener fields. Store per-record state in local variables and use safe, durable
repositories.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 37

pages.title: What triggers a rebalance?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · CONSUMER GROUPS AND SCALINGQUESTION 029 / 100 
What triggers a rebalance?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Membership, subscriptions or partition metadata changes can
require reassignment of group partitions.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Pod joins ➔ Partition assignment ➔ assignment changes
WORKED EXAMPLE
Pod joins -> assignment changes
   Consumer misses progress requirements -> partition revoked
WHY IT WORKS
During ownership changes, unfinished work
and commits need careful handling. Strategies
and group protocols affect how much work
pauses. Handle duplicates after reassignment
rather than assuming an old owner finished
everything.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A rebalance is not itself evidence of a broker
failure.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which logs explain why membership changed?
Check consumer coordinator logs for join/leave, heartbeat expiration, max.poll.interval
expiration, assignment, partitions revoked, and deployment restarts. Correlate with
Kubernetes pod events.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 38
pages.shortAnswer:
Membership, subscriptions or partition metadata changes can

pages.title: How do cooperative assignment and static membership help?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · CONSUMER GROUPS AND SCALINGQUESTION 030 / 100 
How do cooperative assignment and static
membership help?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
They can reduce assignment disruption or unnecessary
membership churn when correctly configured for the selected
protocol.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Subscribed group ➔ Partition assignment ➔ Progress checkpoint
WORKED EXAMPLE
group.instance.id=orders-pod-unique-id
WHY IT WORKS
Static membership requires a stable unique
identity per group member. Cooperative
strategies incrementally transfer ownership
rather than treating all partitions as
immediately revoked. They reduce disruption
but do not remove timeouts or scaling
tradeoffs.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Duplicate static identities can fence a member.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you assign stable identities in Kubernetes?
Use StatefulSet ordinal or another stable per-pod identity combined with a stable group
name. Ensure every live consumer has a unique `group.instance.id` and plan identities for
scaling.

pages.title: What does a committed offset represent?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · OFFSETS AND ACKNOWLEDGMENTQUESTION 031 / 100 
What does a committed offset represent?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It records the next position the group should resume from for a
partition.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Processed offset 41 ➔ Apply durable effect ➔ commit next offset 42
WORKED EXAMPLE
Processed offset 41 -> commit next offset 42
WHY IT WORKS
The consumer's current position can be
ahead of its committed position after polling.
Commit is a progress checkpoint, not deletion
of the record. A restart resumes from
committed progress if the offset remains valid.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Committing 41 after processing 41 can replay
that record.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you inspect current and committed positions?
Use AdminClient or `kafka-consumer-groups --describe` for committed offsets; use
KafkaConsumer.position for its current next fetch position. Compare with log-end offsets
separately.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 41

pages.title: What does auto.offset.reset control?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · OFFSETS AND ACKNOWLEDGMENTQUESTION 032 / 100 
What does auto.offset.reset control?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It chooses behavior when the group has no valid committed offset,
not on every restart.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Read record ➔ Apply durable effect ➔ Commit next offset
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
spring.kafka.consumer.auto-offset-reset=earliest
WHY IT WORKS
With a valid commit, the consumer resumes
there even if earliest is configured. A fresh
group can read retained history. If retention
removed an offset, the reset policy becomes
important. Use controlled resets for intentional
replay.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
earliest does not force an existing group to
reread all records.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you replay without affecting production progress?
Run a new isolated group (or shadow application) with an explicit starting offset and
write to a separate projection. Leave production group IDs and committed positions
unchanged.

pages.title: Why disable Kafka auto-commit for container- managed processing?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · OFFSETS AND ACKNOWLEDGMENTQUESTION 033 / 100 
Why disable Kafka auto-commit for container-
managed processing?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It lets Spring's acknowledgment mode coordinate progress with
listener outcomes instead of periodic client commits.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Read record ➔ Apply durable effect ➔ Commit next offset
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
spring.kafka.consumer.enable-auto-commit=false
   spring.kafka.listener.ack-mode=record
WHY IT WORKS
For a record listener, RECORD commits after
successful record handling under the
container's commit configuration. Default
container modes and transactional behavior
differ. Read the effective configuration rather
than assuming manual acknowledgment is
always required.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Disabling auto-commit alone does not stop the
Spring container from committing.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What controls commits after auto-commit is disabled?
Spring Kafka listener container ack mode, error handler and transactional configuration
govern commits. For example RECORD commits after successful listener handling under
its configured rules.

pages.title: How do RECORD, BATCH and manual acknowledgment differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · OFFSETS AND ACKNOWLEDGMENTQUESTION 034 / 100 
How do RECORD, BATCH and manual
acknowledgment differ?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
They choose record-level, poll-batch-level or application-signaled
progress boundaries for nontransactional container processing.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Read record ➔ Apply durable effect ➔ Commit next offset
WORKED EXAMPLE
MANUAL: acknowledge queues progress by container rules
   MANUAL_IMMEDIATE: immediate on consumer thread
WHY IT WORKS
BATCH commits after the records from a poll
are handled. MANUAL is not a promise of an
immediate commit. Calling acknowledgment
off the consumer thread can alter timing.
Error handling and transactions further affect
commit behavior.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Acknowledging does not make the database
and Kafka atomic.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Why can a successful database write still be replayed?
After committing the DB change, the process can crash before Kafka stores the next
offset. On restart the same record is delivered again; make the database effect
idempotent.

pages.title: CHAPTER 07 · OFFSETS AND ACKNOWLEDGMENTQUESTION 035 / 100
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · OFFSETS AND ACKNOWLEDGMENTQUESTION 035 / 100 
How do at-most-once and at-least-once processing
differ?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Committing before the required effect risks loss; committing
afterward risks duplicates during a crash window.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
commit ➔ charge ➔ crash before charge: lost work
WORKED EXAMPLE
commit -> charge -> crash before charge: lost work
   charge -> crash -> no commit: possible duplicate charge
WHY IT WORKS
At-least-once with an idempotent business
effect is often the practical choice. Define the
exact durable effect and checkpoint. Manual
commits do not eliminate the fundamental
crash interval.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Treating duplicates as impossible is a design
defect.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would a unique eventId make a charge safe?
Put a unique `(paymentId, effectType)` constraint or `(consumerId,eventId)` inbox entry in
the same database transaction as the charge ledger update. Replays then find the
previous result.

pages.title: How do heartbeat and max.poll.interval.ms differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · POLL LOOP AND PROCESSING PRESSUREQUESTION 036 / 100 
How do heartbeat and max.poll.interval.ms differ?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Heartbeats maintain liveness; the poll interval limit checks whether
the consumer continues making polling progress.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Long listener work ➔ Bounded processing ➔ next poll delayed
WORKED EXAMPLE
Long listener work -> next poll delayed
   Heartbeats alone do not justify unlimited processing time
WHY IT WORKS
Classic and newer consumer protocols differ
in which timing settings are client- or broker-
controlled. For the classic baseline, budget the
worst poll batch plus retry time below the
interval. Identify the actual group protocol
first.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Increasing heartbeat frequency does not fix
an oversized poll workload.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which timing is exceeded by a slow batch?
For classic groups, a slow batch risks exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms`, even if heartbeats
occur. Choose batch size and processing budget within the actual protocol's polling rules.
