pages.title: What does max.poll.records limit?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · POLL LOOP AND PROCESSING PRESSUREQUESTION 037 / 100 
What does max.poll.records limit?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It limits the records returned per poll, not the entire broker fetch
byte size.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Consumer poll ➔ Bounded processing ➔ Safe next poll
WORKED EXAMPLE
max.poll.records=100
   100 records * 50 ms serial work = about 5 seconds
WHY IT WORKS
Fetched data may be cached by the client and
returned across polls. Tune returned batch
size against processing time, heap and
downstream capacity. A few exceptionally
expensive records can dominate the budget.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Lowering max.poll.records does not strictly cap
all fetched bytes.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which settings and metrics describe fetch memory?
Consider `fetch.max.bytes`, `max.partition.fetch.bytes`, `fetch.min.bytes`, `fetch.max.wait.ms`,
memory used for deserialization, and bytes per partition. Watch fetch size and heap/GC
metrics.

pages.title: CHAPTER 08 · POLL LOOP AND PROCESSING PRESSUREQUESTION 038 / 100
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · POLL LOOP AND PROCESSING PRESSUREQUESTION 038 / 100 
Can KafkaConsumer be shared across worker
threads?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
KafkaConsumer is not generally thread-safe; coordinate consumer
operations on its owning thread.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Consumer poll ➔ Bounded processing ➔ Safe next poll
WORKED EXAMPLE
Consumer thread: poll, assignment, commit
   Workers: bounded business tasks with explicit ordering
WHY IT WORKS
Delegating records to workers requires
partition-aware completion tracking,
revocation handling and safe commits.
Committing beyond unfinished earlier work
can skip it on restart. Prefer container
concurrency when it meets the requirement.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Offloading and immediately returning marks
work complete too early.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you track the highest contiguous completed offset?
For each partition track completed offsets and hold gaps in an ordered set. Commit only
one past the highest contiguous completed offset; never skip an unfinished earlier
record.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 49

pages.title: When should a listener pause consumption?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · POLL LOOP AND PROCESSING PRESSUREQUESTION 039 / 100 
When should a listener pause consumption?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Pause when temporary downstream saturation requires bounded
intake while retaining controlled polling and membership.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Database saturated ➔ Bounded processing ➔ pause assigned processing
WORKED EXAMPLE
Database saturated -> pause assigned processing
   Capacity restored -> resume
WHY IT WORKS
Use container-supported pause/resume and
observe actual pause state. Maintain a finite
queue and a recovery threshold to avoid
oscillation. Pausing a consumer does not
pause producers or stop topic retention.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
An unbounded in-memory queue only moves
lag out of Kafka.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What would trigger pause and resume?
Pause when queue utilization or DB latency exceeds a high threshold; resume only after
load falls below a lower threshold. Monitor paused duration and retained Kafka backlog.

pages.title: How should you shut down a consumer safely?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · POLL LOOP AND PROCESSING PRESSUREQUESTION 040 / 100 
How should you shut down a consumer safely?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Stop new work, finish or abandon bounded in-flight tasks
deliberately, and let the container close and commit according to
its policy.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Consumer poll ➔ Bounded processing ➔ Safe next poll
WORKED EXAMPLE
Termination budget > listener timeout + commit/close allowance
WHY IT WORKS
Long external calls need deadlines; otherwise
the process may be killed mid-effect. Replayed
work must remain idempotent. Coordinate
readiness and termination grace with the
container's stop behavior.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Graceful shutdown cannot guarantee no
duplicates after every crash.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What test would simulate forced termination?
Terminate a consumer process during a slow DB write, after the DB commit and before
Kafka commit, then restart. Verify safe replay, no skipped durable work, and bounded
shutdown.

pages.title: CHAPTER 09 · FAILURES, RETRIES AND DEAD-LETTER TOPICSQUESTION 041 / 100
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 · FAILURES, RETRIES AND DEAD-LETTER TOPICSQUESTION 041 / 100 
Why should a listener propagate processing
failures?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
The container must observe failure to apply retry, rollback or
recovery rules.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Processing failure ➔ Bounded recovery ➔ DLT or retry
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
try { charge(event); }
   catch (Exception e) { throw e; }
WHY IT WORKS
Logging and returning normally can advance
progress after failed work. Catch only when
you complete a documented alternative
outcome durably. Exception classification
should separate transient infrastructure errors
from permanently invalid events.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A log line is not a recovery action.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which failures should never retry?
Do not blindly retry invalid schemas, unauthorized actions or permanent business
rejections. Quarantine poison records with evidence; use retries for transient failures
under a bounded policy.

pages.title: What does DefaultErrorHandler do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 · FAILURES, RETRIES AND DEAD-LETTER TOPICSQUESTION 042 / 100 
What does DefaultErrorHandler do?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It applies configured retry/backoff and recovery behavior for
listener failures in nontransactional containers.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Processing failure ➔ Bounded recovery ➔ DLT or retry
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, new FixedBackOff(1000L, 2L));
WHY IT WORKS
Two backoff retries means an initial attempt
plus two retries. Seek/replay behavior,
exception classification and acknowledgment
settings control what happens afterward.
Configure a durable recoverer instead of
assuming every exhausted failure is retained
safely.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Exhaustion without a deliberate recovery
policy can skip business work.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you verify recovery failure does not advance progress?
Force the recoverer/DLT producer to fail (for example revoke write permission), restart
the listener, and verify that source progress does not pass the record without the
configured durable recovery guarantee.

How do blocking and nonblocking retries differ?

Blocking retries delay source processing; retry topics move failed
records to later processing on other topics.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Blocking: A fails ➔ A retried ➔ B follows
WORKED EXAMPLE
Blocking: A fails -> A retried -> B follows
   Retry topic: A deferred -> B may run before A
WHY IT WORKS
Nonblocking retries improve source
throughput but can break original ordering.
Spring Kafka 3.3 retry-topic support is for
record listeners and cannot combine with
container transactions. Choose the strategy
from business order and atomicity needs.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Do not attach @RetryableTopic to a
transactional or batch design blindly.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which strategy fits sequential account updates?
For sequential account updates, blocking retries or a partition-preserving queue usually
fit better. Retry topics can let a later account event finish before the earlier one.

CHAPTER 09 · FAILURES, RETRIES AND DEAD-LETTER TOPICSQUESTION 044 / 100 
What belongs in a dead-letter topic?

into DLT headers.

repair, with approval records, event IDs, deduplication policy, target group and audit trail.

How do you handle deserialization failures?

pages.title: What is a Kafka transaction?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · KAFKA TRANSACTIONS AND EXACTLY-ONCE BOUNDARIESQUESTION 046 / 100 
What is a Kafka transaction?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It atomically commits or aborts a set of Kafka writes and, when
included, consumed group offsets.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
begin ➔ publish output ➔ include input offsets
WORKED EXAMPLE
begin -> publish output -> include input offsets -> commit
WHY IT WORKS
Read-process-write pipelines can commit
outputs and progress together. Consumers
must use the appropriate isolation to avoid
observing aborted writes. The transaction does
not include an arbitrary database or external
HTTP service.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Atomic Kafka writes are not a global
distributed transaction.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What happens to an email sent before rollback?
The email provider is outside the Kafka transaction: the email may already be sent even
if Kafka rolls back. Use provider-level idempotency or a durable delivery ledger.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 59

included, consumed group offsets.

pages.title: What does read_committed isolation do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · KAFKA TRANSACTIONS AND EXACTLY-ONCE BOUNDARIESQUESTION 047 / 100 
What does read_committed isolation do?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It returns committed transactional records and nontransactional
records while excluding aborted transactional records.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Read-process-write ➔ Kafka transaction ➔ Atomic Kafka outcome
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
spring.kafka.consumer.properties[isolation.level]=read_committed
WHY IT WORKS
Open transactions can hold back visibility
beyond the last stable offset. Aborted records
still occupy log positions, so visible offsets can
have gaps. Read-uncommitted consumers do
not get the same transactional visibility
guarantee.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
read_committed does not validate business
semantics.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Why can visible consumer lag grow during a long transaction?
A read_committed consumer waits past open transactions and hides aborted data. Its
visible end offset can lag the physical log while a long-running transaction remains
incomplete.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · KAFKA TRANSACTIONS AND EXACTLY-ONCE BOUNDARIESQUESTION 048 / 100 
How does Spring configure a transactional listener
pipeline?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Boot can configure a Kafka transaction manager from a producer
transaction-id prefix and wire it into the default listener container.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Read-process-write ➔ Kafka transaction ➔ Atomic Kafka outcome
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix=${INSTANCE_ID}-
WHY IT WORKS
Use a unique prefix per application instance.
With container transactions, listener output
and input offsets can participate in one Kafka
transaction. Spring Kafka 3.x uses EOS V2.
Validate the custom factory wiring if you
replace Boot defaults.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A shared transactional identity across active
instances can cause fencing.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you verify the listener is actually transactional?
Test that the listener container uses a transactional Kafka producer/transaction manager
and that consumed offsets join its transaction. Inject an exception and verify output and
offsets are not committed.

pages.title: What does exactly-once mean for a Kafka read- process-write pipeline?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · KAFKA TRANSACTIONS AND EXACTLY-ONCE BOUNDARIESQUESTION 049 / 100 
What does exactly-once mean for a Kafka read-
process-write pipeline?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
The committed Kafka outcome can be exactly once even though
processing code is invoked again after rollback.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Attempt 1: compute + publish ➔ Kafka transaction ➔ abort
WORKED EXAMPLE
Attempt 1: compute + publish -> abort
   Attempt 2: compute + publish + offsets -> commit
WHY IT WORKS
Spring documents the read/process steps as
at-least-once; the committed sequence is the
EOS boundary. External effects can repeat, so
a database write or payment request still
needs its own correctness mechanism.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Never claim the listener method executes only
once.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you explain EOS in one interview sentence?
Exactly-once for Kafka read-process-write means produced Kafka records and
consumed offsets commit atomically in one Kafka transaction; external databases and
emails remain outside that boundary.

pages.title: What happens when database and Kafka transactions are synchronized?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · KAFKA TRANSACTIONS AND EXACTLY-ONCE BOUNDARIESQUESTION 050 / 100 
What happens when database and Kafka
transactions are synchronized?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
They still have separate commit boundaries, so a later commit can
fail after the earlier system committed.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
DB commit succeeds ➔ Kafka transaction ➔ Kafka commit fails
WORKED EXAMPLE
DB commit succeeds -> Kafka commit fails
   Required response: recovery / reconciliation
WHY IT WORKS
Spring synchronization can coordinate order
but is not a general two-phase atomic
transaction across both resources. Avoid
deprecated chained transaction manager
designs as a magic solution. Use an outbox or
explicitly accepted compensation boundary.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
@Transactional alone cannot guarantee
atomic database-plus-Kafka publication.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would an outbox close the missing-publication gap?
Write business state and an outbox event in one local DB transaction. A relay retries
publication after crashes; consumers deduplicate the stable event ID, closing the lost-
intent window.

pages.title: How do you build an idempotent consumer?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 · IDEMPOTENCY, OUTBOX AND BUSINESS CORRECTNESSQUESTION 051 / 100 
How do you build an idempotent consumer?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Atomically deduplicate an event and apply its business effect in
the same durable transaction.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Business DB change ➔ Durable event identity ➔ Replay-safe effect
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
BEGIN;
   INSERT processed_event(consumer_name,event_id) VALUES (...);
   UPDATE account SET balance=balance+...;
   COMMIT;
WHY IT WORKS
A unique constraint enforces the deduplication
key under concurrent deliveries. Duplicate
detection must be handled with the database's
transaction semantics in mind; do not
continue in a transaction marked rollback-
only. Commit offsets after success.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A separate check-then-insert can race.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Why include consumer identity in the deduplication key?
Different consumers can legitimately apply the same event for different purposes. A
uniqueness key such as `(consumerName,eventId)` prevents duplicates per effect without
blocking other consumers.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 65

CHAPTER 11 · IDEMPOTENCY, OUTBOX AND BUSINESS CORRECTNESSQUESTION 052 / 100 
Why is a Redis deduplication flag insufficient for a
database effect?

A separate flag and database update have a failure gap unless a
deliberate cross-system protocol closes it.

SET eventId ➔ crash ➔ DB update never happens

   DB update -> crash -> SET never happens
WHY IT WORKS

effects, or an idempotency key accepted by
the external provider. Redis may optimize
reads but should not silently define stronger
guarantees.

A cache hit is not proof a durable effect
committed.

What should the payment provider's idempotency contract say?

fingerprint and final charge result, return the original result on a replay, and reject key
reuse with different input.

pages.title: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 · IDEMPOTENCY, OUTBOX AND BUSINESS CORRECTNESSQUESTION 053 / 100 
What is the transactional outbox pattern?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Save business data and an event row in one database transaction,
then publish the row asynchronously.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Business DB change ➔ Durable event identity ➔ Replay-safe effect
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
BEGIN: insert order + insert outbox event; COMMIT
   Publisher: read committed outbox -> Kafka -> mark delivered
WHY IT WORKS
If publication succeeds but marking fails, the
event can be published again. Therefore the
consumer still deduplicates. The outbox
provides durable publication intent, not
inherently exactly-once transport.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Marking delivered before Kafka confirmation
can lose the event.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you coordinate multiple outbox publishers?
Use database row claims such as `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, leases or version-
checked updates with small batches. Republish safely using stable IDs because a crash
may occur after send.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 · IDEMPOTENCY, OUTBOX AND BUSINESS CORRECTNESSQUESTION 054 / 100 
How do polling and CDC outbox publishing differ?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Polling queries pending rows; CDC reads committed database
changes from a change log through a connector.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Business DB change ➔ Durable event identity ➔ Replay-safe effect
WORKED EXAMPLE
Polling: SELECT pending ORDER BY ...
   CDC: database log -> connector -> Kafka
WHY IT WORKS

CDC needs connector lifecycle, log retention,
snapshots and routing configuration. Both
require stable event IDs, schema contracts
and monitoring of publication delay.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
CDC does not remove consumer duplicate
handling.

What happens when the database log expires during connector downtime?
If the connector stays down past log retention, required database changes may be
unavailable to CDC. Restore from backup/snapshot and rebuild consistently, or use a
durable snapshot-and-resume strategy.

pages.title: How do you prevent stale or reordered events overwriting new state?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 · IDEMPOTENCY, OUTBOX AND BUSINESS CORRECTNESSQUESTION 055 / 100 
How do you prevent stale or reordered events
overwriting new state?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Enforce aggregate version or another explicit monotonic invariant
at the durable projection boundary.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Business DB change ➔ Durable event identity ➔ Replay-safe effect
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
UPDATE projection SET version=8, status='SHIPPED'
   WHERE id=42 AND version < 8;
WHY IT WORKS
For a full-state projection, a newer version can
replace an older state. For incremental deltas,
missing versions may require buffering or
repair rather than skipping. Choose behavior
from the event meaning.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Discarding old deltas can lose required
arithmetic updates.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you reconcile a missing version?
Detect a version gap (received 12 after 10), defer the newer update, fetch the missing 11
from the owner or replay source, and reconcile with a snapshot if the event is no longer
retained.

pages.title: What do serializer and deserializer do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 · SERIALIZATION AND SCHEMA EVOLUTIONQUESTION 056 / 100 
What do serializer and deserializer do?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
They convert application keys/values to bytes and bytes back to
usable data.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
StringSerializer ➔ Serialized payload ➔ UTF-8 bytes
WORKED EXAMPLE
StringSerializer -> UTF-8 bytes
   StringDeserializer -> String
WHY IT WORKS
Both ends need an agreed format. Spring
message conversion is a separate layer that
can convert already-deserialized content for a
method parameter. Explicit contracts simplify
consumers written in other languages.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A matching Java generic type does not prove
matching wire format.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you debug a serializer mismatch?

CHAPTER 12 · SERIALIZATION AND SCHEMA EVOLUTIONQUESTION 057 / 100 
How should a business event envelope look?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Include stable identity, type, version, occurrence time and the
domain payload needed by consumers.

{"eventId":"e-42","type":"OrderPlaced","version":1,
    "occurredAt":"2026-10-08T06:00:00Z","orderId":"42"}

Avoid embedding secrets or a complete
mutable database entity. Separate event
identity from correlation and aggregate
identity. Define required fields, nullable values,
number precision and time zone semantics.

defeats deduplication.

timestamp unchanged. Add separate replay metadata or attempt count rather than
silently minting a new business event.

pages.title: How do you evolve JSON events safely?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 · SERIALIZATION AND SCHEMA EVOLUTIONQUESTION 058 / 100 
How do you evolve JSON events safely?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Prefer compatible additive changes and tolerant readers, while
validating fields required for business correctness.

Producer schema ➔ Serialized payload ➔ Consumer contract
WORKED EXAMPLE
v1: orderId, amount
   v2: orderId, amount, optional currency defaulted by contract
WHY IT WORKS
An optional field is safe only if its default has
an agreed meaning. Renaming, deleting or
changing units can break consumers even
when JSON parses. Test old readers/new
writers and new readers/old records.

Parse success does not imply semantic
compatibility.

How would you change amount from rupees to paise?
Add a new `amountMinorUnits` field with clear currency and transition semantics, backfill
or dual-publish during migration, test old readers, and retire the old rupees field only
after compatibility checks.

pages.title: What does a schema registry provide?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 · SERIALIZATION AND SCHEMA EVOLUTIONQUESTION 059 / 100 
What does a schema registry provide?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It manages schemas and compatibility checks for configured
serialization ecosystems such as Avro or Protobuf.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Writer schema v2 ➔ registry ID ➔ encoded record
WORKED EXAMPLE
Writer schema v2 -> registry ID -> encoded record
   Reader resolves schema and applies compatibility rules
WHY IT WORKS
A schema registry is an additional component,
not a built-in guarantee of every Kafka cluster.
Subject naming, compatibility mode and
deployment sequence matter. It catches
structural changes but not every business
meaning change.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A structurally compatible enum or unit change
can still break business logic.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which compatibility mode suits long historical replay?
For long replay with multiple historical schemas, use compatibility rules that support all
versions a new reader will encounter (often a transitive backward-compatible policy), and
verify actual schemas.

pages.title: Why restrict trusted JSON types?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 · SERIALIZATION AND SCHEMA EVOLUTIONQUESTION 060 / 100 
Why restrict trusted JSON types?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Type metadata from incoming messages must not authorize
arbitrary class deserialization.

Producer schema ➔ Serialized payload ➔ Consumer contract
WORKED EXAMPLE
JsonDeserializer configured with a specific target type
   Trusted package list kept narrow

Spring Kafka JSON settings and class names
differ across major versions. Prefer explicit
type mapping or a fixed target type where

authenticates it.

mappings; reject unrecognized types. Never allow untrusted data to pick arbitrary Java
classes.

pages.title: How do delete retention and compaction differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · RETENTION, COMPACTION AND REPLAYQUESTION 061 / 100 
How do delete retention and compaction differ?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Delete retention removes old segments by policy; compaction
eventually keeps the latest value per key.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Retained log ➔ Replay / compaction ➔ Rebuilt projection
WORKED EXAMPLE
Delete: event history window
   Compact: latest known state for each key
WHY IT WORKS
Compaction is asynchronous and can coexist
with deletion. Older values may remain until
cleaning occurs. A compacted topic is useful
for rebuilding keyed state, but cannot be
assumed to preserve every historical event.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Compaction is not immediate deduplication.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which policy fits an audit ledger?
An audit ledger normally needs a durable append-only history and a retention plan
suitable for compliance. Pure compaction would discard historical changes and is usually
inappropriate.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 77

pages.title: What is a tombstone?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · RETENTION, COMPACTION AND REPLAYQUESTION 062 / 100 
What is a tombstone?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It is a record with a non-null key and null value that represents
deletion in a compacted topic.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Retained log ➔ Replay / compaction ➔ Rebuilt projection
WORKED EXAMPLE
key=customer-42, value=null
WHY IT WORKS
Consumers rebuilding state must apply the
deletion. Tombstone retention and consumer
downtime affect whether a stale local entry
can be removed reliably. An empty JSON
object or the string "null" is not the same wire
value.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A null key cannot express a specific keyed
deletion.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would a long-offline consumer miss a tombstone?
Compaction and retention can eventually remove older tombstones. A consumer offline
too long may miss deletion evidence and need a rebuilt snapshot or an external deletion
ledger.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 78

pages.title: How do you replay safely?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · RETENTION, COMPACTION AND REPLAYQUESTION 063 / 100 
How do you replay safely?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Use a controlled group or offset reset, verify retention coverage,
and isolate or deduplicate external side effects.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Retained log ➔ Replay / compaction ➔ Rebuilt projection
WORKED EXAMPLE
New group: billing-rebuild-2026
   Target: fresh projection table, no real payment calls
WHY IT WORKS
Record replay scope, schema versions, rate
limits and expected result counts. An existing
live group reset can reapply business effects
and disrupt consumers. Rebuilding projections
is often safer than repeating original
commands.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
earliest reads only currently retained data.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you compare the rebuilt and live projection?
Build a shadow projection from a known snapshot plus replay offset, then compare
business aggregates, row counts, hashes or versions with the live view before cutover.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 79

pages.title: How should dead-letter events be replayed?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · RETENTION, COMPACTION AND REPLAYQUESTION 064 / 100 
How should dead-letter events be replayed?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Repair the cause, preserve identity and provenance, then republish
through an authorized rate-limited workflow.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
DLT event e-42 ➔ Replay / compaction ➔ repaired source event e-42
WORKED EXAMPLE
DLT event e-42 -> repaired source event e-42
   Replay audit: operator, reason, original position
WHY IT WORKS
Use the original eventId when replaying the
same business event; a genuinely new
corrective action needs a distinct identity.
Preserve or restore aggregate order where
required. Avoid endless source-to-DLT loops.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Blindly replaying every DLT record can repeat
permanent failures.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you identify a successful previous effect?
Use the stable eventId or business operation ID to query the durable inbox or target
effect. If it already succeeded, mark replay as duplicate rather than repeating the
payment/email.

pages.title: What if a consumer is offline longer than retention?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · RETENTION, COMPACTION AND REPLAYQUESTION 065 / 100 
What if a consumer is offline longer than retention?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It may lose access to unprocessed history and needs a snapshot,
alternate archive or repair process.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Retained log ➔ Replay / compaction ➔ Rebuilt projection
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
Committed next=100; earliest available=900
   Missing history: 100..899 may no longer be recoverable here
WHY IT WORKS
Alert on lag age relative to retention before
the gap occurs. Retention bytes can also
constrain available history. The reset policy
controls resume behavior but cannot
reconstruct removed records.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A large numeric retention setting does not
guarantee unlimited history.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Where would you source a recovery snapshot?
Load a trusted snapshot from the authoritative business database or archived event
stream, record its cutover offset/version, then replay what remains. Do not assume Kafka
retains history forever.

pages.title: What belongs in a unit test?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 · TESTING SPRING BOOT KAFKA APPLICATIONSQUESTION 066 / 100 
What belongs in a unit test?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Business mapping, validation, exception classification and
idempotency decisions that do not require a broker.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Given invalid currency ➔ Inject crash window ➔ reject before publish
WORKED EXAMPLE
Given invalid currency -> reject before publish
   Given duplicate event -> no second business effect
WHY IT WORKS
Mocking KafkaTemplate can test how
application code handles a failed future, but it
does not test partitioning, commits, rebalances
or broker transactions. Keep a smaller set of
real integration tests for those behaviors.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A mocked successful send does not
demonstrate delivery.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which behavior needs a real broker?
Pure validation, mapping, partition-key choice and retry classification fit unit tests.
Partition ownership, offsets, broker failures, transactions and DLT publication require a
real Kafka integration test.

CHAPTER 14 · TESTING SPRING BOOT KAFKA APPLICATIONSQUESTION 068 / 100 
Why are sleeps weak synchronization in Kafka
tests?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
They guess when asynchronous work finishes and make tests flaky
or unnecessarily slow.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Controlled fixture ➔ Inject crash window ➔ Assert durable effect
WORKED EXAMPLE

   Then assert stored state and commit boundary
WHY IT WORKS
Use bounded polling, latches or observability
hooks. A condition should assert the intended
invariant, not merely that a listener was
invoked. Choose timeouts generous enough
for CI but fail with useful diagnostics.

Seeing a callback does not prove the database
committed.

What evidence would your failure message include?
Wait for explicit conditions using polling assertions and time bounds (e.g. Awaitility), not
fixed sleeps. On failure report topic, partition, offset, consumed records, error and
pending assertions.

same group. Verify a replay occurs and the unique inbox/ledger prevents a second
business effect.

CHAPTER 14 · TESTING SPRING BOOT KAFKA APPLICATIONSQUESTION 070 / 100 
How do you test Kafka transactions?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Verify committed outputs are visible to read_committed consumers
and aborted outputs are not, with input progress moving only on
success.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Fail listener after output send ➔ Inject crash window ➔ transaction abort
WORKED EXAMPLE
Fail listener after output send -> transaction abort
   Retry succeeds -> one committed output outcome
WHY IT WORKS
Use the production transaction manager and
compatible broker fixture. Inspect offsets and
output records, not only exception handling.
Also test fencing or instance identity conflicts
where relevant.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP

pages.title: What is consumer lag?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 · OBSERVABILITY AND PERFORMANCEQUESTION 071 / 100 
What is consumer lag?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It measures distance between a partition's end and the group's
progress; its exact interpretation depends on the metric source
and isolation.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Producer / consumer ➔ Signals and lag age ➔ Business SLO
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
Partition end=1000; group committed next=800
   Approximate offset lag=200
WHY IT WORKS
Offset gaps and variable record cost mean lag
is not an exact count of business tasks. Add
age of oldest unprocessed event and
processing rate. Inspect each partition rather
than only group totals.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Zero commit lag does not prove every
business effect succeeded.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How can swallowed exceptions hide failure?
A listener can catch and ignore an exception, return normally and advance its offset. Lag
may look healthy while the durable effect is missing; monitor business completion and
error counters.

pages.title: How do you diagnose increasing lag?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 · OBSERVABILITY AND PERFORMANCEQUESTION 072 / 100 
How do you diagnose increasing lag?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Compare arrival and completion rates, then identify whether the
bottleneck is partition skew, processing, retries or infrastructure.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Producer / consumer ➔ Signals and lag age ➔ Business SLO
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
Input=2000 records/s; completion=1500 records/s
   Backlog grows about 500 records/s for this workload
WHY IT WORKS
Check poll duration, rebalance counts, per-
partition lag, external call latency, database
saturation and broker fetch behavior. Scaling
consumers helps only where partition
ownership and downstream capacity permit.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Increasing concurrency can overload the
database and worsen lag.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What evidence would justify more partitions?
Add partitions only if multiple partitions are saturated and keys can be redistributed
without violating ordering. Confirm CPU, records-per-partition, consumer parallelism and
downstream headroom.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 90

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 · OBSERVABILITY AND PERFORMANCEQUESTION 073 / 100 
Which Kafka application metrics should be
monitored?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Monitor publish errors and latency, consumer lag/age, processing
failures, retries, DLT traffic and dependency saturation.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Producer / consumer ➔ Signals and lag age ➔ Business SLO
WORKED EXAMPLE
SLO: 99% of OrderPlaced projected within 30 seconds
   Alert: oldest pending event age > agreed threshold
WHY IT WORKS
Client metrics and Spring observations
complement business outcome metrics. Bound
labels such as topic and outcome; avoid
unique eventIds as metric tags. Use eventId
and correlationId in structured logs instead.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Consumer running is weaker evidence than
business convergence.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you keep metric cardinality bounded?
Use bounded labels such as topic, group, outcome and environment. Never label metrics
with eventId, customerId or arbitrary payload fields; keep those in sampled traces/logs.

pages.title: How should tracing work across Kafka?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 · OBSERVABILITY AND PERFORMANCEQUESTION 074 / 100 
How should tracing work across Kafka?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Propagate trace context through approved headers and create
spans that reflect asynchronous producer/consumer processing.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
HTTP span ➔ publish span ➔ consumer processing span
WORKED EXAMPLE
HTTP span -> publish span -> consumer processing span
   Logs: eventId, aggregateId, traceId, partition, offset
WHY IT WORKS
Spring Kafka observations must be enabled
and configured for the selected setup.
Preserve business identity separately from
trace identity. Do not log complete sensitive
payloads for debugging.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A traceId is not a business deduplication key.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you diagnose a replay across different traces?
Propagate event correlation IDs and trace context in headers, and store stable event IDs
in logs. Cross-reference replay attempts with the original event even when they belong to
new traces.

pages.title: How do you tune throughput responsibly?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 · OBSERVABILITY AND PERFORMANCEQUESTION 075 / 100 
How do you tune throughput responsibly?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Measure realistic record sizes, keys and downstream work, then
change one limiting factor at a time.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Producer / consumer ➔ Signals and lag age ➔ Business SLO
WORKED EXAMPLE
Benchmark: p95 end-to-end latency, records/s,
   bytes/s, CPU, heap, broker load and error rate
WHY IT WORKS
Producer batching/compression and
consumer concurrency/poll size affect
different boundaries. Include failure and
recovery tests, because a configuration that
wins a healthy benchmark may produce
unstable retry storms.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A throughput number without durability
settings is incomplete.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which SLO must not regress during tuning?
Preserve end-to-end processing freshness, durability and error-rate SLOs (for example
p99 event-to-effect latency). Higher MB/s is not a win if lag age or DLT failures worsen.
SPRING BOOT + KAFKA • PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK | 93

pages.title: How do TLS, SASL and ACLs differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 · SECURITY AND DEPLOYMENTQUESTION 076 / 100 
How do TLS, SASL and ACLs differ?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
TLS protects transport and can authenticate certificates; SASL
authenticates clients; ACLs authorize Kafka operations.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
SASL_SSL ➔ Secure Kafka channel ➔ authenticated encryptedconnection
WORKED EXAMPLE
SASL_SSL -> authenticated encrypted connection
   ACL -> principal may read orders with approved group
WHY IT WORKS
Select mechanisms supported by the cluster
and manage credentials securely. Permissions
cover topic operations, consumer groups and
transactional resources as needed. Transport
security does not determine whether an event
describes an authorized business action.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A valid client credential is not permission to
every topic.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which ACLs does a transactional producer need?
Depending on the Kafka cluster and authorization setup, a transactional producer needs
topic Write/Describe plus permission on its transactional ID (and possibly cluster/
idempotent-write permission). Verify broker policy.

CHAPTER 16 · SECURITY AND DEPLOYMENTQUESTION 077 / 100 
How should secrets be supplied to a Boot Kafka
application?

Use a managed secret delivery mechanism and avoid committing
credentials or exposing them through logs/endpoints.

Trusted identity ➔ Secure Kafka channel ➔ Authorized resource

spring.kafka.properties.security.protocol=SASL_SSL
   Credential material injected from protected runtime configuration

Rotate credentials with a tested reconnect or
deployment plan. Validate TLS trust and
hostname verification instead of disabling
them to fix connectivity. Keep DLTs and
backups within the same data protection
review.

A secret hidden in application.yml is still a
secret in source control.

How would you test credential rotation?

new connections, consumer rebalances, no lost records and eventual removal of old
credentials.

pages.title: What is bootstrap.servers versus advertised.listeners?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 · SECURITY AND DEPLOYMENTQUESTION 078 / 100 
What is bootstrap.servers versus
advertised.listeners?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Bootstrap addresses locate the cluster; advertised addresses tell
clients where to connect to individual brokers.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Bootstrap works ➔ Secure Kafka channel ➔ metadata advertisesbroker:9092
WORKED EXAMPLE
Bootstrap works -> metadata advertises broker:9092
   Remote client cannot resolve broker -> subsequent calls fail
WHY IT WORKS
Docker, Kubernetes and external access often
need different reachable listener addresses.
Diagnose metadata routing, DNS, ports and
TLS names. Replacing the bootstrap address
alone cannot repair unreachable advertised
endpoints.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A successful TCP connection to bootstrap is
insufficient.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you inspect broker metadata from the client network?
From the same network as the app, run Kafka CLI metadata commands or a small
AdminClient against the bootstrap address. Confirm returned broker hostnames/ports
resolve and are reachable from the pod.

pages.title: Should liveness fail whenever Kafka is unavailable?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 · SECURITY AND DEPLOYMENTQUESTION 079 / 100 
Should liveness fail whenever Kafka is unavailable?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Liveness should reflect whether the process can recover; readiness
and health policy should represent whether it can fulfill its
assigned role.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Broker outage ➔ app can reconnect ➔ avoid restart storm
WORKED EXAMPLE
Broker outage -> app can reconnect -> avoid restart storm
   HTTP write readiness may fail if acceptance cannot be durable
WHY IT WORKS
Producer-only APIs and background
consumers have different admission needs.
Define startup behavior, missing-topic
behavior, reconnect strategy and dependency
deadlines. An orchestrator restart cannot
repair a remote cluster.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A healthy JVM does not prove publish
capability.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What degraded behavior is acceptable for your API?
Liveness should usually reflect a stuck application process, not a temporarily unreachable
broker. Readiness may degrade if required event intake is unusable, while read-only APIs
can stay available by policy.

How should rolling deployments affect event

pages.title: How does Kafka Streams differ from @KafkaListener?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 · STREAMS AND ECOSYSTEM CHOICESQUESTION 081 / 100 
How does Kafka Streams differ from
@KafkaListener?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Kafka Streams defines a processing topology with stateful
operations; a listener is an application callback over consumed
records.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Streams: groupByKey ➔ window ➔ aggregate
WORKED EXAMPLE
Streams: groupByKey -> window -> aggregate -> output topic
   Listener: receive order -> call business service
WHY IT WORKS
Streams handles repartitioning, state stores
and recovery within its topology model. A
listener fits explicit workflow integration. Boot
can support Streams configuration, but the
programming model remains distinct.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Kafka Streams is not simply listener
concurrency with a new name.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
When do you need a windowed aggregate?
Use Kafka Streams for stateful event-time joins, aggregates and windowing. A simple
stateless consumer or DB write may be clearer with `@KafkaListener`.

What is a state store and changelog?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
A state store holds local processing state; a changelog topic can
support rebuilding that state after failure.

WORKED EXAMPLE

   Changelog: durable state updates for recovery

and topology naming affect restoration. Local

instance has all keys.

restoration.

How would you estimate cold-start recovery time?

partitions. Measure under cold cache and broker/network load; model restoration time
plus rebalance delay.

What is a repartition topic?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It redistributes records by a new key so downstream keyed
operations can process related records together.

Changing an application key is a logical
operation; stateful operations may need a
physical shuffle. Repartitioning adds network,
storage and topic-management cost. Plan
topic names and topology upgrades
intentionally.

How would you identify unnecessary shuffles?
Inspect Kafka Streams topology descriptions, internal repartition topics and `groupBy`/
key-changing operations. Preserve the key when possible so needless repartition topics
are avoided.

pages.title: How do event-time windows handle late records?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 · STREAMS AND ECOSYSTEM CHOICESQUESTION 084 / 100 
How do event-time windows handle late records?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
They group by event timestamps and use an explicit grace policy
to decide how long late records can update results.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Input topic ➔ State / time window ➔ Output topic
WORKED EXAMPLE
Window: 10:00-10:05
   Late event timestamp=10:04 arrives later
WHY IT WORKS
Window type, timestamp extraction and grace
determine acceptance. Stream time is driven
by observed data, not simply the wall clock.
Define whether results are provisional or final
and what happens to dropped late records.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A five-minute window does not imply five
minutes of wall-clock waiting.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How would you explain grace to a business stakeholder?
Explain grace as extra time after the window end to accept late facts and correct results.
After grace closes, the event needs a separate late-event policy rather than silently
changing finalized totals.

pages.title: CHAPTER 18 · ARCHITECTURE AND SIZINGQUESTION 086 / 100
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 · ARCHITECTURE AND SIZINGQUESTION 086 / 100 
How would you design an order-to-payment
workflow?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Commit order intent durably, publish through an outbox, process
payment idempotently, and emit explicit outcomes.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Order PENDING ➔ PaymentRequested ➔ PaymentSucceeded
WORKED EXAMPLE
Order PENDING -> PaymentRequested -> PaymentSucceeded
   Order CONFIRMED after permitted outcome transition
WHY IT WORKS
The payment provider should accept a stable
idempotency key. Timeouts can mean
unknown outcomes, so reconcile rather than
issuing uncontrolled repeat charges. Apply
valid state transitions using aggregate identity
and version.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A Kafka acknowledgment is not payment
confirmation.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you recover a timed-out payment request?
Keep the original payment operation ID and set the order to PAYMENT_UNKNOWN after
timeout. Query provider status or reconcile before retrying with the same key; do not
charge with a new identity.

pages.title: What is a saga in Kafka-based services?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 · ARCHITECTURE AND SIZINGQUESTION 087 / 100 
What is a saga in Kafka-based services?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
It coordinates a multi-step workflow through local transactions
and explicit compensating actions.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Reserve stock ➔ charge payment ➔ arrange shipment
WORKED EXAMPLE
Reserve stock -> charge payment -> arrange shipment
   Failure -> release stock / refund under policy
WHY IT WORKS
Choreography uses emitted events;
orchestration uses a coordinator. Neither
creates a global ACID transaction.
Compensations can fail and need durable
retries, idempotency and human escalation.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A refund is not a literal rollback of history.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which action is irreversible in your workflow?
Shipping physical goods, sending irreversible messages or externally capturing funds
may be difficult to undo. Choose the point of no return and design compensations, audit
and manual recovery.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 · ARCHITECTURE AND SIZINGQUESTION 088 / 100 
How do you estimate partition count?

Use measured per-partition throughput, desired consumer
parallelism, skew and recovery headroom.

Peak load and keys ➔ Partition / replica plan ➔ Measured headroom
CODE / WORKED EXAMPLE
Required 12000 events/s
   Measured safe partition processing=2000 events/s
   Initial lower bound=6; add reviewed headroom

This is a sizing starting point, not a universal
formula. Include payload bytes, brokers,
replicas, open files, downstream concurrency
and hot keys. Partition expansion can affect
key order, so plan it early.

Average throughput hides burst and skew risk.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What load test would validate the estimate?

consumer processing p99, rebalances and downstream saturation. Check required
headroom after a broker failure.

pages.title: How do you estimate retained storage?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 · ARCHITECTURE AND SIZINGQUESTION 089 / 100 
How do you estimate retained storage?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Start with incoming bytes times retention duration times replica
count, then account for compression and operational overhead.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Peak load and keys ➔ Partition / replica plan ➔ Measured headroom
WORKED EXAMPLE
10 MB/s * 86400 s/day * 3 replicas
   About 2.59 TB/day before compression and overhead
WHY IT WORKS
Use consistent units and measured stored
compression ratio. Include indexes, segments,
growth, rebalance movement and free-space
headroom. Compaction sizing depends on key
churn and cleaner progress.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Replication factor affects physical storage
across brokers.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What happens when one broker loses capacity?
With a broker down, remaining replicas handle leadership and replication load; spare
disk and network capacity must exist. Alert on ISR loss and evaluate under-replication
and retention backlogs.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 · ARCHITECTURE AND SIZINGQUESTION 090 / 100 
How should a multi-tenant Kafka design enforce
isolation?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Combine topic/key design, principal permissions and application
tenant validation appropriate to the required boundary.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Peak load and keys ➔ Partition / replica plan ➔ Measured headroom
WORKED EXAMPLE
Event tenantId must match authorized operation
   Projection writes constrained to tenant-owned data
WHY IT WORKS
Shared topics reduce topic count but rely
more on application isolation. Separate topics
and principals can strengthen operational
boundaries at higher management cost.
Validate DLT/replay paths as carefully as the
happy path.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A tenantId field alone is not access control.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which tenants require dedicated infrastructure?
Regulated, noisy, high-volume or strict-isolation tenants may need separate topics,
quotas, ACLs or clusters. Use risk and measurable resource contention rather than
tenant count alone.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 · PRODUCTION TROUBLESHOOTING SCENARIOSQUESTION 091 / 100 
Events were published but one service sees
nothing. Where do you start?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Check topic/cluster identity, group assignment, committed offsets,
filtering and deserialization before blaming delivery.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Same group as another
service? ➔ Locate failed boundary ➔ they divide work
WORKED EXAMPLE
Same group as another service? -> they divide work
   Different group? -> independent subscription

Verify actual resolved bootstrap addresses and
listener endpoint state. Inspect broker records
with safe tooling and the group's progress.

events.

Two services sharing a group do not each
receive every record.

offsets, reset policy and filters. A new group at latest can skip older retained records
without any broker defect.

CHAPTER 19 · PRODUCTION TROUBLESHOOTING SCENARIOSQUESTION 092 / 100 
A listener runs twice for one event. Is Kafka
broken?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Redelivery is expected after failure or a crash before durable
progress commit; application republishing can also duplicate the
event.

Effect committed ➔ Locate failed boundary ➔ process dies before offsetcommit
WORKED EXAMPLE

   New owner receives same source position

different positions with the same eventId

invariant instead of merely suppressing logs.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Producer idempotence does not prevent this
consumer crash window.

Which database constraint protects the effect?
No. At-least-once processing, retries or crash after business commit before offset
commit can produce a repeat. Protect with a unique `(consumer,eventId)` or
`(tenant,operationId)` database constraint.

Lag grows only on one partition. What is likely?

required per-account ordering while adjusting aggregate design, processing speed or
key strategy.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 · SENIOR DESIGN AND INTERVIEW CHALLENGESQUESTION 098 / 100 
How do you perform a safe consumer-group
migration?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Define replay starting points, duplicate protection, shadow
validation and cutover ownership before launching a new group.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Old billing-v1 ➔ Failure and recovery ➔ live effects
WORKED EXAMPLE
Old billing-v1 -> live effects
   New billing-v2 -> shadow projection -> compare -> cutover
WHY IT WORKS
A new group starts according to reset policy
unless offsets are deliberately established. Two
live groups may both execute external effects.
Record the checkpoint and rollback plan so
cutover does not silently miss history.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Renaming groupId is a behavioral change, not
a cosmetic one.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
How do you choose a consistent cutover point?
Record a source offset or business version watermark, build a shadow group, catch up
and compare effects. Freeze/cutover writes briefly if strict order demands an
unambiguous boundary.

CHAPTER 20 · SENIOR DESIGN AND INTERVIEW CHALLENGESQUESTION 099 / 100 
How do you migrate to newer Kafka consumer
protocols?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
Check broker/client compatibility and protocol-specific assignment
and timeout settings, then validate rebalance behavior under
rollout and failure.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Boot BOM ➔ Failure and recovery ➔ resolved kafka-clients version
WORKED EXAMPLE
Boot BOM -> resolved kafka-clients version
   Broker support + client support -> chosen group.protocol
WHY IT WORKS
Kafka 4.x introduced a new consumer protocol
with different management of some timing/
assignment options. A Boot 3.5 application's
older managed client should not be assumed
to expose newer client behavior. Use official
migration guidance and staged tests.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Broker upgrade alone does not change every
client API or default.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
What would your compatibility matrix include?
List broker/client protocol versions, Spring Kafka/Boot alignment, group protocol feature
flags, assignor compatibility and rollback path. Test mixed versions and rolling
deployments.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 · SENIOR DESIGN AND INTERVIEW CHALLENGESQUESTION 100 / 100 
What makes a strong architect-level Kafka
interview answer?
THE SIMPLE ANSWER
State the business invariant, chosen mechanism, failure window,
recovery process and evidence that it works.
VISUAL MEMORY MAP Read left to right
Business invariant ➔ Failure and recovery ➔ Measured proof
WORKED EXAMPLE
Invariant: payment applied once per paymentId
   Mechanism: provider key + durable ledger
   Evidence: timeout, replay, concurrency and crash tests
WHY IT WORKS
Discuss cost, ordering, retention and
operational ownership. Separate transport
acceptance from business completion. Use
measured sizing and acknowledge boundaries
rather than claiming exactly-once across
every component.
COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Naming Kafka, Redis and retries without an
invariant is not a design.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION
Which assumption would you challenge first in this system?
First challenge the required guarantee and the exact business effect: is ordering global
or per key, does success mean broker append or payment completed, and which failure
can be tolerated?

HANDS-ON PRACTICE · C05 / C10
C05 · Kafka-only transactional transformation
Consume an input event and publish an output with its offset in one Kafka transaction.
Setup: spring-kafka; Boot default listener factory; read_committed consumers
SOURCE WORKED SOLUTION
// application.properties
   spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix=${INSTANCE_ID}-
   spring.kafka.consumer.enable-auto-commit=false
   spring.kafka.consumer.properties[isolation.level]=read_committed
   // listener method; KafkaTemplate<String,String> injected
   @KafkaListener(topics="order-input", groupId="transform-v1")
   public void transform(String value) {
     template.send("order-output", extractOrderId(value), convert(value));
     // A thrown failure rolls back the container transaction.
   }
CHECKS, LIMITATIONS & FAILURE CASES
Verification and boundary Each active instance needs a unique INSTANCE_ID. Supply
extraction/conversion functions, topic provisioning and String serializers/deserializers. Boot
configures a KafkaTransactionManager and the default listener container transaction wiring.
Verify that custom configuration does not remove it. Assert abort hides output from
read_committed and prevents progress advancement. The default rollback processor
handles retries; define any recovery policy explicitly. Do not add an HTTP call and assume it
rolls back.

pages.title: HANDS-ON PRACTICE · C06 / C10
pages.fullText:
HANDS-ON PRACTICE · C06 / C10
C06 · Database inbox deduplication
Atomically claim an eventId and apply the effect without a check-then-insert race. Setup:
SQL database; service transaction; PostgreSQL syntax shown
SOURCE WORKED SOLUTION
CREATE TABLE processed_event (
     consumer_name varchar(100) NOT NULL,
     event_id varchar(100) NOT NULL,
     PRIMARY KEY (consumer_name, event_id)
   );
   -- Inside the same transaction as the business update:
   INSERT INTO processed_event(consumer_name,event_id)
   VALUES ('balance-v1', :eventId)
   ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
   -- If affected rows = 0: duplicate; return without applying effect.
   -- If affected rows = 1: apply validated effect, then COMMIT.
CHECKS, LIMITATIONS & FAILURE CASES
Verification and boundary Use a proxy-invoked @Transactional service and parameterized
SQL. Capture the affected-row count, and roll back both operations on business failure.
Verify simultaneous duplicate deliveries, transaction rollback, restart and replay. PostgreSQL
ON CONFLICT avoids the failed-transaction problem caused by naively catching a
uniqueness exception. Other databases need their own reviewed atomic insert technique.
Deduplication cleanup must respect replay/retention policy.
Focused example: add your project's beans, domain objects, infrastructure and tests. This excerpt is not
verified as a standalone application.

pages.title: HANDS-ON PRACTICE · C07 / C10
pages.fullText:
HANDS-ON PRACTICE · C07 / C10
C07 · Transactional outbox and publisher crash
window
Write order and publication intent atomically, then confirm Kafka before marking delivery.
Setup: SQL transaction; scheduled/CDC publisher; illustrative SQL
SOURCE WORKED SOLUTION
BEGIN;
   INSERT INTO orders(id,status) VALUES (:orderId,'PENDING');
   INSERT INTO outbox(event_id,aggregate_id,payload,state)
   VALUES (:eventId,:orderId,:json,'PENDING');
   COMMIT;
   -- Publisher state machine, not standalone SQL:
   -- claim pending row with lease / reviewed locking strategy
   -- send stable aggregate key and stable eventId; await confirmation
   -- mark DELIVERED only after successful send
   -- retry unconfirmed rows; tolerate confirmed-but-unmarked duplicates
CHECKS, LIMITATIONS & FAILURE CASES
Verification and boundary Add schemas, indexes, lease expiry, bounded batches and a safe
multi-publisher claiming algorithm for the chosen database. Preserve per-aggregate order if
required. Crash immediately before send and immediately after broker confirmation: both
must leave recoverable intent. Test one business row and one logical effect after duplicate
delivery. Monitor oldest pending row age and define archival/cleanup policy. No SQL-only
solution removes the post-send marking ambiguity.
Focused example: add your project's beans, domain objects, infrastructure and tests. This excerpt is not
verified as a standalone application.

pages.fullText:
Q001   •   CHAPTER 01 Foundation
REDIS FOUNDATIONS AND TRADEOFFS
What is Redis and why use it with Spring Boot?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Redis is a low-latency data store with useful data structures; Spring Boot
supplies configuration and Spring Data integration.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Data source → Redis acceleration → Recovery policy
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Common uses include caching, sessions, counters and short-lived coordination. Each use
needs a different durability and failure policy. A catalog cache can be rebuilt; losing a
session or reservation can affect users directly.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Do not treat every Redis key as disposable cache data.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHICH OF YOUR REDIS KEYS COULD BE SAFELY LOST?
Product cards, search suggestions and derived rankings can usually be rebuilt from the
database. Sessions, reservations, payment decisions and audit records need an explicit
recovery policy; never assume they are safe to discard.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
Application -> Redis cache -> fewer repeated database reads

pages.title: Is Redis only a cache?
pages.fullText:
Q002   •   CHAPTER 01 Foundation
REDIS FOUNDATIONS AND TRADEOFFS
Is Redis only a cache?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
No. Redis can hold primary application state, but correctness then
depends on persistence, replication, backup and recovery choices.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Data source → Redis acceleration → Recovery policy
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Separate state by business importance. If Redis is authoritative, define acceptable loss,
restore tests and write semantics. A relational database can remain the durable source for
business transactions while Redis accelerates reads.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Enabling persistence is not a complete recovery strategy.
06   FOLLOW-UP: HOW WOULD YOU CHOOSE THE AUTHORITATIVE STORE FOR BALANCES?
Keep monetary balances and transfers in a durable store with transaction isolation,
constraints, auditability and tested recovery. Use Redis for fast derived reads only unless
its durability model demonstrably meets the financial requirement.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
Rebuildable product cache != sole payment ledger

pages.title: Why is Redis fast?
pages.fullText:
Q003   •   CHAPTER 01 Foundation
REDIS FOUNDATIONS AND TRADEOFFS
Why is Redis fast?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Many operations work on in-memory data with efficient structures and
low protocol overhead.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Data source → Redis acceleration → Recovery policy
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Network round trips, large payloads and command complexity still matter. Long commands
or scripts can delay unrelated work. Redis uses multiple threads for some activities, so
describing the entire server as universally single-threaded is inaccurate.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
In-memory does not mean every command has constant cost.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHAT CAN MAKE A SMALL REDIS DEPLOYMENT SLOW?
Network round trips, CPU-heavy Lua, large keys, eviction pressure, swapping, persistence
I/O, slow clients and hot-key contention can all increase latency. Check server latency
and client/network timings separately.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
GET product:42 -> one keyed lookup, no table scan

pages.title: How does Redis differ from a relational database?
pages.fullText:
Q004   •   CHAPTER 01 Foundation
REDIS FOUNDATIONS AND TRADEOFFS
How does Redis differ from a relational database?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Redis favors key-oriented structures and direct operations; relational
databases offer rich relational queries and transaction/invariant tools.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Data source → Redis acceleration → Recovery policy
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Model Redis access paths deliberately instead of reproducing every relational join with
round trips. Use database constraints for durable business rules when appropriate. The
choice depends on query patterns, correctness and operational needs.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Redis MULTI is not equivalent to all SQL ACID behavior.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHICH INVARIANT WOULD YOU KEEP IN SQL?
Keep rules such as unique payment reference, nonnegative inventory or balanced
ledger postings in a transactional database. Cache a projection in Redis; do not make
cache expiry the only enforcement mechanism.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
Redis: GET catalog:v1:42
   SQL: SELECT ... JOIN ... WHERE ...

Data source → Redis acceleration → Recovery policy

Local hits avoid network latency but need separate invalidation and memory management.
Shared Redis reduces duplicate storage while adding network and service availability
dependencies. A two-level cache inherits both sets of tradeoffs.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Shared storage alone does not make cached values always fresh.

Use Caffeine for extremely frequent, short-lived in-process reads and Redis for a
shared cross-pod cache. Define L1 invalidation or very short TTLs, since local entries
can remain stale after Redis changes.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
Pod A Caffeine entry != Pod B Caffeine entry
   Both pods can read the same Redis key

pages.fullText:
Q006   •   CHAPTER 02 Foundation
DATA TYPES AND ACCESS PATTERNS
When should you use a string value?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use strings for simple values, serialized objects and operations such as
counters.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Access need → Redis data type → Cost and limits
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Redis strings are byte sequences, not automatically JSON documents. A JSON value usually
needs whole-value serialization unless a separately supported JSON feature is used. Use
compact DTOs and explicit schemas.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
GET does not query fields inside ordinary JSON strings.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHEN WOULD A HASH BE BETTER?
A hash fits when callers frequently update or fetch individual fields, such as HSET
profile:42 city Chennai. Use a string for a single serialized value that is usually replaced
as a whole.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
SET product:42 '{"name":"Pen"}' EX 60
   GET product:42
   INCR page:view:42
SPRING BOOT + REDIS | CLEAN PREMIUM EDITION 11

Q007   •   CHAPTER 02 Foundation
DATA TYPES AND ACCESS PATTERNS
When should you use a hash?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use a hash for a map of fields that can be read or updated separately.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Access need → Redis data type → Cost and limits
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Field operations reduce whole-object rewriting. Key expiry affects the hash key; newer Redis
versions may offer field-expiration features, but support must be checked against server/
client versions. A partial read requires clear missing-field semantics.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Do not assume every Redis deployment supports hash-field TTL.
06   FOLLOW-UP: HOW WOULD YOU EVOLVE FIELDS SAFELY?
Add optional fields with sensible reader defaults, retain old names during migration, and
version or dual-read incompatible formats. Verify old and new applications against
existing keys before rolling out.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
HSET profile:42 name Sai city Chennai
   HGET profile:42 city

pages.title: DATA TYPES AND ACCESS PATTERNS When should you use lists and sets?
pages.fullText:
Q008   •   CHAPTER 02 Foundation
DATA TYPES AND ACCESS PATTERNS
When should you use lists and sets?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Lists preserve element order and allow duplicates; sets represent unique
membership without insertion-order guarantees.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Access need → Redis data type → Cost and limits
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Lists fit bounded recent history or queue-like patterns. Sets fit membership and set algebra.
Neither implies a durable acknowledgment workflow for work processing. Bound growth and
evaluate command complexity for large collections.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A plain list pop can lose work if the worker dies.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHAT WOULD YOU USE FOR RECOVERABLE WORK DELIVERY?
Use Redis Streams with consumer groups and pending-entry recovery, or a durable
messaging service such as Kafka. A plain list pop or Pub/Sub notification lacks the
same acknowledgment and replay semantics.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
LPUSH recent:42 order-1 order-2
   SADD user:42:roles viewer editor
SPRING BOOT + REDIS | CLEAN PREMIUM EDITION 13

pages.title: DATA TYPES AND ACCESS PATTERNS What is a sorted set useful for?
pages.fullText:
Q009   •   CHAPTER 02 Foundation
DATA TYPES AND ACCESS PATTERNS
What is a sorted set useful for?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A sorted set stores unique members ordered by score, useful for ranking
and time-based selection.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Access need → Redis data type → Cost and limits
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Scores are numeric, with tie ordering determined by Redis rules. Leaderboards need
explicit tie semantics and score-update policies. Avoid treating floating-point scores as a
universally exact monetary representation.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Sorted-set rank is not an authorization decision.
06   FOLLOW-UP: HOW WOULD YOU REMOVE OLD ENTRIES FROM A SLIDING WINDOW?
Use ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to remove scores older than the window, then count or
rank the remaining entries. Perform cleanup and admission atomically in a bounded
Lua script when the outcome must be consistent.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
ZADD leaderboard 120 user-42 95 user-7
   ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES
SPRING BOOT + REDIS | CLEAN PREMIUM EDITION 14

pages.fullText:
Q010   •   CHAPTER 02 Foundation
DATA TYPES AND ACCESS PATTERNS
When do bitmaps and HyperLogLog help?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Bitmaps represent compact positional flags; HyperLogLog estimates
distinct cardinality with bounded memory.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Access need → Redis data type → Cost and limits
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Bitmaps need stable numeric positions and can become large if offsets are sparse.
HyperLogLog is approximate and cannot enumerate individual members. Choose them
when the operation fits these limitations.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
An approximate visitor count cannot replace exact billing counts.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHAT DATA WOULD REQUIRE A NORMAL SET INSTEAD?
Use a regular Set when you must know whether a particular user exists, enumerate
exact members, or calculate an exact small membership count. HyperLogLog cannot
list members or provide exact cardinality.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
SETBIT active:2026-10-08 42 1
   PFADD visitors user-42 user-7
   PFCOUNT visitors
SPRING BOOT + REDIS | CLEAN PREMIUM EDITION 15

pages.fullText:
Q011   •   CHAPTER 03 Foundation
KEYS, EXPIRATION AND ATOMIC COMMANDS
How should Redis keys be designed?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use a stable namespace that includes the application, purpose and
required identity boundaries.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Key identity → Atomic command → Expiry behavior
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Include tenant and representation versions when needed. Keep sensitive identifiers out of
exposed key names where possible. A consistent namespace supports inspection and
targeted cleanup, but is not access control by itself.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Two services using the same unqualified key can overwrite each other.
06   FOLLOW-UP: HOW DO YOU MIGRATE A KEY FORMAT?
Introduce a v2 namespace, deploy readers that can read v2 and v1, backfill or lazily
populate v2, then switch writes. Monitor misses and preserve old keys until rollback is no
longer needed.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
shop:prod:product:v1:tenant-7:42
SPRING BOOT + REDIS | CLEAN PREMIUM EDITION 17

pages.title: KEYS, EXPIRATION AND ATOMIC COMMANDS How do TTL and PTTL behave?
pages.fullText:
Q012   •   CHAPTER 03 Foundation
KEYS, EXPIRATION AND ATOMIC COMMANDS
How do TTL and PTTL behave?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
They report remaining lifetime in seconds or milliseconds; special results
identify missing keys and keys without expiration.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Key identity → Atomic command → Expiry behavior
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Expiration is a logical access boundary managed through passive and active expiry. A key
may expire between two commands, so do not assume a positive TTL from an earlier read
proves later existence.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Redis TTL is not a precise business scheduler.
06   FOLLOW-UP: HOW WOULD YOU ENFORCE A RESERVATION DEADLINE DURABLY?
Store reservation expiry and status in the authoritative database and use a scheduled or
event-driven expiry worker with idempotent transitions. A Redis TTL can assist cleanup
but is not proof that the reservation was durably canceled.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
TTL key -> -2: key absent
   TTL key -> -1: key exists without expiry
   PTTL key -> positive milliseconds remaining
SPRING BOOT + REDIS | CLEAN PREMIUM EDITION 18

pages.title: KEYS, EXPIRATION AND ATOMIC COMMANDS Why set value and expiry in one command?
pages.fullText:
Q013   •   CHAPTER 03 Foundation
KEYS, EXPIRATION AND ATOMIC COMMANDS
Why set value and expiry in one command?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A combined command avoids the crash gap between creating a value
and separately setting its TTL.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Key identity → Atomic command → Expiry behavior
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
A process dying between separate commands can leave an immortal key.
StringRedisTemplate offers set with Duration. Other structures may need a script or a
reviewed transaction to combine creation and expiry.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Pipelining separate commands is not atomic.
06   FOLLOW-UP: HOW WOULD YOU CREATE AN EXPIRING COUNTER SAFELY?
Use a Lua script that performs INCR and sets PEXPIRE only when the count is first
created, or another single atomic protocol. Test concurrent first increments and retries
after unknown outcomes.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
SET otp:42 123456 EX 120
   // Instead of SET followed later by EXPIRE.
SPRING BOOT + REDIS | CLEAN PREMIUM EDITION 19

pages.title: KEYS, EXPIRATION AND ATOMIC COMMANDS What happens to TTL when a value is overwritten?
pages.fullText:
Q014   •   CHAPTER 03 Foundation
KEYS, EXPIRATION AND ATOMIC COMMANDS
What happens to TTL when a value is overwritten?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
A normal SET replaces the value and clears its previous expiry unless an
expiry or supported preservation option is specified.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Key identity → Atomic command → Expiry behavior
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
In-place operations such as INCR or HSET ordinarily preserve the key expiry, unlike SET
replacement. Verify the precise command semantics. KEEPTTL is a server-version-
dependent option for retaining an existing deadline.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A refresh write can accidentally create a permanent cache key.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHICH TEMPLATE OPERATION ARE YOU USING TO UPDATE VALUES?
Inspect the actual Spring Redis API: opsForValue().set(key,value) normally removes an
existing TTL, while set(key,value,Duration) specifies a new deadline. For TTL preservation,
use explicitly supported Redis options and test the wire behavior.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
SET k one EX 60
   SET k two
   TTL k -> -1
SPRING BOOT + REDIS | CLEAN PREMIUM EDITION 20

pages.title: KEYS, EXPIRATION AND ATOMIC COMMANDS Why is INCR safer than GET plus SET for a counter?
pages.fullText:
Q015   •   CHAPTER 03 Foundation
KEYS, EXPIRATION AND ATOMIC COMMANDS
Why is INCR safer than GET plus SET for a counter?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
INCR performs one atomic counter update, while a read-modify-write
sequence can lose concurrent increments.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Key identity → Atomic command → Expiry behavior
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Atomic increment does not atomically establish a TTL unless the complete policy is
combined. Redis expects a supported integer representation and can reject wrong types or
overflow. Define timeout/retry behavior for increments.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Retrying after an unknown outcome can increment twice.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHEN WOULD YOU NEED AN OPERATION IDENTITY?
An operation ID is essential when a request may be retried after an uncertain INCR
response, especially for billing or quotas. Store/deduplicate request identity and its result
under an atomic, sufficiently durable policy.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
Two callers: GET 10; both SET 11 -> one increment lost
   Two INCR calls: 10 -> 11 -> 12

Q017   •   CHAPTER 04 Foundation
SPRING BOOT WIRING AND CLIENTS
What properties configure a standalone Redis
connection?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
In Boot 3.5, use the spring.data.redis property namespace for host, port,
credentials and timeout settings.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Boot configuration → Redis client → Failure budget
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Connection establishment and command wait budgets are different. Supply authenticated
TLS configuration for the intended environment and avoid storing credentials in source. Old
property namespaces can be misleading after migration.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A longer timeout can turn an outage into thread exhaustion.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHAT BUDGET SHOULD AN API ALLOCATE TO A CACHE LOOKUP?
Reserve a small, measured fraction of the end-to-end request deadline for Redis,
including connection and command time. For a noncritical cache, fail fast to a bounded
fallback rather than consuming the entire request budget.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
spring.data.redis.host=localhost
   spring.data.redis.port=6379
   spring.data.redis.connect-timeout=2s
   spring.data.redis.timeout=1s
SPRING BOOT + REDIS | CLEAN PREMIUM EDITION 24

connection lifecycle; do not cache a raw connection as a singleton.

Q020   •   CHAPTER 04 Foundation
SPRING BOOT WIRING AND CLIENTS
Does Lettuce always need a connection pool?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
No. Ordinary operations can share a native connection; blocking and
transactional use cases need separate consideration.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Boot configuration → Redis client → Failure budget
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
Pooling support needs the appropriate pool dependency/configuration. Multiplexing reduces
connection counts but does not remove head-of-line or server capacity limits. Inspect
actual connection use before increasing pool size.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
A pool of 100 does not create 100 Redis command execution cores.
06   FOLLOW-UP: WHEN WOULD BLOCKING OPERATIONS REQUIRE ISOLATION?
Blocking reads, long-lived Pub/Sub subscriptions, or transactions can monopolize a
connection and may need isolated dedicated connections. Ordinary nonblocking GET/
SET through Lettuce can often share a connection safely.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
Simple GET/SET -> shared native connection by default
   Blocking/transactional usage -> reviewed dedicated connection handling

How do Redis T emplate and StringRedis T emplate differ?

StringRedisTemplate uses string serialization for its normal operations.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Java object → Wire serializer → Versioned key
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH

typed RedisTemplate needs matching key, value and hash serializers. Java generic
parameters do not automatically select the wire format.

the configured key/value serializers. Check hash field serializers separately if using
hashes.

pages.fullText:
Q022   •   CHAPTER 05 Foundation
TEMPLATES, SERIALIZATION AND REPOSITORIES
Why can Redis keys look unreadable in redis-cli?
01   SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The template may use binary Java serialization rather than plain string
serialization.
02   VISUAL MENTAL MODEL
Java object → Wire serializer → Versioned key
04   HOW IT WORKS, IN PLAIN ENGLISH
A default RedisTemplate and the Redis cache manager can have different serialization
settings. Inspect each actual path. Changing serializers affects compatibility with existing
data and requires migration or a versioned namespace.
05   COMMON INTERVIEW TRAP
Switching a serializer does not rewrite old keys.
06   FOLLOW-UP: HOW DO YOU MIGRATE WITHOUT BREAKING ROLLBACK?
Use a versioned namespace and dual-compatible readers; write new values without
rewriting all old keys in place. Keep old-format data or a backfill/rollback strategy until
the old release can be safely retired.
03   ORIGINAL PRACTICAL EXAMPLE
CLI key: binary prefix + encoded text
   StringRedisSerializer -> human-readable key bytes
