pages.title: How does BCNF differ from 3NF?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 12   •   NORMALIZATION AND SCHEMA DESIGN
QUESTION Q058
How does BCNF differ from 3NF?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
BCNF requires every nontrivial functional dependency's determinant to be a
superkey; 3NF permits certain dependencies involving prime attributes.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
R(student,course,instructor)
FDs: (student,course) -> instructor; instructor -> course
Candidate keys: (student,course), (student,instructor)
Entity keys ➜ Dependencies ➜ Normalized tables
WHY THIS WORKS
Assume each instructor teaches one course, and each student has one instructor for a
course. Instructor determines course but is not a superkey, so the relation violates BCNF.
Course is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key), so this dependency is permitted by
3NF. Decomposing into InstructorCourse and StudentInstructor can lose direct
preservation of the student/course instructor rule. BCNF can remove anomalies
remaining in a 3NF design, but dependency preservation can be a tradeoff. Interview
answers should state actual dependencies for an example rather than label a table from
its column count.
WATCH OUT
Every determinant is not automatically a primary key.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What is a prime attribute?
A prime attribute is part of some candidate key. BCNF requires every determinant to be
a superkey; 3NF allows some dependencies whose dependent attribute is prime.

course. Instructor determines course but is not a superkey, so the relation violates BCNF.
Course is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key), so this dependency is permitted by
3NF. Decomposing into InstructorCourse and StudentInstructor can lose direct
preservation of the student/course instructor rule. BCNF can remove anomalies
remaining in a 3NF design, but dependency preservation can be a tradeoff. Interview
answers should state actual dependencies for an example rather than label a table from
its column count.
WATCH OUT
Every determinant is not automatically a primary key.
pages.followup:
QUESTION + ANSWER
What is a prime attribute?
A prime attribute is part of some candidate key. BCNF requires every determinant to be
a superkey; 3NF allows some dependencies whose dependent attribute is prime.

pages.title: How do you model many-to-many relationships?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 12   •   NORMALIZATION AND SCHEMA DESIGN
QUESTION Q059
How do you model many-to-many relationships?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use an association table with references and an appropriate uniqueness
identity.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
CREATE TABLE enrollment (
 student_id INTEGER, course_id INTEGER,
 PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id)
);
Entity keys ➜ Dependencies ➜ Normalized tables
WHY THIS WORKS
Add foreign keys to the relevant tables in a real schema and store relationship attributes
such as grade on the association. Some domains allow repeated enrollment attempts,
requiring another identity dimension.
WATCH OUT
A comma-separated list of course IDs weakens relational integrity/querying.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would multiple attempts change the key?
Use an enrollment/attempt identity, e.g. PRIMARY KEY(student_id, course_id,
attempt_number) or a unique attempt_id plus a documented composite uniqueness rule.

pages.title: When is denormalization reasonable?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 12   •   NORMALIZATION AND SCHEMA DESIGN
QUESTION Q060
When is denormalization reasonable?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Use it for measured read needs with an explicit source, refresh/invalidation
policy and reconciliation plan.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Reporting projection stores paid_total per customer
Source orders remain authoritative
Entity keys ➜ Dependencies ➜ Normalized tables
WHY THIS WORKS
Duplicated/derived facts trade write complexity and freshness for read speed.
Materialized summaries need correct handling of updates, deletes and late events.
Establish whether an inconsistent read is acceptable.
WATCH OUT
Storing a total does not ensure it stays correct.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How do you rebuild or verify the projection?
Rebuild from authoritative events/rows and compare row counts, totals, checksums or
sampled business invariants before switching readers.

pages.title: What does an index provide?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 13   •   INDEXES AND ACCESS-PATH DESIGN
QUESTION Q061
What does an index provide?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It supplies an alternative access path that can reduce lookup, filtering or
ordering work at storage and write-maintenance cost.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_customer_date
ON orders(customer_id,ordered_at,order_id);
Filter pattern ➜ Index access ➜ Row lookup
WHY THIS WORKS
An index is not guaranteed to be selected. Selectivity, statistics, row width and ordering
needs affect cost. Additional indexes consume space and make inserts/updates/deletes
more expensive.
WATCH OUT
More indexes do not monotonically improve performance.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which workload justifies this index?
A measured query repeatedly filters by customer_id and ordered_at, so an index
beginning with customer_id then date may be useful. Verify with the plan.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 067

pages.title: How does composite-index column order matter?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 13   •   INDEXES AND ACCESS-PATH DESIGN
QUESTION Q062
How does composite-index column order matter?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The ordered key structure makes some leading-column predicates and
ordering combinations more useful than others.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
(customer_id,ordered_at,order_id)
WHERE customer_id=? ORDER BY ordered_at,order_id
Filter pattern ➜ Index access ➜ Row lookup
WHY THIS WORKS
Equality, range and requested ordering should guide the design. Leftmost-prefix rules are
a useful baseline, but optimizer/index features can offer exceptions or alternative scans.
Measure rather than declaring later columns never usable.
WATCH OUT
An index on (a,b) is not generally equivalent to (b,a).
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What happens with only ordered_at in the predicate?
A composite index beginning with customer_id may not efficiently locate only ordered_at;
test a separate date-leading index based on actual workload.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 068

pages.title: What is a covering or index-only query?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 13   •   INDEXES AND ACCESS-PATH DESIGN
QUESTION Q063
What is a covering or index-only query?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The access path may supply required columns from an index, reducing table/
heap visits, subject to engine visibility and storage rules.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Query projects columns present in a chosen index
Filter pattern ➜ Index access ➜ Row lookup
WHY THIS WORKS
PostgreSQL index-only scans still depend on visibility information and can require heap
checks. MySQL InnoDB secondary indexes include primary-key information. Include/
payload syntax and index size tradeoffs differ.
WATCH OUT
Covering does not mean zero I/O in every engine.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you verify actual heap/table reads?
Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) in PostgreSQL and check heap fetches; in MySQL
compare index coverage and actual row reads using execution evidence.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 069

pages.title: What makes a predicate sargable?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 13   •   INDEXES AND ACCESS-PATH DESIGN
QUESTION Q064
What makes a predicate sargable?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It can be matched effectively to an available indexed access path, depending
on types, expressions and engine capabilities.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Better baseline: ordered_at>=:start AND ordered_at<:end
Potential issue: DATE(ordered_at)=:day without matching expression index
Filter pattern ➜ Index access ➜ Row lookup
WHY THIS WORKS
Functions, implicit casts, leading wildcards and mismatched collation can affect access.
Expression/generated-column indexes can support some transformed predicates. Explain
the actual plan, not a universal ban on functions.
WATCH OUT
WHERE syntax alone does not prove an index seek.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you support a case-insensitive search?
Use an appropriate normalized/search column with an index, or an engine-supported
expression/function index; compare collation behavior.

pages.title: How do clustered storage and secondary indexes differ across engines?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 13   •   INDEXES AND ACCESS-PATH DESIGN
QUESTION Q065
How do clustered storage and secondary indexes
differ across engines?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
MySQL InnoDB stores rows in its clustered primary-key organization;
PostgreSQL commonly uses a heap with separate indexes.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
InnoDB secondary entry includes primary-key columns
PostgreSQL secondary index points to heap tuples
Filter pattern ➜ Index access ➜ Row lookup
WHY THIS WORKS
PostgreSQL CLUSTER can physically reorder a table but does not continuously maintain
InnoDB-like clustering. A wide InnoDB primary key increases secondary-index storage.
These details affect design and lookup cost.
WATCH OUT
Saying every table has the same kind of clustered index is incorrect.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why might a compact primary key matter?
InnoDB secondary indexes store primary-key values as row locators; a large primary key
increases secondary index size and lookup work.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 071

pages.title: What does EXPLAIN show?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 14   •   EXECUTION PLANS AND QUERY TUNING
QUESTION Q066
What does EXPLAIN show?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It shows the chosen plan and estimates; execution-aware variants can add
actual timing and row counts.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
-- PostgreSQL example:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;
SQL + parameters ➜ Actual plan ➜ Measured cost
WHY THIS WORKS
Analyze forms execute the statement, so do not casually run them on mutating
production SQL. Interpret scan, join, filter, sort and aggregate nodes. Engine output and
timing semantics differ.
WATCH OUT
Estimated cost is not a duration in milliseconds.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Where would you look for unexpected row multiplication?
Find where actual rows exceed estimates after a join; unexpected many-to-many
multiplication often begins at that operator.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 072

pages.title: Why can estimated and actual row counts differ?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 14   •   EXECUTION PLANS AND QUERY TUNING
QUESTION Q067
Why can estimated and actual row counts differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Statistics, data skew, correlations and parameter distributions can make
cardinality estimates inaccurate.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Estimated 10 rows; actual 100000 -> downstream plan may be poor
SQL + parameters ➜ Actual plan ➜ Measured cost
WHY THIS WORKS
Refresh appropriate statistics and investigate distribution/correlation rather than only
forcing an index. Small sample fixtures cannot reproduce every production estimate.
Include representative parameter values.
WATCH OUT
Statistics can be current and still miss important correlations.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which columns are correlated in this workload?
Correlated tenant_id, status and ordered_at values can mislead independent estimates;
inspect per-tenant distribution and supported statistics.

pages.title: What are nested-loop, hash and merge joins?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 14   •   EXECUTION PLANS AND QUERY TUNING
QUESTION Q068
What are nested-loop, hash and merge joins?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
They are physical join strategies using repeated lookups, hashing or ordered
matching, chosen according to supported operators and costs.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Small outer + indexed inner -> nested loop can be good
Large equijoin -> hash may fit, subject to memory/support
SQL + parameters ➜ Actual plan ➜ Measured cost
WHY THIS WORKS
No algorithm is always best. A nested loop can be disastrous with a huge outer result and
expensive inner scans, while efficient indexed lookups can make it ideal. Plan names and
availability differ by engine.
WATCH OUT
Rewriting SQL text does not guarantee a specific physical join.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would a row-estimate error change the decision?
An underestimated outer input may lead to nested-loop work that is much larger than
expected; a correct estimate might favor hash/merge join or a different access path.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 074

pages.title: Why can a sequential/table scan be the best plan?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 14   •   EXECUTION PLANS AND QUERY TUNING
QUESTION Q069
Why can a sequential/table scan be the best plan?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
When much of a table is needed or the table is small, scanning can cost less
than many scattered index/table lookups.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
SELECT most columns WHERE status matches 90% of rows
SQL + parameters ➜ Actual plan ➜ Measured cost
WHY THIS WORKS
Evaluate total work and latency rather than treating every scan as a defect. Storage/
cache state and column width matter. A tiny practice database often favors scans even
with an appropriate production index.
WATCH OUT
Index presence is not proof the optimizer should use it.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What measurement would justify a different access path?
Measure elapsed time, buffers/I/O, row counts and selection ratio on representative data.
An index helps only when savings exceed lookup cost.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 075

pages.title: How do you approach a slow SQL query systematically?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 14   •   EXECUTION PLANS AND QUERY TUNING
QUESTION Q070
How do you approach a slow SQL query
systematically?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Verify semantics and workload, inspect actual plan/rows/waits, then change
the dominant cause and compare results.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Evidence: parameters, row counts, plan, lock waits,
I/O, spills, latency distribution and before/after outputs
SQL + parameters ➜ Actual plan ➜ Measured cost
WHY THIS WORKS
Fix incorrect joins first, then access paths/statistics and resource constraints. Changes
should preserve results on edge cases and representative data. Measure end-to-end
impact, including application fetch and network cost.
WATCH OUT
Optimizing an incorrect query preserves the wrong answer faster.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you validate equivalence after rewriting?
Check that the rewrite yields the same columns, row identities and counts for empty,
NULL, tie and multi-child cases, preferably with EXCEPT comparisons.

pages.title: What is an SQL transaction?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 15   •   TRANSACTIONS AND ACID
QUESTION Q071
What is an SQL transaction?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It groups supported database work into a commit/rollback boundary with
configured isolation and engine behavior.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-10 WHERE account_id=1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+10 WHERE account_id=2;
COMMIT;
Begin ➜ Changes ➜ Commit / rollback
WHY THIS WORKS
The fragment assumes valid rows and business checks within a reviewed transaction. In
MySQL, use a transactional engine such as InnoDB and account for autocommit/implicit
commits. A single connection owns the local transaction.
WATCH OUT
Two separate autocommitted updates are not one transfer.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What if the destination row is absent?
Abort the unit of work; do not debit if the destination is absent. A foreign key and
guarded updates help prevent partial transfer.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 077

configured isolation and engine behavior.

pages.title: What does ACID mean?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 15   •   TRANSACTIONS AND ACID
QUESTION Q072
What does ACID mean?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Atomicity is a database unit-of-work boundary; consistency preserves
enforced invariants; isolation governs concurrent interaction; durability
preserves committed work under configured guarantees.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Atomic rollback != automatic business correctness
Isolation level != universally serial execution
Begin ➜ Changes ➜ Commit / rollback
WHY THIS WORKS
Application rules and constraints must define a valid transfer or order. Durability depends
on database/storage configuration and acknowledged commit boundaries. Avoid saying
ACID automatically makes external calls transactional.
WATCH OUT
Consistency is not proof the database inferred every business rule.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which invariant is actually enforced?
State a concrete invariant, e.g. all committed ledger postings for a transfer balance to
zero; enforce it using constraints plus one transaction.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 078

pages.fullText:

CHAPTER 15   •   TRANSACTIONS AND ACID
QUESTION Q073
How do COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT
differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Commit finalizes the transaction; rollback abandons its supported changes; a
savepoint can allow partial rollback within it.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
SAVEPOINT before_optional;
-- optional work
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_optional;
Begin ➜ Changes ➜ Commit / rollback
WHY THIS WORKS
Savepoints do not commit the earlier work and are not autonomous nested transactions.
Error behavior differs: PostgreSQL commonly leaves a failed transaction needing
rollback/recovery, while MySQL statement/transaction effects vary by error.
WATCH OUT
Catching an SQL exception does not guarantee the connection is ready to continue.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What would the transaction manager do after failure?
Roll back failed work (or to a savepoint when safe), then mark the transaction rollback-
only under the framework's rules and return an accurate outcome.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 079

savepoint can allow partial rollback within it.

Error behavior differs: PostgreSQL commonly leaves a failed transaction needing
rollback/recovery, while MySQL statement/transaction effects vary by error.

Catching an SQL exception does not guarantee the connection is ready to continue.

only under the framework's rules and return an accurate outcome.

pages.title: Why keep transactions short?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 15   •   TRANSACTIONS AND ACID
QUESTION Q074
Why keep transactions short?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Long transactions can hold locks/resources and retain old visibility/version
state, increasing contention and maintenance cost.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Read required data -> mutate -> commit
Avoid slow HTTP call while holding important row locks
Begin ➜ Changes ➜ Commit / rollback
WHY THIS WORKS
A correct workflow may need an external call, but design it with explicit intent/outcome
handling instead of unlimited lock time. Deadlines and connection-pool capacity matter.
PostgreSQL vacuum and InnoDB history cleanup are affected by long-lived snapshots in
different ways.
WATCH OUT
Short does not mean splitting an invariant across unsafe commits.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which work can move outside the transaction?
Move external HTTP calls, reporting and noncritical messages outside the lock-holding
transaction; publish committed intent via an outbox when needed.

pages.title: Does a database transaction atomically include Kafka or HTTP?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 15   •   TRANSACTIONS AND ACID
QUESTION Q075
Does a database transaction atomically include
Kafka or HTTP?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Not by itself. External effects have separate commit/outcome boundaries
unless a specific supported distributed protocol is used.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
DB commit succeeds -> event publish fails
Transactional outbox records publication intent with DB work
Begin ➜ Changes ➜ Commit / rollback
WHY THIS WORKS
An outbox publisher can resend, so downstream deduplication remains required. For
payments, use stable provider idempotency and reconciliation of unknown outcomes.
Spring transaction annotations do not create universal cross-system atomicity.
WATCH OUT
A method-level transaction cannot roll back an already sent email.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How do you recover a confirmed but unrecorded payment?
Reconcile by the provider idempotency key and persisted intent. If the charge
succeeded, record the confirmation without charging again.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 081

pages.title: What anomalies do isolation levels address?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 16   •   ISOLATION AND MVCC
QUESTION Q076
What anomalies do isolation levels address?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Common phenomena include dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, phantoms
and broader serialization anomalies such as write skew.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Nonrepeatable read: same row value changes between reads
Phantom: a predicate query returns a changed matching row set
Snapshot ➜ Concurrent write ➜ Visible result
WHY THIS WORKS
The SQL level names set expectations, but implementations can provide stronger or
different details. Snapshot reads and locking reads may behave differently within one
engine. Describe a concrete two-session schedule.
WATCH OUT
Repeatable reads of one row do not alone prove a cross-row invariant.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What does write skew look like?
Write skew: two doctors each see the other on call, both update their own on-call flag,
and both commit, leaving none available unless protected.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 082

pages.title: How does PostgreSQL Read Committed behave?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 16   •   ISOLATION AND MVCC
QUESTION Q077
How does PostgreSQL Read Committed behave?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Each statement normally sees a snapshot of committed data as that
statement begins; later statements can see newer commits.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
T1 SELECT -> salary 80000
T2 UPDATE + COMMIT
T1 next SELECT -> may see updated salary
Snapshot ➜ Concurrent write ➜ Visible result
WHY THIS WORKS
PostgreSQL treats Read Uncommitted as Read Committed. Locking/data-changing
commands have additional rules for concurrent target-row changes. Do not extrapolate
ordinary SELECT snapshot behavior to every operation.
WATCH OUT
Transaction begin does not freeze one snapshot at Read Committed.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What changes at Repeatable Read?
In PostgreSQL Repeatable Read, ordinary reads use a stable transaction snapshot;
concurrent update conflicts can abort transactions. Recheck whole transaction
semantics.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 083

pages.title: How does MySQL InnoDB Repeatable Read differ from a generic slogan?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 16   •   ISOLATION AND MVCC
QUESTION Q078
How does MySQL InnoDB Repeatable Read differ
from a generic slogan?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Consistent reads typically use a transaction snapshot, while locking reads and
writes use additional current-read/locking behavior.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Ordinary SELECT snapshot != SELECT ... FOR UPDATE semantics
Snapshot ➜ Concurrent write ➜ Visible result
WHY THIS WORKS
InnoDB's default Repeatable Read and PostgreSQL's default Read Committed are distinct
baselines. Gap/next-key locks and access paths affect locking operations. Explain the
exact statements and indexes instead of claiming every read sees an identical universe.
WATCH OUT
Mixing consistent reads and writes needs engine-specific reasoning.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which read establishes the InnoDB snapshot?
Under InnoDB Repeatable Read, the first consistent (nonlocking) read typically
establishes the transaction read view, subject to transaction setup.

pages.title: What is MVCC?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 16   •   ISOLATION AND MVCC
QUESTION Q079
What is MVCC?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Multi-version concurrency control lets readers use suitable row versions while
writers manage changes and visibility under engine rules.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Reader snapshot -> visible older version
Writer commits newer version for later applicable snapshots
Snapshot ➜ Concurrent write ➜ Visible result
WHY THIS WORKS
MVCC can reduce reader/writer blocking but does not eliminate every lock or conflict.
Old versions need cleanup and long snapshots can retain them. Foreign keys, DDL and
explicit locking add other interactions.
WATCH OUT
MVCC is not lock-free execution for all SQL.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What does a long report do to version cleanup?
Long snapshots retain obsolete versions or delay cleanup; monitor long transactions,
undo/history in InnoDB, and vacuum dead tuples in PostgreSQL.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 085

writers manage changes and visibility under engine rules.

pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 16   •   ISOLATION AND MVCC
QUESTION Q080
What does Serializable require from the
application?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It targets results equivalent to some serial execution, but the application must
handle engine-specific blocking/conflict failures and retries.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Two concurrent decisions conflict -> one may need retry
Retry the complete transaction with a bounded policy
Snapshot ➜ Concurrent write ➜ Visible result
WHY THIS WORKS
PostgreSQL uses serialization-conflict detection; MySQL InnoDB has its own stronger
locking behavior for this level. Preserve idempotency for external effects around retries.
Serializable is a correctness choice, not a promise of no exceptions.
WATCH OUT
Retrying just the final statement may reuse a stale decision.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which work must be repeated together?
On serialization failure, retry the entire transaction with all dependent reads and writes,
bounded attempts and idempotent external effects.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 086

pages.title: What does SELECT FOR UPDATE do?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 17   •   LOCKS, DEADLOCKS AND CONCURRENCY CONTROL
QUESTION Q081
What does SELECT FOR UPDATE do?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It acquires locking-read protection on qualifying rows under engine
semantics until the transaction releases it.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
BEGIN;
SELECT available FROM inventory WHERE item_id=:id FOR UPDATE;
-- validate and update within this transaction
COMMIT;
Read / lock ➜ Conflict handling ➜ Commit
WHY THIS WORKS
Exact lock scope depends on engine, access path and isolation. It does not universally
lock all future rows matching any predicate. Use constraints and guarded writes where
simpler. Keep lock duration bounded.
WATCH OUT
Locking an existing row is not a universal solution for absence checks.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What if the row does not exist?
Locking a missing row may not protect absence under every engine/isolation. Use a
unique constraint, insert claim, advisory lock, or proper range-lock protocol.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 087

pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 17   •   LOCKS, DEADLOCKS AND CONCURRENCY CONTROL
QUESTION Q082
How do optimistic and pessimistic concurrency
differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Optimistic control detects conflicting state/version at write time; pessimistic
control coordinates through locks before completing the operation.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
UPDATE orders SET status=:new,version=version+1
WHERE order_id=:id AND version=:expected;
Read / lock ➜ Conflict handling ➜ Commit
WHY THIS WORKS
Zero affected rows means conflict/missing under the contract. Optimistic approaches suit
certain lower-contention workflows; repeated conflicts can make them expensive.
Pessimistic locks can avoid wasted work but increase waits/deadlock risk.
WATCH OUT
Versioning is ineffective if other writers bypass the version rule.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which option fits a highly contended stock item?
A highly contended stock item usually needs a short guarded atomic UPDATE (or
controlled pessimistic lock); optimistic retries may thrash under heavy contention.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 088

pages.title: What causes a deadlock and how do you reduce it?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 17   •   LOCKS, DEADLOCKS AND CONCURRENCY CONTROL
QUESTION Q083
What causes a deadlock and how do you reduce it?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Transactions hold resources while waiting cyclically for each other; consistent
lock order and short transactions reduce opportunities.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
T1 locks account 1 -> waits for 2
T2 locks account 2 -> waits for 1
Read / lock ➜ Conflict handling ➜ Commit
WHY THIS WORKS
The database detects/handles victims under engine rules. Retry a failed transaction with
bounds/backoff and safe effect identity. Indexes and statement ordering can influence
lock footprints. Inspect deadlock evidence rather than only raising timeouts.
WATCH OUT
Deadlock and ordinary long lock wait are different.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you impose a transfer lock order?
Always acquire account locks in deterministic ascending account_id order; keep
transactions short and retry the entire failed transfer on deadlock.

pages.title: What is SKIP LOCKED useful for?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 17   •   LOCKS, DEADLOCKS AND CONCURRENCY CONTROL
QUESTION Q084
What is SKIP LOCKED useful for?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It lets workers skip currently locked qualifying rows for queue-like claiming,
with engine/version-specific syntax.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE state='READY'
ORDER BY job_id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
Read / lock ➜ Conflict handling ➜ Commit
WHY THIS WORKS
This is not a consistent general-purpose report: locked rows are deliberately omitted.
Claim/update in the same transaction, then define lease/recovery for workers that die
after claim. Avoid starvation and keep batches bounded.
WATCH OUT
Skipping a row does not mean the work was completed.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How do you recover abandoned jobs?
Persist a claimed/lease state with deadline and unique job identity; a worker can requeue
timed-out claims and processing remains idempotent.

CHAPTER 17   •   LOCKS, DEADLOCKS AND CONCURRENCY CONTROL
QUESTION Q085
How do unique constraints support idempotent
processing?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
They atomically reject duplicate identities while business effects commit in the
same durable transaction.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
processed_event(consumer_name,event_id) PRIMARY KEY
Insert identity + apply effect + commit together
Read / lock ➜ Conflict handling ➜ Commit
WHY THIS WORKS
Handle engine-specific conflict/transaction behavior correctly. A precheck or Redis flag
stored separately leaves a failure gap. The key must remain stable across retries, and
record cleanup must respect replay policy.
WATCH OUT
Unique event identity alone does not atomically protect a remote provider call.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How do you return the prior result for a repeated API request?
Persist the request ID and immutable request fingerprint with status/result. On duplicate,
return the stored result, or explicit in-progress/unknown status.

pages.fullText:

CHAPTER 18   •   VIEWS, ROUTINES, PARTITIONING AND MAINTENANCE
QUESTION Q086
How do views and materialized views differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
An ordinary view is a stored query definition; a materialized view stores
results that require a refresh/maintenance strategy.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
CREATE VIEW paid_orders AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status='PAID';
Storage policy ➜ Maintenance ➜ Read model
WHY THIS WORKS
PostgreSQL offers native materialized views; MySQL does not offer the same native
materialized-view feature. Views do not automatically index or cache their results.
Updatability and security behavior depend on the definition/engine.
WATCH OUT
A view can still execute expensive joins for every request.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
When would a maintained summary table help?
Maintain a summary table when live aggregation is too costly and updates can be
controlled; define refresh lag, atomic replacement and reconciliation.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 092

QUESTION Q087
How do stored procedures and functions differ?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
They are database-side routines with engine-specific invocation, return, side-
effect and transaction rules.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Function used as an expression where supported
Procedure invoked with CALL under engine rules
Storage policy ➜ Maintenance ➜ Read model
WHY THIS WORKS
Do not assert functions can never mutate or procedures always commit: semantics differ
across PostgreSQL/MySQL and languages. Centralized routines can reduce round trips
but introduce deployment/test ownership. Document boundaries.
WATCH OUT
A routine does not automatically protect invariants better than ordinary SQL.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Who versions and tests the routine?
Database routines should be versioned in migrations, reviewed with application code, and
tested on the target engine with rollback practices.

pages.fullText:

CHAPTER 18   •   VIEWS, ROUTINES, PARTITIONING AND MAINTENANCE
QUESTION Q088
What are triggers useful for and what are their
costs?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Triggers react to supported data events and can enforce/maintain selected
behavior, but introduce less visible work and ordering/error complexity.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
INSERT order -> configured trigger maintains an audit row
Storage policy ➜ Maintenance ➜ Read model
WHY THIS WORKS
Review per-row/per-statement support, transaction behavior and recursion. A durable
audit needs clear identity and access policy. Avoid making remote calls or hidden cross-
table workflows without controlled failure semantics.
WATCH OUT
The application's one INSERT can cause more work than the visible statement suggests.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you trace a trigger-induced failure?
Log the database exception and statement/trigger context without secrets, inspect trigger
definitions and reproduce with a small transaction.

pages.title: and sharding?
pages.fullText:

CHAPTER 18   •   VIEWS, ROUTINES, PARTITIONING AND MAINTENANCE
QUESTION Q089
How does table partitioning differ from indexing
and sharding?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Partitioning divides a logical table into managed pieces; indexing creates
access paths; sharding distributes data across independent database
boundaries.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Partition orders by ordered_at range
Index each relevant access path
Shard tenants across databases only with an explicit routing design
Storage policy ➜ Maintenance ➜ Read model
WHY THIS WORKS
Partition pruning helps only when predicates and bounds permit it. Constraints,
uniqueness, joins and maintenance differ by engine. More partitions are not automatically
faster. Sharding adds cross-boundary consistency and operations costs.
WATCH OUT
Partitioning does not replace all indexes.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which query can prune to one month?
A half-open time range on the partition key, e.g. ordered_at >= month_start AND
ordered_at < next_month, allows pruning when partitions align.

pages.title: Why do statistics and version cleanup matter?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 18   •   VIEWS, ROUTINES, PARTITIONING AND MAINTENANCE
QUESTION Q090
Why do statistics and version cleanup matter?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
The optimizer needs distribution evidence, and MVCC storage needs cleanup
to avoid uncontrolled old-version accumulation.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
PostgreSQL: ANALYZE / VACUUM / autovacuum
MySQL InnoDB: statistics and purge/history mechanisms
Storage policy ➜ Maintenance ➜ Read model
WHY THIS WORKS
Maintenance tasks have different roles; ordinary PostgreSQL VACUUM does not generally
shrink every table file to the minimum size. Diagnose long transactions, growth and stale
estimates. Avoid treating every engine's maintenance commands as interchangeable.
WATCH OUT
A single maintenance command is not a universal slow-query fix.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What evidence indicates old snapshots are delaying cleanup?
PostgreSQL: long-running transactions/replication slots and retained dead tuples;
MySQL: long-running read views and growing InnoDB history list length.

pages.title: TRACE THE EXAMPLE SELECT * FROM customers WHERE customer_id = ?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 19   •   APPLICATION SQL, SECURITY AND PAGINATION
QUESTION Q091
How do parameterized queries prevent SQL
injection?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
They bind values separately from SQL structure rather than concatenating
untrusted text into executable syntax.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE customer_id = ?
-- Bind a value through JDBC; do not concatenate request text.
T enant input ➜ Safe query ➜ Paged output
WHY THIS WORKS
Placeholders generally represent values, not arbitrary table names or ORDER BY
identifiers. Choose dynamic identifiers from an allow-list and keep privilege minimal. ORM
usage is not proof every query path is parameterized.
WATCH OUT
Concatenating a sort expression remains unsafe.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How do you allow multiple safe sort columns?
Use an allowlist mapping user sort choices to fixed column names and ASC/DESC
tokens; bind values, never raw SQL identifiers.

pages.title: How do you prevent cross-tenant SQL leakage?
pages.fullText:

CHAPTER 19   •   APPLICATION SQL, SECURITY AND PAGINATION
QUESTION Q092
How do you prevent cross-tenant SQL leakage?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Constrain access through authenticated tenant identity and enforce it
consistently across reads, writes and relationship checks.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id=:trustedTenant AND order_id=:id;
T enant input ➜ Safe query ➜ Paged output
WHY THIS WORKS
A globally unique order ID does not remove authorization requirements. Composite
constraints and database row-level policies can help where supported. Dynamic/report/
admin paths need deliberate ownership rules too.
WATCH OUT
A tenantId from the request is not automatically trusted.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What happens when joining tenant-scoped tables?
Join using both tenant_id and entity ID, keep tenant predicates/row-level security
enforced, and test crossed-ID attacks.

pages.title: What is the N+1 query problem?
pages.fullText:

CHAPTER 19   •   APPLICATION SQL, SECURITY AND PAGINATION
QUESTION Q093
What is the N+1 query problem?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
One initial query causes many additional per-row queries, increasing round
trips and total work.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Load 100 orders -> 100 separate customer/item lookups
T enant input ➜ Safe query ➜ Paged output
WHY THIS WORKS
Use appropriate joins, batching or staged fetching, while respecting result cardinality and
pagination. Joining several collections can create a different row-explosion problem.
Count queries and inspect actual rows, not only ORM method names.
WATCH OUT
One giant join is not always the correct N+1 fix.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How do you page orders while fetching their items?
First page a stable list of order IDs, then fetch items for those IDs in one query or batch;
assemble results without multiplying page rows.

pages.title: How does keyset pagination work?
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
CHAPTER 19   •   APPLICATION SQL, SECURITY AND PAGINATION
QUESTION Q094
How does keyset pagination work?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
It requests rows after the last ordered key rather than skipping a growing
offset.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
SELECT order_id,ordered_at FROM orders
WHERE ordered_at<:lastTime OR
 (ordered_at=:lastTime AND order_id<:lastId)
ORDER BY ordered_at DESC,order_id DESC LIMIT 20;
T enant input ➜ Safe query ➜ Paged output
WHY THIS WORKS
Use a stable unique tie-breaker, matching sort directions and useful index. Null ordering
and mutable sort values require explicit handling. It improves deep navigation but does
not promise one immutable snapshot across requests.
WATCH OUT
Changing an ordering value can move a row across the cursor.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What if the user needs random page numbers?
Use offset pagination for bounded random access, or page-number metadata plus a
stable snapshot; seek pagination is cursor-based by nature.

CHAPTER 19   •   APPLICATION SQL, SECURITY AND PAGINATION
QUESTION Q095
How should connection pools and query deadlines
be designed?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Bound concurrency, wait time and transaction/query duration according to
database capacity and application SLOs.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Pool wait budget + query budget + response work <= request budget
T enant input ➜ Safe query ➜ Paged output
WHY THIS WORKS
More connections can increase contention rather than throughput. A connection must
return in clean transaction/session state. Cancellation/timeout can leave an uncertain
write outcome, so correct identity and reconciliation matter.
WATCH OUT
Client timeout does not prove a database write rolled back.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What should the API do after an unknown commit outcome?
Reconcile commit outcome via stable request identity before repeating work; return a
pending/unknown status rather than falsely claiming failure.

QUESTION Q096
A revenue query doubled totals. Where do you
investigate?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Check join grain and detail multiplicity before blaming SUM or the database.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
orders -> order_items multiplies order amount per item
Aggregate item totals or avoid unnecessary detail join
Correctness ➜ Plan evidence ➜ Failure recovery
WHY THIS WORKS
Compare counts per order and trace a tiny counterexample. Aggregating each many-
side before joining can restore the desired grain. Add constraints where one-to-one
assumptions are real. Preserve equal-valued legitimate orders.
WATCH OUT
SUM(DISTINCT order.amount) is not a general repair.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which table owns the revenue fact?
The orders header owns order-level booked revenue; order_items owns line-level revenue
if that is the metric. Define grain before summing.

parameter, before/after deploy. Compare statistics and selectivity.

pages.fullText:

QUESTION Q099
How would you design a safe bank transfer?
SHORT INTERVIEW ANSWER
Enforce account validity/funds invariants in one reviewed transaction, lock or
guard writes coherently, and use stable transfer identity for retries.
TRACE THE EXAMPLE
Transaction: validate both accounts -> debit -> credit -> ledger -> commit
Consistent account lock order; same currency/amount contract

WHY THIS WORKS
Check affected rows and constraints. External notifications publish from durable intent
after the database outcome. A timeout after commit is an uncertain result, so reusing the
transfer identity should return/reconcile the existing outcome.
WATCH OUT
Two balance updates alone omit important validation and idempotency.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What if the destination does not exist?
Reject/rollback the full transaction if destination row is missing; constrain accounts and
verify affected row counts before committing.

SQL WORKED LAB C01
Second-highest distinct salary
YOUR TASK
Return one row containing the second-highest known salary value. Tied
employees count as one salary level.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
EXPECTED RESULTS • 1 ROWS
second_salary
90000
WHY IT WORKS
The inner MAX is 100000. The outer MAX of lower values is 90000. Unlike selecting the
second row, duplicates cannot change the distinct-level meaning. An aggregate over no
qualifying rows still returns one row with NULL.
TRY NEXT

NULL. If asked to return people at that level, join/filter by the resulting salary instead.

pages.fullText:

SQL WORKED LAB C02
T op two salary levels per department
YOUR TASK
Return all employees in the two highest distinct salary levels of each assigned
department. Include ties and exclude unknown salaries.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT department_id, employee_id, name, salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (
      PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC
    ) AS salary_rank
  FROM employees
  WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL AND salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT department_id, employee_id, name, salary, salary_rank
FROM ranked WHERE salary_rank <= 2
ORDER BY department_id, salary_rank, employee_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 5 ROWS
department_id employee_id name salary salary_rank

Customers with no orders
YOUR TASK
Return customers with no order of any status. Preserve the meaning if the
orders table is empty.

FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

customer_id name
4 Priya

SQL WORKED LAB C04
Employee count for every department
YOUR TASK
Include empty departments and count matched employees, not null-extended
rows.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
SELECT d.department_id, d.name,
       COUNT(e.employee_id) AS employees_count
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_id, d.name
ORDER BY d.department_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 3 ROWS
department_id name employees_count
10 Engineering 3
20 Sales 2
30 HR 0
WHY IT WORKS
HR creates one null-extended join row; COUNT(e.employee_id) ignores its NULL.
COUNT(*) would give HR a misleading count of one. Nila has no assigned department
and does not belong to these department groups.
TRY NEXT
Add a salary requirement to ON when you must keep empty departments. Check both
COUNT(*) and COUNT(e.employee_id) before and after the change.

pages.fullText:

SQL WORKED LAB C05
Paid revenue including customers with zero
YOUR TASK
Return one paid order-header total per customer; include customers with no
qualifying order.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
WITH paid AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COALESCE(p.revenue, 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN paid p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 4 ROWS
customer_id name revenue
1 Sai 350
2 Meena 270
3 Arun 80
4 Priya 0
WHY IT WORKS
The CTE establishes one row per customer before joining. Its total is 700 across all paid
orders, including the February order. Replacing absent paid revenue with zero is explicit
here.
TRY NEXT
Add a half-open date predicate inside the CTE for a reporting period. January paid
revenue is 630; do not accidentally include order 108.

pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
SQL WORKED LAB C06
Running paid total per customer
YOUR TASK
Return each paid order and the cumulative amount for that customer in
date/ID order.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
SELECT customer_id, order_id, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at, order_id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_total
FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID'
ORDER BY customer_id, ordered_at, order_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 6 ROWS
customer_id order_id amount running_total
1 101 100 100
1 102 150 250
1 106 100 350
2 103 200 200
2 108 70 270
3 105 80 80
WHY IT WORKS
PARTITION BY resets the total per customer. ROWS and a unique order define a row-by-
row progression. Filtering before the window means pending/cancelled orders are absent
from both rows and totals.
TRY NEXT
Insert two paid orders on the same date and verify both steps. Removing the ID tie-
breaker or relying on a default peer-aware frame can change the intended result.

SQL WORKED LAB C07
Previous paid amount and difference
YOUR TASK
Compare each paid order amount with the previous paid order for the same
customer.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
WITH history AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, ordered_at, amount,
    LAG(amount) OVER (
      PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at, order_id
    ) AS previous_amount
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID'
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, previous_amount,
       amount - previous_amount AS difference
FROM history
ORDER BY customer_id, ordered_at, order_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 6 ROWS
customer_id order_id previous_amount difference
1 101 NULL NULL
1 102 100 50
1 106 150 -50
2 103 NULL NULL
2 108 200 -130
3 105 NULL NULL
WHY IT WORKS
The first paid order has no previous paid row, so its previous value and arithmetic
difference are NULL. Using zero as the default would answer a different question.
TRY NEXT

order or previous order of any status.PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 115

pages.fullText:

SQL WORKED LAB C08
Employees above their department average
YOUR TASK
Return assigned employees whose known salary is strictly greater than their
department average.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
WITH averages AS (
  SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
  FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT e.employee_id, e.name, e.department_id, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN averages a ON a.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE e.salary > a.avg_salary
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 2 ROWS
employee_id name department_id salary
1 Sai 10 100000
4 Priya 20 90000
WHY IT WORKS
Engineering averages about 86666.67 and Sales averages 75000. AVG excludes NULL
salaries. A department with only NULL salaries has a NULL average, so no employee
qualifies via a normal comparison.
TRY NEXT
Test an employee exactly at the average, and a department containing one known salary.
Neither should qualify under the strict greater-than rule.

SQL WORKED LAB C09
Latest order per customer
YOUR TASK
Return the latest order of any status for each customer who has orders.
Higher order_id breaks equal-date ties.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, ordered_at, status,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY customer_id
      ORDER BY ordered_at DESC, order_id DESC
    ) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, ordered_at, status
FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 3 ROWS
customer_id order_id ordered_at status
1 106 2026-01-04 PAID
2 108 2026-02-01 PAID
3 107 2026-01-05 PENDING
WHY IT WORKS
ROW_NUMBER picks one complete row. MAX(date) joined back without a tie rule can
return multiple rows. Priya is absent because this query starts from orders; left join the
rn=1 result to customers to preserve her.
TRY NEXT
Add equal-date orders for a customer. Confirm the chosen ID and decide whether the
product actually requires all latest-date ties.

pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
SQL WORKED LAB C10
Revenue without detail-join inflation
YOUR TASK
Compute paid header revenue and paid item value. Collapse item rows to one
row per order before joining.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
WITH item_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS item_value
  FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT SUM(o.amount) AS header_revenue,
       SUM(COALESCE(i.item_value, 0)) AS item_value
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN item_totals i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID';
EXPECTED RESULTS • 1 ROWS
header_revenue item_value
700 700
WHY IT WORKS
Order 101 has two item rows. Summing its header amount after a raw item join produces
800 instead of 700. SUM(DISTINCT amount) gives 600 here because different orders
can both cost 100. Pre-aggregation restores the intended grain.
TRY NEXT
Add an order with no item rows and clarify whether that is valid. Item totals need not
equal header totals in a real system with taxes, fees and discounts.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 118

pages.fullText:

SQL WORKED LAB C11
Deterministic duplicate candidates
YOUR TASK
For each non-null exact email, keep the smallest contact_id and return the
other IDs. Do not delete anything yet.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT contact_id, email,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY email ORDER BY contact_id
    ) AS rn
  FROM contacts WHERE email IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT contact_id, email FROM ranked
WHERE rn > 1 ORDER BY contact_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 1 ROWS
contact_id email
2 a@example.com
WHY IT WORKS
Only ID 2 is a duplicate candidate. This fixture uses exact lowercase values; production
equality depends on collation and any normalization policy. Missing emails are excluded
by the stated requirement.
TRY NEXT
Test three equal emails, case variants and multiple NULLs. Before deletion, review
survivor rules, foreign-key references and concurrent inserts; then enforce the chosen
uniqueness rule.

pages.title: SQL WORKED LAB C12
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
SQL WORKED LAB C12
Consecutive integer islands
YOUR TASK
Find consecutive groups of distinct integers and return their start, end and
length.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
WITH distinct_values AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT n FROM sequence_values
), numbered AS (
  SELECT n, n - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY n) AS island_key
  FROM distinct_values
)
SELECT MIN(n) AS start_n, MAX(n) AS end_n, COUNT(*) AS length
FROM numbered GROUP BY island_key
ORDER BY start_n;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 3 ROWS
start_n end_n length
1 3 3
5 6 2
9 9 1
WHY IT WORKS
For consecutive integers, both n and row number increase by one, so their difference
stays constant. DISTINCT removes duplicate integers before numbering. Date-based
islands require dialect-aware date arithmetic.
TRY NEXT
Insert a duplicate 2 and verify the same groups. Try an empty table, one integer and
negative integers; review arithmetic range when real values approach type limits.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 120

pages.title: SQL WORKED LAB C13
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
SQL WORKED LAB C13
Bounded organization traversal
YOUR TASK
Starting at Sai (employee 1), list the reporting tree with depth. The fixture is
acyclic; limit depth to ten.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT employee_id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth
  FROM employees WHERE employee_id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.employee_id
  WHERE o.depth < 10
)
SELECT employee_id, name, depth FROM org
ORDER BY depth, employee_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 3 ROWS
employee_id name depth
1 Sai 0
2 Meena 1
3 Arun 1
WHY IT WORKS
The anchor emits Sai, and the recursive term follows employees whose manager is a
current node. Priya/Ravi belong to another root. The depth bound stops unbounded
expansion but may truncate a legitimate deeper tree.
TRY NEXT
A production graph needs a deliberate cycle policy and path/visited detection, not only a
depth cap. Test a missing root, a leaf root and a cycle in a disposable fixture.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 121

pages.title: SQL WORKED LAB C14
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
SQL WORKED LAB C14
Seek pagination with tied dates
YOUR TASK
Return the next three orders after cursor (2026-01-03, 105), sorted by date
descending then ID descending.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
SELECT order_id, ordered_at
FROM orders
WHERE ordered_at < '2026-01-03'
   OR (ordered_at = '2026-01-03' AND order_id < 105)
ORDER BY ordered_at DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 3;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 3 ROWS
order_id ordered_at
104 2026-01-03
103 2026-01-02
102 2026-01-02
WHY IT WORKS
The cursor comparison includes both sort fields, so order 104 is not skipped despite
sharing a date with 105. This avoids reading a deep offset, but it does not create a frozen
snapshot across requests.
TRY NEXT
Use bound parameters in application SQL, include tenant/filter context in the cursor
contract, and consider an index matching equality filters then sort keys. Test changed
sort values and a deleted cursor row.

pages.title: SQL WORKED LAB C15
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
SQL WORKED LAB C15
Conditional order-status report
YOUR TASK
Return paid, pending and cancelled counts for every customer, including
customers with no orders.
WORKED SQL SOLUTION
SELECT c.customer_id,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'PAID' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'PENDING' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
EXPECTED RESULTS • 4 ROWS
customer_id paid pending cancelled
1 3 0 0
2 2 0 1
3 1 1 0
4 0 0 0
WHY IT WORKS
Each CASE turns one stated condition into a 1/0 value, so the preserved row for Priya
contributes zero in every column. These three statuses cover the fixture; a new status
needs an explicit reporting decision.
TRY NEXT
Add a new status and an additional pending order. If detail joins are introduced, restore
one row per order before counting.

pages.title: LAST-MINUTE REVISION
pages.fullText:
SQL / ZERO TO HERO / PREMIUM INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK
LAST-MINUTE REVISION
10 traps interviewers test
01 = NULL is UNKNOWN: use IS NULL.
02 COUNT(*) after LEFT JOIN can count preserved empty rows.
03 LEFT JOIN + WHERE on right side can drop unmatched rows.
04 Join detail tables at the right grain to avoid duplicated totals.
05 Define tie policy for top-N and salaries.
06 Window ORDER BY is different from final display ordering.
07 An index does not always beat a scan.
08 DDL rollback depends on the engine and command.
09 MVCC does not eliminate write conflicts or locks.
10 Timeout does not prove a write failed.
THE FIVE TEST INPUTS
Empty input, missing match, duplicate value, NULL and one-to-many child
rows. These catch many SQL mistakes.
PORTABLE SQL   •   POSTGRESQL 17   •   MYSQL 8.4 INNODB 124

pages.title: Four drawings worth memorizing
pages.fullText:
03 / THE BIG PICTURE
Four drawings worth memorizing
Docker becomes easier when you separate build-time, runtime, networking and recovery.
1. Build once → Run anywhere compatible
Source + dependencies → OCI image → Container process
An image packages user-space files. It still needs the right OS/CPU environment.
2. Where data lives
Container layer ≠ Named volume → Backup + restore
A volume outlives the container. It does not automatically give off-host recovery.
3. Container networking
Host port 18080 → Container port 8080 → Java listener
EXPOSE is documentation. A published port and active application listener are separate facts.
4. Safer Java shutdown
Stop new traffic → SIGTERM + drain → Close resources
Runtime shutdown timing must allow Spring, database and worker cleanup to finish.
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO
HANDWRITTEN-STYLE STUDY EDITION • JAVA + SPRING 5

pages.title: What is Docker, and what problem does it solve?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 01 — Docker foundations
What is Docker, and what problem does it
solve?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
Docker packages an application and its user-space dependencies into an image,
then runs that image as an isolated process environment.
↳ Draw this in the interview
Application files ➜ Docker image ➜ Isolated process
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
A service can use the same image in test and production while receiving a different database URL at
startup. Packaging removes many installation differences; it does not remove network, permission or
configuration differences.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
Which production problems remain even when the image is identical?
A. The image does not control network access, database availability, secrets, CPU/memory
limits, file permissions, or deployment configuration. Check these separately in production.
⚠ WATCH OUT A container image does not include its own running kernel. External services still need
compatible contracts and credentials.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 6
Q001
from original guide COMMAND OR MINI EXAMPLE 
Developer: Java 21 + app.jar + OS libraries
Image:     the same packaged runtime and application
Server:    starts that image with its own configuration
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO
HANDWRITTEN-STYLE STUDY EDITION • JAVA + SPRING 6

pages.title: What is the difference between an image and a container?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 01 — Docker foundations
What is the difference between an image and
a container?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
An image is a reusable template; a container is a created runtime instance with
configuration, process state and a writable filesystem layer.
↳ Draw this in the interview
Reusable image ➜ Create container ➜ Run process
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
Pulling downloads an image. Creating records a container without starting its main process. Starting
launches that process. Several containers can use one image and have separate writable layers.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
What survives a restart, and what disappears when the container is removed?
A. A restart keeps the container object's configuration and writable layer. Removing the
container removes its writable layer; named volumes and images normally remain unless
explicitly removed.
⚠ WATCH OUT Editing a running container does not modify the source image or the other containers
created from it.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 7
Q002
from original guide COMMAND OR MINI EXAMPLE 
docker pull nginx:stable
docker create --name dk-q-web nginx:stable
docker start dk-q-web
docker inspect dk-q-web
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO
HANDWRITTEN-STYLE STUDY EDITION • JAVA + SPRING 7

pages.title: How are containers different from virtual machines?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 01 — Docker foundations
How are containers different from virtual
machines?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
A conventional VM has a guest kernel; Linux containers isolate processes that
share the kernel of the Linux host or Docker Desktop VM.
↳ Draw this in the interview
Virtual machine: own OS
kernel ➜ Linux container: shared kernel ➜ Choose isolation boundary
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
Containers commonly start faster because they launch processes rather than boot a full guest OS. A VM
can run a different guest OS; a Linux image requires a compatible Linux execution environment.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
When would you combine VMs and containers?
A. Run containers inside VMs when you need stronger host isolation, different tenant security
boundaries, or cloud VM management combined with fast container deployment.
⚠ WATCH OUT Shared-kernel isolation has a different threat boundary from a separate guest kernel. Startup
and memory savings depend on the workload.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 7
Q003
from original guide COMMAND OR MINI EXAMPLE 
VM workload:        app + libraries + guest kernel
Linux container:    app + libraries
Shared foundation:  Linux host or Desktop VM kernel

pages.title: Why can a Docker image run on different computers?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 01 — Docker foundations
Why can a Docker image run on different
computers?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
It supplies a consistent user-space filesystem, but portability still depends on OS,
CPU architecture, kernel features and runtime configuration.
↳ Draw this in the interview
Image manifest ➜ Select amd64 / arm64 ➜ Compatible native runtime
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
A Linux image on macOS or Windows usually runs through Docker Desktop's Linux VM. Multi-platform
images can supply separate variants for AMD64 and ARM64. Native libraries inside a Java image must
match the selected platform.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
Why can a JNI library work on one image variant and fail on another?
A. JNI contains CPU- and OS-specific native binaries. An amd64 Linux .so cannot automatically
load on arm64 or another OS; package and test the right binary for each platform.
⚠ WATCH OUT Windows containers use Windows compatibility rules. Java bytecode portability does not
make every image architecture-neutral.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 8
Q004
from original guide COMMAND OR MINI EXAMPLE 
docker image inspect IMAGE \
  --format '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'
# Example platform: linux/amd64
# An ARM laptop needs an ARM image or supported emulation.
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO

pages.title: What are Docker Engine, Docker Desktop, Compose and a registry?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 01 — Docker foundations
What are Docker Engine, Docker Desktop,
Compose and a registry?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
Engine manages container objects; Desktop provides a workstation environment;
Compose describes a multi-container application; a registry distributes images.
↳ Draw this in the interview
Docker CLI & Engine ➜ Compose services ➜ Registry stores images
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
Compose uses the Docker API to create services, networks and volumes from configuration. A registry can
store images without running them. Desktop adds integration around the engine for supported desktop
systems.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
How would you confirm which engine receives your commands?
A. Use `docker context show`, `docker context inspect`, and `docker info`. Check the daemon
endpoint and engine identity before running builds or deleting containers.
⚠ WATCH OUT Installing the CLI alone does not prove that a daemon is running or that your selected
context points to the intended machine.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 8
Q005
from original guide COMMAND OR MINI EXAMPLE 
docker version          # client and engine information
docker compose version  # Compose plugin information
docker pull REGISTRY/TEAM/SERVICE:TAG
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO
HANDWRITTEN-STYLE STUDY EDITION • JAVA + SPRING 10

Compose describes a multi-container application; a registry distributes images.

pages.title: How does a Docker command reach a container process?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 02 — Engine architecture and Linux isolation
How does a Docker command reach a
container process?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
The CLI calls the selected engine API; the engine coordinates container creation
and execution through lower-level runtime components.
↳ Draw this in the interview
Client command ➜ Engine API & runtime ➜ Host kernel process
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
The terminal runs on the client machine, but containers and volumes live on the engine's machine. A
remote context can therefore change where data is stored and where published ports appear.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
Where does a bind mount come from when the engine is remote?
A. A bind mount path is resolved on the Docker Engine host, not necessarily on your local CLI
computer. With Docker Desktop, check its VM/file-sharing behavior.
⚠ WATCH OUT A client-side file path is not automatically a path on a remote daemon host. Check context
before troubleshooting mounts or cleanup.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 9
Q006
from original guide COMMAND OR MINI EXAMPLE 
docker context show
docker context ls
docker info
# The selected context can address a remote engine.
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO
HANDWRITTEN-STYLE STUDY EDITION • JAVA + SPRING 11

and execution through lower-level runtime components.

pages.title: What do Linux namespaces do?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 02 — Engine architecture and Linux isolation
What do Linux namespaces do?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
Namespaces give processes separate views of resources such as process IDs,
network interfaces and mounts.
↳ Draw this in the interview
PID / mount / network view ➜ Linux namespaces ➜ Process sees its namespace
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
The process may see a small process tree and its own hostname while still being a process on the host
kernel. Namespaces change visibility and association; they do not allocate CPU or memory budgets.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
How is namespace isolation different from resource limiting?
A. Namespaces control which resources a process can see; cgroups limit how much CPU/memory
it may use. Isolation and resource budgets are different controls.
⚠ WATCH OUT Explicit host namespace options reduce that isolation. Namespace separation alone is not a
complete security boundary.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 10
Q007
from original guide COMMAND OR MINI EXAMPLE 
docker run --rm alpine:3.22 \
  sh -c 'echo "container view"; ps; hostname'
# Compare this view with the Linux host's process list.
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO
HANDWRITTEN-STYLE STUDY EDITION • JAVA + SPRING 12

network interfaces and mounts.

pages.title: What are cgroups, and why do containers need them?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 02 — Engine architecture and Linux isolation
What are cgroups, and why do containers
need them?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
Linux control groups account for and constrain resources consumed by groups of
processes.
↳ Draw this in the interview
Set memory & CPU budget ➜ Linux cgroups ➜ Throttle or OOM control
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
The process receives a memory ceiling and CPU bandwidth allowance. This keeps a runaway workload
from consuming unrestricted resources, provided the host and runtime support the relevant controls.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
What happens when a process exceeds its memory limit?
A. The Linux memory controller can kill a process in the container; Docker may report
OOMKilled. Inspect the memory limit, exit details, and host events.
⚠ WATCH OUT A CPU quota is not a dedicated physical core. Container limits also do not reserve sufficient
cluster capacity by themselves.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 10
Q008
from original guide COMMAND OR MINI EXAMPLE 
docker run --rm --memory=256m --cpus=0.5 \
  alpine:3.22 sleep 10
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO
HANDWRITTEN-STYLE STUDY EDITION • JAVA + SPRING 13

processes.

pages.title: What are containerd, runc and OCI?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 02 — Engine architecture and Linux isolation
What are containerd, runc and OCI?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
containerd manages runtime lifecycle and image-related tasks; runc is a low-level
Linux container runtime; OCI defines interoperable image and runtime
specifications.
↳ Draw this in the interview
OCI image format ➜ containerd / runc ➜ Kubernetes CRI
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
Separating these responsibilities helps explain why an image built with Docker can be consumed by other
compatible runtimes. It also helps locate failures: image retrieval, runtime creation and application
startup are different steps.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
Does Kubernetes need Docker Engine to run a Docker-built image?
A. No. Kubernetes talks to a CRI-compatible runtime such as containerd or CRI-O; it can run
OCI images built with Docker without using Docker Engine.
⚠ WATCH OUT Product architecture can evolve. Do not assume a specific daemon chain is required by every
OCI-compatible platform.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 10

Engine/runtime stack -> container process
# The registry stores content, not a running runc process.

pages.title: How does the writable container layer work?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 02 — Engine architecture and Linux isolation
How does the writable container layer work?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
Filesystem changes go into the container's own layer above the image's read-only
layers; mounted storage has separate behavior.
↳ Draw this in the interview
Read-only image layers ➜ Per-container write layer ➜ Remove = layer gone
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
The change can be inspected after the process exits while the container object exists. Removing that
object removes its writable layer. A later container from the same image has no note.txt unless it was in
the image or a mount.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
How does a named volume change this lifecycle?
A. A named volume has its own lifecycle. It keeps mounted data when the container is removed
and can be attached to a replacement container.
⚠ WATCH OUT This is not a persistence strategy for a database. A committed image also is not a consistent
backup of a running database.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 11

docker run --name dk-q-edit alpine:3.22 \
  sh -c 'echo changed > /note.txt'
docker diff dk-q-edit
docker rm dk-q-edit

pages.title: What is the difference between run, create and start?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 03 — Container lifecycle and essential commands
What is the difference between run, create
and start?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
run creates and starts a new container; create only creates it; start launches an
existing stopped container.
↳ Draw this in the interview
docker create ➜ docker start ➜ docker run = both
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
The two start commands execute the existing container's configured command again. They do not create
two new objects. In contrast, two unnamed run commands create two separate containers.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
Can you change the startup environment with docker start?
A. No. `docker start` reuses the container's original environment and configuration. Create a
replacement container with updated `-e` or Compose settings.
⚠ WATCH OUT start does not rebuild an image or pick up a new image tag automatically. Recreate to change
most container configuration.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 12

docker create --name dk-q-once alpine:3.22 echo hello
docker start -a dk-q-once
docker start -a dk-q-once
docker rm dk-q-once

existing stopped container.

pages.title: Why does a container exit immediately after starting?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 03 — Container lifecycle and essential commands
Why does a container exit immediately after
starting?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
A container normally lives as long as its main process. A command that finishes,
crashes or cannot execute makes the container exit.
↳ Draw this in the interview
Start main process ➜ Process exits ➜ Container stops
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
echo prints once and exits successfully, so an exited container is expected. A missing executable or
application exception requires a different diagnosis. Detached mode changes terminal attachment, not
process lifetime.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
How would you distinguish a successful batch job from a failed API server?
A. Check exit code, logs, and the expected process type. Exit 0 is fine for a short batch task; an
API that should stay up is failing its service contract.
⚠ WATCH OUT Adding sleep forever hides startup failure and does not turn a broken service into a
healthy one.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 12

from original guide COMMAND OR MINI EXAMPLE 
docker run --name dk-q-short alpine:3.22 echo done
docker ps -a --filter name=dk-q-short
docker logs dk-q-short
docker inspect dk-q-short --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO

crashes or cannot execute makes the container exit.

docker ps -a --filter name=dk-q-short
docker logs dk-q-short
docker inspect dk-q-short --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'
pages.explanation:
echo prints once and exits successfully, so an exited container is expected. A missing executable or
application exception requires a different diagnosis. Detached mode changes terminal attachment, not
process lifetime.
pages.pitfall:
Adding sleep forever hides startup failure and does not turn a broken service into a
healthy one.
pages.followup:
How would you distinguish a successful batch job from a failed API server?
A. Check exit code, logs, and the expected process type. Exit 0 is fine for a short batch task; an
API that should stay up is failing its service contract.

pages.title: What is the difference between exec and attach?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 03 — Container lifecycle and essential commands
What is the difference between exec and
attach?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
exec starts an additional process inside a running container; attach connects to
the main process's standard streams.
↳ Draw this in the interview
docker exec: new process ➜ docker attach: existingstreams ➜ Inspect the right process
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
nginx -t runs a separate configuration check. An exec shell can inspect files if the image contains a shell.
Attach does not create a shell and interactive signals may affect the main process.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
How would you inspect a crashed container when exec cannot run?
A. Use `docker logs`, `docker inspect`, `docker cp` on a retained container, and image metadata.
Reproduce or debug with a separate disposable container if needed.
⚠ WATCH OUT exec requires a running container and a present executable. Minimal images may provide
neither sh nor bash.

# attach targets the existing main process streams.

pages.title: How do stop, kill and rm differ?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 03 — Container lifecycle and essential commands
How do stop, kill and rm differ?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
stop requests graceful termination before a timeout; kill sends a signal directly;
rm removes the container object.
↳ Draw this in the interview
SIGTERM grace period ➜ SIGKILL if needed ➜ Remove container object
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
The default stop signal is SIGTERM unless configured otherwise; a surviving process is forcibly killed after
the timeout. Removing the stopped container discards its writable layer, while its image remains available.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
How do you align Docker's timeout with a Spring shutdown timeout?
A. Set Docker's stop grace period longer than the Spring shutdown phases plus request drain
and cleanup time. Verify SIGTERM reaches the JVM.
⚠ WATCH OUT rm -f combines forced termination with removal. It gives the application no normal drain
window and can erase useful diagnosis state.
ORIGINAL QUESTION PRESERVED Source guide p. 13

docker inspect dk-q-web --format '{{.State.Status}}'
docker rm dk-q-web
INTERVIEW NOTEBOOK / DOCKER ZERO TO HERO
HANDWRITTEN-STYLE STUDY EDITION • JAVA + SPRING 19

rm removes the container object.

pages.title: When should you use --rm, -d and -it?
pages.fullText:
FOUNDATION CHAPTER 03 — Container lifecycle and essential commands
When should you use --rm, -d and -it?
THE 20-SECOND ANSWER
--rm removes an exiting container, -d detaches the terminal, and -it supplies
interactive input plus a pseudo-terminal.
↳ Draw this in the interview
--rm: auto-clean ➜ --detach: background ➜ -it: interactive terminal
WHY / HOW IT WORKS
An ephemeral command is suitable for --rm; a server can run detached; a shell benefits from interactive
terminal behavior. The flags solve different problems and can sometimes be combined.
THE INTERVIEWER MAY ASK…
Would you use --rm on a container whose crash you must investigate?
A. Usually no. Retain the exited container so `inspect`, filesystem differences, and logs are
available; remove it after capturing incident evidence.
⚠ WATCH OUT --rm does not remove explicitly named volumes. Automatic removal can also discard
container metadata needed after a failure.

docker run -d --name dk-q-server nginx:stable
docker run --rm -it alpine:3.22 sh

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE STUDY EDITION • JAVA + SPRING 20

interactive input plus a pseudo-terminal.
