pages.title: What triggers a Deployment rollout?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 · Deployments, ReplicaSets and rollouts FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q017. What triggers a Deployment rollout?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Changing the Pod template starts a rollout; changing replicas only scales
it.
Interview precision: A change to the Pod template triggers a new rollout; changing the desired
replica count alone does not create a new template revision.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl set image deployment/orders \
  api=TEAM/APP:NEW_TAG -n interview
kubectl scale deployment/orders --replicas=4 -n interview
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The image change alters the template. Scaling changes how many
replicas are requested. Updating an external ConfigMap may leave the template unchanged
unless your delivery process deliberately changes a checksum or restarts it.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do you roll out an environment-variable configuration update?
Answer: Use a controlled restart or a template checksum/version change for
environment values that Pods read at startup.
Watch out: Reapplying identical YAML does not force every Pod to restart.
Original guide: page 16 · K03 (source directory).
Template changed New ReplicaSet New Pods

pages.title: How do maxSurge and maxUnavailable work?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 · Deployments, ReplicaSets and rollouts FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q018. How do maxSurge and maxUnavailable
work?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
maxSurge allows extra Pods; maxUnavailable sets how many may be
unavailable during an update.
Interview precision: They bound extra replicas and unavailable replicas during a rolling update,
with percentage rounding rules where percentages are used.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · For a three-replica workload, this policy can temporarily need a
fourth replica while retaining available capacity. Readiness and sufficient node resources
determine whether the rollout can progress.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if there is no room for the surge Pod?
Answer: The rollout waits for spare capacity, unless you safely adjust surge/
unavailability or add capacity.
Watch out: The policy is not an end-to-end zero-error guarantee. Terminating Pods can
consume resources beyond a simple replica calculation.
Original guide: page 16 · K03 (source directory).

pages.title: Does Kubernetes automatically roll back a failed Deployment?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 · Deployments, ReplicaSets and rollouts FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q019. Does Kubernetes automatically roll back a
failed Deployment?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Kubernetes marks a stalled rollout; it does not automatically undo every
failed release.
Interview precision: A Deployment reports stalled progress under its configured conditions; an
automatic rollback requires an external delivery policy or operator action.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl rollout status deployment/orders -n interview --timeout=120s
kubectl describe deployment orders -n interview
# After reviewing compatibility and intent:
kubectl rollout undo deployment/orders -n interview
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A progress deadline helps surface a stalled rollout. undo restores a
retained template revision; it does not restore database state or all external configuration.
Delivery systems can enforce additional rollback rules.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What must be checked before rolling application code back after a
migration?
Answer: Check database backward compatibility, the migration's rollback path
and whether old code understands new rows.
Watch out: A timeout from your kubectl client is not itself a completed server-side
rollback.
Original guide: page 17 · K03 (source directory).

pages.title: Why are Deployment selectors important?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 04 · Deployments, ReplicaSets and rollouts FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q020. Why are Deployment selectors important?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Selectors tell a Deployment which Pod template it owns and must match
the template labels.
Interview precision: The selector defines the Pod set a controller owns and must align with the
Pod template labels; apps/v1 Deployment selectors are immutable after creation.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
selector:
  matchLabels:
    app: orders
template:
  metadata:
    labels:
      app: orders
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Matching labels establish ownership. A stable app selector avoids
making release version changes into ownership changes. A changed immutable selector
needs a deliberate replacement or new Deployment plan.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How can a correct Deployment still receive no traffic from its Service?
Answer: Service labels may not match, Pods may be unready, or targetPort may
not reach the listener.
Watch out: Avoid overlapping ownership selectors between independent controllers.
Service selectors have a separate traffic role.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 · Services, DNS and traffic paths FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q021. What does a Kubernetes Service provide?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
A Service gives clients a stable name and port while its matching Pods
change.
Interview precision: A Service defines a stable access abstraction for a backend set; its type
and networking implementation determine how clients reach that set.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: orders}
spec:
  selector: {app: orders}
  ports:
    - {port: 80, targetPort: 8080}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Clients use orders:80 while selected backend Pods listen on 8080.
Pod replacement does not require clients to memorize the new Pod IP.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would you inspect if the Service exists but connections fail?
Answer: Check selectors, Ready Pods, EndpointSlices, targetPort, listener address,
DNS and network rules.
Watch out: A Service does not start an application or make a wrong listener port valid.

Q022. How do port, targetPort, containerPort and
nodePort differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Service port is the caller's port; targetPort is the Pod's listener; nodePort
exposes a node port.
Interview precision: port is the Service endpoint, targetPort is the backend listener target,
containerPort is declarative container metadata, and nodePort is an external node-level port
when allocated.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Client -> Service port 80 -> Pod targetPort 8080
NodePort client -> reachable node IP:NODE_PORT -> Service backend
# containerPort: 8080 does not make Java listen on 8080.

targetPort can refer to a named container port. Host access and cluster-internal access use
different endpoints.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why could port-forward work while a NodePort URL fails on a laptop?
Answer: Port-forward uses an API tunnel. NodePort needs a reachable node
address and permitted network path.
Watch out: Do not confuse a Service port with the node-level port or a port-forward's
local port.

Q023. How do ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer
and headless Services differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
ClusterIP is internal, NodePort opens a node port, LoadBalancer needs
provider support, and headless gives backend DNS.
Interview precision: They provide cluster virtual access, node-level exposure, supported load-
balancer integration and DNS-based backend discovery respectively.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
ClusterIP:    cluster-facing virtual endpoint
NodePort:     reachable node address plus allocated port
LoadBalancer: integration with a supporting provider/controller
Headless:     clusterIP: None; backend discovery without a VIP
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A headless Service is useful for discovering individual StatefulSet
members. LoadBalancer provisioning depends on the environment; a local cluster may
need tunnel or another integration.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which type would you use for a private database and why?
Answer: Use ClusterIP for an internal database entry point; use headless DNS
when individual stable members are required.
Watch out: A pending external address does not necessarily mean the Pods are broken.
Provider policy and internal/external settings matter.

pages.title: How does Kubernetes Service DNS work?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 · Services, DNS and traffic paths FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q024. How does Kubernetes Service DNS work?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Cluster DNS translates Service names into network addresses, usually
with namespace-based search rules.
Interview precision: Cluster DNS supplies Service names, with short names commonly resolving
within the caller's namespace and qualified names identifying other namespaces.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
# Same namespace:
jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders
# Another namespace:
jdbc:postgresql://db.data.svc.cluster.local:5432/orders
# cluster.local is a common default, not a universal cluster domain.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The Pod's DNS configuration and search domains influence lookup.
Resolve the name, then test the required protocol. A successful lookup is not evidence of
database readiness or authorization.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you distinguish DNS failure from a refused TCP connection?
Answer: Test name resolution first, then TCP connection separately; a refused
connection means DNS likely worked.
Watch out: localhost normally refers to the calling Pod, including its sidecars, not a
different database Pod.
Original guide: page 20 · K04, K20, K21, K35 (source directory).
Service name DNS address TCP connection

pages.title: What are EndpointSlices useful for in troubleshooting?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 05 · Services, DNS and traffic paths FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q025. What are EndpointSlices useful for in
troubleshooting?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
EndpointSlices list backend Pod addresses and their readiness conditions
for a Service.
Interview precision: EndpointSlices show Service backend addresses and conditions, helping
verify selection and readiness before investigating the network datapath.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl get svc orders -n interview -o yaml
kubectl get pods -n interview -l app=orders --show-labels
kubectl get endpointslices -n interview \
  -l kubernetes.io/service-name=orders -o yaml
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · An empty backend set can mean the selector matches nothing. Not-
ready endpoints point toward Pod readiness. Correct ready endpoints shift attention toward
the listener, policy or traffic implementation.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What check comes after a ready endpoint with the correct target port?
Answer: Test the actual listener and network policy from a client Pod, then
inspect packet routing if needed.
Watch out: Special settings such as publishNotReadyAddresses change assumptions.
Prefer EndpointSlices over relying on legacy Endpoints output for modern diagnosis.
Original guide: page 20 · K04, K20, K21, K35 (source directory).

pages.title: What is the difference between a Service and an Ingress?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · Ingress, Gateway API and external routing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q026. What is the difference between a Service
and an Ingress?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
A Service names backends; an Ingress declares HTTP routes
implemented by an installed controller.
Interview precision: A Service exposes a backend set; Ingress expresses HTTP(S) routing rules
implemented by an ingress controller.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
External request -> ingress controller -> Service -> ready Pod
# Rules can select a backend by host and path.
kubectl get ingress -n interview
kubectl get ingressclass
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · An ingress object without a supporting controller does not create a
working proxy. Its backend references a Service port, which then maps to the Pod listener.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which controller and class own a specific routing object?
Answer: Inspect ingressClassName/IngressClass and the controller's status,
events and logs.
Watch out: Ingress is not a general protocol gateway for every TCP/UDP workload. Its API
is frozen; Gateway API supports newer routing models.
Original guide: page 21 · K05, G01, K35 (source directory).

pages.title: How do Exact and Prefix paths work, and who rewrites paths?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · Ingress, Gateway API and external routing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q027. How do Exact and Prefix paths work, and
who rewrites paths?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Exact matches a whole path; Prefix matches a path prefix. Rewriting is a
separate controller feature.
Interview precision: Path types define matching semantics; URI rewriting is a separate
controller or routing-feature decision.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
paths:
  - path: /reviews/v1
    pathType: Prefix
    backend:
      service:
        name: reviews-v1
        port: {number: 80}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · This routes matching requests but does not universally remove /
reviews/v1 before forwarding. The backend must support that path or the chosen controller
must apply a supported rewrite policy.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why could routing reach the right Pod but return an application 404?
Answer: The upstream may receive /reviews/v1 while the app only serves /; verify
forwarded path and rewrite rules.
Watch out: Controller-specific annotations are not portable Kubernetes semantics. Avoid
assuming all controllers interpret one annotation identically.
Original guide: page 22 · K05, G01, K35 (source directory).
Match path Optional rewrite App handler

pages.title: Why does a host-based route fail when called by raw IP?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · Ingress, Gateway API and external routing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q028. Why does a host-based route fail when
called by raw IP?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
A host rule needs the correct HTTP Host header; requesting by IP may
select another route.
Interview precision: The request's host identity may not match the configured rule even if the
controller address is reachable.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
curl -H 'Host: reviews.local' http://CONTROLLER_IP/reviews/v1
# Or configure local DNS/hosts so reviews.local reaches the controller.
# HTTPS additionally requires correct SNI and certificate identity.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · HTTP host matching selects the rule. A raw-IP request can hit a
default backend instead. For HTTPS, use a client setup that preserves the intended
hostname for TLS validation and routing.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would curl --resolve help test HTTPS before updating DNS?
Answer: Use curl --resolve to connect to a test IP while preserving the hostname
for HTTPS and SNI.
Watch out: Disabling TLS verification is not a proper production fix for a hostname
mismatch.
Original guide: page 22 · K05, G01, K35 (source directory).
Hostname TLS SNI Route match

STUDY • DRAW • EXPLAIN • VERIFY 37

pages.title: What is Gateway API, and how is it organized?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · Ingress, Gateway API and external routing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q029. What is Gateway API, and how is it
organized?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Gateway API separates traffic infrastructure from application-owned
routes.
Interview precision: Gateway API separates infrastructure ownership from route ownership
through resources such as GatewayClass, Gateway and HTTPRoute.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Platform team: GatewayClass and Gateway policy
App team:     HTTPRoute attached to an allowed Gateway
# Requires installed Gateway API CRDs and a supporting controller.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The separation helps teams delegate routes while retaining listener
and attachment policy. Read resource status to confirm acceptance and backend resolution.
Controller support and feature conformance still matter.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What must be allowed before a route can attach across namespaces?
Answer: Check listener allowedRoutes plus cross-namespace ReferenceGrant
where required, then inspect route status.
Watch out: These are not automatically installed on every Kubernetes cluster. API
presence alone does not prove traffic implementation.
Original guide: page 23 · K05, G01, K35 (source directory).

pages.title: How do you troubleshoot an external HTTP 503?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 06 · Ingress, Gateway API and external routing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q030. How do you troubleshoot an external HTTP
503?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Trace the 503 from ingress controller through Service and endpoints to
the application.
Interview precision: Trace the external controller, route acceptance, Service selection, ready
backend set and actual application response.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl describe ingress ROUTE -n interview
kubectl get svc,pods -n interview
kubectl get endpointslices -n interview
# Inspect controller logs and test backend reachability separately.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · 503 can arise because no healthy upstream is available, but
controller-specific behavior differs. A backend request returning 503 itself is a different
cause from a proxy generating it. Use response and log evidence.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you compare proxy access logs with application request logs?
Answer: Match request IDs and timestamps; see whether the proxy generated
503 or forwarded an app response.
Watch out: Recreating every Pod can erase evidence and worsen an outage. First identify
the layer generating the response.
Original guide: page 23 · K05, G01, K35 (source directory).

pages.title: When should you use a ConfigMap versus a Secret?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · ConfigMaps, Secrets and runtime configuration FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q031. When should you use a ConfigMap versus a
Secret?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
ConfigMaps hold regular settings; Secrets hold sensitive values with
restricted access.
Interview precision: Use ConfigMaps for ordinary configuration and Secrets for sensitive
values, with explicit access and storage protections.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
env:
  - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef: {name: app-config, key: profile}
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: {name: db-auth, key: password}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The values enter the container at startup. The Secret object type
supports dedicated handling but does not automatically make every consumer or operator
safe.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you rotate a credential without rebuilding the image?
Answer: Update the Secret through approved delivery, allow credential overlap,
then restart/reload Pods safely.
Watch out: Secret data encoded as base64 is not encrypted by that encoding. Restrict
API access, logs and backup exposure.

pages.title: Do ConfigMap and Secret updates immediately update application behavior?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · ConfigMaps, Secrets and runtime configuration FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q032. Do ConfigMap and Secret updates
immediately update application behavior?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Environment variables are read at startup; mounted files may update
later, but apps must reload them.
Interview precision: It depends on injection mode and application reload: environment values
are startup snapshots, while projected files can update eventually with important exceptions.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Environment injection -> recreate/restart workload for new values
Projected volume -> file update can propagate eventually
Application binding -> may still need explicit reload/restart
# subPath mounts do not receive the ordinary projected update behavior.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A refreshed file is not proof that a Spring bean re-bound its
configuration. A controlled rollout can be simpler than a hot-reload design when changes
are infrequent.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if a database revokes the old password before every replica
reconnects?
Answer: Replicas still using the old credential may lose connections. Rotate with
overlap and confirm all replicas first.
Watch out: Immutable objects and subPath use change the update plan. Coordinate
credential overlap with live connection pools.
Original guide: page 25 · K10, K11, K42, K48, S03 (source directory).

pages.title: Why is base64 not encryption, and how should Secrets be protected?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · ConfigMaps, Secrets and runtime configuration FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q033. Why is base64 not encryption, and how
should Secrets be protected?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Base64 only changes the representation. Secret protection needs real
access rules and encryption.
Interview precision: Base64 is reversible representation; protection requires configured at-rest
safeguards, secure transport, limited authorization and safe consumption.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
printf 'ZGVtbw==' | base64 -d
# Produces demo with no decryption key.
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n interview
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Knowing how values are represented prevents a false security
assumption. Verify the cluster's encryption policy and who can read Secrets or create Pods
that consume them.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you review service-account and developer access separately?
Answer: Review human identities and service-account RBAC independently, plus
who can create Pods reading Secrets.
Watch out: Pod-creation authority can expose namespace secrets indirectly. A deny on
get secrets is not the entire threat model.
Original guide: page 25 · K10, K11, K42, K48, S03 (source directory).

pages.title: What is the Downward API used for?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · ConfigMaps, Secrets and runtime configuration FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q034. What is the Downward API used for?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Downward API gives a container selected Pod details without broad API
permissions.
Interview precision: It supplies supported Pod metadata and resource information to
containers without requiring general Kubernetes API access.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
env:
  - name: POD_NAME
    valueFrom:
      fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}
  - name: POD_NAMESPACE
    valueFrom:
      fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.namespace}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The app can add instance identity to logs. This avoids giving the
process broad API credentials just to learn its own name. Supported field choices and
update behavior depend on the injection form.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which identity should remain stable across Pod replacement?
Answer: Business IDs such as order ID, tenant ID or customer ID must not
depend on replaceable Pod names.
Watch out: Pod names are not stable business identifiers. Avoid using them as durable
order or customer keys.

pages.title: How can Spring Boot read mounted secret files?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 07 · ConfigMaps, Secrets and runtime configuration FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q035. How can Spring Boot read mounted secret
files?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Spring can read a directory of mounted secret files as configuration
properties.
Interview precision: A supported configuration-tree import maps file names to properties, with
required versus optional startup semantics chosen deliberately.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
SPRING_CONFIG_IMPORT=configtree:/run/secrets/

pages.title: How do startup, readiness and liveness probes differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · Startup, readiness, liveness and shutdown FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q036. How do startup, readiness and liveness
probes differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Startup gives an app time to boot; readiness controls traffic; liveness
decides whether to restart.
Interview precision: Startup gates initial initialization, readiness controls normal traffic
admission, and liveness can trigger container restart after repeated failure.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
startupProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /livez, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 24
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /readyz, port: 8080}
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /livez, port: 8080}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · With a startup probe configured, normal readiness and liveness
probing wait for startup success. The example gives about two minutes of failure tolerance
at the specified interval; actual timing includes execution details.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which probe should fail while a service deliberately drains traffic?
Answer: Readiness should fail during drain, while liveness may remain healthy
until the process stops.
Watch out: Paths must exist and have a correct access policy. Probe configuration does
not create endpoints.

pages.title: Why should liveness usually avoid checking a shared database?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · Startup, readiness, liveness and shutdown FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q037. Why should liveness usually avoid checking
a shared database?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
If the database is down, restarting every healthy JVM usually makes the
outage worse.
Interview precision: A shared dependency failure often cannot be repaired by restarting every
application process, and mass restarts can worsen the incident.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Database unavailable -> possibly unready or degraded API
JVM deadlocked -> liveness failure may justify restart
# Decide from the recovery action, not merely the dependency list.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Readiness may include dependencies needed for the intended
traffic, but that choice must consider whether removing every instance is useful. Liveness
should target failures where restarting this instance helps.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would your API behave during a short database failover?
Answer: Fail or degrade database-dependent requests, retry carefully, and
recover connections without a restart storm.
Watch out: A trivial always-200 liveness endpoint may miss a stuck request subsystem.
Choose a meaningful but stable contract.

pages.title: Does a successful readiness probe guarantee no requests fail?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · Startup, readiness, liveness and shutdown FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q038. Does a successful readiness probe
guarantee no requests fail?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Readiness is a useful sample, not a guarantee that every request
succeeds.
Interview precision: No. It is a sampled admission signal, and traffic propagation, application
races and downstream failures can occur between samples.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Probe interval -> observed readiness
Endpoint/controller update -> traffic propagation
Request handling -> current application and dependency state
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Readiness helps reduce avoidable routing to unsuitable instances. It
does not prove all routes, payloads or dependencies work at every instant. Monitor request
outcomes and test transitions.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would you test during rollout beyond waiting for Ready Pods?
Answer: Test HTTP behavior, error rate, latency, graceful drain, database access
and new/old version compatibility.
Watch out: Existing connections and external load balancers can have independent drain
behavior.

pages.title: How does terminationGracePeriodSeconds interact with preStop and SIGTERM?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · Startup, readiness, liveness and shutdown FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q039. How does terminationGracePeriodSeconds
interact with preStop and SIGTERM?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
preStop and Spring shutdown share one termination grace period before
forced kill.
Interview precision: The grace budget includes termination work; a preStop hook runs before
the normal stop signal, and final forced termination follows budget expiry.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
    - name: api
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec: {command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A brief delay can help with traffic propagation only when the image
includes sh and the measured deployment needs it. The hook consumes the budget, leaving
less time for application drain.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you budget a 20-second Spring drain plus propagation time?
Answer: Budget measurable propagation delay, at least 20s drain time, plus
margin; e.g. 45s after testing.
Watch out: Do not add a shell-based hook to a shell-free image. A sleep is not proof that
traffic has stopped, and exact termination behavior has version details.
Original guide: page 29 · K06, S01, S02 (source directory).

pages.title: How should Spring Boot health endpoints be exposed for probes?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 · Startup, readiness, liveness and shutdown FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q040. How should Spring Boot health endpoints
be exposed for probes?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Expose a real application-port probe that reflects the running Spring
HTTP server.
Interview precision: Configure supported probe endpoints on the application path and make
their access and listener contract explicit.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
management.endpoint.health.probes.add-additional-paths=true
server.shutdown=graceful
# Supported Boot baseline supplies /livez and /readyz on the main port.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Probing the main server can catch failures hidden by a separate
healthy management listener. Verify endpoint availability with the actual Actuator
dependency, Spring version and Security configuration.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would a separate management port fail to detect?
Answer: A separate healthy management listener can miss a stuck or unbound
main application listener.
Watch out: Avoid exposing sensitive diagnostic endpoints publicly while enabling probe
access. A passing health group is not a full business transaction test.

pages.title: What is the difference between resource requests and limits?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 · Requests, limits, QoS and JVM sizing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q041. What is the difference between resource
requests and limits?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Requests reserve scheduling capacity; limits cap CPU and memory
behavior at runtime.
Interview precision: Requests guide scheduling and resource allocation; limits constrain
supported runtime consumption through mechanisms appropriate to each resource.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
resources:
  requests: {cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi"}
  limits: {cpu: "1", memory: "512Mi"}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The scheduler accounts for the requested budget. CPU use can be
throttled by a limit, while exceeding memory constraints can cause termination. 250m
means a quarter CPU unit; Mi is binary memory sizing.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why can a Pod remain Pending even while a node looks mostly idle?
Answer: Scheduling uses requested CPU/memory and placement rules, not
current dashboard idle percentages alone.
Watch out: Requests are not a promise of unlimited throughput or independent physical
cores. Defaults can be injected by namespace policy.

pages.title: How do CPU throttling and memory OOM termination differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 · Requests, limits, QoS and JVM sizing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q042. How do CPU throttling and memory OOM
termination differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
CPU throttling slows a process; memory exhaustion can kill it.
Interview precision: CPU limits can delay execution through throttling; memory enforcement
can kill a process when the relevant budget is exhausted.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl describe pod POD -n interview
kubectl top pod POD -n interview
kubectl logs POD -n interview --previous
# Combine with cgroup and JVM time-series telemetry.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · High tail latency can reflect throttling even without an application
exception. A kernel memory kill may prevent Java from emitting a heap dump. Use
termination reason and resource history to separate them.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What evidence would distinguish GC pressure from CPU quota pressure?
Answer: Compare CPU throttling time, heap/GC logs, CPU quota and termination
state together.
Watch out: Exit 137 is evidence to investigate, not a universal proof of memory exhaustion.
Metrics Server snapshots can miss spikes.
Original guide: page 32 · K07, K29, K30, K31, J01 (source directory).

pages.title: What are Guaranteed, Burstable and BestEffort QoS classes?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 · Requests, limits, QoS and JVM sizing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q043. What are Guaranteed, Burstable and
BestEffort QoS classes?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
QoS depends on how all containers' CPU and memory requests and
limits are declared.
Interview precision: They classify Pod resource configuration and influence behavior under
resource pressure; they are not application availability guarantees.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
# Traditional per-container Guaranteed pattern:
requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi"}
limits:   {cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi"}
# Every relevant container must meet the class requirements.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Without relevant requests or limits, a traditional Pod may be
BestEffort. Partial or unequal configuration generally leads to Burstable. Inspect the actual
qosClass instead of inferring from one container.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How can a sidecar change the Pod's class and total budget?
Answer: A helper container adds resources and can change the Pod's QoS
classification.
Watch out: Newer resource features can affect details. Priority and consumption also
matter in eviction decisions; Guaranteed does not mean never killed.

pages.title: How should Java heap relate to a container memory limit?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 · Requests, limits, QoS and JVM sizing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q044. How should Java heap relate to a container
memory limit?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Leave memory for JVM heap plus threads, metaspace, direct buffers and
native code.
Interview precision: Heap must leave measured room for native allocations, metaspace, direct
buffers, thread stacks and other charged memory.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
# Illustrative 512 MiB limit, not a universal sizing rule:
env:
  - {name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, value: "-Xms128m -Xmx320m"}
# Measure peak total use with realistic traffic and thread counts.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The remaining space is a starting hypothesis, not established safety.
Modern supported JDKs on Linux detect container limits, but the exact update and cgroup
setup must be verified.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
When would you choose explicit Xmx rather than a percentage?
Answer: Use explicit Xmx when workloads need a tested fixed heap budget; leave
safety room under memory limit.
Watch out: MaxRAMPercentage sizes heap ergonomically; it does not cap total process
memory. Probe subprocesses and agents can consume additional memory.

pages.title: How do ResourceQuota and LimitRange differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 · Requests, limits, QoS and JVM sizing FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q045. How do ResourceQuota and LimitRange
differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
ResourceQuota limits a namespace total; LimitRange sets defaults and
bounds for individual resources.
Interview precision: ResourceQuota restricts aggregate namespace usage or object counts;
LimitRange sets supported per-object defaults and bounds during admission.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl get resourcequota,limitrange -n interview
kubectl describe resourcequota -n interview
# Inspect effective admitted Pod requests and limits.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A quota can block a new replica even when nodes have free
capacity. A LimitRange can supply missing defaults that change scheduling or runtime
behavior. Compare the rendered input with the admitted object.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why might the same manifest be accepted in one namespace and rejected in
another?
Answer: Namespaces can have different quota, security or admission settings, so
the same YAML may be rejected.
Watch out: These policies do not provision capacity or automatically scale nodes. Runtime
memory tuning still belongs to the workload team.

pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · Scheduling, affinity and topology FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q046. How do nodeSelector and node affinity
differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
nodeSelector requires exact labels; node affinity supports richer
scheduling rules.
Interview precision: nodeSelector matches simple node labels; node affinity supports richer
required and preferred placement expressions.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
nodeSelector:
  workload.example.com/pool: java
# Verify the eligible nodes:
kubectl get nodes --show-labels
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Only nodes with the declared label are eligible for this selector.
Required affinity constrains placement; preferred affinity influences scoring without the
same absolute gate. Resources and other constraints still apply.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if every eligible node lacks memory for the request?
Answer: The Pod remains Pending until an eligible node gains enough allocatable
memory or constraints change.
Watch out: User-controllable labels are not automatically trusted isolation evidence.
Choose secured label practices for sensitive placement.

pages.title: What is the difference between a taint and a toleration?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · Scheduling, affinity and topology FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q047. What is the difference between a taint and
a toleration?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Taints repel Pods unless tolerations allow them; tolerations do not force
placement.
Interview precision: A node taint repels workloads under its effect; a matching Pod toleration
permits placement despite that taint but does not require placement there.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
tolerations:
  - key: dedicated
    operator: Equal
    value: java
    effect: NoSchedule
# Pair with deliberate node selection if a dedicated pool is required.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · This Pod can tolerate that NoSchedule taint. It may still land
elsewhere if no selection rule constrains it. NoExecute has eviction-related behavior beyond
scheduling.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How do you make a dedicated node pool both eligible and exclusive?
Answer: Use node affinity to target the pool and taints/tolerations to keep
unrelated Pods out.
Watch out: Tolerating all taints can expose workloads to nodes they were not intended to
use. Avoid modifying shared node taints as a casual exercise.

pages.title: How do Pod affinity, anti-affinity and topology spread differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · Scheduling, affinity and topology FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q048. How do Pod affinity, anti-affinity and
topology spread differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Affinity groups or separates Pods; topology spread distributes them
across failure domains.
Interview precision: They express attraction to peer placement, separation from peer
placement and balanced distribution across topology domains.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector: {matchLabels: {app: orders}}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The rule tries to distribute matching Pods across eligible node
domains under the specified constraint. Zone-level spreading needs accurate zone labels
and enough eligible capacity.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which failure domain matters for your availability requirement?
Answer: Choose the zone for zone-failure resilience and the node for a single-
machine failure.
Watch out: A strict spread rule can deliberately leave replicas Pending. Distribution across
nodes is not distribution across independent zones.

pages.title: Why can a Pod be Pending despite apparent free CPU?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · Scheduling, affinity and topology FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q049. Why can a Pod be Pending despite
apparent free CPU?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Free CPU alone is not enough: requests, storage, taints and topology
must all fit.
Interview precision: Placement uses declared requests and eligibility, not merely a current CPU
utilization snapshot; storage, topology and policy can also block it.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl describe pod POD -n interview
kubectl get nodes
kubectl describe node CANDIDATE_NODE
kubectl get pvc -n interview
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Events can report insufficient requested resources, unmatched
affinity, taints or unbound storage. Prioritize the actual scheduler message before changing
resource settings.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What evidence justifies adding nodes rather than changing the workload?
Answer: Events showing insufficient capacity across eligible nodes justify adding
nodes after checking requests.
Watch out: Lowering requests to force scheduling can create unstable oversubscription. A
PVC with delayed binding can have an intentional scheduling dependency.

pages.title: What do PriorityClass and preemption provide?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 · Scheduling, affinity and topology FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q050. What do PriorityClass and preemption
provide?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Priority affects which pending Pods get preference and may allow lower-
priority Pod preemption.
Interview precision: Priority influences scheduling order and can allow eligible lower-priority
workloads to be displaced, subject to scheduler policy and constraints.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
priorityClassName: TEAM_APPROVED_PRIORITY
# Use an approved class rather than inventing a cluster-wide value.
# Inspect Pending Pod Events for preemption-related evidence.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Preemption can free resources but cannot make an incompatible
node label or storage constraint disappear. Priority should reflect business importance and
team policy.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you allocate priority to APIs, batch jobs and critical platform
services?
Answer: Protect cluster essentials first, then customer-facing APIs, then batch
tasks; avoid unnecessary evictions.
Watch out: Raising every workload's priority does not create capacity and can harm other
services. PDB interaction does not make preemption an absolute disruption-free
guarantee.

pages.title: How do a PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim relate?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 · Volumes, claims and storage lifecycle FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q051. How do a PersistentVolume and
PersistentVolumeClaim relate?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
A PVC asks for storage; a PV is the allocated storage object to which it
binds.
Interview precision: A PV represents available persistent storage; a PVC requests supported
capacity and access, then binds to a suitable volume.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: data}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests: {storage: 1Gi}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · An eligible StorageClass can dynamically provision the backend. The
Pod mounts the claim, not a guessed node directory. Binding depends on class, capacity,
access mode and topology.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would you inspect before changing a stuck claim's requested size?
Answer: Inspect StorageClass resize support, volume mode, binding state,
capacity, events and current data first.
Watch out: An accepted claim can remain Pending if no suitable provisioner or volume is
available.
Original guide: page 37 · K08, K24, K25 (source directory).

pages.title: What does a StorageClass control?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 · Volumes, claims and storage lifecycle FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q052. What does a StorageClass control?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
StorageClass chooses the provisioner and storage behavior, including
when binding waits.
Interview precision: A StorageClass names provisioning policy, including a supported
provisioner and settings such as binding mode, reclaim behavior and expansion capability.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl describe storageclass CLASS
kubectl describe pvc data -n interview
# WaitForFirstConsumer can delay binding until placement is known.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Delayed binding helps choose storage compatible with the Pod's
topology. Different classes can have different performance and durability contracts. Select a
class intentionally rather than assuming all persistent storage is equivalent.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why can immediate provisioning place a volume in the wrong zone?
Answer: Immediate binding can create storage before a node/zone is chosen,
making the Pod unschedulable.
Watch out: Setting an expansion flag does not make an unsupported backend resize
correctly. Provider and filesystem behavior matter.

pages.title: What do RWO, ROX, RWX and RWOP mean?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 · Volumes, claims and storage lifecycle FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q053. What do RWO, ROX, RWX and RWOP
mean?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Access modes describe how a volume can be mounted; they do not make
an application multi-writer safe.
Interview precision: They request supported mount-access patterns, with ReadWriteOnce
referring to one node rather than necessarily one Pod; ReadWriteOncePod provides a
supported single-Pod constraint.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
ReadWriteOnce:     read/write from one node
ReadOnlyMany:      read-only from multiple nodes
ReadWriteMany:     read/write from multiple nodes
ReadWriteOncePod:  supported CSI single-Pod access
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Multiple Pods on one node can sometimes share an RWO volume.
The storage driver must support the requested mode. Access modes do not design
database locking or make concurrent writers safe.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why is a shared database data directory unsafe despite successful mounts?
Answer: Two database writers can corrupt files even when mounted successfully;
use a database replication protocol.
Watch out: RWX does not mean arbitrary applications can concurrently modify the same
data safely. RWOP has driver/version requirements.

pages.title: How do emptyDir, hostPath and PVC-backed storage differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 · Volumes, claims and storage lifecycle FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q054. How do emptyDir, hostPath and PVC-backed
storage differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
emptyDir lasts for a Pod, hostPath uses node files, and a PVC follows
storage's own lifecycle.
Interview precision: emptyDir follows Pod lifetime, hostPath exposes a node path, and a PVC
binds workload storage to a persistent-storage contract.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
volumes:
  - name: scratch
    emptyDir: {sizeLimit: 64Mi}
# Mount scratch at an application temp path.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · emptyDir survives a container restart within the Pod but disappears
with Pod removal. A hostPath ties data and access to a node, creating portability and
security concerns. A PVC can preserve data across Pod replacement under its backend
policy.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What is a safe temp-storage choice for a replaceable Java API?
Answer: Use size-limited emptyDir for disposable temporary Java files, with a
controlled memory/disk budget.
Watch out: Memory-backed emptyDir contributes to memory use; disk-backed scratch
still has node and ephemeral-storage limits.

pages.title: Does deleting a PVC always preserve or always delete the data?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 · Volumes, claims and storage lifecycle FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q055. Does deleting a PVC always preserve or
always delete the data?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Deleting a PVC can delete or retain backing storage depending on
reclaim policy.
Interview precision: The resulting behavior depends on reclaim policy, backend, protection/
finalization and workload ownership; deletion is a data-lifecycle decision.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl get pv
kubectl get pv VOLUME -o yaml
# Inspect persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy and provider policy.
# Test restore before retiring real business storage.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Delete can request backend removal, while Retain leaves an
administrative recovery and cleanup task. A retained backend is not automatically safe,
backed up or reusable without review.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which recovery objectives should guide your backup and reclaim policy?
Answer: Set recovery-point and recovery-time goals, backups and tested restores
independently from reclaim policy.
Watch out: Deleting a lab namespace can delete its PVC and trigger backend deletion.
StatefulSet claim retention has additional configuration.

pages.title: When should you choose StatefulSet instead of Deployment?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 · StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q056. When should you choose StatefulSet instead
of Deployment?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Use StatefulSet for stable Pod identities and ordered stateful lifecycle,
not as a substitute for replication.
Interview precision: Use StatefulSet when supported stable identities, ordered lifecycle or per-
replica storage matter; choose Deployment for interchangeable application replicas.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
orders-api replicas -> Deployment
db-0, db-1 identities -> possible StatefulSet
Per-member PVCs -> explicit stable storage ownership
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Stable ordinals and suitable discovery can support a clustered
application. The database software still needs explicit replication, membership and failover
configuration.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would a database operator add beyond a bare StatefulSet?
Answer: An operator can handle backups, leader changes, upgrades, repair and
application-aware failover.
Watch out: StatefulSet does not automatically make a database highly available or
synchronize its data.

pages.title: What is a headless Service's role with StatefulSet?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 · StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q057. What is a headless Service's role with
StatefulSet?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Headless Service exposes individual stable members instead of a single
virtual IP.
Interview precision: It supports discovery of individual member identities rather than hiding
them behind only a virtual service address.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: {app: db}
  ports: [{port: 5432, targetPort: 5432}]
# StatefulSet serviceName must follow the intended discovery contract.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Clients or peer nodes can discover particular members through
supported DNS patterns. Readiness publication and startup membership requirements must
be designed for the application.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would Kafka member identity and advertised endpoints fit this model?
Answer: Use stable member DNS in Kafka configuration, with correct advertised
listener addresses and broker identities.
Watch out: A stable DNS name does not guarantee the member is ready or holds the
leader role. Do not hard-code a current Pod IP.

pages.title: What does a DaemonSet do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 · StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q058. What does a DaemonSet do?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
DaemonSet ensures a node-level agent runs on each eligible node.
Interview precision: It maintains a Pod on each eligible node, commonly for node-local
infrastructure such as log agents or networking components.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Node A -> log agent Pod
Node B -> log agent Pod
Node C -> log agent Pod
# Eligibility can be restricted by selection and tolerations.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Adding an eligible node can add another agent automatically.
Resource usage is multiplied by eligible node count, and required host access must be
reviewed carefully.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you safely roll out an agent that reads host logs?
Answer: Roll out gradually, limit host permissions, monitor agent overhead and
verify log ingestion.
Watch out: A DaemonSet is not a general API horizontal-scaling strategy. Node agents
can have substantial privileges.

pages.title: How is a Job different from a Deployment?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 · StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q059. How is a Job different from a Deployment?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
A Job finishes bounded work; a Deployment keeps service replicas
running.
Interview precision: A Job tracks successful completion of bounded work; a Deployment
maintains running application replicas.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
spec:
  backoffLimit: 2
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 60
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - {name: task, image: busybox:1.37, command: ["echo", "done"]}
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The Job can retry failed attempts within its policy. Limits bound the
exercise, but a retry can repeat effects already performed before failure. Build idempotency
into real work.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you make a payment reconciliation job safe to retry?
Answer: Use unique reconciliation IDs, durable checkpoints and deduplication so
a retry does not pay twice.
Watch out: A successful Pod exit does not prove the business operation was correct
unless the job verifies it.

How would you make a payment reconciliation job safe to retry?
Answer: Use unique reconciliation IDs, durable checkpoints and deduplication so
a retry does not pay twice.

pages.title: Does a CronJob guarantee exactly-once execution?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 · StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q060. Does a CronJob guarantee exactly-once
execution?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
A CronJob schedules Jobs but cannot guarantee that the business effect
happens exactly once.
Interview precision: No. Scheduling and retry behavior require the underlying job to tolerate
missed, duplicated or overlapping execution under the selected policy.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
startingDeadlineSeconds: 120
# Use a supported timeZone field if explicit timezone policy is required.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Forbid prevents certain overlaps for that CronJob but does not
establish a distributed business lock across unrelated jobs or clusters. Deadline and
scheduling policy define what happens after a delay.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you recover a missed daily settlement without double processing?
Answer: Track settlement date in durable state, reconcile missed dates and reject
duplicate processing.
Watch out: A trigger every five minutes is not a transaction guarantee. Track business
windows and completed work durably.

pages.title: How do authentication, authorization and admission differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · Authentication, RBAC and workload identity FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q061. How do authentication, authorization and
admission differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Authentication proves identity; authorization checks permission;
admission validates or changes a request.
Interview precision: Authentication identifies the caller, authorization decides whether the
requested API action is allowed, and admission can validate or modify admitted objects.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Identity -> permission decision -> admission -> stored object
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n interview
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n interview
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A caller may have permission to create a Pod yet be rejected by
resource or security policy. Separating these gates makes Forbidden and admission errors
easier to explain.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you debug an allowed action whose manifest is rejected?
Answer: Check admission webhook messages or namespace policy after
confirming RBAC allowed the API action.
Watch out: A Kubernetes API identity does not automatically define the logged-in user for
your HTTP application.
Original guide: page 43 · K09, K26, K27, K33 (source directory).

pages.title: How do Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · Authentication, RBAC and workload identity FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q062. How do Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding and
ClusterRoleBinding differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Role/RoleBinding scope permissions in a namespace; ClusterRole may
define broader rules.
Interview precision: Roles define namespaced permissions, ClusterRoles define reusable or
cluster-scoped permissions, and bindings grant them to subjects at a selected scope.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
# Role rule fragment:
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [configmaps]
    verbs: [get, list]
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A RoleBinding can grant a ClusterRole within one namespace. A
ClusterRoleBinding grants its permissions cluster-wide. The example allows ConfigMap
reads, not Secret reads or Deployment changes.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Can a RoleBinding give access to cluster-scoped nodes?
Answer: A namespaced RoleBinding cannot grant access to cluster-scoped nodes,
even if it references a ClusterRole.
Watch out: Wildcards and broad bindings expand authority as APIs grow. Review what a
subject can indirectly do, not only explicit Secret reads.

pages.title: What is a ServiceAccount used for?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · Authentication, RBAC and workload identity FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q063. What is a ServiceAccount used for?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
A ServiceAccount gives a workload its Kubernetes identity when API
access is needed.
Interview precision: A ServiceAccount identifies a workload to Kubernetes API authentication
and can participate in supported external workload-identity integration.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
serviceAccountName: orders-api
automountServiceAccountToken: false
# Use false when the application does not need the Kubernetes API.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · An ordinary order API may need no API token at all. If access is
required, give its own account narrowly scoped permissions and use supported short-lived
projected-token behavior.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you let a job read one configuration object without granting
cluster-admin?
Answer: Bind a narrow Role allowing get on only the named ConfigMap to that
job's ServiceAccount.
Watch out: Namespace default accounts are not a least-privilege design by themselves.
Cloud workload identity also needs provider configuration.

pages.title: How do securityContext and Pod Security Admission work together?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · Authentication, RBAC and workload identity FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q064. How do securityContext and Pod Security
Admission work together?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
SecurityContext sets process security; admission policy rejects Pods that
violate required controls.
Interview precision: securityContext requests runtime settings; admission policy can reject
workloads that do not meet the namespace's security standard.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 10001
  seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
# Container settings also include allowPrivilegeEscalation: false.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Runtime identity and syscall policy constrain execution. A non-root
declaration must match the image contract, file permissions and mount access. Pod-level
and container-level settings apply to different fields.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What writable path does your Java image need under a read-only root
filesystem?
Answer: Mount a writable /tmp emptyDir and avoid writing to the read-only root
filesystem.
Watch out: Passing admission does not prove the application is secure or that a mounted
host path is harmless.
Original guide: page 45 · K09, K26, K27, K33 (source directory).

pages.title: Why are Pod creation, exec and cluster- admin sensitive permissions?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 · Authentication, RBAC and workload identity FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q065. Why are Pod creation, exec and cluster-
admin sensitive permissions?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Pod creation, exec and admin privileges can expose data or control
other workloads.
Interview precision: They can expose workload credentials, modify execution or control broad
cluster resources, including indirect access beyond a simple read rule.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Review subjects that can:
  create Pods consuming Secrets
  exec into credential-bearing workloads
  bind/escalate privileged roles or alter policy
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A subject denied direct get secrets may still access a Secret through
an allowed Pod. Exec permission can reach an application's files and process environment.
Use separate operational identities and audit sensitive actions.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you provide production diagnosis access with a reviewed
escalation path?
Answer: Use read-only diagnostics by default and time-limited, audited escalation
with approval.
Watch out: A namespace is not a sufficient boundary when a subject can gain node or
cluster authority.
Original guide: page 45 · K09, K26, K27, K33 (source directory).

pages.title: What does NetworkPolicy control?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 · NetworkPolicy and layered traffic security FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q066. What does NetworkPolicy control?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
NetworkPolicy selects Pod traffic allowed by an enforcing network
implementation.
Interview precision: It restricts supported ingress and egress traffic for selected Pods when the
network implementation enforces the policy API.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: deny-incoming}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · This selects Pods in its namespace and allows no ingress under this
policy. It leaves egress unchanged unless other egress-isolating policies apply. Verify the
CNI's actual support with traffic tests.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you distinguish policy parsing from policy enforcement?
Answer: Create the policy, then run allowed and denied traffic tests; a parsed
policy may not be enforced.
Watch out: Creating a policy object on a non-enforcing network does not prove isolation.
Original guide: page 46 · K18, K09 (source directory).

pages.title: Are NetworkPolicy allow rules ordered firewall rules?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 · NetworkPolicy and layered traffic security FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q067. Are NetworkPolicy allow rules ordered
firewall rules?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Matching policies add allowed traffic together; they are not ordered
deny/allow firewall rules.
Interview precision: No. Applicable allow policies are additive; a connection must meet relevant
source egress and destination ingress requirements.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Policy A allows app=api to database TCP 5432.
Policy B allows an approved maintenance client.
Their allowed ingress sets combine for selected destinations.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A broad extra policy can reopen access that a narrow policy was
meant to restrict. Review all policies selecting each endpoint, including the source's egress
isolation.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why might adding a second policy unexpectedly make a blocked client work?
Answer: A second policy may permit traffic already denied by the first because
allow results are additive.
Watch out: NetworkPolicy is not evaluated as first matching deny/allow lines in a
conventional ordered ACL.
Original guide: page 47 · K18, K09 (source directory).

pages.title: How do namespaceSelector and podSelector combine?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 · NetworkPolicy and layered traffic security FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q068. How do namespaceSelector and
podSelector combine?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Combining namespaceSelector and podSelector in one rule selects
labeled Pods within selected namespaces.
Interview precision: Selectors in the same peer entry are combined; separate peer entries
represent alternative allowed sources.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
ingress:
  - from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: apps}
        podSelector:
          matchLabels: {role: api}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · The peer must be a role=api Pod in the apps namespace. Splitting
the two selectors into separate entries would allow a broader union. This rule fragment
needs the destination selection and policy declaration.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would separate entries allow that this combined entry does not?
Answer: Separate peer entries allow either matching namespaces or matching
Pods, a wider traffic set.
Watch out: Label-management authority matters because labels can affect network
eligibility.
Original guide: page 47 · K18, K09 (source directory).

pages.title: Why does deny-all egress often break otherwise healthy applications?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 · NetworkPolicy and layered traffic security FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q069. Why does deny-all egress often break
otherwise healthy applications?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Denying egress also blocks DNS and required upstream connections
unless allowed.
Interview precision: It can block DNS and required dependency paths as well as unwanted
traffic; every necessary route needs a supported explicit allowance.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Required egress may include:
  DNS queries: UDP and TCP 53 to the actual resolver path
  Database: approved destination and port
  HTTPS dependencies: architecture-specific controlled access
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · DNS failure can hide the true policy issue behind an unknown-host
exception. Resolver placement, host networking and CNI behavior affect a correct rule.
Standard NetworkPolicy does not provide portable domain-name authorization.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you verify DNS, TCP connection and application authentication
separately?
Answer: Resolve DNS, test TCP to the destination, then check TLS and application
credentials independently.
Watch out: Do not permit all egress merely to make tests pass. IP-based controls for
changing external services need a deliberate design.
Original guide: page 48 · K18, K09 (source directory).

Q070. How are NetworkPolicy, TLS, mTLS and
application authorization different?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
NetworkPolicy limits reachability, TLS encrypts traffic, mTLS verifies
peers, and authorization checks users.
Interview precision: NetworkPolicy limits network reach, TLS protects supported transport,
mTLS authenticates transport peers, and application policy authorizes business actions.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Reachability: may this Pod connect to this port?
Transport:   is this encrypted and who is the peer?
Application: may this caller cancel this order?
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · An allowed TCP connection is not authorization to read customer
data. A service mesh can automate some transport policy but still needs identity, certificate
and operational controls.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which controls protect an internal Spring endpoint containing personal data?
Answer: Use restricted network paths, TLS/mTLS and app-level object
authorization with audited access.
Watch out: Kubernetes does not provide every layer merely because Pods are in separate
namespaces.

Q071. What does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
do?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
HPA changes desired replicas using metrics; it does not directly add
nodes.
Interview precision: HPA adjusts a target workload's replica count using supported observed
metrics and configured scaling policy.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
# Resource metric: CPU utilization relative to requests.
# Custom/external metrics require the relevant metrics integration.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · CPU-based scaling usually requires Metrics Server and meaningful
requests for the relevant containers. HPA controls replicas; it does not itself provision nodes
or solve a saturated database.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What would you inspect when the HPA reports an unknown utilization value?
Answer: Check metrics-server/custom metrics availability, Pod requests and HPA
conditions/events.
Watch out: Missing or stale metrics can prevent the intended decision. Inspect HPA
conditions and events.

pages.title: How is CPU utilization calculated for a typical HPA target?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 · Autoscaling and downstream capacity FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q072. How is CPU utilization calculated for a
typical HPA target?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Typical CPU HPA usage compares measured CPU to requested CPU for
eligible Pods.
Interview precision: The resource-utilization metric compares observed CPU use against the
configured CPU request, not the CPU limit.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
CPU request: 250m
Observed use: 150m
Utilization: 150 / 250 = 60 percent
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Changing the request changes the metric denominator and
scheduling budget. Keep resource tuning and autoscaling policy coordinated. The actual
controller also accounts for readiness, missing data, tolerance and policy limits.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why could lowering CPU requests unexpectedly trigger more replicas?
Answer: Reducing the request raises utilization percentage for identical CPU
usage and may scale sooner.
Watch out: Do not interpret 60 percent as 60 percent of an entire physical machine.

pages.title: When is a queue or demand metric better than CPU?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 · Autoscaling and downstream capacity FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q073. When is a queue or demand metric better
than CPU?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Queue size/age can show overload when CPU does not match work
waiting.
Interview precision: Use a metric closer to the bottleneck when waiting work, latency or
consumption demand is not reflected reliably by CPU use.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Kafka worker: lag plus processing rate and partition parallelism
HTTP API:    concurrency, latency and CPU under measured demand
Batch work:  queued work with bounded downstream capacity
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A CPU-idle consumer can still be blocked on a dependency while
lag grows. More workers may help only until partition and downstream limits are reached.
Any external metric needs a trusted adapter and meaningful stale-data behavior.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What caps useful replicas for a Kafka consumer group?
Answer: Kafka consumer-group partition count and downstream capacity cap
useful consumer parallelism.
Watch out: Lag alone can be misleading during rebalances or long tasks. Scaling must
not create unbounded database or API concurrency.

pages.title: How do HPA, VPA and node autoscaling differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 · Autoscaling and downstream capacity FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q074. How do HPA, VPA and node autoscaling
differ?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
HPA changes replica counts, VPA recommends/adjusts Pod resources,
and node autoscaling adds compute.
Interview precision: HPA changes replica count, VPA recommends or adjusts workload
resource sizing, and node autoscaling changes available node capacity through its integration.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
HPA:  more/fewer application replicas
VPA:  resource sizing for workload execution
Nodes: capacity for eligible scheduled workloads
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Vertical updates can use different rollout or resize modes depending
on the installed implementation and feature support. Coordinate CPU-resource
recommendations with CPU-utilization HPA to avoid a moving denominator.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What happens if HPA requests more Pods but no eligible nodes can fit them?
Answer: Extra Pods wait Pending until a node scaler adds eligible capacity or
resource constraints change.
Watch out: None of these guarantees storage compatibility, instant startup or a responsive
dependency.

pages.title: How do you prevent autoscaling from causing oscillation or overload?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 · Autoscaling and downstream capacity FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q075. How do you prevent autoscaling from
causing oscillation or overload?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Keep scale decisions stable and protect databases, queues and other
shared services.
Interview precision: Use measured thresholds, stabilization and rate policy, while bounding
expensive concurrency and validating scaling transitions.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
API replicas: 8
DB pool per replica: 20
Potential API connections: 160, plus other clients
# Reserve dependency and node headroom for failure and rollout.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A scale-up can stress the database before it reduces HTTP pressure.
Scale-down needs connection and worker drain. Test spike response, recovery and
sustained load rather than only steady throughput.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which metrics would stop a harmful scale-up and guide a different
mitigation?
Answer: Watch connection saturation, p99 latency, error rate and throttling; cap
growth and fix shared bottlenecks.
Watch out: Adding replicas is not a repair for a shared lock, schema issue or external
outage.

pages.title: How do you diagnose CrashLoopBackOff?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 · Observability and evidence-driven diagnosis FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q076. How do you diagnose CrashLoopBackOff?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Find why containers are restarting using events, previous logs, probes
and exit codes.
Interview precision: Inspect previous container logs, last termination state, command/
configuration and probe events before changing restart behavior.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl describe pod POD -n interview
kubectl logs POD -n interview -c api --previous
kubectl get pod POD -n interview -o yaml
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A missing secret, JVM flag error, permission denial or failing
liveness probe can cause repeated restarts. Backoff describes retry pacing, not the root
cause. Check the exact image and admitted configuration.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you prove the next Pod will start with corrected inputs?
Answer: Compare new image digest, config, Secret mount, runtime command and
probe behavior before rollout.
Watch out: Deleting the Pod can remove useful local evidence without repairing its
template.

pages.title: How do you diagnose ImagePullBackOff?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 · Observability and evidence-driven diagnosis FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q077. How do you diagnose ImagePullBackOff?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
ImagePullBackOff means the node could not fetch an image; inspect
registry, tag and credentials.
Interview precision: Read pull events and inspect the image reference, registry access,
credentials, architecture and pull policy.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl describe pod POD -n interview
kubectl get secret REGISTRY_SECRET -n interview
# Inspect imagePullSecrets names without printing secret data.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Not-found and unauthorized errors require different repairs. A
private-registry Secret must be accessible in the workload namespace under the intended
reference. A local minikube image has a separate loading and pull-policy contract.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Why might an image visible to Docker on the laptop be invisible to minikube?
Answer: Minikube may use a separate container runtime/image store from laptop
Docker; load into the correct node.
Watch out: Retrying an invalid tag does not fix it. Avoid exposing credentials while
collecting evidence.

pages.title: What should you check for a Service with no working traffic?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 · Observability and evidence-driven diagnosis FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q078. What should you check for a Service with
no working traffic?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Trace client name, Service selector, ready endpoints, targetPort and Pod
listener.
Interview precision: Trace DNS, selector matches, ready EndpointSlices, port mapping, actual
listener and applicable ingress/egress policy.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl get svc orders -n interview -o yaml
kubectl get pods -n interview -l app=orders -o wide
kubectl get endpointslices -n interview \
  -l kubernetes.io/service-name=orders
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · If no Pod matches the selector, network debugging is premature. If
the direct Pod port works but Service access fails, investigate the Service datapath and
policy. Compare clients from the intended namespace.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
What does an HTTP 401 prove about the network path?
Answer: HTTP 401 proves a response reached an HTTP endpoint; authentication
still denied the request.
Watch out: A ping does not verify HTTP readiness, database login or Kafka metadata
reachability.

pages.title: How do you debug a minimal image without a shell?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 · Observability and evidence-driven diagnosis FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q079. How do you debug a minimal image without
a shell?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Use logs, describe, metrics and authorized ephemeral debugging instead
of assuming bash exists.
Interview precision: Use logs, status and approved diagnostic tooling such as ephemeral
containers, with deliberate permissions and namespace access.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
kubectl logs POD -n interview -c api
kubectl debug POD -n interview -it \
  --image=APPROVED_DEBUG_IMAGE --target=api
# Support, privileges and process visibility depend on the environment.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · A diagnostic container can supply tools without baking them into the
application image. Targeted process visibility and attach permissions require checking. Use
the least authority appropriate to the incident.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
How would you collect a thread dump while respecting production access
policy?
Answer: Use policy-approved JVM diagnostics or a debug image/process with
audit and minimal permissions.
Watch out: An ephemeral container is not a normal restartable application sidecar. Do
not assume it can read every target filesystem or collect every JVM artifact automatically.

pages.title: What is the difference between monitoring and observability in practice?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 · Observability and evidence-driven diagnosis FOUNDATION → ARCHITECT
Q080. What is the difference between monitoring
and observability in practice?
20-SECOND ANSWER • IN SIMPLE WORDS
Monitoring checks chosen signals; observability uses logs, metrics and
traces to explain failures.
Interview precision: Monitoring tracks known health and performance signals; observability
combines evidence to investigate why behavior occurred, including previously unanticipated
failures.
→ →
YAML / COMMAND EXAMPLE
Metrics: request rate, errors, duration, throttling, heap, queueing
Logs:    events with request and instance context
Traces:  request flow and dependency latency
Events:  scheduling, pull, probe and lifecycle transitions
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS · Correlate timestamps and release identity across signals.
Infrastructure Ready status can coexist with high user error rates. Alerts should lead to a
tested investigation or recovery action.
INTERVIEWER FOLLOW-UP
Which user-facing signal would detect a broken order flow that health probes
miss?
Answer: Measure completed orders and checkout errors, not just Pod readiness
or CPU.
Watch out: kubectl top is not a substitute for historical telemetry. Avoid recording sensitive
payloads while adding context.
Original guide: page 54 · K34, K35, K39, K40, K46 (source directory).
Metrics Traces/logs Business SLI

STUDY • DRAW • EXPLAIN • VERIFY 99
