pages.title: What can interactive rebase do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 / Cherry-pick, amend and interactive cleanup Q 039 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q039
What can interactive rebase do?
THE SHORT ANSWER
It lets you reorder, reword, combine, edit or drop selected commits while
replaying the series. The selected range must match what you intend to rewrite.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git branch backup/cleanup
   git rebase -i HEAD~3
   # todo actions: pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop
✎ REMEMBER git branch backup/cleanup
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Squash combines changes and lets you compose a message; fixup normally discards the fixup
message. Reordering can break dependencies and dropping removes a change from the
result. Keep a reference to the original and inspect the final series.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you split one large commit into two coherent changes?
Run interactive rebase with `edit` on that commit, `git reset HEAD^`, stage the first logical
part and commit, then stage and commit the remainder; continue rebase.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Interactive cleanup can produce intermediate commits that do not compile.

Run interactive rebase with `edit` on that commit, `git reset HEAD^`, stage the first logical
part and commit, then stage and commit the remainder; continue rebase.

pages.title: How do fixup commits and autosquash help a review workflow?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 08 / Cherry-pick, amend and interactive cleanup Q 040 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q040
How do fixup commits and autosquash help a
review workflow?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A fixup commit identifies the earlier commit it should correct, and autosquash
arranges it in an interactive rebase. This preserves review activity until the
intentional cleanup step.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git add -- src/OrderTest.java
   git commit --fixup=TARGET_COMMIT
   git rebase -i --autosquash BASE_COMMIT
✎ REMEMBER git add -- src/OrderTest.java
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Choose a base before the target commit so both target and fixup appear in the todo list. This
still rewrites commits and must follow the team's policy. Verify that the fixup attached to the
intended change, especially when messages are similar.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What happens if the target commit is outside the selected rebase range?
Autosquash cannot match a target absent from the todo list. Select an earlier base that
includes the target and its fixup, then review the plan.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Autosquash is not automatically safe for a branch others are already using.

pages.title: How do restore, reset and revert differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Restore, reset and revert without confusion Q 041 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q041
How do restore, reset and revert differ?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Restore replaces selected file/index content. Commit-form reset moves the
current branch/HEAD and optionally changes index/files. Revert creates a new
inverse commit without removing the original history.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Unstage: git restore --staged -- Order.java
   Discard unstaged tracked edit: git restore -- Order.java
   Undo a shared change: git revert BAD_COMMIT
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Safe undo keeps shared ancestry visible.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Restore of the working file can discard edits, so inspect them first. Revert is normally the
suitable starting point for a published change because existing ancestry remains. Reset is
often useful for private cleanup but has multiple modes.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Must the original commit remain visible to collaborators?
If collaborators already rely on it, usually yes: use `git revert` to undo while keeping shared
history, rather than rewriting it.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: The word undo does not identify which of these outcomes you need.

pages.title: How do soft, mixed and hard reset affect state?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Restore, reset and revert without confusion Q 042 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q042
How do soft, mixed and hard reset affect state?
THE SHORT ANSWER
All three commit-form modes move the current branch/HEAD to the target. Soft
leaves index/files; mixed resets the index but keeps files; hard resets both index
and tracked files.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
# Disposable repository only; inspect and preserve useful work first.
   git reset --soft HEAD~1
   git reset --mixed HEAD~1
   git reset --hard HEAD~1
✎ REMEMBER # Disposable repository only; inspect and preserve useful work first.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
These are alternative demonstrations, not a sequence for one task. Hard reset discards
tracked local changes and can remove untracked items that obstruct writing tracked paths. It
is not a general removal of every untracked file.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which mode keeps undone commit content staged?
`git reset --soft TARGET` moves the tip while leaving the old commit's changes in the index,
ready to recommit.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Reflog may recover an old commit, but it does not restore arbitrary edits never
recorded by Git.

pages.title: How does path-form reset differ from commit-form reset?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Restore, reset and revert without confusion Q 043 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q043
How does path-form reset differ from 
commit-form reset?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A reset with paths changes selected index entries without moving the branch tip.
A reset to a commit without paths can move the branch and apply a mode.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git reset HEAD -- src/Order.java
   git rev-parse HEAD
   git diff -- src/Order.java
✎ REMEMBER git reset HEAD -- src/Order.java
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The path form is an older way to unstage selected files. It leaves working content intact. A --
separator clearly distinguishes paths from revision arguments. Avoid applying the branch-
moving mental model to every reset invocation.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why is HEAD unchanged after unstaging one path?
Path-form reset updates only chosen index entries. It does not move the current branch
or HEAD commit.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: You cannot use path-form reset to move only part of a branch history.

pages.title: How do you revert a bad commit on a shared branch?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Restore, reset and revert without confusion Q 044 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q044
How do you revert a bad commit on a shared
branch?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Inspect the commit and later dependencies, create an inverse commit, resolve
any conflicts, test and publish through the team's review policy.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git show BAD_COMMIT
   git revert BAD_COMMIT
   git show --stat HEAD
✎ REMEMBER git show BAD_COMMIT
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Later code may depend on the removed behavior, so a mechanical inverse can still break the
application. Reverting records a new history event and does not erase the original. Deploying
an old artifact and reverting source are related but separate release actions.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you revert one bug fix while preserving later unrelated changes?
Use `git revert BAD_COMMIT`, resolve any conflicts, and test. Revert adds an inverse
commit instead of deleting later commits.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A successful revert command does not establish that the resulting application is
correct.

pages.title: Why does reverting a merge need a mainline parent?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 09 / Restore, reset and revert without confusion Q 045 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q045
Why does reverting a merge need a mainline
parent?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A merge has multiple parents, so Git needs to know the parent relative to which
the merge's change should be reversed. Inspect parent order before selecting it.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git show --no-patch --format=%P MERGE_COMMIT
   git revert -m 1 MERGE_COMMIT
✎ REMEMBER git show --no-patch --format=%P MERGE_COMMIT
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Parent 1 is commonly the previous checked-out branch tip, but verify it. The original merge
remains an ancestor, so merging the same old branch again will not simply reapply all
reverted changes. A later reintroduction needs an intentional strategy.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why might reverting the revert be needed before reintroducing the old feature?
Git still sees the old merge as integrated. Reverting the revert can restore its changes so
future integration is deliberate; test for intervening changes.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Choosing -m 1 without checking the graph can undo the wrong side.
Original question & example: uploaded Git guide, source page 27. Follow-up answer: added for this edition.

pages.title: What is the reflog and how is it different from the log?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 / Reflog, recovery and clean-up Q 046 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q046
What is the reflog and how is it different from the
log?
THE SHORT ANSWER
The log traverses commit ancestry. A reflog records local reference updates,
including previous checkout or branch positions that may no longer be
reachable from current branches.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git log --oneline -5
   git reflog show HEAD -10
   git reflog show main -10
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Preserve the old object before changing more refs.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Reflogs are local and have expiration policies. They are not normally pushed to another clone.
A reflog entry can help find the old tip after reset, rebase or a detached experiment, but it is
not a permanent backup.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which view helps find a tip removed by a local reset?
`git reflog show HEAD` or the branch's reflog shows previous local tip positions even after
a reset.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Your colleague's reflog is not automatically available in your clone.

pages.title: How do you recover a commit after an accidental reset?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 / Reflog, recovery and clean-up Q 047 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q047
How do you recover a commit after an accidental
reset?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Find and verify the intended old commit, then create a rescue reference before
doing further history changes. Recovering the branch can be a later deliberate
step.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git reflog
   git show RECOVERED_OID
   git branch rescue/lost-work RECOVERED_OID
✎ REMEMBER git reflog
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
A rescue branch makes the object reachable and lets you compare it safely with current work.
The correct reflog selector depends on the operations performed; do not assume HEAD@{1}
is always the lost commit. Preserve the current tip too if it contains useful changes.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How do you confirm the rescued commit contains the expected files?
Inspect `git show --stat RECOVERED_OID`, `git ls-tree -r --name-only RECOVERED_OID`
and the file's contents before moving branches.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Another reset before inspection can make a confused recovery even harder to
reason about.

pages.title: Can Git recover an uncommitted deleted edit?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 / Reflog, recovery and clean-up Q 048 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q048
Can Git recover an uncommitted deleted edit?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Only if that content was recorded somewhere Git can still find, such as a commit,
stash or staged blob. Never-added working edits are generally outside Git's
recovery history.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Check: commits, stash list, reflog, editor local history.
   If staged content became unreachable, object inspection may help.
   Use backups for content Git never stored.
✎ REMEMBER Check: commits, stash list, reflog, editor local history.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Staged objects can exist without a convenient commit reference, but locating them is less
direct and retention is limited. Start with known references and preserve evidence rather than
running aggressive cleanup. Editor recovery and filesystem backup are independent
mechanisms.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Was the missing content ever added, committed or stashed?
That decides the recovery path: commits/reflog, stash, or potentially a staged blob may
help. Never-saved working edits need editor or filesystem backups.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Reflog does not record every keystroke or every working-tree version.

pages.title: How does git clean differ from reset --hard?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 / Reflog, recovery and clean-up Q 049 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q049
How does git clean differ from reset --hard?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Clean removes selected untracked files; hard reset aligns index and tracked files
with a commit. Clean has explicit options for directories and ignored paths and
should be previewed.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git clean -nd          # preview untracked files/directories
   git clean -fd -- tmp-demo/  # delete only this intended path
   # -x also includes ignored paths; do not add it casually.
✎ REMEMBER git clean -nd # preview untracked files/directories
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Use a disposable lab or a clearly scoped path. Ignored files can contain local configuration,
secrets or valuable generated output. Clean does not create a commit or a Git undo record
for removed untracked content.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What does the dry-run say will be deleted?
`git clean -nd` lists the untracked paths Git would remove if you ran the destructive form
with matching flags. Inspect every listed path first.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: git clean -fdx can remove ignored local files that the repository never backed
up.

pages.title: What are ORIG_HEAD and repository integrity checks useful for?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 10 / Reflog, recovery and clean-up Q 050 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q050
What are ORIG_HEAD and repository integrity
checks useful for?
THE SHORT ANSWER
ORIG_HEAD can retain a previous tip for certain operations; integrity tools
inspect objects and references. They help diagnosis but are not universal
recovery guarantees.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git show ORIG_HEAD
   git fsck --full
   git count-objects -vH
✎ REMEMBER git show ORIG_HEAD
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
ORIG_HEAD may be replaced by a later operation, so verify rather than assuming it refers to
a particular incident. Fsck can report unreachable objects without those necessarily being
corruption. Garbage collection and retention determine how long unreachable content
survives.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Is the repository corrupt or merely holding unreachable old commits?
`git fsck` output must be interpreted: unreachable valid commits are common after resets/
rebases. Object corruption needs different evidence and repair steps.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Do not run aggressive pruning while trying to rescue unreachable work.

pages.title: What are origin, upstream and origin/main?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Remotes, fetch and pull Q 051 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q051
What are origin, upstream and origin/main?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Origin is a conventional remote name created by clone. Upstream can be
another remote name or the tracking branch relationship. Origin/main is
normally a local remote-tracking reference.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git remote -v
   git branch -vv
   git rev-parse refs/remotes/origin/main
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Fetch inspects incoming history without integrating.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Remote names are configurable. The remote-tracking reference is not a live query to the
server, and your local main can differ from it. Clarify whether upstream means a named
remote in a fork workflow or the branch used for comparison and default operations.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What updates your local view of the remote branch?
`git fetch` updates your repository's configured remote-tracking references, such as `origin/
main`, without merging them into your branch.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: origin/main and local main are different references even when they currently
have the same ID.

pages.title: What does git fetch change?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Remotes, fetch and pull Q 052 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q052
What does git fetch change?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Fetch downloads needed objects and updates references according to the
refspec, normally remote-tracking branches. It does not ordinarily integrate
those changes into your checked-out branch.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git fetch origin
   git log --oneline main..origin/main
   git diff main origin/main
✎ REMEMBER git fetch origin
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
This lets you inspect incoming work before choosing merge or rebase. FETCH_HEAD also
records fetched tips. Fetch configuration can limit which references update, and fetching tags
has separate rules. Your files can remain unchanged while origin/main advances.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you review incoming commits without integrating them?
Run `git fetch origin`, then `git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main` and `git diff HEAD..origin/
main` before merging or rebasing.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A successful fetch is not the same as updating local main.

How would you review incoming commits without integrating them?

main` before merging or rebasing.

pages.title: How does git pull differ from fetch?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Remotes, fetch and pull Q 053 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q053
How does git pull differ from fetch?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Pull fetches and then integrates the selected upstream into the current branch
using a merge, rebase or fast-forward-only policy. Make the policy explicit when
learning or diagnosing divergence.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git pull --ff-only
   git pull --rebase
   git pull --no-rebase
✎ REMEMBER git pull --ff-only
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
These are alternative policies. Ff-only refuses divergence; rebase replays local commits; no-
rebase uses merge integration. Defaults depend on version and configuration, so inspect them
rather than assuming pull always creates a merge.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which pull policy should reject accidental divergent local main commits?
`git pull --ff-only` refuses divergent histories; choose it when main must update only by
fast-forward.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Pull can modify local history or working content after the fetch stage.

pages.title: How do you set and inspect a branch's upstream?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Remotes, fetch and pull Q 054 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q054
How do you set and inspect a branch's upstream?
THE SHORT ANSWER
An upstream links a local branch to a tracking target used by several default
operations and comparisons. Set it deliberately and inspect branch
configuration.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main main
   git branch -vv
   git rev-parse --abbrev-ref '@{upstream}'
✎ REMEMBER git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main main
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The target remote-tracking reference must exist. Upstream does not automatically push, grant
permissions or make branch content identical. Push behavior also depends on push
configuration and an explicitly provided refspec.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why can a branch be ahead even when it tracks origin/main?
Ahead is based on your local upstream-tracking reference, not a live server call. Your local
commits can be ahead until you push or realign history.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Tracking configuration is not a background synchronization service.

pages.title: What do fetch --prune and remote branch deletion mean?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 11 / Remotes, fetch and pull Q 055 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q055
What do fetch --prune and remote branch
deletion mean?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Prune removes stale local tracking references covered by the fetch/prune
mapping when their remote counterparts are gone. Deleting a remote branch is
a separate server mutation.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git fetch --prune origin
   git branch -r
   git push origin --delete feature/finished
✎ REMEMBER git fetch --prune origin
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The deletion line requires the team's authorization and can be rejected by server policy.
Prune does not normally delete your unrelated local feature branch. Tag pruning is sensitive
to the configured refspec and explicit tag-prune options.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why can a local feature still exist after its remote branch is deleted?
Removing a remote branch deletes a server name. Your independent local `refs/heads/
feature` remains until you delete it.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Do not assume pruning always affects only branches under every possible
configuration.

pages.title: What does git push actually do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Push, rejected updates and leases Q 056 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q056
What does git push actually do?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Push transfers required objects and asks the remote to update specified
references. The requested update must satisfy Git's checks and the server's
policy.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git push -u origin feature/orders
   git ls-remote --heads origin
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Lease helps detect an unexpected remote update.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The -u option records an upstream for a successful or up-to-date branch push. It does not
create review approval. Explicit remote and branch names reduce surprises from defaults,
especially when fetch and push destinations differ.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What does the server check before advancing a branch?
For a normal push, the server checks permissions, hooks/policy and whether the new tip
fast-forwards the existing branch; exceptions require authorization.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A push can transfer objects yet still fail to update the requested reference.

pages.title: Why is a non-fast-forward push rejected?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Push, rejected updates and leases Q 057 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q057
Why is a non-fast-forward push rejected?
THE SHORT ANSWER
For a normal branch update, the old remote tip should be an ancestor of the
new tip. If it is not, updating would discard remote reachability from that branch
and is normally rejected.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git fetch origin
   git log --left-right --oneline HEAD...origin/feature/orders
   # integrate or coordinate after inspecting both histories
✎ REMEMBER git fetch origin
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Another person may have pushed, or you may have rewritten local history. Fetching first
reveals the actual divergence. Merge or rebase according to policy, test, and push the
integrated result. A rejection is useful evidence, not a reason to force blindly.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Are the remote-only commits someone else's work or your old rewritten series?
Fetch and graph the tips; compare `git log --left-right --cherry-pick` or `git range-diff` to
learn whether remote commits are new work or rewritten equivalents.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Retrying the same ordinary push does not resolve divergent ancestry.

pages.title: How does --force-with-lease differ from --force?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Push, rejected updates and leases Q 058 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q058
How does --force-with-lease differ from --force?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Force bypasses the usual ancestry protection. Force-with-lease also requires the
remote reference to match an expected value, which can prevent overwriting a
concurrent update.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
# Authorized rewrite only; EXPECTED_OID is the reviewed old remote tip.
   git push --force-with-lease=refs/heads/feature:EXPECTED_OID origin HEAD:feature
✎ REMEMBER # Authorized rewrite only; EXPECTED_OID is the reviewed old remote tip.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
An explicit expected object ID makes the reviewed expectation clear. The shorthand form
commonly relies on local remote-tracking state; background fetches can update that state and
weaken your intended protection. A lease does not make rewriting shared history socially or
semantically safe.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What happens if a coworker pushes after you record EXPECTED_OID?
The explicit lease no longer matches, so the remote rejects the force update. Fetch, inspect
the coworker's commit and coordinate a safe next step.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Force-with-lease can still replace work if your expected tip includes work you
did not preserve.

pages.title: How do push refspecs select the destination?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Push, rejected updates and leases Q 059 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q059
How do push refspecs select the destination?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A push refspec maps a source object/reference to a destination reference.
Explicit full destinations are useful for scripts where ambiguity is unacceptable.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/review/order-fix
   git push origin refs/tags/v1.0.0:refs/tags/v1.0.0
✎ REMEMBER git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/review/order-fix
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The first command publishes the current commit under a chosen server branch name, which
can differ from the local branch. A leading plus requests a forced update and needs the same
caution as force. Deletion has a dedicated command form.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Can you push a detached HEAD to a named review branch?
Yes. Use an explicit refspec such as `git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/review/my-fix` if you
are allowed to create that branch.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Choosing the wrong destination can publish to an unintended branch even with
correct content.

pages.title: How do you diagnose authentication, authorization and policy push failures?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 12 / Push, rejected updates and leases Q 060 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q060
How do you diagnose authentication, authorization
and policy push failures?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Read the failure category, inspect the remote URL and intended ref, and check
credentials versus server policy separately. Preserve local commits while
diagnosing the network operation.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git remote get-url --push origin
   git branch --show-current
   git status
✎ REMEMBER git remote get-url --push origin
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Authentication proves an identity; authorization permits access; protected-branch or hook
policy can reject an otherwise authenticated update. Do not expose tokens in diagnostic
output. A local commit remains local even if its push fails.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Does the failure occur before repository access or after reference-update validation?
Check the exact error: DNS/SSH/HTTPS failures happen before access, while 'non-fast-
forward', hooks and protected-branch errors happen during update checks.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Changing user.email usually does not repair a transport permission error.

pages.title: How do lightweight and annotated tags differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 / Tags, releases and reproducible builds Q 061 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q061
How do lightweight and annotated tags differ?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A lightweight tag is a reference to an object. An annotated tag has a tag object
containing metadata and a message, and can also carry a signature.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git tag demo-light
   git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0.0"
   git cat-file -t v1.0.0
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Tags are release pointers; verify artifacts too.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Both can identify a release commit, but annotated tags provide a separate tagger identity and
message. A tag can point to objects other than commits, though release workflows commonly
use commits. Normal commits do not move existing tags.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What extra object exists for an annotated tag?
An annotated tag has its own `tag` object holding tagger, message and target. A lightweight
tag is only a ref pointing directly to an object.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A tag name is a reference, so it can be changed unless policy prevents it.

pages.title: Are tags pushed automatically with branches?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 / Tags, releases and reproducible builds Q 062 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q062
Are tags pushed automatically with branches?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Do not assume they are. Push the selected release tag explicitly, or use a
deliberate tag-publishing policy such as follow-tags for eligible annotated tags.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git push origin v1.0.0
   git push --follow-tags origin main
   git ls-remote --tags origin
✎ REMEMBER git push origin v1.0.0
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Follow-tags is not identical to pushing every local tag. An explicit tag push is easiest to review
for one release. Server policy may restrict tag creation or updates. Check the remote
reference rather than assuming a successful branch push published the release name.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which exact tag should a release pipeline create and publish?
Use a reviewed, immutable release commit and a uniquely named annotated tag such as
`v2.4.0`; publish via the approved release process.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: git push --tags can publish unintended local tags as well.

pages.title: Why should release tags usually be immutable?

CHAPTER 13 / Tags, releases and reproducible builds Q 063 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q063
Why should release tags usually be immutable?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Moving an existing release name makes the same name refer to different
source across clones and time. New release or correction names preserve
reproducibility and audit meaning.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Deployed artifact metadata:
   release = v1.0.0
   commit = full object ID
   artifact digest = verified build output identity

immutability is a team rule to enforce. A source ID does not fully specify a build without
dependency, toolchain and configuration information.

Embed the source commit OID and artifact digest/build ID in release metadata; compare
them to the deployed artifact and CI provenance.

target.

pages.title: What does git describe do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 / Tags, releases and reproducible builds Q 064 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q064
What does git describe do?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Describe produces a human-readable name based on reachable tags and
commit distance, subject to its options and available history. It can help
diagnostics but is not a replacement for the full commit ID.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git describe --tags --always
   git rev-parse HEAD
   git status --porcelain
✎ REMEMBER git describe --tags --always
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
A shallow clone or missing tags can produce a different description. The dirty option can
signal working-tree modifications, but build reproducibility requires more than a label. Save
exact source and artifact identities in build metadata.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why can local and CI descriptions differ for the same checked-out commit?
`git describe` depends on which tags are present/fetched and the history graph. CI clones
may be shallow or may not fetch all tags.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A description may change when additional reachable tags are fetched.

pages.title: How should a Java release branch receive a hotfix?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 13 / Tags, releases and reproducible builds Q 065 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q065
How should a Java release branch receive a
hotfix?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Backport the smallest coherent fix, test it against the release's dependencies and
JDK, and publish a new version under the release policy. Record the relationship
to the original fix.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git switch release/1.4
   git cherry-pick -x FIX_COMMIT
   ./mvnw verify
   git tag -a v1.4.1 -m "Fix quantity validation"
✎ REMEMBER git switch release/1.4
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Also ensure the required fix exists on future development lines so it is not lost in the next
release. Database migrations and feature flags can make rollback more complex than
selecting an old Git tag. A new source tag should correspond to a tested artifact.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Does the fix depend on a schema change unavailable in production?
Check the current production schema and code dependencies; adapt or stage the
migration safely before backporting a fix that relies on them.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A hotfix that compiles on main may fail on an older release toolchain.

pages.title: What does git stash save by default?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Stash and multiple worktrees Q 066 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q066
What does git stash save by default?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A normal stash records tracked working-tree and index changes, then cleans
those changes from the checkout. Untracked and ignored files require additional
options.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git stash push -m "unfinished order validation"
   git stash list
   git stash show -p 'stash@{0}'
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Stash and worktrees serve different task changes.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Use -u to include untracked files and -a when deliberately including ignored files too. Ignored
paths may contain large output or local secrets, so choose consciously. A stash is stored
locally and is not sent by an ordinary branch push.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which option includes the new file without including ignored build output?
Use `git stash push -u` to include untracked files; ignored outputs remain excluded unless
you deliberately use `-a`.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A new untracked Java file is not saved by the default stash.

pages.title: How do stash apply and stash pop differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Stash and multiple worktrees Q 067 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q067
How do stash apply and stash pop differ?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Apply restores a stash without dropping it. Pop restores and removes it on
success; if conflicts prevent a clean application, the stash normally remains for
resolution.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git stash apply 'stash@{0}'
   git status
   # after verifying, deliberately drop the intended entry:
   git stash drop 'stash@{0}'
✎ REMEMBER git stash apply 'stash@{0}'
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Apply followed by verification is useful when preserving the saved state matters. Use --index
when attempting to restore the staged state as well, understanding that conflicts can prevent it.
Stash numbers can change after list operations.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What should you check before dropping a stash after resolving conflicts?
Confirm your intended edits exist and work, `git status` has no unresolved conflicts, and
nothing still needed remains only inside that stash.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Pop does not guarantee a conflict-free restoration on a changed base.

pages.title: When is stash branch useful?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Stash and multiple worktrees Q 068 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q068
When is stash branch useful?
THE SHORT ANSWER
It creates a branch from the stash's original base and applies the saved work
there, which can reduce conflicts caused by the current branch having moved
far away.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git stash branch recover/order-work 'stash@{0}'
   git status
   git log --oneline -3
✎ REMEMBER git stash branch recover/order-work 'stash@{0}'
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
When successfully using a stash reference, the applied stash entry is dropped according to
the command's semantics. Review the recovered work and commit it deliberately. This is not
the same as applying the stash on today's main.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why can the original base be easier to restore onto?
`git stash branch` checks out the original base where the stash was created, which may
avoid conflicts caused by applying on a newer branch.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Do not assume the resulting branch includes all later main commits.

pages.title: What is git worktree useful for?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Stash and multiple worktrees Q 069 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q069
What is git worktree useful for?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Worktree lets one repository have multiple working directories with separate
checked-out positions and indexes while sharing objects and most references. It
supports parallel tasks without constant stashing.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git worktree add -b hotfix/order ../order-hotfix main
   git worktree list
   git -C ../order-hotfix status
✎ REMEMBER git worktree add -b hotfix/order ../order-hotfix main
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
You can fix a release while keeping an unfinished feature checkout intact. Build output and
environment files belong to each working directory, but common refs still affect the shared
repository. Git normally prevents checking out the same branch in two worktrees.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What state is private to a worktree and what is shared?
Working files, index and HEAD checkout are per worktree; repository objects and most
refs/branches are shared. Git restricts one branch being checked out twice.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A worktree is not an independent clone with its own separate object database.

pages.title: How do you remove or repair worktree metadata?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 14 / Stash and multiple worktrees Q 070 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q070
How do you remove or repair worktree metadata?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Use worktree-aware commands so Git can check state and update
administrative records. Inspect status before removing a directory with useful
work.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git -C ../order-hotfix status
   git worktree remove ../order-hotfix
   git worktree prune --dry-run
✎ REMEMBER git -C ../order-hotfix status
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Remove normally refuses problematic working state unless explicitly forced. Prune cleans stale
administrative entries for missing worktrees; it is not the same as deleting a branch. Moving
directories manually may require repair. Keep external or removable worktrees locked when
appropriate.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why might a branch still appear checked out after its directory was removed?
A worktree can have stale administrative records after manual deletion. Inspect `git
worktree list --porcelain` and prune only confirmed stale entries.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Deleting a worktree directory manually can leave stale records and lose
uncommitted files.

pages.title: Does .gitignore stop tracking an already committed file?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Ignore rules, attributes and cross-platform files Q 071 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q071
Does .gitignore stop tracking an already
committed file?
THE SHORT ANSWER
No. Ignore rules apply to untracked discovery; an already tracked file remains
tracked. To stop future tracking while keeping the local file, deliberately remove it
from the index.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
# after deciding this file should no longer be tracked:
   git rm --cached -- local.properties
   # add the ignore rule, then commit the tracking change
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Already tracked files need separate untracking.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The removal becomes part of the next commit, while the file stays locally when the command
succeeds. Other collaborators may lose their checked-out copy when adopting that removal,
so communicate. Existing history still contains previous committed content.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What additional action is needed if the file contained an active credential?
Rotate or revoke the credential immediately. Removing the file from a commit does not
disable a secret already exposed in history.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Adding a secret file to .gitignore does not remove the secret from history.

pages.title: How do ignore patterns and negation work?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Ignore rules, attributes and cross-platform files Q 072 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q072
How do ignore patterns and negation work?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Patterns match paths within their scope; a leading exclamation can re-include a
match. You cannot re-include a file inside an excluded directory without also
making the relevant directory traversable.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
target/
   *.log
   config/*
   !config/example.yml
✎ REMEMBER target/
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
This keeps an example under a traversable config directory while excluding its siblings. Root
anchoring, directory slashes and nested ignore files change matching. Use check-ignore to
identify the rule rather than guessing.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which rule explains why a new file is ignored?
Use `git check-ignore -v PATH` to reveal the matching ignore rule and its source file.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: config/ followed only by !config/example.yml will not behave like config/* in this
example.

pages.title: Which files should a Java project commonly ignore?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Ignore rules, attributes and cross-platform files Q 073 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q073
Which files should a Java project commonly
ignore?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Ignore generated build outputs and machine-specific local state, while tracking
source, tests, intended build configuration and the wrapper files required by the
project's build policy.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Typical ignored output: target/, build/, *.class.
   Track by policy: pom.xml, build.gradle, wrapper scripts/config.
   Keep real credentials outside committed local configuration.
✎ REMEMBER Typical ignored output: target/, build/, *.class.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Do not blindly ignore every .jar: some build-wrapper layouts or deliberately vendored
dependencies need tracked binary files. Check the specific wrapper version and repository
policy. Share sanitized example configuration rather than committing a developer's actual
secrets.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Can a clean clone build without files from your laptop?
A clean clone must have all required tracked sources, build scripts and dependency
access. Run CI from a fresh clone to catch machine-only files.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A broad ignore rule can hide a required new build file and break CI.

pages.title: What does .gitattributes control?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Ignore rules, attributes and cross-platform files Q 074 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q074
What does .gitattributes control?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Attributes define path-based behavior such as text normalization, diff/merge
drivers, binary treatment and filters. They can make repository behavior more
consistent across platforms.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
* text=auto
   *.java text eol=lf
   *.sh text eol=lf
   *.png binary
✎ REMEMBER * text=auto
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Line-ending normalization affects index content and checkout behavior under the configured
rules. Introduce renormalization as a separate reviewed change where needed, then test
rather than mixing it with a functional patch. Filters need consistent installation and trust
decisions.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you separate normalization from a production bug fix?
Make a separate commit for line-ending/format changes and another for the bug fix;
confirm `.gitattributes` and compare with whitespace-insensitive tools.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Changing attributes can create many apparent diffs without changing
application logic.

pages.title: How do you diagnose unexpected ignored files or line-ending diffs?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 15 / Ignore rules, attributes and cross-platform files Q 075 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q075
How do you diagnose unexpected ignored files or 
line-ending diffs?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Inspect the matching ignore rule, effective attributes and relevant configuration.
Distinguish an intentional content change from normalization or executable-
mode differences.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git check-ignore -v -- config/local.yml
   git check-attr text eol -- src/Order.java
   git diff --check
   git config --show-origin --get core.autocrlf
✎ REMEMBER git check-ignore -v -- config/local.yml
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Check-ignore normally focuses on untracked paths; tracked-path investigation may need its
no-index option. Diff --check flags certain whitespace errors but does not prove semantic
equality. Investigate the exact patch before applying a global setting.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why does a file appear wholly changed after a Windows checkout?
CRLF/LF conversion can change nearly every line. Inspect `git diff --ignore-space-at-eol`
and repository `.gitattributes` before assuming logic changed.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Turning off all whitespace checks can hide real formatting problems without
fixing normalization.

pages.title: What are blob, tree, commit and tag objects?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 / Git objects, references and the index Q 076 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q076
What are blob, tree, commit and tag objects?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A blob stores file content; a tree maps names and modes to objects; a commit
points to a tree and parents with metadata; an annotated tag adds named-object
metadata.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git cat-file -t HEAD
   git cat-file -p HEAD
   git ls-tree HEAD
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Content objects are identified by their data.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
File names belong to tree entries, not the blob itself, so identical content can be reused at
different paths. Trees also represent subtrees and special entry modes. The branch name is a
reference outside the commit object.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why can two files with identical bytes share a blob ID?
Blob IDs hash file content, not names or paths. Identical bytes therefore reference the
same blob object when using the same object format.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A blob does not inherently know which Java filename contained its content.

pages.title: Why do references matter for object reachability?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 / Git objects, references and the index Q 077 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q077
Why do references matter for object reachability?
THE SHORT ANSWER
References name starting points from which commit/tree/object relationships
make content reachable. Removing a branch name does not immediately delete
every object formerly reachable through it.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git show-ref --heads --tags
   git for-each-ref --format='%(refname) %(objectname)'
   git rev-list --all
✎ REMEMBER git show-ref --heads --tags
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Another branch, tag or reflog may still protect the commits. Eventually unreachable objects
may be pruned according to retention and maintenance rules. Preserve a rescue reference
before relying on uncertain retention.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which other references could still retain a deleted feature's commits?
Tags, remote-tracking refs, other branches, stash and reflog entries may still make
commits reachable after deleting one branch name.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Deleting a branch is not a secure content-erasure operation.

pages.title: What is the index during a conflict?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 / Git objects, references and the index Q 078 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q078
What is the index during a conflict?
THE SHORT ANSWER
In ordinary state the index holds one proposed entry per tracked path. During
an unresolved merge it can hold base, ours and theirs entries in separate stages.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git ls-files -u
   git show :1:src/Order.java
   git show :2:src/Order.java
   git show :3:src/Order.java
✎ REMEMBER git ls-files -u
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Stage 1 is the base, 2 ours, and 3 theirs when those entries exist. A stage can be missing in
add/delete conflicts. Staging a resolved file replaces the unmerged entries with the chosen
normal entry. Operation-specific ours/theirs meaning still matters.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What changes in the index after git add marks a path resolved?
Git replaces the path's conflict-stage entries (1/2/3) with a normal stage-0 index entry
containing your resolved content.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Not every conflict has all three file versions available.

Does Git track renames directly?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Git stores snapshots and can infer renames when comparing them using
similarity detection. A move command records the path/content changes; there
is no universal permanent rename object.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git mv src/OldOrder.java src/Order.java
   git diff --staged --find-renames
   git log --follow -- src/Order.java
✎ REMEMBER git mv src/OldOrder.java src/Order.java
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Rename detection depends on comparison context, thresholds and limits. Large content edits
can make a move harder to recognize. Follow is useful for a single path's history but should
not be treated as an infallible record of identity.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why might Git show a delete and add instead of a rename?
Rename detection is a similarity-based presentation of delete/add changes. Major edits or
thresholds may prevent Git from recognizing a rename.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A rename-only commit and a rename-plus-rewrite can be displayed differently.

pages.title: What do packfiles and garbage collection do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 16 / Git objects, references and the index Q 080 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q080
What do packfiles and garbage collection do?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Packfiles compress and organize objects, potentially using delta representations.
Maintenance can consolidate storage and eventually remove unreachable
objects under retention rules.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git count-objects -vH
   git gc  # normal maintenance; not a recovery step
✎ REMEMBER git count-objects -vH
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The logical snapshot model remains the same even when objects are packed. Loose-object
count alone is not total repository size. During recovery, avoid aggressive pruning that
removes objects you are trying to rescue. Large historical binaries can keep storage large
even after deletion from today's tree.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why can deleting a large file leave the repository large?
The old large blob remains reachable through historical commits. Deleting the current
path does not rewrite prior snapshots or automatically shrink history.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Garbage collection is not a substitute for intentional history cleanup or backup.

pages.title: How does git bisect find a regression?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Debugging with bisect, blame and history search Q 081 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q081
How does git bisect find a regression?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Bisect narrows a known good/bad history interval by checking intermediate
commits and classifying their behavior. It is efficient when the test and good/bad
boundary are reliable.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git bisect start
   git bisect bad BAD_TIP
   git bisect good GOOD_TIP
   # test each selected revision, then mark good, bad or skip
   git bisect reset
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Automate a reliable pass/fail test.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The selected checkout may be detached while testing. Preserve local edits first and reset
bisect when done. Flaky tests, environmental changes or a regression that disappears and
returns can invalidate a simple monotonic interpretation.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What evidence establishes the last known good revision?
Use a known passing CI build, release tag or tested deployment commit, then confirm it
still passes the same deterministic reproduction check.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: The newest failing commit is not necessarily the commit that introduced the
problem.

pages.title: How does automated bisect use exit codes?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Debugging with bisect, blame and history search Q 082 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q082
How does automated bisect use exit codes?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Bisect run executes a supplied test command. Zero means good; ordinary failure
codes indicate bad, while 125 means the selected revision cannot be tested and
should be skipped.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git bisect run ./regression-check.sh
   # test script contract:
   # 0 = regression absent; 1 = regression present; 125 = untestable
✎ REMEMBER git bisect run ./regression-check.sh
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Certain special exit codes stop the run, so use the documented contract. A Java test wrapper
must distinguish the target regression from missing dependencies, incompatible JDKs or
unrelated compilation failures. Otherwise it may blame an infrastructure break.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How will the script classify an old commit requiring a different toolchain?
Return 'skip' (exit 125) for commits that cannot be tested fairly, such as those lacking
required tools. Bad test setup must not count as product failure.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Mapping every build failure to bad can identify the wrong change.
Original question & example: uploaded Git guide, source page 48. Follow-up answer: added for this edition.

pages.title: What does git blame tell you and what are its limits?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Debugging with bisect, blame and history search Q 083 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q083
What does git blame tell you and what are its
limits?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Blame attributes current lines to commits that last changed them under its
traversal rules. It provides context for investigation, not proof of who introduced
a behavioral bug.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git blame -L 20,50 -- src/OrderService.java
   git blame -w -- src/OrderService.java
   git show COMMIT_FROM_BLAME
✎ REMEMBER git blame -L 20,50 -- src/OrderService.java
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Formatting, moves and earlier dependencies can make the last line edit unrelated to the root
cause. Inspect the patch, parent version and tests. Options can ignore whitespace or selected
mechanical revisions when configured deliberately.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Could the bug come from a caller that did not modify these lines?
Yes. `blame` identifies the last change to a line, not the full cause. Investigate callers,
config, data and earlier design decisions.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: The author of the last formatting commit may not own the behavior being
investigated.

pages.title: How do -S and -G history searches differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Debugging with bisect, blame and history search Q 084 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q084
How do -S and -G history searches differ?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Pickaxe -S searches for changes in the occurrence count of a string; -G
searches for added or removed patch lines matching a regular expression. They
answer different questions.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git log -S 'validateQuantity' --oneline -- src/
   git log -G 'quantity.*<.*0' -p -- src/
✎ REMEMBER git log -S 'validateQuantity' --oneline -- src/
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
A moved string with the same count may not match -S even though relevant patch lines
changed. Combine the search with path scope and inspect candidate commits. Search deleted
history through suitable revisions instead of looking only at current files.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which query helps find when a validation expression changed?
Use `git log -S'validationText' -- path` for a changed string count, or `git log -G'regex' --
path` for matching patch lines.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Neither command is equivalent to a simple search of today's source tree.

pages.title: How does git grep help during an investigation?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 17 / Debugging with bisect, blame and history search Q 085 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q085
How does git grep help during an investigation?
THE SHORT ANSWER
It searches tracked content in the selected working/index or tree context,
making it useful for finding related code at a particular revision without switching
checkouts.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git grep -n 'validateQuantity'
   git grep -n 'validateQuantity' v1.0.0 -- src/
   git log --oneline -- src/OrderService.java
✎ REMEMBER git grep -n 'validateQuantity'
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The tagged search can reveal an older caller or implementation while leaving working files
untouched. Choose options deliberately if untracked or ignored files also matter. Pair search
results with history rather than concluding from one occurrence.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you locate all uses in an older release snapshot?
Use `git grep 'symbol' RELEASE_TAG -- '*.java'` or `git grep 'symbol' COMMIT` to search
the old snapshot without switching the working tree.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Today's grep result does not prove the same code existed in the release under
investigation.

pages.title: What is a shallow clone and what can it affect?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Large repositories, sparse checkout, submodules and LFS Q 086 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q086
What is a shallow clone and what can it affect?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A shallow clone truncates commit ancestry at a chosen depth or boundary. It
can speed acquisition but limits history-based commands until more history is
fetched.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git clone --depth 20 REPOSITORY_URL demo
   git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository
   git fetch --unshallow
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Git pointers need reachable backing content.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The final command requires a suitable remote with the missing history. Merge-base discovery,
bisect, describe and release tooling may need deeper ancestry or tags. CI's actual checkout
settings determine which data is present.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why might a pull-request diff fail to find the expected merge base?
A shallow or partial history may omit the common ancestor. Fetch/deepen the relevant
history and verify refs before comparing.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A shallow clone is not merely a smaller working directory.

pages.title: How does a partial clone differ from a shallow clone?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Large repositories, sparse checkout, submodules and LFS Q 087 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q087
How does a partial clone differ from a shallow
clone?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A partial clone can omit selected objects, such as blobs, while keeping relevant
commit structure and fetching promised objects when needed. Shallow clone
limits ancestry.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout REPOSITORY_URL demo
   git -C demo sparse-checkout set service-a common
   git -C demo checkout
✎ REMEMBER git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout REPOSITORY_URL demo
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Server support and Git configuration matter. Reading missing content can trigger a network
fetch, so offline behavior differs from a full clone. Combine partial clone with sparse checkout
only when both serve the workload. These are illustrative commands, not a tested remote-
server lab here.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What happens when an offline command needs a missing blob?
In a partial clone, Git may attempt lazy fetching; offline access to an absent blob fails.
Prefetch required objects before disconnecting.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Partial clone does not guarantee that later checkout avoids all network
transfers.

pages.title: What does sparse checkout change?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Large repositories, sparse checkout, submodules and LFS Q 088 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q088
What does sparse checkout change?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Sparse checkout limits which tracked paths are populated in a working tree. It
does not, by itself, erase the remaining paths from history or turn the repository
into separate projects.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git sparse-checkout init --cone
   git sparse-checkout set service-a common
   git sparse-checkout list
   git sparse-checkout disable
✎ REMEMBER git sparse-checkout init --cone
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Cone mode expresses directory-oriented selections with its own inclusion rules. Build files and
shared modules may still be needed. Sparse index support and tool compatibility depend on
version and configuration. Choose paths from the actual build dependency graph.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which shared directories must a Java service build still include?
Include every build input: project modules, shared libraries, parent POMs, wrappers, scripts
and resources. Sparse patterns must not hide required paths.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Hiding another module from the checkout does not remove its Git history.

pages.title: What is a submodule and how do you initialize it?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Large repositories, sparse checkout, submodules and LFS Q 089 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q089
What is a submodule and how do you initialize it?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A submodule records a specific commit of another repository, with location
metadata normally in .gitmodules. Updating the submodule checkout and
updating the parent pointer are separate changes.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git clone --recurse-submodules REPOSITORY_URL demo
   git submodule update --init --recursive
   git submodule status
✎ REMEMBER git clone --recurse-submodules REPOSITORY_URL demo
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The parent stores a gitlink entry for the selected submodule commit, not a copy of its
ordinary history. To adopt a new submodule revision, commit the pointer change in the
parent. Ensure the referenced commit is available to collaborators before publishing that
pointer.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What happens if the parent points to a submodule commit never pushed?
The submodule checkout fails to obtain that commit from its remote, and CI cannot
reproduce the build. Publish the submodule commit before the parent reference.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Cloning the parent without initialization may not provide the submodule's
source files.

pages.title: What problem does Git LFS solve, and what are its limits?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 18 / Large repositories, sparse checkout, submodules and LFS Q 090 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q090
What problem does Git LFS solve, and what are
its limits?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Git LFS stores pointer files in Git while keeping selected large content in a
separate LFS store. It helps binary workflows but adds tooling, transfer and
retention dependencies.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
# Requires Git LFS installation and a compatible remote:
   git lfs install
   git lfs track '*.psd'
   git add .gitattributes
✎ REMEMBER # Requires Git LFS installation and a compatible remote:
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Tracking a new pattern does not automatically migrate every old binary in history. Clones and
CI need access to the LFS objects, not just Git pointers. Storage policy and cleanup require
coordination; deletion of a current path may leave historical content retained.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Can CI build if it has the Git commit but cannot download the LFS object?
No, not if the build needs its bytes. The Git pointer alone is insufficient; CI must
authenticate and fetch the matching LFS object.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: An LFS pointer is not the actual binary artifact.

pages.title: How do trunk-based development and Gitflow-style workflows differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 / Team workflows, review and Java CI Q 091 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q091
How do trunk-based development and 
Gitflow-style workflows differ?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Trunk-based work emphasizes frequent integration and short-lived branches.
Gitflow-style work uses additional long-lived development and release/support
lines. Choose based on release needs and operational cost.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Frequent deployment: short feature branch -> reviewed main.
   Supported product versions: main plus deliberate release lines.
   Incomplete feature: controlled feature flag when appropriate.
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Test the exact source tree being delivered.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Long-lived lines increase divergence and backport work; very short-lived lines require reliable
tests and change isolation. Workflow names do not guarantee quality. Define who owns a
release, how fixes propagate and which history can be rewritten.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Does the product need several independently supported release versions?
If multiple versions need fixes independently, release branches and controlled backports
may be worthwhile; one maintained version can use a simpler trunk flow.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Keeping a branch open for months increases integration risk even if each
commit is small.

lines. Choose based on release needs and operational cost.

Frequent deployment: short feature branch -> reviewed main.
   Supported product versions: main plus deliberate release lines.
   Incomplete feature: controlled feature flag when appropriate.
pages.explanation:
Long-lived lines increase divergence and backport work; very short-lived lines require reliable
tests and change isolation. Workflow names do not guarantee quality. Define who owns a
release, how fixes propagate and which history can be rewritten.
pages.pitfall:
Keeping a branch open for months increases integration risk even if each
commit is small.
pages.followup:
Does the product need several independently supported release versions?
If multiple versions need fixes independently, release branches and controlled backports
may be worthwhile; one maintained version can use a simpler trunk flow.

pages.title: What is the difference between a pull request and a merge?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 / Team workflows, review and Java CI Q 092 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q092
What is the difference between a pull request and
a merge?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A pull request is a hosting-platform review and integration workflow. Merge is a
Git operation joining histories. A platform may integrate an approved request
using merge, squash or rebase policies.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Review: inspect requirements, diff, tests and compatibility.
   Integration policy: merge commit, squash or rebase.
   After integration: delete short-lived branch by team policy.
✎ REMEMBER Review: inspect requirements, diff, tests and compatibility.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Review can detect semantic mistakes Git cannot see. Approval, required checks and protected
branches belong to hosting configuration. The reviewed diff must match the final integration
result, especially after late conflict resolution or base changes.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which exact commit or combined result did CI validate?
Record the exact integration commit/tree (merge queue or final merge result), not only
the feature tip. Test what will actually ship.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A green branch build does not always test the eventual merge result with
current main.

pages.title: How should CI select and record source for a Java build?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 / Team workflows, review and Java CI Q 093 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q093
How should CI select and record source for a
Java build?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Build an explicit commit or defined integration result, record its identity and run
the intended toolchain and checks from a clean environment. Detached HEAD in
CI can be intentional.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git rev-parse HEAD
   git status --porcelain
   ./mvnw verify
   # attach source ID, JDK/build-tool versions and artifact digest
✎ REMEMBER git rev-parse HEAD
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
If tooling needs tags, history or submodules, configure checkout accordingly. A clean source
tree does not fix unpinned dependencies or environment-specific behavior. Deployment
should use the tested artifact rather than rebuilding differently later.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How do you link the deployed artifact to the exact tested source?
Publish the commit SHA, dependency/build metadata and immutable artifact digest with
the deployment; verify the artifact against CI records.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A mutable branch name can advance after the pipeline starts.

pages.title: How should Java teams handle generated files and schema migrations in Git?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 / Team workflows, review and Java CI Q 094 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q094
How should Java teams handle generated files and
schema migrations in Git?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Give generated artifacts an explicit tracking policy, keep semantic source review
clear and treat deployed migrations as versioned operational history. Avoid
mixing mechanical regeneration with unrelated logic changes.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Review separately: generated client regeneration and business change.
   Ignore ordinary target/build output.
   New DB correction: add a new migration under the migration policy.
✎ REMEMBER Review separately: generated client regeneration and business change.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Some generated sources are deliberately committed for distribution, while others are
reproducibly generated during build. Database rollback depends on the migration system and
data, not just Git revert. Changing an already applied migration can invalidate checksums or
history.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Can a clean clone generate exactly the committed client code?
Run code generation in clean CI, verify reproducible output and compare generated files
or expected checksums; no developer-only tool should be required.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Reverting Java source does not automatically undo a production database
change.

pages.title: How do you make conflict resolution part of code review?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 19 / Team workflows, review and Java CI Q 095 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q095
How do you make conflict resolution part of code
review?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Treat the resolved result as a new decision to inspect and test. Compare it with
both sides and confirm that important requirements still hold before accepting
the integration.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git show --cc MERGE_COMMIT
   git diff MERGE_COMMIT^1 MERGE_COMMIT -- src/
   git diff MERGE_COMMIT^2 MERGE_COMMIT -- src/
✎ REMEMBER git show --cc MERGE_COMMIT
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Parent comparisons expose what the merge added relative to each line. Combined display has
its own filtering semantics, so it should not be your only inspection. Ask the responsible
reviewers to verify nontrivial resolutions and rerun integration tests.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which requirement could be lost by the chosen resolution?
Conflict choices can drop validation, authorization, error handling or transaction checks;
add tests for both branches' intended requirements.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A conflict-free final index does not prove that both branches' behavior was
preserved.

pages.title: What are Git hooks and are local hooks enough to enforce policy?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Hooks, credentials and secure history Q 096 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q096
What are Git hooks and are local hooks enough to
enforce policy?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Hooks run at defined Git events. Local hooks help developers catch problems,
but can be absent or bypassed. Critical shared policy needs suitable server or CI
enforcement.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
pre-commit: fast style or secret checks.
   commit-msg: message policy.
   pre-receive/update: server reference-update policy.
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Local hooks are not a server security boundary.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Hook files are not automatically installed just because another person cloned the source
repository. A configured hooks path can share reviewed scripts, but adoption and trust still
matter. Avoid putting long unreliable checks in every local edit cycle.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Where is the required security check enforced if a local hook is missing?
Server-side branch protection, required CI checks and review rules enforce policy
independently of optional developer-side hooks.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: --no-verify can bypass certain local hooks; it does not bypass server policy.

pages.title: How do HTTPS and SSH authentication compare?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Hooks, credentials and secure history Q 097 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q097
How do HTTPS and SSH authentication compare?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Both can authenticate transport when configured correctly. HTTPS commonly
uses a credential helper or token; SSH uses keys and host verification.
Repository authorization remains a separate server decision.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git remote get-url origin
   git config --get credential.helper
   # use the organization's approved credential/key setup
✎ REMEMBER git remote get-url origin
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Choose the mechanism that fits the environment rather than claiming one is always more
secure. Use least-privilege credentials, protect private keys and verify server identity. Avoid
embedding tokens in URLs, shell history or committed configuration.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Is the failing identity authorized for this specific repository and operation?
Verify the remote URL, selected SSH key/token identity, its scope and repository/branch
rights; a credential can be valid but not authorized here.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Disabling host verification to fix a connection error removes an important trust
check.

pages.title: What do signed commits and sign-off mean?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Hooks, credentials and secure history Q 098 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q098
What do signed commits and sign-off mean?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A cryptographic signature can support verification of commit provenance under
a trusted key policy. A sign-off is a text trailer expressing a project's attestation
convention; it is not the same as a signature.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git commit -S -m "Fix order validation"  # signing configured first
   git verify-commit SIGNED_COMMIT
   git commit -s -m "Fix order validation"  # adds sign-off trailer
✎ REMEMBER git commit -S -m "Fix order validation" # signing configured first
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Key trust, revocation and allowed signing identities determine what verification means. A
signature does not prove the code is correct or approved. Rewriting a signed commit creates
a different object that requires a new signature if the policy demands one.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What should CI verify beyond the existence of a signature field?
Verify the cryptographic signature, trusted key identity, allowed signer policy and that
protected build/ref policy used the verified commit.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A Signed-off-by line is not cryptographic proof of identity.

pages.title: What should you do if a secret was committed?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Hooks, credentials and secure history Q 099 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q099
What should you do if a secret was committed?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Revoke or rotate the exposed credential, assess its use, and coordinate removal
from active files and history where required. Removing the latest file does not
invalidate a copied credential.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Immediate action: revoke/rotate through the credential owner.
   Repository action: remove active secret; add safe example/config policy.
   History cleanup: coordinated rewrite with clones/forks and server handling.
✎ REMEMBER Immediate action: revoke/rotate through the credential owner.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
History rewrite is a separate operation with affected references, backups and collaborators.
Use reviewed tooling and documented hosting guidance rather than assuming a force push
erases every copy. The urgent guarantee is that the old credential stops working.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How will you verify the exposed credential is no longer accepted?
Revoke/rotate it at the provider and prove the old credential fails a safe authentication
test. Rewrite history only when warranted, with coordination.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: .gitignore and git revert do not erase the credential from existing historical
objects.

pages.title: Why does a repository need trust boundaries for automation?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 20 / Hooks, credentials and secure history Q 100 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q100
Why does a repository need trust boundaries for
automation?
THE SHORT ANSWER
A repository can contain build scripts, hooks configuration and workflow
changes. Reviewing source or a pull request should not automatically grant
untrusted code privileged execution with secrets.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
External contribution: test in an appropriately limited environment.
   Trusted release: scoped credentials and protected approval path.
   Build output: verify provenance and source identity.
✎ REMEMBER External contribution: test in an appropriately limited environment.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
CI behavior depends on the platform's trigger and permission model. Keep secret-bearing
jobs separated from untrusted execution as required by that model. Git ownership checks and
server controls solve different trust problems.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which identity and secrets are available to the proposed pipeline run?
Review whether untrusted PR code receives any tokens, cloud roles, secrets or write
permissions; use minimal scoped, short-lived permissions.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A change to a workflow file can be as sensitive as a change to production Java
code.

pages.title: How do HEAD~2 and HEAD^2 differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 21 / Advanced revisions, patches and repeated resolutions Q 101 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q101
How do HEAD~2 and HEAD^2 differ?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Tilde follows the first-parent chain a given number of steps. Caret selects a
particular parent of one commit. HEAD^2 therefore requires a second parent,
such as a merge commit.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git show HEAD~2
   git show HEAD^1
   git show HEAD^2  # only if HEAD has a second parent
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Always check parentage and dependencies.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
For ordinary one-parent history, HEAD~1 and HEAD^1 agree. At a merge, HEAD~2 follows
parent 1 twice, while HEAD^2 selects the other parent immediately. Quoting revision
expressions can be necessary in some shells.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
How would you inspect the feature tip recorded by a merge's second parent?
`git show MERGE_COMMIT^2` inspects the second parent's commit; `git log
MERGE_COMMIT^2` follows its history.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: ^2 does not mean two commits back.

pages.title: How do git apply and git am differ?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 21 / Advanced revisions, patches and repeated resolutions Q 102 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q102
How do git apply and git am differ?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Apply applies a patch to files and optionally the index without creating the
corresponding commit. Am imports suitable mail-format patches as commits
with their metadata.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git apply --check fix.patch
   git apply fix.patch
   # separate workflow for format-patch output:
   git am 0001-fix-order-validation.patch
✎ REMEMBER git apply --check fix.patch
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Inspect patch origin and scope before applying. Apply --check checks applicability, not
whether the code is safe or correct. Am has its own continue/abort flow when applying a
series fails. Different patch formats preserve different metadata.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which workflow preserves the author and message from a format-patch series?
`git am` imports the mailbox patch series and typically preserves the supplied author and
commit messages; check conflicts and results.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Applying a patch is not automatically committing it.

pages.title: What is format-patch used for?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 21 / Advanced revisions, patches and repeated resolutions Q 103 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q103
What is format-patch used for?
THE SHORT ANSWER
It exports commits as mail-style patch files containing change content and
commit information. It supports review or transfer workflows that do not depend
on a hosting pull-request interface.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git format-patch -1 FIX_COMMIT
   git format-patch BASE_COMMIT..feature/orders
✎ REMEMBER git format-patch -1 FIX_COMMIT
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The receiver can inspect and apply the series with an appropriate am workflow. The resulting
commit IDs may differ because destination ancestry and metadata differ. Patch transfer does
not include every referenced object or large external artifact.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What dependencies must be present for the series to apply and compile?
Ensure earlier patches, prerequisite types/APIs, and target dependencies are present.
Apply in dependency order, then build and run tests.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A patch series is not a complete backup of all repository references.
