pages.title: What is rerere and why should you still review its result?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 21 / Advanced revisions, patches and repeated resolutions Q 104 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q104
What is rerere and why should you still review its
result?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Rerere records a conflict resolution and can reuse it when a matching conflict
reappears. It saves repetitive work, but does not establish that an old resolution
remains semantically correct.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git config --local rerere.enabled true
   git rerere status
   git diff
✎ REMEMBER git config --local rerere.enabled true
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Automatic staging is controlled separately. After reuse, inspect the resolved content and test it
under the new surrounding code. The feature is useful for repeated integrations or rebases
with similar conflicts. Remove an unsuitable recorded resolution deliberately rather than
repeatedly accepting it.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Should a reused resolution be staged automatically in this repository?
Usually inspect and stage the resolution deliberately. `rerere.autoupdate` can stage reused
resolutions automatically, but team policy and tests should control it.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A syntactically matching conflict can have different business context later.

Rerere records a conflict resolution and can reuse it when a matching conflict
reappears. It saves repetitive work, but does not establish that an old resolution
remains semantically correct.
pages.codeExample:
git config --local rerere.enabled true
   git rerere status
   git diff
✎ REMEMBER git config --local rerere.enabled true
pages.explanation:
Automatic staging is controlled separately. After reuse, inspect the resolved content and test it
under the new surrounding code. The feature is useful for repeated integrations or rebases
with similar conflicts. Remove an unsuitable recorded resolution deliberately rather than
repeatedly accepting it.
pages.pitfall: A syntactically matching conflict can have different business context later.
pages.followup:
Should a reused resolution be staged automatically in this repository?
Usually inspect and stage the resolution deliberately. `rerere.autoupdate` can stage reused
resolutions automatically, but team policy and tests should control it.

pages.title: How can merge-base and ancestry tests support automation?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 21 / Advanced revisions, patches and repeated resolutions Q 105 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q105
How can merge-base and ancestry tests support
automation?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Merge-base finds common ancestry, while an ancestor check answers whether
one commit is reachable from another. They let scripts reason about topology
instead of counting visible log lines.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git merge-base main feature/orders
   git merge-base --is-ancestor BASE_COMMIT HEAD
   # exit 0: ancestor; exit 1: not ancestor; errors are separate
✎ REMEMBER git merge-base main feature/orders
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Handle missing objects, shallow history and multiple merge bases under the script's
requirements. A successful ancestry check says nothing about review, security or semantic
equivalence. Squash-integrated patches can be present without original ancestry.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Why can a squash-merged feature fail an ancestry check?
A squash merge copies combined changes into a new commit but not the original
commits' parent links. An ancestry check therefore still reports them absent.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Equivalent content does not necessarily imply that the source commit is an
ancestor.

pages.title: You committed on the wrong branch: how do you move the work?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Senior interview scenarios and judgment Q 106 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q106
You committed on the wrong branch: how do you
move the work?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Preserve the commit under the intended branch, then decide how to repair the
wrong branch according to whether it was shared. Avoid losing the only
reference before creating the new one.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
# if the accidental tip is private and should become a new feature:
   git switch -c feature/intended-work
   # inspect the old branch and deliberately restore its intended tip
DRAW IT TO REMEMBER ✎
Explain which refs, files and people were affected.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
If the target branch already exists, cherry-pick the needed commits there instead. A private
wrong branch may be reset after preserving work; a shared wrong branch normally needs an
inverse or corrective commit. Verify uncommitted files as a separate concern.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Was the accidental commit already published and used by teammates?
If published, protect teammates' history and normally add a correction/revert. If private,
an amend/reset may be acceptable after saving work.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Deleting or resetting the original reference first can make recovery harder.

pages.title: A teammate force-pushed and your branch diverged: what do you do?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Senior interview scenarios and judgment Q 107 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q107
A teammate force-pushed and your branch
diverged: what do you do?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Preserve your current tip, inspect old and new upstream histories, identify your
unique work, and replay or integrate only what is intended. Coordinate before
changing the server again.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git branch backup/local-before-repair
   git fetch origin
   git log --left-right --oneline HEAD...origin/main
✎ REMEMBER git branch backup/local-before-repair
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Blind pull can reintroduce commits the teammate deliberately replaced. The correct repair
depends on the old base, equivalent patches and team agreement. Range-diff and explicit
rebase --onto can help once boundaries are known. Test the reconstructed result.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which local commits represent your changes rather than the old upstream series?
Fetch the new upstream; inspect `git log --left-right --cherry-pick` and `git range-diff`
against your backup to distinguish your patch series from upstream replacements.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Another force push can overwrite new valid work while trying to undo the first
incident.

pages.title: A merge succeeds but Java tests fail: why can that happen?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Senior interview scenarios and judgment Q 108 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q108
A merge succeeds but Java tests fail: why can that
happen?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Git merges textual/tree changes, not business semantics. Independent edits can
combine into invalid behavior even without overlapping lines, and clean
integration still needs tests and review.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Branch A changes validation rules.
   Branch B changes the caller's assumptions.
   Merge has no text conflict, but checkout behavior regresses.
✎ REMEMBER Branch A changes validation rules.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Inspect each parent's changes and the resulting interaction. Use a targeted regression test
and consider whether the fix belongs in one branch or the integration layer. Avoid assuming
that lack of conflict establishes application correctness.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which integration test covers the interaction between these two changes?
Create a test exercising both changes together, including the boundary where they interact
(for example stock reservation and payment retry), not just separate unit tests.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Compiling alone can miss a behavioral or transaction-boundary regression.
Original question & example: uploaded Git guide, source page 63. Follow-up answer: added for this edition.

pages.title: Your local branch says ahead but pushing updates nothing: how do you investigate?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Senior interview scenarios and judgment Q 109 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q109
Your local branch says ahead but pushing updates
nothing: how do you investigate?
THE SHORT ANSWER
Inspect the exact upstream, push destination and refspec rather than assuming
all defaults refer to the same server branch. Ahead is a comparison against a
local tracking reference.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
git branch -vv
   git remote -v
   git config --get push.default
   git remote get-url --push origin
✎ REMEMBER git branch -vv
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
The tracking view may be stale or the configured push target may differ. Confirm whether the
intended remote reference has the expected object ID. Do not expose credentials while
printing configuration or URLs. An explicit reviewed source/destination can remove ambiguity.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
Which reference is the status comparison using?
The status compares against the branch's configured upstream tracking ref (shown by `git
branch -vv`), which may differ from the push destination.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: Ahead/behind is not a live measurement of every remote.
Original question & example: uploaded Git guide, source page 63. Follow-up answer: added for this edition.

pages.title: How should you answer an unfamiliar Git failure in an interview?
pages.fullText:
CHAPTER 22 / Senior interview scenarios and judgment Q 110 of 110
INTERVIEW QUESTION / Q110
How should you answer an unfamiliar Git failure
in an interview?
THE SHORT ANSWER
State what must be preserved, inspect status and topology, explain the probable
category, and choose a reversible diagnostic before a destructive repair. Be
precise about what you do not yet know.
COMMAND EXAMPLE / SCENARIO
Inspect: status, operation state, refs, diffs, recent reflog.
   Preserve: backup branch and valuable working files.
   Decide: integrate, undo, rescue or fix permissions/policy.
✎ REMEMBER Inspect: status, operation state, refs, diffs, recent reflog.
WHAT REALLY HAPPENS
Explain expected effects on HEAD, index, working tree and remote references. Confirm the
outcome with an appropriate diff, graph and tests. A command is correct only relative to the
desired end state and the collaboration boundary.
FOLLOW-UP QUESTION + ANSWER
What observable result would show that your repair succeeded?
Show the repaired state with a clean/reviewed graph, correct target ref and expected
tests/CI. Confirm the intended remote OID if publication was part of the task.
⚠ INTERVIEW TRAP: A memorized reset --hard answer can destroy the very evidence needed to
diagnose the problem.
Original question & example: uploaded Git guide, source page 64. Follow-up answer: added for this edition.

pages.title: HANDS-ON GIT PRACTICE L01 / L14
pages.fullText:
HANDS-ON GIT PRACTICE L01 / L14
TESTED BASH LAB • PASS
L01 Commit the staged version, not the later edit
Run from a new empty directory. Requires Bash and Git; works in Git Bash on Windows.
set -eu
# Run in a new, empty disposable directory.
test -z "$(ls -A)"
git init -q -b main
git config --local user.name "Git Learner"
git config --local user.email "learner@example.test"
git config --local commit.gpgsign false
git config --local core.autocrlf false
printf 'quantity=10\n' > Order.txt
git add Order.txt
git commit -qm "Initial quantity"
printf 'quantity=20\n' > Order.txt
git add Order.txt
printf 'quantity=30\n' > Order.txt
git commit -qm "Stage quantity 20"
test "$(git show HEAD:Order.txt)" = 'quantity=20'
test "$(cat Order.txt)" = 'quantity=30'
test -z "$(git diff --staged)"
test -n "$(git diff -- Order.txt)"
printf 'committed=20; working=30; unstaged diff remains\n'
VERIFIED OUTPUT
committed=20; working=30; unstaged diff remains
Why it works: git add recorded quantity 20 in the index. The later edit to 30 affected only the working
tree. The normal commit used the index, then the staged diff became empty while the working diff
remained.
CAUTION: A normal commit does not automatically include a later unstaged edit. Inspect both diff
views before assuming all work was saved.
GIT / PREMIUM NOTEBOOK ZERO TO HERO • JAVA TEAM WORKFLOWS
Understand • Practice • Explain 115

L02 Fast-forward versus an explicit merge commit
Run from a new empty directory. Requires Bash and Git; works in Git Bash on Windows.
set -eu
# Run in a new, empty disposable directory.
test -z "$(ls -A)"
git init -q -b main
git config --local user.name "Git Learner"
git config --local user.email "learner@example.test"
git config --local commit.gpgsign false
git config --local core.autocrlf false
printf 'base\n' > base.txt
git add base.txt
git commit -qm "Base"
git switch -qc feature
printf 'feature\n' > feature.txt
git add feature.txt
git commit -qm "Feature"
feature_tip=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
git switch -q main
git merge --ff-only feature > /dev/null
test "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" = "$feature_tip"

printf 'next\n' > next.txt
git add next.txt
git commit -qm "Next feature"
git switch -q main
git merge --no-ff -m "Integrate next feature" next-feature > /dev/null
test "$(git rev-list --parents -n 1 HEAD | wc -w)" -eq 3
printf 'fast-forward reused tip; no-ff created a two-parent commit\n'

fast-forward reused tip; no-ff created a two-parent commit
Why it works: A fast-forward moves main to the existing feature commit. The second feature is also fast-
forwardable, but --no-ff deliberately creates a commit whose parent list has two entries.

well as parent count.

L03 Abort and then resolve a real merge conflict
Run from a new empty directory. Requires Bash and Git; works in Git Bash on Windows.
set -eu
# Run in a new, empty disposable directory.
test -z "$(ls -A)"

printf 'price=100\n' > price.txt
git add price.txt
git commit -qm "Base price"
git switch -qc feature
printf 'price=90\n' > price.txt
git commit -qam "Feature price"
git switch -q main
printf 'price=110\n' > price.txt
git commit -qam "Main price"
if git merge feature > /dev/null 2>&1; then exit 1; fi
test -n "$(git ls-files -u)"
git merge --abort

test -z "$(git status --porcelain)"

printf 'price=95\n' > price.txt

pages.fullText:

TESTED BASH LAB • PASS
L05 Measure soft, mixed and hard reset
Run from a new empty directory. Requires Bash and Git; works in Git Bash on Windows.
set -eu
# Run in a new, empty disposable directory.
test -z "$(ls -A)"
git init -q -b main
git config --local user.name "Git Learner"
git config --local user.email "learner@example.test"
git config --local commit.gpgsign false
git config --local core.autocrlf false
printf 'A\n' > value.txt
git add value.txt
git commit -qm "A"
a=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
printf 'B\n' > value.txt
git commit -qam "B"
git branch keep-B
git reset --soft "$a"
test "$(git show :value.txt)" = B
test "$(cat value.txt)" = B
test -n "$(git diff --staged)"
git reset --hard keep-B > /dev/null
git reset --mixed "$a" > /dev/null
test "$(git show :value.txt)" = A
test "$(cat value.txt)" = B
test -z "$(git diff --staged)"
test -n "$(git diff)"
git reset --hard keep-B > /dev/null
git reset --hard "$a" > /dev/null
test "$(cat value.txt)" = A
test "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" = "$a"
test -z "$(git status --porcelain)"
printf 'soft: B staged; mixed: B unstaged; hard: files A\n'
VERIFIED OUTPUT
soft: B staged; mixed: B unstaged; hard: files A
Why it works: The target commit is A in every case. Soft keeps the B index and files; mixed restores the A
index while retaining B files; hard restores A in both areas. keep-B deliberately preserves the original B
commit throughout the exercise.
CAUTION: The hard resets here are confined to the disposable fixture. They can discard useful local
edits in a real repository.

git commit -qm "Later docs"

git revert --no-edit "$bad" > /dev/null

commits are still ancestors. History now contains four commits, including the new revert.

L07 Rescue a detached commit with the reflog
Run from a new empty directory. Requires Bash and Git; works in Git Bash on Windows.
set -eu
# Run in a new, empty disposable directory.
test -z "$(ls -A)"

printf 'experiment\n' > note.txt

experiment=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

test "$lost" = "$experiment"

Why it works: In this exact sequence, the most recent previous HEAD position is the detached
experiment tip. Creating rescue/experiment makes it reachable under a deliberate name without
changing main.
CAUTION: HEAD@{1} is correct only for this known sequence. In an incident, inspect the reflog and
verify content instead of assuming that selector always identifies lost work.

L09 Fetch, fast-forward pull and a stale push lease
Run from a new empty directory. Requires Bash and Git; works in Git Bash on Windows.
set -eu
# New empty disposable directory; no network server is used.
test -z "$(ls -A)"
git init --bare -q --initial-branch=main remote.git
git clone -q remote.git alice
for who in alice; do
  git -C "$who" config user.name "Git Learner"
  git -C "$who" config user.email "learner@example.test"
  git -C "$who" config commit.gpgsign false
done
printf 'base\n' > alice/base.txt
git -C alice add base.txt
git -C alice commit -qm "Base"
git -C alice push -qu origin main
git clone -q remote.git bob
git -C bob config user.name "Git Learner"
git -C bob config user.email "learner@example.test"
git -C bob config commit.gpgsign false
base=$(git -C bob rev-parse HEAD)
printf 'A\n' > alice/a.txt
git -C alice add a.txt
git -C alice commit -qm "Alice A"
git -C alice push -q origin main
git -C bob fetch -q origin
test "$(git -C bob rev-parse HEAD)" = "$base"
test "$(git -C bob rev-parse origin/main)" != "$base"
git -C bob pull -q --ff-only
expected=$(git -C bob rev-parse origin/main)
printf 'B\n' > bob/b.txt
git -C bob add b.txt
git -C bob commit -qm "Bob B"
printf 'C\n' > alice/c.txt
git -C alice add c.txt
git -C alice commit -qm "Alice C"
git -C alice push -q origin main
if git -C bob push --force-with-lease=refs/heads/main:"$expected" \
    origin HEAD:refs/heads/main > /dev/null 2>&1; then exit 1; fi
test "$(git --git-dir=remote.git rev-parse main)" = \
    "$(git -C alice rev-parse HEAD)"
printf 'fetch left bob main unchanged; pull advanced it\n'
printf 'stale explicit lease rejected; Alice C stayed on remote\n'
VERIFIED OUTPUT
fetch left bob main unchanged; pull advanced it
stale explicit lease rejected; Alice C stayed on remote
Why it works: Fetch advances Bob's local origin/main, then ff-only pull moves his main. Bob records the
reviewed remote tip before Alice publishes C. His later explicit lease no longer matches the remote, so the
forced rewrite is rejected.
CAUTION: All pushes target remote.git under this disposable directory. A lease is an update guard, not
authorization to rewrite a real shared branch. This exercise intentionally simulates divergence.

git commit -qm "Save restored work"

printf 'current-side\n' > work.txt

leaves the stash entry. Later, a conflicting pop produces unmerged entries and keeps the saved stash
rather than dropping it.

stash; do not treat the saved entry as a permanent backup.

L11 Parallel worktrees and independent checkouts
Run from a new empty directory. Requires Bash and Git; works in Git Bash on Windows.

# Run in a new, empty disposable directory.
test -z "$(ls -A)"
git init -q -b main

git config --local core.autocrlf false
printf 'base\n' > base.txt
git add base.txt
git commit -qm "Base"
main_tip=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
git worktree add -q -b hotfix ../hotfix main
printf 'fix\n' > ../hotfix/fix.txt
git -C ../hotfix add fix.txt
git -C ../hotfix commit -qm "Hotfix"
test "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" = "$main_tip"
test ! -e fix.txt

test ! -d ../hotfix

printf 'main unchanged; hotfix committed separately; branch survives removal\n'

main unchanged; hotfix committed separately; branch survives removal
Why it works: Each checkout has its own working files and checked-out HEAD. Objects and branches are
shared, so main can inspect hotfix by reference while its own files remain unchanged. Removing the
clean worktree keeps the hotfix branch.

parent directory; worktree add should not be forced over an existing task.

L12 Automated bisect finds the first failing commit
Run from a new empty directory. Requires Bash and Git; works in Git Bash on Windows.
set -eu
# Run in a new, empty disposable directory.
test -z "$(ls -A)"
git init -q -b main
git config --local user.name "Git Learner"

git config --local commit.gpgsign false
git config --local core.autocrlf false
printf '3\n' > limit.txt
git add limit.txt
git commit -qm "Limit 3"
good=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
printf '5\n' > limit.txt
git commit -qam "Limit 5"
printf '11\n' > limit.txt
git commit -qam "Limit 11: regression"
first_bad=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
printf '12\n' > limit.txt
git commit -qam "Limit 12"
printf '15\n' > limit.txt
git commit -qam "Limit 15"
tip=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
git bisect start "$tip" "$good" > /dev/null
git bisect run sh -c 'test "$(cat limit.txt)" -le 10' > /dev/null 2>&1
test "$(git rev-parse refs/bisect/bad)" = "$first_bad"
git bisect reset > /dev/null 2>&1
test "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" = "$tip"
test "$(git branch --show-current)" = main
printf 'bisect found Limit 11; reset returned to original main tip\n'
VERIFIED OUTPUT
bisect found Limit 11; reset returned to original main tip
Why it works: The test succeeds at limits 3 and 5 and fails from 11 onward. The final refs/bisect/bad
identifies the first failing revision; HEAD can remain at the last tested revision. Reset exits bisect and
restores the original checkout.
CAUTION: A Java regression wrapper needs a policy for unbuildable revisions, typically skip rather
than falsely bad. Flaky or non-monotonic behavior requires further diagnosis.

L13 Ignore does not untrack existing content

Why it works: The ignore entry does not remove a tracked path. Removing it from the index records a
deletion while the local copy remains. The older committed content is still reachable in history.

tracking or changing history does not revoke copied credentials.

pages.title: Quick command decisions
pages.fullText:
Quick command decisions
See what changed: git status --short and git diff
Review staged work: git diff --staged
Unstage and keep files: git restore --staged -- FILE
Discard unstaged tracked edit: git restore -- FILE (destructive)
Undo private tip, keep staged: git reset --soft TARGET
Undo private tip, keep unstaged: git reset --mixed TARGET
Undo shared change: git revert COMMIT
Rescue lost commit: git reflog then git branch rescue/name OID
See incoming work: git fetch then compare tracking refs
Spot the first bad commit: git bisect
Core model: working files → git add → index → git commit → history →
git push → remote. Always name which part a command changes.
